text:
During the visit, H.E. Ambassador Huh Jeong-ae met with farmers, cooperative representatives, and beneficiary groups of the Sustainable Agricultural Productivity and Market Linkage Project (SAPMP). 

The beneficiaries showcased their achievements and shared personal experiences of how the project has contributed to improving agricultural productivity, strengthening their livelihoods, and creating new business opportunities.

Among the beneficiaries was IMARIRWAKURUSHA, a farming group based in Gisagara District. The group comprises 20 members who collectively cultivate five hectares of land. During the visit, the group presented its agricultural activities and highlighted the opportunities created through its participation in the project.

The Ambassador also heard from Jean Claude Mukeshimana, president of a beneficiary cooperative, who explained how training and study visits facilitated by SAPMP had helped farmers improve their production practices and increase agricultural yields. These capacity-building initiatives have enabled farmers to gain practical knowledge, learn from successful agricultural approaches, and identify opportunities to improve their farming activities.

Another beneficiary who shared his experience was Victor Ndikumagenge, a farmer from Ntazo Sector in Nyanza District. Through his participation in SAPMP, he has experienced improvements in his rice-farming activities and discovered new opportunities to diversify his income.

Reflecting on the challenges farmers previously faced, Victor explained that heavy rainfall frequently caused flooding in the marshland, damaging rice crops and resulting in significant losses.

He said:

“During the rainy season, the marshland used to experience severe flooding because of excessive water accumulation. The floods damaged our rice crops and caused us financial losses. However, when SAPMP began its interventions, it first supported the construction of erosion-control structures on the surrounding hillsides to manage runoff. The project later developed the marshland itself. Today, farmers can grow rice under improved conditions without facing the same flooding challenges as before.”

The project’s combined interventions in the surrounding hillsides and marshland have helped address challenges associated with runoff and water management, creating better conditions for rice production.

For farmers such as Victor, these improvements represent more than better farming conditions. They create an opportunity to protect their investments, sustain production, and build a more secure economic future.

Victor’s story goes beyond improvements in rice farming. Through a study visit organized by SAPMP, he discovered an additional opportunity to diversify his agricultural business through rabbit farming.

Inspired by the knowledge and experience gained during the visit, Victor decided to reinvest part of the profits from his rice-farming activities into a new livestock enterprise. He started with just eight rabbits.

Nine months later, his rabbit population had grown to more than 200, and he estimated the value of his rabbit-farming business at approximately RWF 5 million.

Victor explained:

“SAPMP took us on a study visit, and I returned with the idea of starting a rabbit-farming business. I took some of the profits I had earned from rice farming and invested them in eight rabbits. Now, after nine months, I have more than 200 rabbits, and my business is worth approximately RWF 5 million.”

His experience illustrates how agricultural development projects can create opportunities that extend beyond their initial objectives. By combining improved crop production with exposure to new business ideas, farmers can diversify their income sources, reduce dependence on a single enterprise, and explore additional opportunities within the agricultural value chain.

The experiences shared by the beneficiaries demonstrate the importance of combining agricultural infrastructure with knowledge transfer and entrepreneurship development.

Through SAPMP, farmers are benefiting from interventions aimed at improving land and water management, strengthening agricultural production, building practical skills, and connecting them with new opportunities.

Victor’s journey from a rice farmer facing repeated flood-related losses to an entrepreneur who has diversified into rabbit farming highlights the potential of these combined interventions.

His experience also offers an important lesson for other farmers: agricultural development does not end with increasing crop yields. It can also involve reinvesting profits, learning from others, diversifying production, and building complementary enterprises that strengthen household incomes.

Ultimately, the success of agricultural development is reflected not only in the land developed or infrastructure constructed, but also in the knowledge farmers gain, the businesses they establish, and the opportunities they create for their families and communities.

text:
BORN IN THE YEAR TWO THOUSAND
Biologically, they are exactly the same age. They were both born in the year 2000. But on the grid of Pattaya, chronological time is an entirely useless metric. Time here is not measured in years; it is measured in mileage, in trauma, and in the sheer volume of human desperation you have had to process just to survive.

She arrived in the city when she was eighteen. Over the last eight years, she has worked thousands of shifts under the neon lights. She has survived two impossible choices, built a cinderblock house for her mother in the provinces, and navigated the darkest, most manipulative corners of male psychology. Her mental age is approximately sixteen hundred years. She has lived through enough condensed human tragedy to rival the entire history of an ancient Irish bloodline. She has casually witnessed things that would permanently shatter the minds of normal people, and she has learned how to bury it all behind a perfectly calibrated smile.

He arrived in the city two days ago. He has a freshly printed Master’s degree, a completely unblemished record of existence, and his youth. Because he has spent the last twenty-six years in a wealthy, insulated Western society, reading theoretical articles and debating politics in campus coffee shops, he genuinely believes that he "knows life."

They are sitting next to each other in a dimly lit bar, breathing the same air. He is entirely captivated by her quiet, heavy presence. He looks at her, deeply moved by a brief conversation they just had about family responsibility, and says, "You are so incredibly wise for your age."

He is saying this to a woman who has emotionally outlived his entire ancestry. She looks at him—at his soft hands, his unburdened posture, and his naive, searching eyes. She doesn't laugh. She doesn't explain the brutal mechanics of exactly how that wisdom was acquired. She just offers a bright, practiced smile.

"Thank you," she says softly. "I watch a lot of educational channels on TikTok."

That night, in a standard hotel room, she quietly becomes his first.

When the morning sun bleeds through the heavy curtains, the transaction becomes chaotic for him. He doesn't know how to simply hand over the three thousand baht and let it be what it is. He couples the cash with a desperate, heavy confession of love. He sits on the edge of the mattress, talking intensely about how they have a special connection, how he wants to take care of her, and how he wants to be with her forever.

She nods. She agrees with everything he says, smiling sweetly, promising to see him again tomorrow, validating his emotions—doing absolutely whatever is necessary to accelerate the interaction so she can finally put her shoes on and get out of the room.

Twenty minutes later, she is sitting sideways on the back of an orange-vested motorbike taxi, the hot morning wind hitting her face. She clutches her purse with the three thousand baht folded inside. As the bike weaves through the heavy Sukhumvit traffic, she squints against the harsh sunlight and casually tries to remember which country he told her he was from.

She searches her memory for a few seconds. Was it Belgium? Canada? She can't remember.

And as the bike accelerates toward her apartment, she realizes it doesn't matter at all.

text:
The Attempt to Erase "Mother"

The most brazen assault on the traditional family came in March of 2024, when the government pushed the 39th and 40th Amendments. 

The state apparatus threw its full weight behind the "Care Amendment," a proposal designed to rip Article 41.2 out of the Irish Constitution. That specific article explicitly recognizes that a mother's life within the home gives a vital support to the State, ensuring that mothers shouldn't be forced into the labor market out of economic necessity.

The government’s solution wasn't to offer tangible financial support to mothers; it was to delete the word "mother" entirely, replacing it with sterile, gender-neutral language about "caregivers." 

The Irish people saw right through the sleight of hand. In a massive, roaring rebuke to the ruling class, the electorate decisively crushed the amendments at the ballot box. They refused to allow the unique biological and societal role of the mother to be legislated out of existence.

text:
On the other hand, those who founded sects committed to erroneous doctrines proceeded in a way that is opposite to this. The point is clear in the case of Muhammad. He seduced the people by promises of carnal pleasure to which the concupiscence of the flesh goads us. His teaching also contained precepts that were in conformity with his promises, and he gave free rein to carnal pleasure. In all this, as is not unexpected, he was obeyed by carnal men. As for proofs of the truth of his doctrine, he brought forward only such as could be grasped by the natural ability of anyone with a very modest wisdom. Indeed, the truths that he taught he mingled with many fables and with doctrines of the greatest falsity. He did not bring forth any signs produced in a supernatural way, which alone fittingly gives witness to divine inspiration; for a visible action that can be only divine reveals an invisibly inspired teacher of truth. On the contrary, Muhammad said that he was sent in the power of his arms—which are signs not lacking even to robbers and tyrants. What is more, no wise men, men trained in things divine and human, believed in him from the beginning. Those who believed in him were brutal men and desert wanderers, utterly ignorant of all divine teaching, through whose numbers Muhammad forced others to become his followers by the violence of his arms. Nor do divine pronouncements on the part of preceding prophets offer him any witness. On the contrary, he perverts almost all the testimonies of the Old and New Testaments by making them into fabrications of his own, as can be seen by anyone who examines his law. It was, therefore, a shrewd decision on his part to forbid his followers to read the Old and New Testaments, lest these books convict him of falsity. It is thus clear that those who place any faith in his words believe foolishly.
——Thomas Aquinas, Summa Contra Gentiles, Book I, Chapter 6, translated by Anton C. Pegis (Notre Dame, IN: University of Notre Dame Press, 1975).

1. Is your fridge really bigger than my room?
I am not sure, but my fridge has 4 doors. It’s also navy blue. 
2. Do cowboys have phones?
Yes, at least the ones I know have them. 
3. Have you seen a bald eagle with your own eyes? Was it as cool as on TV?
Yes. They are huge and majestic. But they do not sound like what you hear on TV. That sound is actually a hawk.
4. What's the biggest pizza you've ever eaten?
Oh, I am not sure. Don’t tell anyone, but I don’t really like pizza. 
5. Do you have a horse? If not, why not?
Yes, I do.  
6. Which state is the best? (Our teacher said not to ask this. We are asking anyway.)
Texas and Alabama. But honestly, all of our states have so much to offer. We have desserts, forests, mountains, prairies, tropical environments, gorgeous beaches. 
7. Is it true you can drive for a whole day and still be in Texas? Yes. 
8. What should we eat first when we come to America? This is hard, we have so many things here! But if I have to choose, start with brisket in Texas, Conecuh sausage in Alabama, and fried okra in Alabama.

text:
Must've been ROUGH! You have my empathy… My heart goes out to you and wishing you the best 

After my accident, Marvel asked me to come back… but they wanted to pay me only half what I made before.”
January 1, 2023, everything changed in a heartbeat

I was in Nevada helping my nephew move a truck that was stuck in deep snow. A six-ton snowplow lost control and started sliding. I jumped in front of my nephew to protect him—and the machine ran right over me.
I lived, but just barely.
More than thirty broken bones

A collapsed lung.

My whole body crushed.
Months in hospitals, surgeries, and painful therapy followed. Learning to walk again, to breathe without hurting, to feel like myself—it was a fight every single day.

Little by little I got stronger. I thought I was ready to go back to work.
That’s when Marvel called. They wanted me for the same role, but only offered half my old paycheck.
It felt like they were saying, “You’re worth less now because you got hurt.”

So I turned them down.
Not because I was mad or proud.
Just because surviving taught me something huge: my worth isn’t decided by a salary.
These days I’m focused on getting better, being with my family, and working only when it feels right for my body.
I’m still acting.
I’m still healing.

And most of all—I’m still here. Still pushing. Still standing.

— Jeremy Renner

text:
The best airplane of the Korean War was the F-86 Sabre. But the story everyone tells about it is only half true, and the other half involves secret Soviet pilots and a jet engine Britain sold to Stalin.

November 1950. The US had been bombing North Korea for months with almost no resistance in the air. Then, near the Yalu River, swept-wing jets started streaking down from China and tearing into American bombers.

It was the MiG-15. Fast, fast-climbing, heavily armed with cannons, and able to fly higher than anything the Americans had in Korea. Overnight, US air superiority was in danger.

And here's the twist. The MiG's engine was British.

In 1946, Britain's government had sold the Soviet Union Rolls-Royce Nene jet engines as a gesture of goodwill. Soviet engineers took them apart and copied them. The story goes that even Stalin was shocked anyone would sell them such a thing.

Four years later, that copied engine was powering MiGs over Korea.

The US rushed its best fighter to Korea: the North American F-86 Sabre. It arrived in December 1950. On December 17, a Sabre scored its first MiG kill.

The battle zone became known as "MiG Alley," the stretch of northwest Korea near the Chinese border. And the rules were maddening. MiGs could take off from bases inside China, attack, and run back across the Yalu. American pilots were forbidden to follow them. Some did anyway and kept quiet about it.

On paper, the MiG had real advantages. It climbed faster. It flew higher. Its cannons could tear apart a bomber with a few hits.

But the Sabre had things that mattered more in a dogfight. Powered controls that let it roll and maneuver smoothly at high speed. A radar-assisted gunsight. G-suits for its pilots. Better visibility. And above all, many of its pilots were veterans who had flown in WW2.

And the MiG pilots weren't who they appeared to be.

Officially, they were Chinese and North Korean. In reality, many of the best were Soviet pilots, secretly sent to fight. They wore Chinese uniforms. Their planes had North Korean or Chinese markings. They were told to speak Korean on the radio, which quickly broke down into Russian the moment combat started. Moscow kept this hidden for decades.

So the war in MiG Alley was really an undeclared war between the United States and the Soviet Union, jet against jet.

After the war, the US Air Force claimed Sabres had shot down nearly 800 MiGs while losing fewer than 80 in air combat. Roughly 10 to 1.

That number became legend. It's also wrong.

Once Soviet records opened, historians found that the real numbers were much closer. Pilots on both sides had overclaimed badly. Against experienced Soviet pilots, the real ratio was probably closer to 2 to 1. Against less experienced Chinese and North Korean pilots, it was much more lopsided in the Sabre's favor.

Still a win. Just not the blowout everyone believed.

Then came one final twist.

In 1953, the US offered $100,000 to any communist pilot who would defect with a MiG. On September 21, 1953, after the armistice, a North Korean pilot named No Kum-sok landed his MiG-15 at an American airbase in South Korea.

He later said he had never even heard of the reward.

American test pilots, including Chuck Yeager, flew the MiG and finally got to see what the Sabre had been up against all along.

The MiG-15 was a great airplane. The Sabre was a better one, flown by better-trained pilots. And the war it won was even stranger than anyone knew at the time.

#China and #Djibouti have reaffirmed Somalia’s territorial integrity and opposed international recognition of Somaliland’s independence, days after US President Donald Trump described the breakaway African territory as “a totally different country” from Somalia.

👉 China and Djibouti issued a joint statement reaffirming Somalia's territorial integrity and opposing international recognition of #Somaliland’s independence.

👉 This stance comes days after US President Donald Trump described Somaliland as distinct from Somalia, sparking celebrations in #Somaliland.

👉 China and Djibouti signed a memorandum on security cooperation and called for freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab el-Mandeb Strait.

👉 The joint communiqué emphasized support for regional sovereignty and addressed security in the Horn of Africa and vital maritime routes.

According to Vue sur Djibouti (@View_of_Djib), an independent Djiboutian digital news platform, the two countries issued a joint statement following a meeting between their foreign ministers in Beijing and signed a memorandum of understanding on security cooperation under China’s Global Security Initiative.

The statement explicitly opposed recognizing #Somaliland as an independent entity and reaffirmed that the territory remains part of the Federal Republic of Somalia. It also called for freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, support for coastal states protecting maritime routes, and respect for regional sovereignty.

China’s Foreign Ministry confirmed that Wang Yi met Djibouti’s Foreign Minister Abdoulkader Houssein Omar on October 21, 2026. The joint communique also addressed peace and stability in the Horn of Africa and security along shipping routes in the Red Sea and Gulf of Aden.

Trump made his remarks at a rally in Youngstown, Ohio, on October 12, distinguishing #Somaliland from Somalia while suggesting the territory should change its name. His comments prompted celebrations in #Somaliland, where officials welcomed the description as recognition of its separate identity.

However, Trump’s statement did not amount to formal US recognition of #Somaliland, and Washington has not officially changed its recognition policy.

China’s position contrasts with the US approach, as both countries seek to protect their strategic interests around the Horn of Africa and its vital maritime trade routes. Somaliland has offered the United States access to its port facilities, mineral resources and potential military bases in a bid to secure stronger American support.

For Washington, closer ties with #Somaliland could provide access to Berbera port, located near the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a critical passage connecting the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. A US military foothold there could strengthen its ability to monitor shipping and project power across the region.

For China, which operates its first overseas military base in neighbouring Djibouti, a stronger US presence in Somaliland could intensify competition over regional ports, military access and maritime security. Beijing has significant interests in keeping trade routes open, particularly those connecting China with European and African markets.

By reaffirming Somalia’s territorial integrity and opposing recognition of #Somaliland’s independence, China is reinforcing a position that conflicts with Somaliland’s efforts to attract US backing.

text:
I appreciate that you have been exploring the LDS Church, and I respect your desire to understand its teachings. However, several of these explanations overlook important historical facts and serious differences between LDS doctrine and what Scripture teaches.

I want to address each point using the Word of God and the LDS Church's own historical records.

1. Yeshua is NOT the spirit brother of Satan.

This is one of the most significant theological disagreements between biblical Christianity and Mormonism.

John 1:1–3 declares that the Word existed in the beginning, that the Word was God, and that everything created came into existence through Him.

John 1:14 identifies that eternal Word as the One who became flesh.

Colossians 1:16–17 declares that all things in heaven and earth, visible and invisible, were created through Him and for Him.

Hebrews 1:5–8 distinguishes the Son from the angels and addresses Him as God.

Satan is a created being who rebelled against his Creator. Yeshua is the eternal Word through whom all things were created.

Isaiah 43:10 declares that no God was formed before YHWH, nor shall there be one after Him.

Yeshua is YHWH, the eternal Word manifested in flesh. He is not Satan's spirit brother.

The LDS explanation of a premortal family relationship does not resolve this fundamental disagreement about the eternal identity of Christ.

2. Joseph Smith's multiple wives were not simply women he married to help.

The LDS Church's own historical essay, Plural Marriage in Kirtland and Nauvoo, acknowledges that Joseph Smith was married or sealed to approximately 30–40 women.

Among them was Helen Mar Kimball, who was 14 years old.

Others were already legally married to living husbands.

The historical record distinguishes between marriages intended for eternity alone and those involving relationships during earthly life, including the possibility of sexual intimacy.

We cannot establish physical intimacy in every marriage, but neither can we dismiss the entire controversy by claiming these were merely charitable arrangements.

Furthermore, the claim that Joseph married additional women because there were too few female Church members is not an established historical explanation.

The LDS Church itself attributes the practice to claimed revelations involving plural marriage, obedience, and eternal exaltation.

We must also examine Matthew 22:30, where Yeshua teaches that people in the resurrection neither marry nor are given in marriage.

Why should Joseph Smith's later revelations establish marriage requirements for the highest heavenly exaltation when Yeshua taught this about the resurrection?

3. Sacred temple garments are not commanded under the New Covenant.

I would not mock someone's religious clothing or call it magical underwear.

Latter-day Saints understand these garments as reminders of sacred covenants.

However, nowhere does Yeshua command His disciples to wear special temple undergarments as part of the New Covenant.

The Old Testament contained priestly clothing requirements, but those instructions do not establish the modern LDS temple garment ceremony.

Hebrews 10:19–22 teaches that believers approach God through the blood of Yeshua.

Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches that salvation is by grace through faith, not through human works.

The issue is not whether someone enjoys wearing religious garments. The issue is whether the practice has a foundation in the teachings of Christ and His apostles.

4. Baptism for the dead is not established as a Christian commandment.

I understand why giving deceased people an opportunity to receive the gospel may sound compassionate.

The LDS Church teaches that deceased individuals can accept or reject ordinances performed on their behalf.

However, we must distinguish what sounds beautiful from what Scripture actually commands.

First Corinthians 15:29 mentions people being baptized for the dead.

But Paul does not explicitly command Christians to perform proxy baptisms.

His larger argument in 1 Corinthians 15 concerns the resurrection of the dead.

The passage is debated among biblical scholars, and its existence should not be denied. Nevertheless, a reference to a practice is not automatically an instruction to continue that practice.

The LDS system of temple baptisms for deceased individuals depends heavily on later revelations attributed to Joseph Smith.

First Timothy 2:5 teaches that there is one mediator between God and humanity: Yeshua the Messiah.

Salvation rests in Him, not in a religious institution's authority to perform ordinances on behalf of deceased people.

5. The LDS Church prohibits polygamy today, but that does not erase its history or remaining teachings.

It is correct that the mainstream LDS Church no longer permits living members to enter plural marriages.

However, it is misleading to discuss the matter without acknowledging the history.

Joseph Smith introduced plural marriage.

Brigham Young and other early LDS leaders continued the practice.

The 1890 Manifesto began its formal discontinuation, but additional plural marriages occurred afterward.

The 1904 Second Manifesto strengthened the prohibition.

Even today, Doctrine and Covenants 132 remains part of LDS scripture and contains teachings concerning plural marriage.

The Church also permits a widower to be eternally sealed to another woman after the death of his wife, even if his earlier sealing remains in effect.

The Church says the precise nature of those relationships in eternity is not fully known.

Therefore, the accurate statement is that the mainstream LDS Church prohibits entering plural marriages today, while retaining historical teachings and certain eternal sealing arrangements.

Those are important distinctions.

6. Being treated kindly does not establish that a church's teachings are true.

I do not believe we should automatically label an entire religious community a cult.

Many Latter-day Saints are sincere, loving, and generous people.

However, spending two months among friendly members cannot establish the divine authority of Joseph Smith or prove the truth of his revelations.

Religious organizations must be evaluated by their doctrines, historical claims, leadership, and treatment of questioning members.

Acts 17:11 commends the Bereans because they examined the Scriptures to determine whether the teachings they received were true.

First Thessalonians 5:21 instructs believers to test all things and hold fast to what is good.

Even the Apostle Paul did not expect people to abandon scriptural examination simply because someone claimed religious authority.

Why should Joseph Smith be treated differently?

Kindness is important, but truth requires evidence.

7. Scripture does not establish the LDS doctrine of three eternal kingdoms of glory.

The LDS Church teaches three kingdoms: celestial, terrestrial, and telestial.

It also teaches a condition called outer darkness, so saying Mormonism has no concept of hell is inaccurate.

Latter-day Saints sometimes appeal to 1 Corinthians 15:40–42 to support the three kingdoms.

But read the passage in context.

Paul is explaining the resurrection and the differences between earthly and heavenly bodies.

His comparison of the sun, moon, and stars does not explicitly establish three separate eternal destinations for humanity.

The detailed LDS system comes primarily from revelations attributed to Joseph Smith, particularly Doctrine and Covenants 76.

Now consider what Yeshua actually taught.

Matthew 25:31–46 describes the final judgment.

John 5:28–29 describes the resurrection of life and the resurrection of judgment.

Revelation 20:11–15 describes the final judgment before the great white throne.

Revelation 21 describes the new heaven and new earth.

You suggested that heaven and hell seem too narrow because most people are neither completely good nor completely evil.

But Scripture does not teach that salvation is determined by whether someone is relatively better than another person.

Romans 3:23 declares that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.

Romans 6:23 teaches that eternal life is the gift of God through Yeshua the Messiah.

Our salvation depends on God's grace and the redeeming work of Christ, not on humanity being divided into three categories of moral achievement.

My final concern is the authority of Joseph Smith's revelations.

Galatians 1:8 warns that even if an angel from heaven preaches a gospel contrary to the one the apostles proclaimed, that message must be rejected.

This passage is particularly relevant because Joseph Smith claimed to receive angelic instructions and revelations.

His revelations cannot simply be assumed true because they were attributed to heavenly messengers.

They must be tested against the revelation already given through God's prophets and apostles.

Isaiah 43:10 declares that no God was formed before YHWH or will be formed after Him.

Yet Doctrine and Covenants 132:20 describes exalted individuals becoming gods.

That creates another serious theological question.

How does that teaching agree with YHWH's declaration in Isaiah?

I do not question your sincerity or the kindness you have experienced.

But I encourage you to examine the Scriptures, the historical evidence, and Joseph Smith's revelations carefully before accepting these doctrines.

My faith rests in Yeshua the Messiah, the eternal Word made flesh, the fullness of deity manifested bodily, the One who conquered death and offers salvation through His finished work.

He is not Satan's brother.

He is not merely one among many divine beings.

He is not dependent on Joseph Smith to reveal His identity.

He is the eternal Lord, and His Word is the standard by which every religious claim must be tested.

I share this not to condemn Latter-day Saints, but because I believe knowing the truth about Yeshua matters more than defending any denomination or institution.

text:
How Magic Works in Early Oz: The Scepter, Witches, and Transformation

The original Oz story gives us several different ways to look at magic. There are practitioners such as Glinda and the witches, an artifact powerful enough to drive the entire journey, creatures used in magical attacks, and people whose bodies have been changed by someone else's power. Each example tells us something about what magic can do, but they do not all work in the same way.

This guide stays with that first Oz adventure. It does not use later revelations to fill in the early story's unanswered questions. That matters especially when discussing where power comes from, who can use a particular artifact, or whether a magical condition can be reversed.

Practitioners and artifacts

A useful starting distinction is between a person who performs magic and an object through which an effect is achieved. Glinda is a magical practitioner with knowledge Dorothy needs. Lynessa can use magic against other people and direct threats against the group. The Veridian Scepter, meanwhile, is an object whose recovery could change their situation dramatically.

Those things should not be collapsed into one category. A witch's demonstrated abilities tell us about that practitioner. An effect achieved with the Scepter tells us about the artifact and the circumstances in which it is being used. Neither automatically establishes a complete list of powers for everyone else in Oz.

The first story also does not offer a comprehensive technical account of the realm's magical energy. It establishes that particular powers and effects exist, while leaving other explanations open. That is a limit on what can be confidently explained from this part of the story, rather than an invitation to invent a hidden system of spell levels or energy reserves.

The Veridian Scepter and why its pieces matter

The Scepter is the central magical object of the original adventure. Dorothy and her allies need to recover its separated pieces, and the search takes them through locations where both the object and the knowledge needed to find it are difficult to obtain.

That separation has practical consequences. Having one piece does not bring the quest to an end. The group must continue travelling, keep what it has recovered out of enemy hands, and survive long enough to obtain the rest. Access to the artifact is therefore a major limitation before its power is even put to use.

The search also links several goals. The Scepter offers a means of opposing the witch, helping Glinda, and getting Dorothy home. Its significance comes from those different applications. It is useful to people with very different intentions, which is why recovering it and controlling it become matters of conflict.

The artifact's demonstrated effects include destructive force. In the final confrontation, Dorothy uses it against Lynessa and the attacking forces. That establishes substantial offensive power in those circumstances. It does not establish that every possible target is equally vulnerable or that anyone who picks it up can reproduce everything Dorothy does.

The story makes Dorothy's interaction with the Scepter important without giving a complete user manual for it. A careful explanation can identify what happens while leaving questions about eligibility, resistance, and the full extent of its power unresolved.

Healing has conditions

Glinda's injury is one of the clearest reminders that magic does not remove vulnerability. During the search for a Scepter piece at the Temple of Despair, she is endangered by a trap and then badly hurt by an attacking creature. The other characters have to help her rather than assume that her magical ability will automatically protect or restore her.

The subsequent effort to save her involves the Scepter. The story distinguishes an initial improvement in her condition from the further healing effort made after the artifact is assembled. That makes access to the right means important. A useful magical intervention does not necessarily mean the injured person is immediately ready to continue as though nothing happened.

There is no need to turn this into a numerical healing system. The demonstrated point is that serious injury can demand rescue, protection, and a particular magical resource. The successful treatment of Glinda should not be stretched into a claim that any injury can be repaired, that every practitioner is a healer, or that death can be reversed at will.

Transformation and its consequences

The Tin Man's metal body provides a different kind of example. Lynessa's magic has changed Nicholas, and that alteration affects his life beyond the original act of casting it. Transformation can leave a continuing condition rather than a brief effect that vanishes when a fight ends.

That makes it important to separate an altered body from an actively performed spell. Nicholas does not have to cast something each time he uses his metal form. His present condition is itself the result of someone else's magic.

The possibility of reversing that condition also affects his choices. A person who wants to be restored can be drawn toward someone claiming to offer that restoration. Magical harm can create an ongoing dependency, giving its perpetrator or a supposed rescuer influence over the victim.

The early story does not give us enough grounds to assume that transformations are universally reversible, that killing a caster always ends their work, or that every curse follows the same rules. Each of those would need its own evidence.

Magical creatures as an extension of an attack

Thora's work with dangerous creatures, including the giant insects sent against Dorothy's group, shows another application of magic. A practitioner can create or deploy a threat that the victims must deal with directly. The caster does not have to stand beside every target and attack them personally.

That changes the practical problem for the defenders. They may be fighting an immediate creature attack while the person responsible remains elsewhere. Stopping the creature and stopping the source of the attack are different objectives.

It is also worth distinguishing magical origin from magical technique. A creature's strength, flight, or dangerous sting may matter in the scene without the creature being a spellcaster. The example tells us how a witch extends her reach, not that every member of a creature type possesses a particular collection of spells.

This is where creatures belong in a magic guide: as examples of effects and abilities relevant to the story. A full inventory of the peoples and creatures of Oz would be a separate discussion.

Crossing the boundary between Oz and Earth

Movement between Oz and Earth is possible, and the original story makes it consequential. Toto's arrival connects the two worlds, the witches' pursuit reaches Kansas, and Dorothy's attempt to get home becomes part of the Scepter quest.

The existence of crossings does not make them ordinary travel. Dorothy can know where she wants to go without having a way to get there. Recovering an appropriate magical means matters precisely because wanting to return is insufficient.

The distinction also applies within Oz. A story that permits inter-realm travel can still require a difficult journey through forests, fortresses, and guarded locations. One successful crossing does not prove that the same characters can transport themselves anywhere, at any time, or past every obstacle.

Limits, risks, and costs

The clearest limits in the original story are practical ones. An artifact may be incomplete or held by an enemy. A knowledgeable ally may be injured. A traveller may not understand the power involved. An attack may put several people in danger at once, requiring cooperation rather than a single overwhelming spell.

Some costs fall on the person targeted rather than the person performing the magic. Nicholas lives with an imposed transformation. Glinda suffers the consequences of a magically generated attack. Dorothy is drawn into a conflict reaching beyond the world she knows. Looking only for a caster becoming exhausted would miss much of what makes these powers dangerous.

The original Oz story therefore gives a substantial picture of magic without explaining everything. It establishes powerful artifacts, destructive and restorative effects, lasting transformation, magically engineered threats, and travel between realms. It also shows that knowledge, access, timing, and the actions of allies affect whether those abilities can solve a problem.

The most useful questions remain specific: what produced this effect, who could use it, what had to happen first, and what consequences followed? Keeping those questions attached to the actual examples makes the magic understandable without turning a few dramatic scenes into rules the story has not established.

text:
Oz in Grimm Fairy Tales: The World Beyond the Yellow Brick Road

Oz comes into Grimm Fairy Tales carrying some very familiar names. Dorothy, Glinda, the Scarecrow, the Tin Man, the Lion, and the Emerald City all give you something recognisable to start with. Zenescope places those familiar figures in a dangerous world with its own conflicts, powerful magical objects, and inhabitants whose lives have already been affected by the witches.

This overview stays with the original Oz story. It treats that first adventure as its own foundation rather than using later books to explain every mystery or settle what happens next.

The first important thing to understand is that Oz is a real place within the Grimm universe. Dorothy enters an existing realm. Its people have histories, loyalties, and problems before she meets them. Getting Dorothy home matters, but that is only one of the things at stake. The people she encounters still have to live with whatever happens to their world.

How Oz reaches Kansas

The original adventure starts with the search for the Veridian Scepter, a powerful magical artifact. The witches' pursuit brings the danger of Oz to Kansas and into Dorothy's life. That connection matters because her involvement grows out of something happening in the other realm. She does not simply walk into a disconnected fantasy that exists for her benefit.

Toto is part of that connection. In this version, he is a wolf from Oz rather than an ordinary little Kansas dog. His presence ties Dorothy's familiar surroundings to a world she has not yet learned to understand. Before there is a travelling group or a journey toward the Emerald City, there is already a threat crossing the boundary between worlds.

Once Dorothy reaches Oz, she needs to learn whom she can trust and how she might return home. Glinda and Thorne become important allies, while the Scepter gives the journey a practical objective. Recovering it offers a way to oppose the witch's power and help Dorothy get back to Kansas. Those goals bring her personal predicament together with the struggle facing the realm.

A journey through an inhabited world

The Emerald City is the obvious destination, but the journey shows why Oz cannot be reduced to that one place. Dorothy and her companions encounter fortresses, dangerous forests, and the Temple of Despair. Moving through the realm involves threats that do not disappear just because the group knows where it wants to go.

The search for the Scepter's pieces gives those places a purpose in the story. A fortress may hold information the group needs. A temple may contain something vital while also exposing the travellers to a trap. The landscape creates practical problems: how to reach a location, how to survive inside it, and how to keep moving when someone is injured.

The Temple of Despair sequence brings several of those difficulties together. Glinda is endangered while retrieving a Scepter piece, and the group also has to contend with a magical attack. Her abilities do not make the rest of the party unnecessary. Other people have to react, help, and deal with the consequences when she is hurt.

That gives the travelling group a reason to exist beyond assembling recognisable Oz characters. The journey demands different kinds of help. Magical knowledge, physical strength, quick thinking, and the willingness to protect someone else all have a place. Someone who cannot match a witch spell for spell can still be essential to keeping the others alive.

The Emerald City

The Emerald City is a centre of authority as well as the destination of the journey. King Jarl and the city's guards establish a political structure that exists independently of Dorothy. Arriving there brings her into contact with people who have responsibilities toward the city and its inhabitants.

The final missing piece of the Scepter also makes the city important to the quest. Dorothy's arrival does not turn the walls into a guarantee of safety, though. The approaching enemy brings the struggle to the city itself, and the story moves from the dangers facing a small group to the danger facing a much larger population.

That change of scale is important. A road adventure can make it easy to focus on whether the travellers survive the next encounter. A threatened city forces attention onto everyone who cannot simply accompany them to the next location. Defending Oz involves people who may never become members of Dorothy's group.

The familiar characters belong to this Oz

Thorne is the lion figure, but his role is that of a warrior with ties to the world around him. Toto's origin links him to Oz before Dorothy arrives. Bartleby the Scarecrow and Nicholas the Tin Man bring their own circumstances into the group. Their presence helps establish that Dorothy has joined other people's lives rather than collected companions waiting to be discovered.

The Tin Man is particularly important to the darker side of the setting. His metal body is the result of Lynessa's magic. That makes the transformation something done to a person, with consequences for what he wants and the choices he makes. His appearance is connected to a history of power being exercised over him.

The promise of changing an unwanted condition can also give a powerful figure leverage. Someone who desperately wants to recover what has been lost may be vulnerable to the person claiming to offer it back. The original story uses that kind of vulnerability to complicate trust within the group.

Bartleby's straw body brings a more immediate vulnerability into the adventure: fire is a real danger to him. Different bodies create different risks, and the group cannot assume that an attack will affect everyone in the same way. That is a useful example of how the unusual inhabitants influence the action without needing to stop for a complete catalogue of Oz's creatures.

Witches, armies, and the use of power

The witches' influence extends beyond their personal spellcasting. Their forces can pursue travellers, capture enemies, and threaten a city. Flying attackers and dangerous creatures allow the conflict to reach people who are nowhere near a witch herself.

This gives the world more than one level of danger. Dorothy may need to survive a creature sent against her, find a way out of captivity, or prevent an artifact from falling into enemy hands. None of those problems is exactly the same as confronting the person directing the attack.

The Scepter's importance makes control of magical resources part of that struggle. It is something people can seek, conceal, recover, lose, and fight over. Magic affects where the characters travel and what their enemies want. It has consequences for the shape of the adventure before anyone uses it in a final confrontation.

Hope within a dangerous realm

The first Oz story repeatedly puts its characters in situations where they cannot solve everything alone. They need information from others, help when they are trapped, protection when they are hurt, and allies willing to act when the danger grows. Those dependencies give friendship and trust practical weight.

Dorothy's arrival brings the reader into the realm, but understanding Oz means looking beyond her route home. There are people living under threats they did not choose, bodies changed by another person's magic, and a city whose inhabitants need defending. The familiar fairy-tale setting becomes a world in which the use of power has lasting consequences.

That is the foundation of Zenescope's early Oz. The first adventure establishes a connected realm, a dangerous journey, and a group of characters whose differences matter to their survival. It also leaves a useful distinction between having extraordinary power and using it to help someone. The magic can be spectacular, but the decisions made around it are what determine who benefits and who suffers.

I’m still putting together a guide to how magic works in this world. I’ll be posting that shortly.

1. Professional Background & Alleged Intelligence Career

The Intelligence Community: Leah claims a two-decade career supporting top-tier defense and intelligence agencies, specifically the NGA, DIA, NSA, and CIA, focusing on financial modeling, risk, and strategy.
Northrop Grumman: She got her start here fresh out of college after a coworker at the Cheesecake Factory told her about the industry. She started in dark rooms building cost models for satellites and software. She was quickly read into a Special Access Program (SAP) inside a secure vault, which she says was her first indication that "government lies to people to protect them".

Booz Allen Hamilton & The NRO: Moving into high-level consulting, she worked as a contractor for the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO). She notes she preferred contracting because trauma made it hard for her to sit still, allowing her to pop around to various agencies.
CIA & DIA Work: At the CIA, she claims she worked directly for the CFO and Comptroller. She uncovered that government tax dollars rarely align with actual missions, revealing a massive amount of "fluff" in contracts. She helped build a "gold standard" financial asset tracking model adopted by the ODNI. She also claims she was a "blue badger" (staff employee) for the DIA for 10 months.

Social Media Backlash: Leah answers critics who say her credentials cannot be verified by stating she used a pseudonym on social media to protect her privacy and her kids. She claims she blew up too fast by yelling about Jeffrey Epstein and the government shutdown, drawing targeted internet attacks from a "mentally unstable" group of ex-special forces influencers.

2. Black Widow Global & Corporate Cases

The Firm: Leah founded Black Widow Global about a year prior to the interview, focusing on private equity mergers, acquisitions, and deep executive due diligence.
Corporate Fraud: She assesses if corporate leaders are actually capable of committing fraud, noting cases where CEOs hid private jet purchases inside vendor payments. She compares the deceptive "stories" sold by modern companies to Theranos and WeWork.

The Lethal London Case: Her most jolting case involved a social media client from England who hired her to look into a shady potential investment partner in Tennessee. Two to three days into her investigation, her healthy, 40-something client suddenly died right after hosting his daughter's sleepover. She strongly suspects foul play.

Hiding Assets in Divorce: She does pro bono work for women to locate hidden assets. She explains that LLCs are the most common hiding method, alongside cryptocurrency. She debunks the narrative that crypto is un-trackable, stating the public blockchain makes it very easy to trace once you acquire a person's exact wallet address.

3. Traumatic Childhood & Mental Resilience

Rolesville, NC: She grew up in a tiny, rural, one-stoplight town on 23 acres next to tobacco fields.
Severe Childhood Amnesia: Leah reveals she has virtually zero memories before the age of 14 due to the extreme trauma and abuse she witnessed. She didn't realize regular people actually possessed childhood memories until later in life.

Domestic Abuse: Her earliest, fleeting memories involve calling emergency services at age 4 or 5 while her father brutally beat her mother. Another memory involves her alcoholic mother driving drunk, kicking her out of a Chuck-E-Cheese birthday party, dropping her at the end of a long driveway, and vanishing to rehab for a year.
The Breakpoint at Age 14: Her first concrete, continuous memory began at 14 during a freshman English class. She went home to find her parents missing, dog food scattered everywhere, and a vacuum cleaner on the floor. Her father had beaten her mother unrecognizable with a 20-pound bag of dog food and the vacuum, landing her mother in the ICU. This was the day her mother finally left for good.

Survival Mode & Escape: Leah was the oldest of four siblings and actively raised them, shielding them from their toxic parents. She ran track and cross-country exceptionally well, earning recruitment offers across North Carolina. She chose the University of Tennessee Knoxville purely to escape the environment, a move for which her youngest sister still resents her. She has completely forgiven both of her now-deceased parents, attributing her survival to an unusual brain chemistry or mindset that simply refuses to absorb insults or depression.

4. Turning Point USA (TPUSA) & Charlie Kirk Allegations

Charlie Kirk's Death: Leah notes that Kirk's "assassination" was a massive catalyst for division on the political right. She notes that eight days before he was killed, Kirk requested a highly unusual forensic financial and operational audit of TPUSA—indicating he suspected an executive was doing something wrong.
Dark Money Funding: TPUSA grew over 300%, jumping from $85 million to $115 million between 2024 and 2025. Leah states that 80%+ of this money comes from just five dark money donors. Through tax filings, she unmasked three: the Wilks brothers, the Bradley Fund, and Robert Schillman (who allegedly pulled $2 million out of a shell charity two days before Kirk died).

Vendor Siphoning: Leah alleges mass financial irregularities, pointing out that TPUSA spent a staggering $70 million more than it brought in during 2023. She states that over $20 million went to internal marketing vendors and LLCs tracing directly back to friends and executive leadership within the nonprofit. She notes that while they only have to name their top five vendors publicly, they have over 60 random vendors getting paid over $100,000 each.

Narrative Capture: She claims current TPUSA leadership (Tyler Boyer, Andrew Kolvet, Rob McCoy) has gained immense financial and social real estate since Kirk's death. She targets Resolute Media (a for-profit entity running the Charlie Kirk show) for using a nonprofit's likeness without paying royalty fees. She states they are paid by hidden entities to push specific political narratives (e.g., pro-Israel, merging militaries, AI data centers).

5. Foreign Influence, Paid Influencers & The Right's Division

Brad Parcale & FAR Campaigns: Shawn cites a Time magazine article detailing Trump's 2020 campaign manager, Brad Parcale, running a paid, Foreign Agents Registration Act (FARA)-registered influence campaign on behalf of Israel targeting young MAGA conservatives. Leah confirms she has gone deep into Parcale’s operation.

The Israel Funding Loop: Leah explains the money trail: Israel pays a German advertising firm starting with an "H" (presumably Havas), which then passes millions to Parcale's US operations. This creates a legal loop where influencers can claim they aren't taking money from Israel. She states Parcale's monthly funding spiked from $3 million to $12–15 million within a week of Charlie Kirk's death, utilizing AI bots like Nucleus to text citizens and gather compliance data on foreign policy.

Influencer Capture: Shawn and Leah discuss how the administration and foreign operatives "capture" right-wing influencers. Shawn remarks that many aren't undercover agents ("feds") but are simply overwhelmed by their own inflated egos after being invited to the White House or high-tier social events. Once they take photos holding up binders or posting coordinated scripts ($7,000 per post), they are trapped on the team and cannot back out.

FARA Rollbacks: Leah claims Pam Bondi stripped strict FARA requirements back in 2025, meaning individuals no longer have to register as foreign agents unless they are a literal direct agent of that country.

6. Tech Surveillance: Waze, Flock Cameras & Israeli Tech

The Waze App Hidden Terms: Leah warns that Waze is entirely operated out of and run by Israel, founded by three former members of the IDF's elite cyber-warfare Unit 8200. Hidden deep in the terms of service is a clause stating that if a user sues Waze, they cannot do it in a US court—they must travel to Israel and waive their right to a jury. Google bought it for $1.3 billion but allowed them to keep these sovereign data terms.

Flock Safety Cameras: Flock license plate readers are exploding across America (jumping from 40k in 2024 to over 100k). She highlights an incredibly invasive add-on called Flock Nova. 

Nova scans a license plate and instantly cross-references open-source data and leaked dark web databases to pull up the driver's emails, LinkedIn, Social Security Number, and bank account info in real-time. It also features Bluetooth integration to track the identities of passengers in the car.

"Have I Been Flocked?": Leah highlights a whistleblower activist website, https://t.co/eGegGafqMU, which FOIA'ed police audit logs mapping 430 million hits. The data reveals that only 9% of police searches were for an actual crime; the other 91% were blank or completely unauthorized. The biggest abusers are Nashville PD and Harris County Sheriff's Office, with logs showing officers tracking ex-girlfriends and women crossing state lines for abortions.

The Ultimate Surveillance Overlap (Toka & Carbine): Leah notes that the primary investors behind Flock cameras are the exact same entities funding major Israeli surveillance firms. She names Toka, a company founded by former Israeli Defense Minister Ehud Barak (who had documented emails with Jeffrey Epstein about it). Toka has the terrifying capability to tap into any internet-connected live camera feed (Ring, Flock, iPhones), alter or delete the footage in real-time, and leave zero forensic trace.

The "Military Tech Merge": Leah and Shawn heavily criticize the NDAA's massive 1,700-page defense bill, specifically highlighting a hidden component allowing a tech and data-sharing merge between the US and Israel. She notes this sets up an entirely un-auditable, classified Special Access Program (SAP) budget pipeline for Israel that completely bypasses public or congressional oversight.

THE LOVE THE BRANIFF BUILT - The brand new 1958 Dallas Love Field Terminal located at the end of Cedar Springs Road was dedicated amidst a full-week of fanfare and ceremony from October 20-27, 1957. The third day, Tuesday, October 22, 1957, was the quietest of the eight-day celebration because there were no events planned. Originally, the Love Field Pioneer Day was scheduled for Tuesday but was moved to Friday prior to the George Haddaway Banquet that evening.

By 1973, Braniff International had opened its new Terminal of the Future located on the south end of the East/Red Concourse in 1968, and debuted the world's first airport overhead people mover dubbed the Jetrail Fastpark System in April 1970. Braniff began flying a single Boeing 747 between Dallas and Hawaii, in January 1971, and offered the most departures of any other airline at Love Field. Several years earlier the, Jet-Age mid century themed Operations and Maintenance Base on the East Side of Love Field was opened in October 1958.

Photo: The spectacular new 1958 Terminal Building Main Lobby featured massive and modern spaces that were indicative of the arrival of the jet age. Braniff’s elegant ticket counter was the largest and the first of the long row of airline counters in the new Ticket Hall, which stretched south from the Main Lobby along Cedar Springs Drive passenger drop-off area. The elegant mid century styled staircase lead up to a beautiful and breathtaking mezzanine that overlooked the busy new terminal concourse and ramp areas.

text:
✡️ WHY DID JESUS SAY “SALVATION IS FROM THE JEWS”?

The Jewish Jesus | Day 6 of 8

What if Jesus Himself challenged the way many believers understand Israel today?

Speaking to a Samaritan woman, He made a declaration that should stop every Gentile believer in their tracks.

“Salvation is from the Jews.”

Not was from the Jews.

IS from the Jews.

What did He mean? And why does it still matter?

JOHN 4:20–26

“Our fathers worshiped in this mountain, and you Jews say that in Jerusalem is the place where people ought to worship.”  Jesus said to her, “Woman, believe me, the hour comes, when neither in this mountain, nor in Jerusalem, will you worship the Father.  You worship that which you don't know.   We worship that which we know; for salvation is from the Jews.  But the hour comes, and now is, when the true worshipers will worship the Father in spirit and truth, for the Father seeks such to be his worshipers.God is spirit, and those who worship him must worship in spirit and truth.”  The woman said to him, “I know that Messiah comes, he who is called Christ.   When he has come, he will declare to us all things.”Jesus said to her, “I am he, the one who speaks to you.”

1. WHY WAS THIS CONVERSATION EXTRAORDINARY?
 
Jesus was speaking across centuries of religious division.

Samaritans claimed an Israelite heritage, revered the Torah, and worshiped on Mount Gerizim.
Jews worshiped in Jerusalem, where God's Temple stood.

The disagreement involved sacred history, Scripture, and the proper location of worship.
Yet Jesus willingly engaged this Samaritan woman.
He did not dismiss her because of her background.
Neither did He abandon the truth God had revealed through Israel.

Notice His words:

“WE worship that which WE know.”

Jesus openly identified Himself with the Jewish people.
Then He made His extraordinary declaration.

“Salvation is from the Jews.”

2. WHY DOES SALVATION COME FROM THE JEWS?

The answer begins with Abraham.

Genesis 12:3 records God's promise:

“All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.”

God chose Abraham and his descendants for a purpose extending far beyond themselves.

Through Israel came the covenants, the Scriptures, the prophets, and ultimately the Messiah.

Romans 9:4–5 identifies these blessings as belonging to Israel.

But consider how specific God's promises became.

Genesis 49:10 associates royal authority with Judah.

2 Samuel 7 promises David an enduring royal dynasty.

Micah 5:2 identifies Bethlehem as the birthplace of Israel's future ruler.

The Messiah did not appear without a history.

He came through a particular people, tribe, and royal line.

God chose Israel not to exclude the nations, but to bring His blessing to the nations.

3. THE PROPHETS ANTICIPATED SALVATION FOR THE WORLD

Isaiah 49:6 declares concerning the Lord's Servant:

“I will also give you as a light to the nations, that you may be my salvation to the end of the earth.”

Notice the progression.

Israel's Messiah would bring God's salvation beyond Israel.

Isaiah 2:3 also declares:

“For the law shall go out of Zion, and the LORD’s word from Jerusalem.”

God's revelation has a particular historical origin, but its saving purpose extends to all nations.

Salvation comes from the Jews, but it was never intended for the Jews alone.

4. THE WOMAN AT THE WELL REVEALS GOD'S PURPOSE

Consider the setting.

Jesus did not make this declaration while addressing Jerusalem's religious authorities.

He spoke to a Samaritan woman.

The conversation crossed ethnic, religious, and social boundaries.

Yet He personally offered her living water (John 4:10–14).

He affirmed the Jewish foundation of salvation while extending its invitation beyond the Jewish community.

And when she spoke of the coming Messiah, Jesus answered:

“I am he, the one who speaks to you.”

Here was Yeshua HaMashiach (Jesus the Messiah) revealing His identity to a Samaritan woman.

The Messiah promised through Israel was offering salvation beyond Israel.

5. TWO DECLARATIONS THAT CHANGE EVERYTHING

Here is perhaps the most remarkable feature of John 4.

JOHN 4:22 — JESUS DECLARES:

“Salvation is from the Jews.”

JOHN 4:42 — THE SAMARITANS CONFESS:

“This is indeed the Christ, the Savior of the world.”

Did you catch that?

Within a single chapter, John establishes both the Jewish origin and universal reach of salvation.

FROM THE JEWS. FOR THE WORLD.

Jesus did not need to erase Israel's significance to extend salvation to Samaritans.

Israel's covenant history explains how the Messiah came into the world.

And His saving work extends far beyond Israel.

6. DOES UNIVERSAL SALVATION ERASE ISRAEL'S PROMISES?

Jesus announced that true worship would no longer depend upon traveling to Jerusalem or Mount Gerizim.

The Father seeks worshipers who worship in spirit and truth.

But does freedom from a geographical worship requirement mean Israel's prophetic future has been canceled?

Not necessarily.

Isaiah 2 anticipates nations streaming to Zion.

Zechariah 14 describes nations worshiping the King.

And Romans 11:28–29 affirms God's continuing faithfulness to Israel because of His promises to the patriarchs.

The universal availability of salvation does not require the cancellation of God's particular covenant promises.

Spiritual unity and covenant faithfulness are not competing truths.

7. PAUL'S WARNING TO GENTILE BELIEVERS

Romans 11 describes Gentile believers as wild olive branches grafted among the natural branches.

Paul warns against arrogance toward Israel.

Then he declares:

“You don't support the root, but the root supports you.” (Romans 11:18)

What a remarkable warning!

Gentile believers did not establish a new foundation independent of Israel's history.

They were graciously brought into blessings rooted in God's ancient promises.

Jesus did not conceal His Jewish identity.

He did not apologize for Israel's role in God's redemptive plan.

And He never suggested that salvation's universal reach erased its Jewish foundation.

“Salvation is from the Jews.”

Yet the Samaritans recognized Him as:

“The Savior of the world.”

Two declarations.

One chapter.

One Messiah.

FROM THE JEWS. FOR THE WORLD.

If Jesus acknowledged Israel's place in God's plan, and Paul warned Gentile believers against boasting over Israel, why should we do otherwise?

Tomorrow | Day 7

Why Did Jesus Stop Reading Isaiah Mid-Prophecy?

🚩 Mother Jogulamba 🚩

In Alampur, Telangana, on the banks of the Tungabhadra River, the Mother does not smile at you. She sits upon a *preta* (a corpse or spirit of the dead); her tongue hangs out, and her hair is tied up in a wild, disheveled knot. Within that hair, a lizard, a frog, a scorpion, an owl, and a human skull crawl about. Look at her directly—for she is looking straight at you.

Those well-versed in the ways of the household interpret this as a diagnosis. When a home forgets its sanctity and proper upkeep, the lizard arrives first. As dampness and neglect allow toxins to seep into the rooms, the frog and the scorpion follow. When the house falls into darkness and ruin, and nocturnal birds begin to nest in the rafters, the owl appears. Finally, there is the skull—the symbol of death itself. There are four stages to destruction, and the Mother wears all four, bound within her own hair. She is *Griha Chandi*—the fierce guardian of the home. It is her hand that prevents decay from reaching your threshold; she performs this task by wearing that very decay as her own adornment.

In the *Lalita Sahasranama*, she is described as *Pancha-pretasana-shila*—meaning one who is seated upon five *pretas* (corpses). Brahma, Vishnu, Rudra, Maheshwara, and Sadashiva are five great powers; yet, without *Shakti* (the Divine Feminine Energy), they remain inert. They cannot create, sustain, or dissolve anything. It is only when she resides upon them that they gain the capacity to act. Creation, preservation, dissolution, concealment, and the bestowal of grace—all are her handiwork.

Alampur is also the land associated with the *Rasa Siddha* tradition and the text *Siddha Rasarnavam*. According to this tradition, when *upasana* (devotional practice) is performed according to the prescribed rules, mercury is said to manifest—emanating from the *Bala Brahma Linga*, the thighs of Subrahmanya, the navel of Ganapati, and the mouth of Jogulamba. This substance, known as *paradum* (mercury), is referred to by alchemists as *Shiva Beeja* (the seed of Shiva). It is believed to possess the power to transmute iron into gold and transform a perishable human body into a perfect vessel for *yoga*. It is said that the nine specific herbs required for this alchemical process are concealed within the nine *Nava Brahma* temples, with the mouth of the Goddess herself serving as the furnace.

This is the site where the upper teeth of Mata Sati fell, making it the fifth of the eighteen *Shakti Peethas*. In 1390, the Bahmani Sultans destroyed the temple; however, devotees managed to relocate the idol of the Goddess to the *Bala Brahmeswara* temple, ensuring her preservation. Her *ugra rupa*—the fiery intensity of her form—is so potent that, in ancient times, the temple architects constructed a pool of water around her *garbhagriha* (sanctum sanctorum) to cool her energy. They did not attempt to restrain her; rather, they sought to soothe her. They ensured that she remained as a living presence before the householder. For the seeker who desires her in her natural, unadorned form, that fire still burns there.

She is the Mother of the Yoginis—the Divine Mother of all ascetics. Offer your fear to her; she will accept it.

🚩Jai Ma Jogulamba🌹🙏 🌹🌺

text:
The Binding of Isaac is the account in Genesis 22 in which God commands Abraham to offer his son Isaac as a sacrifice on a mountain in the land of Moriah. Jewish tradition calls it the Akedah, from the Hebrew word for "binding." Isaac was the child Abraham and Sarah had waited for into old age. Through him God had promised Abraham countless descendants, so the command seemed to cancel the promise itself.

The narrative is spare. Abraham rises early, saddles his donkey, and travels for three days with Isaac and two servants. Isaac carries the wood and asks where the lamb for the offering is. Abraham replies that God will provide. At the summit he binds his son on the altar and lifts the knife. An angel calls out and stops him, and Abraham sacrifices a ram caught by its horns in a thicket. He names the place "The Lord will provide." The text then says that Abraham returned to his servants. It does not say that Isaac came down with him, and father and son never speak to each other again in Genesis. Rabbinic commentators noticed this silence and debated it for centuries.

The episode holds a central place in three religions. In Judaism it is read on Rosh Hashanah, and the shofar, a ram's horn, recalls the animal offered in Isaac's place. Tradition identified Moriah with the Temple Mount in Jerusalem. Early Christian writers read the story as a foreshadowing of the crucifixion. The Quran tells a parallel account, and most Muslim commentators identify the son as Ishmael, an event remembered each year at Eid al-Adha. In 1843 the Danish philosopher Søren Kierkegaard built Fear and Trembling around it, asking how faith could demand an act that ethics condemns.

< Be John Marshall
< Born 1755, a log cabin on the Virginia frontier
< Eldest of fifteen children
< Your father surveys land for Lord Fairfax. You learn to read property lines before you learn Latin.
< No formal schooling until you're fourteen
< One year at a tiny academy. One semester of law lectures at William & Mary. That's it.
< The Revolution starts. You enlist at nineteen.
< Valley Forge, winter of 1778. You watch men die of cold while Congress debates.
< You never forget what a weak central government looks like.
< War ends. You pass the bar in Virginia with six weeks of legal training.
< Richmond loves you. Tall, sloppy dresser, tells better stories than anyone in the tavern.
< Clients don't care that your briefs are a mess. You win.
< 1788, Virginia ratification convention. Patrick Henry argues against the Constitution for seven hours.
< You argue back. Virginia ratifies by ten votes.
< President Adams offers you Secretary of State in 1800. You take it.
< Then Adams loses to Jefferson. The Federalists are finished.
< Five weeks before Jefferson's inauguration, Adams makes you Chief Justice.
< A midnight appointment. Jefferson is furious.
< You are 45. You will hold that seat for 34 years.
< Marbury v. Madison, 1803. William Marbury wants his judgeship. You say he deserves it.
< Then you say the court cannot give it to him.
< The Judiciary Act of 1789 is unconstitutional. The Supreme Court just voided a federal law.
< Jefferson wanted you to lose. Instead you invented judicial review.
< You write 519 of the 1,106 decisions issued during your tenure. Most are unanimous.
< McCulloch v. Maryland. Gibbons v. Ogden. The federal government grows with every opinion.
< Your cousin Thomas Jefferson despises you until the day he dies.
< You outlast him by nine years.
< 1835, you die in Philadelphia. The Liberty Bell cracks tolling for your funeral.
< You served under six presidents. You disagreed with most of them.
< You had almost no legal education. You built the third branch of government anyway.

The Constitution doesn't mention judicial review. You wrote it in.

Six weeks of law school, thirty-four years on the bench.

Every Supreme Court decision since 1803 exists because you decided the Court could say what the law is.

text:
THE DAILY MARKET BRIEF | OCTOBER 22, 2026
Well, that didn't take long. Just when investors were starting to feel comfortable with AI stocks again, Wall Street delivered another reminder of how quickly sentiment can change. The Nasdaq plunged 2.60% on Thursday to close at 26,008.86, while the S&P 500 dropped 1.21% to 7,663.43. Interestingly, the Dow actually managed a tiny 0.02% gain, finishing at 52,867.98. What caught my attention wasn't simply the size of the Nasdaq's decline. It was the divergence underneath the surface. Most stocks actually advanced, even as the major technology names dragged the indexes lower. That's not what a uniform market panic looks like. Investors are becoming much more selective about where they're willing to put money, and some of the most crowded AI trades are feeling the pressure.

The biggest problem right now isn't that demand for AI has suddenly disappeared. It's that investors are starting to question how much capital companies must commit before that demand produces sustainable returns. $META became a particularly important example after reporting strong revenue growth but also disclosing substantial AI-related spending and its first cash outflow in more than a decade. Investors weren't simply judging the latest earnings numbers. They were reassessing the financial consequences of the company's expansion plans. $TSLA also came under pressure despite reporting positive quarterly free cash flow and reducing its planned capital expenditure. That's an important lesson from this earnings season: beating expectations doesn't automatically protect a stock when the market is already questioning its valuation. Meanwhile, Treasury yields declined as investors grew more cautious, but falling yields alone weren't enough to support technology shares. With inflation still a concern and energy prices exposed to geopolitical risks, I don't think we can assume the Federal Reserve will quickly come to the market's rescue.

I've been bullish on AI for years, and Thursday's selloff hasn't changed my long-term conviction. But there's something I want to emphasize. A company can operate in an extraordinary industry and still be a poor investment at the wrong valuation or with the wrong financing structure. That's particularly relevant for AI infrastructure companies, where enormous capital requirements can turn impressive revenue growth into disappointing returns for shareholders. I'm continuing to watch $CRWV closely because I believe the underlying demand for computing infrastructure remains significant, but I also want to see greater confidence in the company's financing position. The same discipline applies across the semiconductor and data-center ecosystem. I'm interested in businesses that can turn AI demand into sustainable earnings and cash flow, not simply companies that announce the largest spending budgets. Thursday's decline doesn't prove the AI investment cycle is ending. It does suggest that investors are no longer prepared to reward every AI-related announcement without asking harder financial questions.

Friday, October 23, should give us a few more clues. At 9:45 AM ET, we'll get the preliminary October S&P Global manufacturing, services and composite PMI readings, which should help clarify whether the economy is maintaining momentum despite high borrowing costs. At 10:00 AM ET, the University of Michigan releases its final October consumer sentiment and inflation expectations figures. Those inflation expectations could be particularly important for Treasury yields and the market's interpretation of the Fed's next move. Earnings from $AXP and $SLB before the opening bell will also be worth watching. American Express offers a useful window into consumer spending and credit quality, while SLB can tell us something about energy-sector investment at a time when oil prices and geopolitical tensions remain elevated. I'll be watching whether the Nasdaq can stabilize, whether selling pressure spreads beyond technology, and whether bond-market conditions offer any meaningful relief.

My view is straightforward: I'm still bullish on the long-term AI cycle, but I'm not going to confuse a compelling investment theme with an immediate buying signal. The Nasdaq has now given back a substantial part of Wednesday's recovery, and I'd rather see evidence of stronger buying support than rush into every decline. If the upcoming economic data show resilient growth without another inflation scare, and if Treasury yields remain stable, we could see buyers return to quality technology names. But if earnings continue to expose weak cash conversion, aggressive borrowing or unrealistic valuations, the correction could extend further. I'm keeping capital available, staying selective, and watching the companies I understand best. I've been through enough market cycles to know that volatility can create excellent opportunities, but only when the price compensates you for the risk. 📈
