text:
*The 4:00 AM Awakening: Reconciling the Contradictions of a Long Life*

*To my dear friends and contemporaries —*

We have walked long paths, built careers through shifting times, and raised families along the way. In the quietest hours, our minds return to choices made at home and at work. I share this as a reminder that our contradictions are not a sign of failure, but the definition of a deeply lived life. May it bring you peace during your own quiet dawns.

The clock reads 4:00 AM. Outside, Hyderabad is still. Inside, you have just awoken from six hours of deep sleep. Your body feels rested, but your mind feels heavy.

While you slept, your brain was auditing your life — not a nightmare, but a vivid processing of old compromises and enduring contradictions. A realization settles in: the ledger of a long life rarely balances perfectly. And perhaps some contradictions were never meant to be resolved.

If you have experienced this, you are far from alone. As our outer lives slow down, our inner minds speed up.

*The Life Review*

Psychologist Erik Erikson called this final stage Ego Integrity versus Despair — a natural life review where we evaluate who we were at home and what we achieved at work.

For many of us, identity was tied to a title for thirty or forty years. We entered offices where staying late was loyalty and a transfer meant progress. We climbed with single-minded focus because that is what the time demanded. In deep sleep, the brain drops the distractions of retirement and forces us to look at what we set aside. We see both the milestones and the friction that came with them.

*From Doer to Witness*

Indian philosophy offers a way to live through this tension. The Gita begins not with glory, but with crisis. Arjuna is paralyzed between his duty as a warrior, his Swadharma, and his conscience. Krishna does not make the conflict disappear. He teaches Nishkama Karma — to act with full duty without letting the role swallow your identity.

Applied to a life review, this means compassion. The focus you maintained in your thirties belonged to that time, its pressures and limited choices. To judge your younger self with the wisdom of your seventies is an unfair trial.

Our tradition gives this shift a stage: Vanaprastha. Not a move to a forest, but a psychological move from the active Doer, the Karta, to the Observer, the Sakshi. You are no longer the designation on your old visiting card. You are the awareness witnessing the story.

*The Dual Paradox*

Nowhere is this clearer than in a long marriage after retirement. For decades, life was synchronized around office timings. Then the stage disappears.

A retired executive here in Hyderabad still wakes at seven and opens a diary where meetings used to be. To stay useful, he begins to manage the kitchen, suggesting how the steel dabbas could be stacked. His wife, who ran that kitchen with quiet precision for thirty years, feels her space crowded. His focus once built their life. Now they must learn each other’s quiet rhythms for the first time.

*Living with Parallel Truths*

Peace does not require resolving every contradiction. Psychologists call it psychological flexibility; our tradition called it Titiksha — the strength to hold two opposite truths without breaking.

You can be proud of what you built while acknowledging the distance it created. You can love your family deeply while recognizing your attention was often elsewhere.

When you wake at 4:00 AM, try this: Name the work — “My mind did night duty; this is health.” Change your seat — from Karta to Sakshi. Put time back in its time — judge the 35-year-old with the context of the 35-year-old. And practice Kintsugi — do not hide the cracks. Light them with gold.

The goal of old age is not a perfect ledger. It is a whole life.

text:
𝟳 𝗟𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗻𝘀 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗠𝘆 𝗠𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗼𝗿𝘀 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗲𝗱 𝗠𝘆 𝗟𝗶𝗳𝗲
Some advice earns a place in your notebook. Other advice changes the decisions you make for the rest of your life.
Through people I’ve worked with, conversations I’ve had, and teachers I’ve listened to, these seven lessons have stayed with me. They’ve challenged how I do business, face disappointment, and live my faith.
Here are the words as I remember them—and what I took from them.
𝟭. 𝗔𝗹 𝗡𝗲𝘂𝗵𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗵 — 𝗛𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗼𝘂𝗿𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗱.
“You can’t let the fucking lawyers run your business.”
Al certainly knew how to make a point memorable.
My takeaway: get sound legal advice, understand your obligations, and take responsibility for your decisions. A leader must exercise judgment rather than turn every difficult choice into another meeting.
𝟮. 𝗦𝗵𝗮𝗻𝗲𝗲 𝗠𝗼𝗿𝗲𝘁 — 𝗦𝘁𝗼𝗽 𝗽𝗼𝗹𝗶𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗮𝘄𝗮𝘆 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆.
“𝗧𝗿𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼 𝗯𝗲 𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗰𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗺𝗼𝗻𝗲𝘆.”
There is always another sentence to rewrite, another detail to adjust, another reason to delay.
Do good work. Release it. Listen to the response. Improve it.
An idea sitting in your drafts cannot help a customer or pay a bill.
𝟯. 𝗗𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗹𝗱 𝗧𝗿𝘂𝗺𝗽 — 𝗠𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗮𝘀𝗸.
“Ask for something you don’t deserve—what if they say yes?”
How many opportunities have we rejected on someone else’s behalf?
Ask for the meeting. Present the proposal. Give someone a reason to consider the possibility.
Let them make their decision. You don’t need to supply the rejection in advance.
𝟰. 𝗗𝗿. 𝗔𝗿𝘁𝗵𝘂𝗿 𝗖𝗮𝗹𝗶𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗿𝗼 — 𝗥𝗲𝗳𝘂𝘀𝗲 𝘁𝗼 𝘀𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗽𝘂𝗿𝗽𝗼𝘀𝗲.
“𝗚𝗶𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘂𝗽 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗮𝗻 𝗼𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻.”
Sometimes the plan fails. Sometimes you need rest, better advice, or a different approach.
Change the approach when necessary. Keep working toward the purpose that matters.
Persistence requires enough humility to learn along the way.
𝟱. 𝗥𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗻𝗱 𝗕𝗶𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝗪𝗲𝗯𝗯𝗲𝗿 — 𝗞𝗲𝗲𝗽 𝗚𝗼𝗱 𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗰𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿.
“𝗛𝗼𝗻𝗼𝗿 𝗚𝗼𝗱 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗱𝗼 𝗴𝗼𝗼𝗱.”
That instruction reaches into every transaction.
Did I tell the truth? Did I keep my word? Did I treat the other person fairly when being fair cost me something?
Those questions belong in the business plan.
𝟲. 𝗘𝘃𝗮𝗻 𝗖𝗮𝗿𝗺𝗶𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗲𝗹 — 𝗧𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗼𝘄𝗻𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽 𝗼𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴.
“Wake up early and tackle the day before it tackles you.”
For me, the early hours beside the sea offer time to pray, think, and prepare before the demands begin.
A quiet morning gives me a better chance of making deliberate decisions throughout the day.
𝟳. 𝗠𝗶𝗰𝗵𝗮𝗲𝗹 𝗙𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘇𝗲𝘀𝗲 — 𝗦𝘁𝗼𝗽 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘄𝗮𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴.
Michael’s message challenged me to listen for God’s purpose and stand boldly for Jesus.
It made me examine my own excuses. Was I waiting for direction—or postponing something I already knew I needed to do?
Faith asks something of us. Eventually, we have to answer with action.
These lessons are still working on me. Remembering them is easy; practicing them when the stakes are high takes effort.
𝗪𝗵𝗶𝗰𝗵 𝗹𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗼𝗻 𝗱𝗼 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗻𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗮𝗰𝘁 𝗼𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗸—𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗱𝗼?
Pastor David Vogel
The Godly Shark
Proudly from New Hampshire.

text:
summer 2025 i was an intern on a trading desk in nyc, sneaking out of the office to work on @WisprFlow

9 months prior i had just quit d1 soccer and the only things i had left were studying finance and making content

so i started looking for creator jobs on linkedin and landed on some random company called wispr flow. after a few calls tanay extended me an offer to join the team of 6

i would sit in class with slack open all day and excuse myself to the "bathroom" for random huddles with tanay

it felt like i had finally found something i enjoyed outside of soccer, and i was making good money from my personal content

but i come from a very traditional immigrant family. we moved to the us from ireland when i was 7 and my parents are from spain, so the expectation was that i would study finance and then work in finance

i also believed the creator stuff wasn't sustainable, and wispr was still really early with a couple thousand users

so junior year i applied to over 600 finance internships and finally got one reply back, from a trading firm in nyc

landing that on my own was a huge moment for my family, but it also meant balancing 2 summer classes, wispr flow, a finance internship and my personal brand

when i finally got to nyc, the first 2 weeks i was learning a ton, asking a million questions, and i actually enjoyed being there (or so i thought)

but soon the novelty wore off and i started hating all of it. being a creative with severe adhd, this felt like a living hell. the robotic work, the drinking culture, slop bowls at the desk, traders who couldn't even get up from their seats

i felt defeated. the one thing i was counting on to be my future was the thing i hated most

then on a random monday i hopped on my usual train into wtc station and looked around. older guys in quarter zips from all these prestigious firms. half of them asleep trying to get 10 more min before clocking in, the other half looking pissed off and miserable

it hit me that there was no amount of money that would make me live this life. i had no other choice but to make content and wispr work out

so i started sneaking out. i'd sit down at the trading desk, say i was going to see my mentor on another floor, and walk out of the building

then i'd post up at a cafe in soho, meet up with founders and app developers i knew from ig, and work on content and wispr all day

those next 2 months i had so much anxiety and doubt, wondering if missing out on a return offer would f*ck up my life and if maybe my parents were right

fast forward to today, i'm the #2 marketing hire at wispr flow at 22, and in my time here we've gone from pre product to series b at a $2b valuation

everyone talks about finding what you love, but nobody talks about how valuable it is to find what you hate. forever grateful for nyc and finding what i hated so young

text:
Come and See, "Dear Bastard"

...It all started with a cake. When casting the young boy for "Come and See," Elem Klimov showed the candidates military footage – executions, trenches filled with bodies, concentration camps. And then he offered them tea and cake. One teenager, Alyosha Kravchenko, refused. He was the one they chose.

More than 40 years later, his face is being sold on Stoleshnikov Lane. For 38,600 rubles, in a limited edition. With piercings, tattoos on his face, acid-wash colors, and machine guns on the sleeves. Over the burning village is the address of the store. On the chest, the inscription "Marking Distance."

Egor Creed starred in the music video for "Dear Bastard" wearing this long-sleeved shirt. The song is about how invincible he is: a white Rolls Royce drives across a bridge, a girl beside him, social media accounts are "going wild," and he's "going wild too." And the main punchline: "They wanted to cancel me, but I cancelled their culture." Underneath this rap, the face of the boy who is watching his village burn alive is printed on the artist's chest.

He cancelled culture. That's the most accurate way to put it.

Let me remind you what the film is about, since neither the "couturier" nor the singer have bothered to say it. Belarus, 1943. People are herded into a barn, covered with straw, and set on fire. Those who try to escape are shot down by machine guns. Klimov wrote the script with Ales Adamovich, who spent years recording the stories of survivors. Their book, co-authored with Yanka Bryl and Vladimir Kolesnik, is called "I am from a burning village." There were 628 such villages in Belarus. They were burned to the ground, along with their inhabitants. 186 people never emerged from the ashes. In Khatyn alone, there were 149 people, including 75 children. The youngest was only seven weeks old...

Klimov took the title from the Book of Revelation: "...I heard a voice of the fourth animal saying, 'COME AND SEE.' And I looked, and behold, a pale horse, and he who sat on it had a name called Death..." The director put these three words on the poster for what is considered the most terrifying film about war. The creatives – on a t-shirt, next to the address of the boutique.

The item was created in collaboration (what a fitting word!) between the Moscow "concept store" KM20 and the New York brand Marking Distance, which sells "punk aesthetics." The demand from Americans is not high – for them, Khatyn is somewhere on the far side of the moon. But the founder of KM20, Olga Karpuk, is from Minsk. From Minsk to Khatyn is 54 kilometers. That's the "Marking Distance."

And there's no need to talk about "reinterpretation" or "freedom of expression." In the West, which they so admire on Stoleshnikov Lane, something like this would be pulled from shelves in a matter of hours. In 2014, Zara pulled a striped children's t-shirt with a yellow star from sale – it too closely resembled the uniform of a concentration camp prisoner, even though the star was a sheriff's star. That same year, Urban Outfitters apologized for a Kent State University sweatshirt with stains that looked like blood: in 1970, four students were shot there.

Creed sings that he won't change. But it's too late, of course. Just do what's written on the poster, the face they've put on your t-shirt. Come and see. The entire 145 minutes. You can have cake.

text:
THE EVIDENCE™ | NFL INVESTIGATION | OCTOBER 22, 2026

DO THE SEATTLE SEAHAWKS NEED A MODERN-DAY CONRAD DOBLER?

What the NFL's Most Notorious Guard Can Teach Seattle About Protecting Sam Darnold

By Kim Wojcinski | USA Best Selling Author

The evidence will be presented. The verdict is yours.

There was a time when offensive linemen did more than execute blocking assignments. They established ownership of the line of scrimmage, made pass rushers earn every inch and treated the protection of their quarterback as a personal obligation. Few men embodied that attitude more aggressively—or more controversially—than Conrad Dobler, the three-time Pro Bowl guard whom Sports Illustrated labeled “Pro Football's Dirtiest Player” in 1977.
Dobler was accused of biting, kicking and other acts that have no legitimate place in football. Yet reducing him to those incidents overlooks his ability. Alongside Hall of Fame tackle Dan Dierdorf, he helped anchor the St. Louis Cardinals' remarkably effective pass protection during the 1970s. His legacy raises an uncomfortable question for today's defending Super Bowl champions: Do the Seattle Seahawks need some of Dobler's uncompromising mentality, even if they should want none of his methods?

EXHIBIT ONE — A CHAMPIONSHIP LINE UNDER PRESSURE

Seattle's offensive line helped make the 2025 championship possible. After allowing 54 sacks in 2024, the Seahawks cut that total to 27 the following regular season. Their rushing attack improved from 28th to 10th in total yards, while the offense became more balanced and the quarterback less vulnerable to relentless pressure. Offensive line coach John Benton deserved credit for producing a unit that was more coordinated, reliable and capable of winning demanding matchups.

Six games into the 2026 season, however, the protection picture has changed. Seattle lost 32–29 to San Francisco on October 11 and 17–14 in overtime to Denver on October 15. Sam Darnold was sacked five times in each game. Through six contests, Seattle's quarterbacks had been sacked 16 times, a pace approaching 45 over 17 games. A projection is not destiny, but the contrast with the championship season is difficult to ignore.

Against Denver, the Seahawks ran 82 plays and gained 353 net yards, yet scored only three points through three quarters. Repeated disruption interfered with their rhythm, while turnovers compounded the damage. Mike Macdonald acknowledged that Darnold was being hit too often, without pretending that all ten sacks across those two losses belonged exclusively to his offensive linemen. He was right. The quarterback, backs, tight ends, receivers, protection calls and offensive design all play a part. But when the pocket repeatedly breaks down, the men up front cannot escape scrutiny.

EXHIBIT TWO — WHAT MADE DOBLER FORMIDABLE?

Dobler played for St. Louis, New Orleans and Buffalo between 1972 and 1981. He earned three consecutive Pro Bowl selections from 1975 through 1977. During his Cardinals years, the offense allowed only eight sacks in 1975 and 40 across the 1975–77 seasons. Those figures speak to the effectiveness of an outstanding line, though they cannot establish how much credit belongs to Dobler rather than Dierdorf, the other blockers, Don Coryell's offense or the quarterback's decisions.

What separated Dobler in the public imagination was his apparent determination to make every encounter miserable for the defender across from him. Opponents knew his reputation before the first snap. That could confer a psychological advantage, but its precise effect is impossible to measure, and it does not excuse his misconduct. The useful lesson is not that Seattle should recruit someone willing to hurt an opponent. It is that a gifted blocker who competes with relentless intensity can help establish a standard that teammates recognize and opponents must respect.

The distinction is essential. Intimidation achieved by illegal contact invites penalties, discipline and retaliation. Intimidation achieved through superior leverage, relentless effort and repeated successful blocks can change the course of a game without a flag being thrown. Seattle needs the second kind.

EXHIBIT THREE — AN OFFENSIVE LINE NEEDS AN IDENTITY

The Seahawks have talent. Charles Cross and Abraham Lucas give them established tackles. Grey Zabel showed considerable promise as a rookie. Jalen Sundell handles the communication demands at center, while Anthony Bradford brings size and power to the interior. These players contributed to a championship. There is no evidentiary basis for accusing them of cowardice or questioning their willingness to compete because the offense has struggled for two weeks.

But collective identity is a different matter. The Raiders' lines of the 1970s, featuring Art Shell and Gene Upshaw, were remembered for more than their individual credentials. Washington's Hogs became the foundation of a bruising attack that helped Joe Gibbs win three Super Bowls. They imposed a standard through coordinated execution, physical control and the ability to perform when an opponent knew what was coming. The Seahawks do not need to copy either group's personnel or era to understand the principle.

Seattle's championship defense has already demonstrated what a coherent identity can accomplish. Macdonald's defenders communicate, disguise intentions, respond to adjustments and challenge opposing offenses on their terms. The offensive line should aspire to comparable consistency. A defender ought to anticipate four quarters of difficult work against Seattle, not because someone might take a cheap shot, but because cleanly defeating these blockers will be exhausting.

That sort of reputation cannot be declared at a press conference. It is earned on third-and-short, against a difficult stunt, after surrendering an early sack and in the fourth quarter when the defense knows a run is coming. The test is whether five linemen can continue winning together once an opponent has discovered their weaknesses.

EXHIBIT FOUR — AGGRESSION CANNOT REPLACE EXECUTION

The Denver loss illustrated why a Dobler comparison must be handled carefully. Reported protection confusion involving Lucas and running back George Holani created problems that no display of aggression could repair. If two players misunderstand who is responsible for a rusher, the solution is improved identification, communication and coordination. A missed assignment does not become acceptable because the blocker plays angrily on the following snap.

Darnold bears responsibility too. A quarterback can invite pressure by holding the ball, misreading coverage or failing to recognize a blitz. His interceptions against Denver cannot automatically be charged to the offensive line. Nor can an inconsistent rushing attack be explained entirely by a lack of brute force. Play design, defensive fronts, timing and execution must all be examined. The change from Klint Kubiak to Brian Fleury at offensive coordinator adds another variable to an offense attempting to defend its title.

Still, the physical confrontation begins up front. Linemen must recognize twists, recover when beaten initially, establish a firm pocket and move defenders in the running game. When opponents repeatedly penetrate, defensive coordinators grow more willing to attack, play-callers become more cautious and the quarterback starts operating under pressure before he has completed his reads. The offense gradually begins responding to the defense rather than forcing the defense to respond to it.

A modern-day enforcer cannot correct a blown assignment by glaring at someone. He can, however, lead by refusing to repeat mistakes, demanding sharper preparation and setting a physical standard that survives a difficult afternoon. That is the version of Dobler's mentality worth considering.

EXHIBIT FIVE — WHO WILL PROTECT DARNOLD?

Darnold's work is demanding enough without requiring him to become his own bodyguard. He must identify coverages, adjust protections, anticipate openings and deliver accurate throws while defenders attack the pocket. Some hits are unavoidable, and no offensive line can promise an untouched quarterback. But ten sacks in consecutive defeats should command the attention of everyone responsible for the offense.

Protection failures carry consequences beyond lost yardage. They can shorten progressions, disrupt routes, compromise play-action, alter play-calling and increase the temptation to force throws. None of those possibilities excuses Darnold's mistakes. They explain why quarterback performance cannot be evaluated independently of the environment in which he operates. Blaming every interception on the passer is as careless as blaming every sack on the offensive line.

Who supplies the leadership? Bradford has the physical tools to set a tone inside. Lucas offers experience against dangerous edge rushers. Zabel could grow into a commanding presence as he gains experience. Cross can establish authority through steady performance, while Sundell occupies the position where much of the unit's coordination begins. Seattle may not need to acquire a new personality. The necessary leadership might already be in the room.

John Schneider should not mistake an aggressive reputation for a sound personnel decision. A lineman who blocks poorly and draws personal fouls is not an upgrade simply because opponents dislike him. Technique, availability, intelligence and competitive resilience must come first. If Seattle adds someone, the objective should be better football, not better theater.

EXHIBIT SIX — THE CASE AGAINST THE PREMISE

There is an obvious objection to this entire investigation: Seattle won the Super Bowl with substantially the same line, and without anyone resembling Conrad Dobler. That fact cannot be brushed aside. The 2025 improvement shows that coaching, coordination, talent and disciplined execution can deliver a championship without a notorious enforcer. Two poor performances do not establish that the Seahawks suddenly lack toughness or character.

History makes the same point. Dobler was not the Cardinals' entire offensive line; he played alongside excellent teammates in a productive system. The eight-sack season cannot be assigned to intimidation by itself. Today's rules also make an imitation of his misconduct both unacceptable and strategically foolish. A player who turns anger into penalties can sabotage the very quarterback he claims to protect.

The strongest conclusion, therefore, is narrower than the headline might suggest. Seattle has demonstrated protection problems, not a proven shortage of courage. What the Dobler example contributes is a reminder that pass protection is both a technical responsibility and a collective commitment. Physical dominance becomes meaningful when it is consistent, controlled and backed by excellent execution.

THE VERDICT — DOBLER'S COMPETITIVE STANDARD, NOT HIS DIRTY PLAY

Seattle does not need a guard who bites, kicks, punches after the whistle or invites unnecessary penalties. It needs five offensive linemen determined to make every legitimate block count and to correct every avoidable mistake. Benton must restore the communication and fundamentals that cut the sack total in half. Fleury must help put his blockers and quarterback in advantageous situations. Darnold must deliver the ball on time and protect possession. Macdonald must ensure that those responsibilities operate as one system.

But technique without determination can be overwhelmed, just as determination without technique can be exploited. Dobler's enduring lesson is that protecting the quarterback should never become a passive assignment. It should be a shared competitive obligation, approached with the expectation that the men in the opposite jerseys will have to fight for everything they gain.

The Seahawks have already shown that they possess championship ability. Now, after successive five-sack games, they must demonstrate that they can recover their standard against opponents determined to take it away. They do not need the NFL's dirtiest offensive lineman. They need an offensive line that opponents cannot push around—and one that wins its arguments between the whistles.

text:
Tesla Q3 2026 earnings call / Q&A webcast (Oct 21) - HIghlights, Elon’s words, and My Take

I was listening to the Tesla Q3 2026 earnings call while riding in a Model Y on Full Self-Driving, heading to the UT Austin campus for a podcast recording. There is no real competitor to Tesla when it comes to FSD. Demand is so strong that Tesla is having a hard time keeping up with production, and Robotaxis (Ys and including Cybercabs) are already running all over Austin.

A few key facts from the call:

- Demand is exceeding production, with FSD as the main driver and no real competitor.
- Robotaxi and Cybercab growth in Austin is exponential (nearly 2 million unsupervised miles, fleet scaling rapidly).
- Optimus is in early production; the S-curve is real (bumpy and slower at the start), with the AI, hands, reliability, and external deliveries expected around the end of next year—and no one is close.
- Energy/Megapacks are essentially sold out into 2027.
Semi is now in volume production, and Tesla is aiming for roughly 5 million vehicles a year by ~2030.
- Terafab is progressing (first test chip targeted for mid-next year, volume around Q3 2028); Elon also reiterated that Tesla could eventually do a majority of passenger miles in places where it is allowed to operate freely.

Elon spoke about demand, FSD, and the shift to growth,

“The third quarter was very strong… Demand is growing rapidly for our vehicles. It’s exceeding our production by a significant margin. And obviously, we’re going to be ramping, and we are ramping production meaningfully. The biggest driver for demand is Full Self-Driving. And today, there’s really no competitor for FSD in any car that you can buy… We’re now approved in many countries in Europe, and we’re hoping for an EU-wide approval. It’s hard to predict, but maybe within a few months, but I would be surprised if it takes longer than Q1… So in a nutshell, after many years of sort of grind and things being fairly flat, I think we’re now headed for a lot of fun and significant growth.”

With Robotaxi exponential scaling, Elon spoke of Austin,

“Regarding Robotaxi, we’re seeing the Robotaxi miles driven, or fully autonomous miles driven, scale exponentially… It really is an extremely fast week-over-week growth in autonomous miles, and I don’t think there’s any company in the world that can match our scale with autonomous vehicles as we continue to ramp. The Cybercab fleet in Austin, for example, has grown by a factor of 10 since launch about a month ago. And the cumulative mileage, when I look at the weekly chart, it’s, wow. I mean, it looks like a rocket going to orbit, basically. It’s growing very fast. If you want to try it out, come to Austin, and you’ll see Cybercabs in use at scale.”

Elon was realistic about Optimus realities and timelines,

“Regarding Optimus, we’ve started what I’d call early production on a high-volume line in Fremont… The growth of Optimus is an S-curve, but the initial part of the S-curve has a shallow slope and is somewhat bumpy because it is such a radically new product. The way to think about it is there’s like 10,000 things that have to go right for production of the robot, and it’ll move as fast as the slowest, least likely of the 10,000… I would expect that the AI, the electromechanical design, the reliability, and the usage life of the robot… these issues to be solved around the end of next year. So that’s the time to expect when we’re delivering Optimus to companies outside of Tesla. And I remain convinced that Optimus will be the biggest product on Earth… But to the best of my knowledge, there is no one that is even close to Tesla with respect to a general-purpose humanoid robot.”

On Optimus training, Elon was realistic,

“Crowdsourcing is not the issue for Optimus. There’s a lot of things we have to get right about the AI architecture that we’re still working on… In order for Optimus to get the training data we need, we actually need to make a lot of Optimi. So we need to make, I think, on the order of 10,000 or 20,000 bots and then have them do self-play… We actually need Optimus to play at scale in order to have it be really good at tasks in the real world… I think we may be ready to release an Optimus video in a month or so. I want to make sure that when we release this video, it’s not a canned demo… It’s Optimus doing things that are not pre-programmed.”

Elon’s comments about Cybercab ownership were expected

“Cybercab is primarily going to be something that is offered as transport as a service, whereas our other cars would be more the cars that you’d want to own, like the 3 and the Y and whatnot, and Roadster, obviously. But the vast majority of the Cybercab stuff will be essentially Tesla-owned and transport as a service.”

Elon explained Terafab, and the great value it will have to humanity.

“Regarding the Terafab, the Austin-based research lab is progressing quickly. We’ll begin commissioning machinery in the first half of next year. And hopefully, if things go well, we’ll make our first test chip… around May or June… And then our aspiration is to be making some kind of useful chip at volume around Q3 of 2028… The Terafab, I think, will be the most valuable building in the world and will probably have an economic value that will place it in the top 20 of countries.”

My Take
I saw Tesla training Optimus firsthand at a recent public event in Austin, and it was eye-opening. You can see Optimus training to be a ticket-taker for hundreds of people! There is a very serious push happening through parallel components that are working simultaneously but separately, and they will soon come together. 
In response to a question from Colin Rusch (Oppenheimer), Elon said: “So we’re doing all these things in parallel: this giant production line at our Fremont factory, a massive supply chain, and then fine-tuning the design and engineering simultaneously with the AI software. So all these things are happening simultaneously, and we’re going as fast as humanly possible here.” 
This does not shock me. Elon has been running multiple companies in parallel for years, so it is in his nature to build humanoid robots the same way.

Sources: EVwire full transcript; official Tesla webcast replay.

 Elon Musk — The Receipts Behind the Headline        By Rosalinda Baby Manuskript™

Documentaries, headlines, and talking points keep saying the same things: “He just bought the company.” “He’s not an inventor.” “He’s no genius.” “It’s all hype.”

Insults are easy. Receipts are harder to argue with. So here they are, year by year: what they said, and what actually happened.

“Test all things; hold fast what is good.” — 1 Thessalonians 5:21

📅 2004 — Tesla
 They said: “He just bought the company and called himself a founder.”
 What happened: Tesla was started in July 2003 by Martin Eberhard and Marc Tarpenning. In early 2004, before Tesla had a factory or a car, Elon put in about $6.5 million and led its first big funding round. In 2009, a legal settlement officially named five co-founders, and Elon is one of them.

📅 2019 — Starship’s Steel
 They said: “SpaceX just copies NASA. Elon is only the face.”

 What happened: Elon decided to build Starship from stainless steel rather than expensive carbon fiber. He has explained why in public: steel is cheaper, it gets stronger when super-cold, and it handles the heat of coming back from space.

📅 2021 — Self-Driving with Cameras
 They said: “Self-driving needs expensive laser sensors. Cameras alone will never work.”

 What happened: Elon pushed Tesla to drive with cameras only, the way human eyes do, and Tesla removed radar from its cars. Former Tesla AI chief Andrej Karpathy has described this shift on the record. It’s still a work in progress, and Tesla keeps expanding where its cars can drive without anyone at the wheel.

📅 September 2024 — The Colossus Supercomputer
 They said: “Building an AI supercomputer takes years.”

 What happened: xAI built Colossus in Memphis in 122 days, starting with 100,000 AI chips. To power it before the permanent grid connection was ready, it relied on gas turbines and batteries, prompting environmental reviews and community debate. That’s part of the record too.

📅 October 2024 — Catching a Rocket
 They said: “Catching a rocket with a tower? Science fiction.”

 What happened: On October 13, 2024, on Starship’s fifth test flight, the launch tower’s giant arms caught the Super Heavy booster, about 232 feet tall, as it came back down. It happened live on camera.

📅 2024 → 2026 — The Cybercab
 They said: “A car with no steering wheel is just a stage prop.”

 What happened: Tesla showed the Cybertruck in October 2024, began building it in 2026, and since September 2026 has been offering paid rides in Austin, Texas.

📅 September–October 2026 — The “Musk” Documentary
 They said: The film presents a former partner as a key witness. At its Venice premiere, she said she turned down a $40 million offer to stay silent.
 
What happened: Elon answered twice, on the record.
September 9: He said she was never offered that and has a history of making false claims.

October 11: He said she was not his girlfriend and they had only seen each other a few times.

No contract has been shown. A claim about a contract isn’t documentary proof. It’s a contractual claim, and contracts leave a paper trail.

 Produce the contract. A claim is not a receipt.

📅 2017 → 2026 — The Flying Roadster (RDSTAR)
 They said: “A flying car? Pure vaporware.”

 What happened: Elon first talked about a rocket-thruster Roadster in 2017. On October 15, 2026, at SpaceX’s site in McGregor, Texas, the new Roadster used 10 air thrusters to jump over five other Teslas. Production is planned for 2028.

The Bottom Line
Money and publicity can’t catch a rocket, fly a car, or put driverless cabs on real roads. That takes big decisions at the top and thousands of engineers doing the work. Elon makes the big calls, and his teams build them. Both are part of the receipts.

Narratives get thrown. Receipts come back.

Super Intelligence is the tool, not the master. It is only ever as wise, as safe, and as capable as the Handler at the controls.

 AI is only as good as its Handler.

text:
On #OTD October 22nd 1911, Cal Rodgers flew from Kyle, Texas, taking off at 10:50 in the morning and landing in San Antonio at 12:40 — 49 miles in 50minutes. What makes that day vivid isn’t the flight itself, it’s what the towns along the way did. In New Braunfels, at the Gruene store and saloon, the owner Ernst Gruene had telegraphed ahead and invited his customers up onto the mercantile roof with their drinks to greet the birdman. When the plane came over, men fired six-shooters into the air, kids cried, and the bartender launched a giant sky rocket that arched in front of the Vin Fiz and burst red. Rodgers saw it and deliberately wobbled his wings back at them. A teenager named Oscar Haas watched from downtown with borrowed binoculars and described the plane as a long framework with two white wings, the pilot sitting out on the edge of the lower wing working two levers, feet on rudder pedals, a broad leather strap around his waist holding him in.
In San Antonio itself, about 10k  people packed Fort Sam Houston’s polo grounds. When the Vin Fiz rolled to a stop on the grass, the crowd surged forward pawing and rocking the airplane, souvenir hunters already at work. Rodgers was shivering from the freezing air at altitude, so they took him to the Officers Club and offered him a drink. He turned it down and asked for milk instead. He was a teetotaler. #Texas #vinfiz #calrodgers #pioneer https://t.co/CjOOYBjSlG

Texas just said “YES” to Tesla's $10.1 billion solar factory ☀️

Fort Bend County commissioners near Houston approved every Tesla agreement on the table this afternoon. All four passed 4-0, with one abstention. That covers the property tax abatement, an economic development deal, and two payment-in-lieu-of-taxes agreements for "Project Crystal Sun," a planned plant that would make solar cells and full solar modules on about 3,000 acres.

Tesla's state filing projects 9,712 permanent jobs by 2033, with production starting in early 2029 if this site wins.

Tesla is clearly treating solar as one of its core businesses, not a side project. Bringing cell manufacturing back to the US at this size would be a big deal for energy independence. The state still has to sign off, and Tesla is still looking at sites in other states, but Texas is making a strong offer.

Sagat Singh was born in Kusumdesar Village in the Churu region of the Bikaner Kingdom on 14 July 1919 to Brijlal Singh Rathore (a soldier in the Bikaner King’s army) and his wife Jadao Kanwar.   In 1938, after his Intermediate exam, Sagat Singh was enrolled as a Naik in the Bikaner State Forces.  
When World War II broke out, he received a commission as a Second Lieutenant from the King of Bikaner.  In 1949, he was absorbed in the Indian Army with the 3 Gorkha Rifles Regiment.

In 1961, Sagat Singh was promoted to the rank of Brigadier and was given the command of India’s Paratroopers -  50 Parachute Brigade. ‘Operation Vijay’, for the liberation of Goa from the Portuguese commenced on 17 December, 1961. Although, 50 Parachute Brigade was given a secondary role in the original operational plan, the rapid advance and initiative under the dynamic leadership of Brigadier Sagat Singh from Belgaum towards Goa, made it the first to reach Panjim, the capital of Goa.    On the morning of 19 December 1961, Panjim fell to the forces of 50 Para Brigade under Brigadier Sagat Singh.

The Portuguese Governor General and Commander – in – Chief, Major General Vassalo De’ Silva fled to Marmagao, but surrendered later.    
At 11 am on19 December 1961, the Indian Tricolour was hoisted on the Secretariat Building at Panjim, by Brigadier Sagat Singh’s forces.   

In 1965, China issued an ultimatum to India to vacate the border outposts of Nathu la and Jelep La in Sikkim, which belonged to India.  Lt. Gen. Manekshaw was the Eastern Army Commander and Lt. Gen. J S Aurora was the Corps Commander of 33 Corps, responsible for Sikkim.  Major General Sagat Singh was the General Officer Commanding (GOC) of 17 Mountain Division which controlled Nathu La.    

Orders to 17 and 27 Divisions were that in case of hostilities they were to vacate outposts and fall back to the main defences. Sagat Singh, however, refused to pull back.  The GOC of 27 Division (deployed East of 17 Div.) pulled back from Jelep La and to this day, this vital pass leading to the Chumbi Valley is still with the Chinese. During August – September 1967, the Chinese tried their best to make Indians withdraw from Nathu La, but General Sagat Singh made his forces hold on, though as per orders, he could have vacated this outpost. During this engagement, both sides suffered casualties, but Nathu La in 1967 gave a bloody nose to the Chinese under General Sagat’s audacious leadership and helped the Nation and the Indian Army, overcome some regrets of the military defeat in 1962.

During his posting in Shillong, the Mizo separatist rebellion under Mizo National Front (MNF) had started and since the area was under his responsibility, General Sagat Singh set into motion the strategy for counter – insurgency operations in Mizoram which quelled the rebellion for sometime.

In December 1970, he was promoted to Lieutenant General and assigned the command of IV Corps. The initial plans for the liberation of Bangladesh did not involve the capture of Dacca. The plan was to liberate areas upto the major rivers surrounding Dacca and thereafter to declare Bangladesh as liberated. The Army Headquarters directive to Eastern Command did not envisage Dacca as the final objective of the campaign in the East.

text:
Ninety years ago, on October 22, a small place called Jiangtaibao (将台堡) in northwestern China witnessed a moment that would change the course of Chinese history.

After enduring countless life-and-death ordeals, the Chinese Red Army joined forces there, bringing the epic Long March (长征) to an end.

It was an astonishing outcome for an army that had once seemed destined for destruction.

These were troops once surrounded by enemies far superior in numbers and firepower. Over those two years, Red Army soldiers had marched some 12,500 kilometers across more than ten provinces, crossed nearly 100 rivers, climbed snow-covered mountains, waded through swampy grasslands, and fought more than 600 battles and engagements (top right).

Nine decades later, Chinese President Xi Jinping commemorated that extraordinary journey in a speech at Beijing's Great Hall of the People (top left).

"The history of the Long March has never faded. The journey continues," he declared.

For those unfamiliar with modern Chinese history, that may sound puzzling. How can a military expedition that ended 90 years ago still matter so much? And why does China's leader believe his country is still on a "new Long March"?

Major Western media outlets gave relatively brief coverage to Xi's speech. Reuters, for example, briefly mentioned on his remarks about economic development and military modernization.

Interestingly, 90 years ago, before American journalist Edgar Snow traveled to northwestern China to interview Mao Zedong and the Red Army, Western media knew surprisingly little about these forces either. Many reports relied heavily on information supplied by the Kuomintang, portraying the Red Army's strategic retreat as a march toward inevitable defeat.

History had other plans.

As a historian and observer of contemporary China, I find this extraordinary reversal of fortune fascinating. How did an army that many believed was doomed to destruction not only survive, but eventually help reshape the destiny of China?

And what is it about that remarkable journey that still resonates with Xi 90 years later?

To find the answers, we need to go back even further-to a time when China itself was struggling for survival.

The story begins in the 19th century. Following the First Opium War of 1840, China suffered repeated military invasions by Western powers and Japan, along with unequal treaties, territorial concessions, enormous indemnities, and a succession of devastating wars.

Just how far did these humiliations go? Consider two examples. In 1860, British and French troops looted Beijing's magnificent Old Summer Palace, taking away countless priceless treasures, before they burned it to the ground. And what happened next? Did Britain have to compensate China for the destruction? Quite the opposite. China paid enormous indemnities instead, plus giving part of the Kowloon Peninsula away to Britain.

Then came Japan, a country that had once faced many of the same pressures from Western powers. In 1894, Japan took a gamble and launched a surprise naval attack on China, destroying China's prized fleet. China was forced to cede Taiwan and pay Japan an enormous indemnity, money that would help fuel Japan's rise as a power to invade China again and again.

For centuries, China had regarded itself as one of the centers of world civilization. But by the late 19th and early 20th centuries, growing numbers of Chinese began to question whether a civilization with thousands of years of history could still find its place in the modern world.

Some sought a better life abroad. Others placed their hopes in reform. Still others concluded that the entire political system had to go.

One of the most prominent among the latter was Sun Yat-sen (孙中山). In 1911, his revolution broke out. The following year, China's last emperor abdicated. The Republic of China, Asia's first republic, was born.

At last, it seemed, a glimmer of dawn had appeared after a long night. But overthrowing an empire was one thing. Building a strong, modern nation was quite another.

Sun and his fellow revolutionaries commanded only limited military forces. When the revolution erupted, much of northern China remained under the imperial control, while the dynasty's most powerful modern army was commanded by a deceitful minister named Yuan Shikai (袁世凯).

The revolutionaries had little assurance of victory if they attempted to unify the country by force. Eventually, the two sides reached a political compromise: Yuan would secure the emperor's abdication, while Sun would step down as provisional president and allow Yuan to succeed him.

Yet the compromise brought China neither genuine democracy nor lasting unity.

Yuan was authoritarian, even audaciously restored the monarchy and crowned himself emperor in 1915.

After his death in 1916, China descended to endless fighting between warlords.

Time and again, Sun Yat-sen tried to organize military campaigns against Yuan and other warlords, but his efforts were repeatedly frustrated by his lack of military strength.

He also looked abroad for help. Sun once spent years living and studying in the United States, so he turned to Washington for support, even writing to the US president. But the assistance he hoped for never came.

The turning point came from an unexpected direction: the Soviet Union. It offered Sun financial, military and organizational assistance. It helped reorganize Sun's Kuomintang (KMT) into a more disciplined and effective political party and supported the establishment of the Whampoa Military Academy (黄埔军校), which trained a new generation of brilliant modern military officers loyal to the revolutionary cause.

As part of this cooperation, Sun paved the way for the united front between CPC and KMT.

In January 1924, the Kuomintang held its First National Congress in Guangzhou (广州), formally establishing this new alliance. Among the delegates was a 31-year-old Mao Zedong, who served as the acting head of the KMT Central Publicity Department.

It is a remarkable twist of history: Mao, who would later lead the Communist Party of China (CPC) to victory over the KMT, once served in the leadership of the very party he would eventually defeat.

The alliance also fueled the rapid growth of the CPC.

When the CPC was founded in 1921, it had just over 50 members. By 1925, that number had grown to around 1,000. By 1927, it had surged to nearly 60,000.

In 1925, Sun Yat-sen died of illness. Having devoted much of his life to the pursuit of China's revolution and modernization, he never lived to witness the military breakthrough his revolutionary movement was about to achieve.

In 1926, the KMT and CPC jointly launched the Northern Expedition from Guangdong in southern China.

This time, the outcome was dramatically different from Sun's earlier failed military campaigns. The revolutionary forces swept northward, defeating one warlord army after another and advancing rapidly into central and eastern China.

The reunification of China seemed within reach. But just as the revolution appeared to be on the verge of triumph, the alliance that had made it possible began to fall apart.

In the spring of 1927, Chiang Kai-shek, a self-proclaimed disciple of Sun and one of the most powerful commanders of the National Revolutionary Army, launched a purge of Communists. Large numbers of CPC members were slaughtered. Chiang soon took over the supreme leadership within KMT.

For the CPC, this was a struggle for its very survival. On August 1, 1927, Communist leaders, together with units of the National Revolutionary Army under their command or influence, launched an armed uprising in Nanchang (南昌), Jiangxi Province. Other uprisings ensued.

Beginning in 1928, the Communist-led forces gradually adopted the name Red Army. Decades later, August 1 would be designated as the founding anniversary of the People's Liberation Army (PLA). But the Communists now faced a fundamental question:

Where could this newly independent revolutionary army go, and more importantly, how could it survive?

In the early stages of their armed struggle, some CPC leaders, influenced by the Soviet revolutionary experience, believed that capturing major cities was essential to achieving nationwide victory.

Yet China was a very different country from Russia. When the Bolsheviks seized power in 1917, Russia was engulfed in World War I, with much of its army fighting at the front.

The overwhelming majority of China's population lived in the countryside, and major cities were firmly controlled by the KMT and other military forces.

The Communists repeatedly attempted armed uprisings in major cities, only to suffer defeat after defeat.

Mao began charting a different course.

If the Red Army was not yet strong enough to capture major cities, why not turn instead to the countryside, where most Chinese people lived and the KMT's military grip was weaker? There, the Communists could establish revolutionary bases, mobilize the peasantry, build up their armed forces and gain the strength to challenge the KMT.

In the autumn of 1927, Mao led the surviving forces of the Autumn Harvest Uprising to the mountains in Jiangxi and Hunan provinces, where he began establishing a rural revolutionary base.

In 1930, Mao wrote "A Single Spark Can Start a Prairie Fire (星星之火可以燎原)", expressing his conviction that a small revolutionary force could grow into a powerful movement.

In 1931, the Provisional Central Government of the Chinese Soviet Republic was established. Mao was elected chairman of both its Central Executive Committee and its Council of People's Commissars.

It was around this time that the title "Chairman Mao", by which he would later become known around the world, began to gain widespread use.

But as the Red Army grew stronger and its revolutionary bases expanded, Chiang Kai-shek became determined to stamp out the movement.

He wanted to extinguish Mao's spark before it could spread into a prairie fire.

Between 1930 and 1934, the KMT launched five major encirclement and suppression campaigns against the Communist-controlled Central Soviet Area.

The KMT enjoyed overwhelming advantages in manpower, weapons and resources.

Yet its first several campaigns failed to crush the Red Army.

During the earlier campaigns, Mao Zedong played a leading role in directing the Red Army's operations. But by the fifth encirclement campaign, the situation had changed dramatically.

Having learned from his earlier failures, Chiang Kai-shek adopted a new strategy: building fortified blockhouses, advancing step by step, and tightening the economic blockade to steadily squeeze the Red Army's territory.

Meanwhile, Mao Zedong had already been stripped of his main military command responsibilities. In 1934, the Red Army suffered devastating losses, and the situation deteriorated. By October, the Red Army could no longer hold its hard-won revolutionary base.

It faced an agonizing decision: Abandon the territory it had spent years building up and set out into the unknown.

Today, we know the Long March as a historic journey with a clear beginning, an ending, and a place in history. But for the soldiers who embarked on it, the road ahead was filled with uncertainty.

They had to evade enemy forces that vastly outnumbered them while battling hunger, disease, raging rivers, snow-covered mountains and swampy grasslands (bottom left). It was at this desperate moment that Mao Zedong's previously sidelined military ideas began to regain influence. He gradually assumed the leading role in military strategy and in the party again.

As the Red Army struggled to survive, Mao's once-dismissed military ideas began to gain ground. He gradually emerged as the dominant figure in the Party's military leadership.

Against extraordinary odds, the Red Army eventually reached northwestern China, where it found a new foothold.

Why does the Long March hold such special significance for Xi Jinping? Beyond its importance in the history of the CPC, there is a personal connection that many observers may not be fully aware of.

Xi's own family history and formative years are deeply intertwined with northwestern China.

In the 1930s, Xi's father, Xi Zhongxun (习仲勋), together with fellow Communists such as Liu Zhidan (刘志丹), helped establish and expand a revolutionary base along the border between Shaanxi and Gansu provinces.

Its existence played a crucial role in the Central Red Army's decision to establish a new foothold in northern Shaanxi, when the exhausted army finally reached northwestern China after its grueling journey.

In the years that followed, the Communist Party made Yan'an its main center of leadership, rebuilding its strength, promoting a united front against Japanese aggression, and taking part in China's resistance against Japan.

After WWII, the Communists emerged from this northwestern stronghold and, following several years of civil war, established the People's Republic of China in 1949.

Decades later, Xi Jinping's own political journey would also begin in northern Shaanxi. In 1969, not yet 16 years old, Xi left Beijing for a rural village in Yan'an. He spent the next seven years living and working alongside local farmers.

It was in that village that he joined the Communist Party, became the village Party secretary, and developed his understanding of rural life, grassroots society and public service.

For Xi, therefore, Yan'an and northern Shaanxi are more than historic places associated with the Chinese revolution. They are also places that profoundly shaped his own life and political outlook.

As a young man, Xi developed a keen interest in the history of the Long March.

According to the wife of writer Wang Yuanjian, who had interviewed numerous Red Army veterans and devoted much of his work to telling their stories, Xi would carefully take out a notebook and jot down notes whenever Wang recounted their experiences during their conversations in the 1980s.

In the years that followed, both as a provincial official and later as China's top leader, Xi repeatedly visited historic sites along the Long March route.

For Xi, the Long March is far more than a military expedition to be commemorated. It also offers enduring lessons about confronting crises, finding the right path forward, mobilizing the people, and remaining committed to long-term goals.

In the 1930s, the CPC faced a fundamental question: how could it survive military encirclement and a deepening political crisis?

Today, China faces a very different set of challenges. How can a country of more than 1.4 billion people achieve modernization on such an unprecedented scale?

How can it ensure that the benefits of development are shared more widely, rather than concentrated in a handful of regions or among a privileged few?

How can it achieve technological breakthroughs amid intensifying global competition?

How can it continue to grow economically while protecting and restoring the environment?

And how can it stay the course toward its long-term goals amid geopolitical upheaval and growing external pressures?

None of these challenges can be overcome overnight.

As Xi once put it:
"The Long March of our generation is to achieve the Two Centenary Goals and realize the Chinese Dream of national rejuvenation."

In Xi's vision, Chinese modernization means common prosperity for all, cultural and intellectual advancement, harmony between humanity and nature, and national rejuvenation through peaceful development (bottom right).

Since 2012, China has achieved its goal of lifting nearly 100 million rural residents out of extreme poverty, while continuing to invest in infrastructure, industrial upgrading, technological innovation and the transition to greener development.

From electric vehicles and robotics to artificial intelligence and space technology, China is seeking to position itself at the forefront of a new wave of technological change. But these achievements do not mean that China's modernization is complete.

An aging population, regional disparities, technological bottlenecks, foreign trade restrictions and an increasingly complex international security environment all pose long-term challenges.

Xi has often drawn on the imagery of the Long March to describe the difficulties China still faces:
"There are still many 'snowy mountains' and 'grasslands' for us to cross."

Of course, history is not a straight road leading inevitably to victory.

Every major decision during the Long March involved enormous risks, and countless soldiers never lived to see its end. China's subsequent development has also involved setbacks, mistakes, costs and adjustments.

Ninety years ago, the Long March confronted one fundamental question:
How could the Chinese revolution survive and move forward when almost every road seemed blocked?

Ninety years later, Xi's vision of a "new Long March" seeks to answer another:
How can a nation of more than 1.4 billion people chart its own path toward modernization in a world of profound uncertainty and change?

The era has changed. The mission has changed. But for Xi, one spirit remains worth passing down from generation to generation: The determination to hold fast to one's convictions, find a way forward, and keep going, no matter how daunting the obstacles.

And perhaps that is what makes his words on the 90th anniversary of the Long March's victory especially worth reflecting on:

"The history of the Long March has never faded. The journey continues."

EVENING NEWS:
A legend of the day gone by

On October 22, 1929, the future great goalkeeper Lev Yashin was born. His widow, Valentina Timofeevna, shortly before her own passing, told the magazine "Rodina" what kind of person he was.

- In the autumn of 1941, the aircraft factory where his father worked was moved from Moscow to Ulyanovsk. 12-year-old Lev also went to work at the machines. Later, he recounted: he didn't have the strength to leave the workshop, he slept in a box for ammunition.

Ivan Petrovich was afraid that his son would fall asleep at the machine from exhaustion and get injured. When Lev started to doze off again, his father himself offered him a cigarette. The strong tobacco brought tears to his eyes, and sleep receded for a while. And that's how his attachment to smoking began. For life...

- Lev's first award was the medal "For Valiant Labor in the Great Patriotic War." He was very proud of it.

- We first met at the dance floor near the "Salut" factory. Some acquaintances pointed him out: "That's Lev, he plays for the Dynamo reserve team." I remember that Lev came to the dance in army rubber boots.

- Sometimes I was annoyed by his willingness to help anyone who asked. He would rush to help, rescue, or lend something, even before they had a chance to ask. You should have seen how many gifts he brought from abroad! I would ask: "Did you buy anything for yourself?" And he would reply: "I have everything I need."

- A real tragedy happened when "Dynamo" went to play against their counterparts from Tbilisi. Our team was leading 4-0, but before halftime, the Georgians scored four goals against Lev. Later, the guys told me that he was the last one to return to the locker room, sat down on a bench, and cried.

- At the 1958 World Cup, in the game against England, he suffered a severe cut under his chin. Knockout! The doctors stitched up the wound. But substitutions were not allowed. They somehow brought my husband to his senses, and he returned to the field. Tolya Il'in scored the winning goal, and we reached the quarter-finals. Everyone was hugging, but Lev sat down on the grass and asked: "What's the score? Who won?"

Today, a sick Russia is praising the young forward who has gone to Turkey and scored two goals for "Galatasaray." Heroes are not made...

Podcast Summary | The Diary Of A CEO with Steven Bartlett: President Zelenskyy: Peace Is A Huge Compromise, The Horrific Atrocities Of Russian War Crimes!

Overview
Volodymyr Zelenskyy presents the war in Ukraine as a conflict that is both deeply personal and profoundly strategic. He traces a direct line from the 2014 occupation of Crimea to the February 24, 2022 invasion, arguing that a failure to push back earlier made the full-scale war possible. At the same time, he resists the idea that peace can be achieved through simple compromise. He describes mass atrocities in Bucha as a threshold that cannot be ignored or easily forgiven, and he frames any ceasefire as a major concession rather than a natural solution. The conversation also covers his family background, his unexpectedly close previous life in comedy and television, and his insistence that Ukraine's resistance changed the war's trajectory.

Key Themes
- Zelenskyy portrays the war as personally consuming, citing sleeplessness, loss of children and soldiers, and an ongoing struggle to hold himself and the country together.
- A full-scale invasion might not have happened if Ukrainian authorities had ordered defenses in 2014, when Russia's "creeping occupation" began.
- The Soviet Union was an empire held together by autocracy and an information vacuum, and Putin, a purely Soviet man, viewed its collapse as the greatest catastrophe of the twentieth century.
- Western warnings about the invasion were extensive and public, yet many European leaders doubted them, and preemptive sanctions and weapons deliveries did not materialize.
- Ukraine's defense of Kyiv depended on mass mobilization, with the army growing from about 200,000 to about 800,000, and on civilians resisting Russian armor.
- The battle for Hostomel airport was pivotal; destroying the runway and retaking the airport prevented a large Russian landing force from seizing the capital.
- Bucha became a defining atrocity, with mass graves, torture, and killings that created lasting hatred and make forgiveness and simple compromise extraordinarily difficult.
- Zelenskyy argues a just peace requires accountability, because without justice the emotional wounds of losing loved ones will not heal and could fuel revenge.
- He frames a ceasefire as the biggest compromise already being made and questions what security guarantees Ukraine would have if it withdrew further.

Detailed Summary
Zelenskyy describes the war as something that consumes him entirely. He says he does not sleep and calls the pain of losing children and soldiers terrifying, something he would not wish on anyone. He acknowledges that people can be shattered inside, especially families who lose loved ones, while describing hope as necessary for survival. His children, he says, keep him strong, and he wants to set an example for them, though he insists he should not hide his pain. He calls himself neither the strongest man in the world nor a perfect person.

He recounts the start of the full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022. He says he did not initially think a full-scale invasion would happen. When Biden called and offered to evacuate him, he was in a bunker built inside his office. His response became a defining line of the war: I need ammunition, not a ride. He emphasizes that he could not abandon the Ukrainian people, and he frames staying in Kyiv as a duty bound to human decency and Ukraine's constitution rather than a special act of bravery.

He describes the scale of the threat. A Russian military convoy 64 kilometers long backed up along a single highway toward Kyiv, and he says defending against 200,000 people was simply impossible. Ukraine's main forces were concentrated in the east facing the strongest Russian and separatist grouping, leaving Kyiv lightly defended when Russia advanced through Belarus. Russia occupied the Chernobyl nuclear plant and the route, blockaded Kyiv, and cut off food, water, and other supplies.

Kyiv's defense, he argues, came down to mass mobilization and volunteer turnout. People volunteered, and the army grew from about 200,000 to about 800,000. Russia lacked enough troops to hold occupied territory and eventually pulled back. He says taking Kyiv would have required roughly 300,000 to 400,000 troops, about twice as many as were deployed. Russian assault units reportedly carried three to ten days of combat rations and parade uniforms, and Zelenskyy confirms parade uniforms were found in Russian military vehicles.

Early war decision-making, he says, was crisis management rather than fear. He worked from a bunker while the area was secured by snipers and special services, communicating with world leaders and organizing rapid logistics for weapons, food, water, and basic systems like card payments in cut-off cities. He slept about fifteen minutes at a time. He made a video call with Europeans pleading for unity and help, and says it worked. About twenty days in, he says, he began to realize the scale of the tragedy. Russia's information campaign claiming he had fled was aimed at demoralizing Ukrainians, and he responded by communicating publicly multiple times a day from Bankova so people and the military could see he had not abandoned them.

He identifies the 2014 occupation of Crimea as the real start of the war, describing it as a creeping occupation and saying Ukraine's mistake was not pushing back when it could have. He argues a full-scale war might not have happened if Ukrainian authorities had given orders to defend the country in 2014. In that context he describes little green men with unclear uniforms, shots fired, Russia denying involvement, and no clear Ukrainian orders to defend the land. He agrees with Trump that if Crimea had not been allowed to fall, there might have been no full-scale war, arguing a response then would have shown Putin there would be consequences.

He explains the war's roots through the Soviet Union, which he describes as an empire held together by autocracy and an information vacuum, a fish tank. Putin, he says, is a purely Soviet man and former KGB officer whose stated goal is reversing what he called the greatest collapse of the twentieth century, the fall of the Soviet Union, and rebuilding the empire. Ukraine was central to the Soviet Union as a forge of talent, with scientists, engineers, universities, rocket manufacturing, and nuclear weapons, so Ukraine moving toward Europe would mean Russia's collapse. He says Putin uses language as a pretext to divide society and justify occupation, starting with Crimea and the Donbas by claiming to protect Russian speakers, which he says was not true. Putin's pre-invasion statement denying Ukrainian statehood is framed as signaling to Russians a return to the Soviet past.

Zelenskyy rejects the idea of easy compromise or forgiveness in response to mass atrocities. He describes visiting Bucha after its liberation and seeing dead bodies, including children, adults, and elderly people, with hands tied and evidence of torture. He cites around 500 people in a mass grave and describes looting of homes and shooting people from military vehicles. He says he brought journalists to Bucha and told them not to touch anything so the world could see the bodies and witnesses. A witness cited, an elderly man who survived the WWII occupation of Bucha, said the fascists did not treat people that way. Zelenskyy describes never before wanting to kill anyone, but after Bucha feeling pure revenge, and says the experience irreversibly changed him and re-evaluated his values.

He also describes a missile strike on a playground where the siren did not help because the strike came within seconds, killing children and adults. He describes a tradition of bringing flowers for adults and toys for children at such tragedy sites. He says there are children in Ukraine who have never known peace and go to bomb shelters every night when alarms sound. He speaks nightly with air defense operators and coordinates needs across regions by text. He describes presenting the Hero of Ukraine award to parents who lost children, some of whom ask for a hug.

The conversation touches on his path to politics, which he frames as a coincidence of societal mood and personal determination rather than a calculated plan. He was born in the Soviet Union when Ukraine was part of it and grew up in an independent Ukraine. He describes his family as ordinary and not well off, and he says he is grateful for education, upbringing, and parental love. His grandfather fought through WWII from start to finish, and several brothers in the family were killed by the Nazis, leaving his grandfather the only surviving brother. Zelenskyy uses this family history to reject Russian claims that Ukraine is fascist, calling the accusation absurd given Ukraine's experience of total occupation in WWII.

As a child he wanted to be a diplomat and a border guard. He studied law but became more interested in media. He became interested in comedy at 17, worked as a scriptwriter and sometimes acted, and got his own company at 26. He won Ukraine's Dancing with the Stars at 28 and later voiced Paddington Bear in Ukrainian. He starred in the satirical series Servant of the People as a history teacher who accidentally becomes president, and he says the idea was ten to twelve years old before it came to fruition. After Crimea's occupation and the Donbas conflict, his business ties with Russia and offices and projects in Belarus and Kazakhstan made him want to drop it all, citing a sense of betrayal by Russia. He registered Servant of the People as a real political party amid government instability, noting the series was very popular and he had prior experience with a political satire project. He says he declined signals to voice another Paddington film after becoming president.

On the war's broader politics, Zelenskyy says Putin's core goal is occupation of Ukraine and that the US president's identity matters less than Putin remaining in power. On whether Trump could have prevented the invasion, he says nobody knows, noting it did not happen under Trump and did happen under Biden, while crediting Trump's friendly relationship with Putin as a possible factor. He disputes Trump's claim that Ukrainian strikes on Russian diesel infrastructure affect US diesel prices, calling the claim totally false and saying Russian diesel export volume is negligible for US prices. He says Ukraine strikes Russian energy infrastructure in retaliation for Russian attacks on Ukraine's energy grid, and that he has asked Trump to broker an energy ceasefire, but Putin refuses.

He says if Trump cannot force Putin to stop the war or agree to an energy truce, the US should provide air defense missiles, and he would not fire at anyone and would protect Ukraine's energy sector. He says the missiles are not requested for free and that Europeans are funding support, and he claims the US has given everything to the Middle East instead. He says Trump could bring Putin to the negotiating table easily and should use toward Putin the kind of rhetoric he uses about Zelenskyy. He says he does not know why Trump does not act, speculating about a possible special relationship or economic deals, and suggests Trump may be concerned about US energy prices ahead of midterms. He says he doubts Russia would use nuclear weapons because it would lose remaining allies, including the US and China, and he describes Putin as tied to his system and likely to remain in power until the end of his life. He says roughly 18 to 19 percent of Ukrainian territory is occupied, and he describes ongoing strikes across the country, including in Lutsk in the west and attacks on Kyiv and Poltava.

He frames a just peace as requiring accountability. The guilty must be punished, or at minimum a credible path to future justice must be shown. Without justice, he argues, the hole in people who lost loved ones will not heal and could fuel revenge and ongoing conflict risk. He says his only dream is to end the war and that justice and moral accountability are essential because the loss people suffered will not heal otherwise. He notes that about 76 percent of Ukrainians would not want an election now. He says his mother calls every day, sometimes many times until he answers, asking how he feels, about the children, and when Putin will end the war. He says his wife Alina would say he has changed a lot, and he describes their relationship as based on love, respect, and mutual interest. His daughter and all Ukrainian children, he says, have grown up during the war, and childhood passed during wartime.

In Acts 15:28/29, James explicitly states to gentile believers that the only parts of the law that they need to follow are as in Act 15:28  For it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us, to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things;
Act 15:29  That ye abstain from meats offered to idols, and from blood, and from things strangled, and from fornication: from which if ye keep yourselves, ye shall do well. Fare ye well”. The entire discussion at that point in time was regarding  Judaizers who were trying to get the gentiles to follow the law. That discussion occurs in a good part of the New Testament. Granted the law had governed much of every aspect of the lives of Jews for some 2000 years, and the sudden change would be hard to handle. But the point was to bring the minds of the slaves in Egypt to the Christ as He is woven throughout the law if they would only ask why do this or that? What could it mean? As Paul says it was a schoolmaster to bring us to Christ. Gal 3:21  Is the law then against the promises of God? God forbid: for if there had been a law given which could have given life, verily righteousness should have been by the law.
Gal 3:22  But the scripture hath concluded all under sin, that the promise by faith of Jesus Christ might be given to them that believe.
Gal 3:23  But before faith came, we were kept under the law, shut up unto the faith which should afterwards be revealed.
Gal 3:24 **Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, **that we might be justified by faith.
Gal 3:25  But after that faith is come, we are no longer under a schoolmaster.
Gal 3:26  For ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus.”

Jas 2:10  For whosoever shall keep the whole law, and yet offend in one point, he is guilty of all.
Jas 2:11  For he that said, Do not commit adultery, said also, Do not kill. Now if thou commit no adultery, yet if thou kill, thou art become a transgressor of the law.
Jas 2:12  So speak ye, and so do, as they that shall be judged by the law of liberty

One of the key points of the law was to demonstrate to His chosen people and teach them that they could not keep it! That they were guilty of sin and could not save themselves by keeping it, by doing some works, that the mediator, the provided son, the lamb would be a sacrifice for their sins in the future.

You point out that God sanctified the seventh day at creation and that sabbath keeping was therefore predating the law. But by that reasoning(as it isn’t mentioned at all until the law is given), then ought not we to offer sacrifices just as Abel did in the garden? It predated the law, and appears to be similar to those prescribed in the law later. Or circumcision, it too predated the law when it was given to Abraham, yet it was done away with in the New Testament as well. 
 
Regarding Col 2:17, Pauls use of the greek word σαββάτων for the sabbath, the Septuagint also uses the same word in the 10 commandments, rendered the same… μνήσθητι τὴν ἡμέραν τῶν σαββάτων ἁγιάζειν αὐτήν 

Apart from this point I am very much in agreement with everything I have seen you post about.
I certainly agree with you that the Roman Kirche was wrong in making Sunday the new holy sabbath. That keeping the sabbath laws and applying them to Sunday was not right. When I was younger I recall culture treating Sunday as if it were the sabbath day, stores closed, no one labored(but we sure did travel!)

text:
Macron’s Absurd Response to France’s Riots

France is facing a crisis of social cohesion, public order, and political credibility. Yet instead of confronting the underlying problems with honesty, Emmanuel Macron has once again offered comments that risk sounding detached from the reality experienced by ordinary French citizens.

When people take to the streets in anger, the first responsibility of a president is to understand why, restore public order, and address legitimate grievances. Dismissing public frustration, shifting blame, or relying on political rhetoric only deepens the divide between the government and the people it claims to represent.

France has long prided itself on liberty, equality, and fraternity. But these ideals lose their meaning when citizens feel that their concerns are ignored, that law and order are applied inconsistently, or that political leaders live in a world far removed from everyday life.

Macron cannot expect public confidence to be restored through clever remarks or carefully crafted speeches. Leadership requires accountability, practical solutions, and the courage to confront uncomfortable realities.

Riots are never a substitute for democratic debate, and violence should not be excused. But neither should political leaders use disorder as an excuse to avoid examining the deeper causes of social unrest.

France needs less presidential grandstanding and more honest leadership. Macron's credibility will ultimately be judged not by what he says about the crisis, but by whether he can address it effectively.

A president who lectures his country while failing to reassure it risks becoming part of the problem rather than the solution.
