text:
We are going through a difficult stage when a range of groups and individuals seem determined to repeat serious errors of judgment going back to the darkest periods of our history.

Recent assertions from some unionist figures have been depressing rather than surprising, but the Westminster speech earlier this week from David Davis, a former British government minister and chair of the Conservative Party, clearly crossed a line into much more alarming territory.

During a debate on the latest contentious Troubles-related legislation, Mr Davis referred to the planned Legacy Commission, saying that he “would rather see the dispassionate actions of the commission rather than the activities of IRA lawyers in the courts”.

He went on to quote the words of an acquaintance who also talked about “IRA lawyers”, claiming they “are more interested in drama than justice”, in the course of a contribution described by the DUP MP Carla Lockhart as “powerful”.

This appalling intervention from Mr Davis inevitably drew comparisons with claims made by another former Conservative minister, Douglas Hogg, when he stood up in the House of Commons in January 1989 and said that certain lawyers were “unduly sympathetic to the IRA”.

The prominent Belfast solicitor Pat Finucane was shot dead by loyalists, plainly facilitated by elements within state forces, in front of his family at their home in the north of the city less than four weeks later, and Rosemary Nelson, the lawyer who represented the nationalist residents of Garvaghy Road in Portadown, was also assassinated by loyalists in equally shocking circumstances in 1999.

Mr Hogg was specifically criticised by the Stevens Inquiry, established by the British government to investigate cases of collusion, and it is verging on the astonishing that Mr Davis chose to go along the same road.
The North Belfast Sinn Féin MP John Finucane, who was eight when he witnessed his father’s murder, and is now also a solicitor, was fully entitled to described the comments as “contemptible”.

In a letter to Mr Davis, he wrote: “Would you dare speak about English solicitors in this way? Or do you believe Irish lawyers deserve less protection, less respect and fewer rights when they dare to challenge the British state?”

The chair of the Bar Council, Denise Kiley KC, and the president of the Law Society, Mark Borland, who are both based in Belfast, also expressed their deep concerns, and spoke trenchantly of the dangers involved in blurring lines between lawyers and their clients.

Mr Davis has a duty to respond without delay, when it must be hoped that he will take the opportunity not only to withdraw his statement but offer a full apology to the Finucane and Nelson families.

text:
Cozy Mysteries Versus Thrillers Compared
#fiction #cozymystery #Dogs
A body may appear in both books, but the feeling you carry into bedtime is very different. In cozy mysteries versus thrillers, the question is not simply whether there is a crime to solve. It is whether you want to follow clues with a cup of tea nearby or turn pages with your heart doing a fast little tap dance.

Both genres celebrate the satisfying click of a puzzle piece falling into place. Both can surprise us, mislead us, and make us suspect the person who seemed nicest at the church bake sale. Their differences lie in the atmosphere, the level of danger, and the kind of company a reader keeps along the way.

## Cozy Mysteries Versus Thrillers: The Essential Difference

A cozy mystery is a whodunit with a welcoming front porch. The crime matters, often deeply, but the story makes room for friendship, humor, community, and the everyday rituals that make a setting feel like home. The amateur sleuth might be a librarian, baker, shop owner, veterinarian, or a sharp-eyed neighbor who knows when someone is acting squirrelly.

A thriller is built to tighten the screws. The danger often feels immediate and personal. A protagonist may be chased, trapped, framed, watched, or racing to stop something terrible before time runs out. Thrillers often ask, “Will they survive?” while cozies more often ask, “Who could have done this, and how on earth did they hide it?”

That does not mean a cozy mystery lacks suspense. A well-placed clue can be as irresistible as the smell of bacon to a determined dog. The suspense simply tends to be gentler. Readers are invited to investigate rather than endure.

## Setting Changes the Whole Reading Experience

Cozy mysteries love a place with personality. A small Florida town, historic district, seaside village, family farm, or close-knit neighborhood gives the mystery a living, breathing backdrop. The reader gets to know the café owner, the eccentric town historian, the grumpy sheriff, and the neighbor with a suspiciously perfect rose garden.

That familiarity raises the stakes in a special way. When a crime disrupts a small community, everyone feels it. The sleuth has relationships to protect and local knowledge to use. A decades-old photograph, a forgotten bit of town history, or a stray comment at a fundraiser may become the clue that changes everything.

Thrillers can certainly have vivid settings, but their locations often increase pressure. Think isolated cabins, storm-battered roads, unfamiliar cities, locked facilities, or houses where every creak sounds like bad news. The setting may feel less like a community to settle into and more like a maze to escape.

Neither approach is better. It depends on what you need from a book. Some nights call for a charming town where the local gossip is nearly as useful as a fingerprint. Other nights, you may want an unfamiliar road, a ticking clock, and the feeling that no one can be trusted.

## The Sleuth Is Often the Biggest Clue

In a cozy, the investigator is commonly an ordinary person with an extraordinary knack for noticing what others miss. They are not usually trained detectives with a tactical team behind them. Their strengths are curiosity, patience, empathy, local connections, and a stubborn refusal to ignore a loose thread.

This is where cozy mysteries can feel especially companionable. The sleuth may be smart, but they are also human. They make dinner, care for family, worry about friends, and occasionally get distracted by a mischievous pet with an opinion about the evidence. Their life continues around the mystery, giving readers both a puzzle and people to root for.

The Doc and Daisy Mysteries bring a playful variation to that tradition. Dr. Sue MacVety has veterinary knowledge and professional instincts, while Daisy offers canine observations, warm-snouted determination, and a point of view that notices the scents, sounds, and behavior humans may miss. Canine forensics add a modern twist without losing the cozy spirit.

Thriller protagonists may also be relatable, but they often operate under harsher conditions. They can be investigators, journalists, attorneys, spies, first responders, or everyday people forced into a nightmare. Their choices may carry life-or-death consequences, and their emotional journey can be intense. That urgency is thrilling for many readers, but it can feel like a lot when the real world has already been noisy enough.

## How Much Darkness Feels Right?

This is often the deciding factor. Cozy mysteries generally keep violence off the page or handled with restraint. A murder has happened, but graphic descriptions are not the point. The story focuses on motive, opportunity, alibis, and the social ripples caused by the crime.

Thrillers may include more explicit violence, psychological menace, danger to children or families, frightening villains, and scenes designed to make readers hold their breath. Some are relatively mild, while others are dark and relentless. The label “thriller” alone does not tell you exactly how intense a book will be.

If you are sensitive to graphic content, a cozy mystery is often a safer choice, though every author handles material differently. If you enjoy high stakes and do not mind a shadowier ride, a thriller can deliver a powerful rush. Reading descriptions and sample pages can help you find the right match for your comfort level.

## Pace: A Pleasant Stroll or a Full Sprint?

Cozies usually move at a steady, clue-driven pace. There may be a body in chapter one, but there is also time to question suspects, compare notes, visit familiar places, and enjoy side threads involving family, food, animals, or town events. The mystery unfolds like a knot being patiently untied.

Thrillers tend to accelerate. Chapters may be short, viewpoints may shift, and each revelation pushes the characters toward a new threat. The book wants you to say, “Just one more chapter,” at midnight, then glance at the clock in disbelief an hour later.

A cozy can still have twists, red herrings, and a dramatic final reveal. A thriller can have tender character moments. The difference is in the dominant rhythm. Cozies offer room to breathe. Thrillers often borrow your breath and return it only at the end.

## What Both Genres Do Beautifully

At their best, cozy mysteries and thrillers honor the same readerly pleasure: order restored through careful attention. Someone notices what others overlook. A secret comes into the light. The truth matters.

Both genres also reward curiosity. Readers get to test their own theories, study suspicious behavior, and decide whether the friendly cousin is truly innocent or simply too eager to offer pie. The pleasure of being fooled fairly is one of the finest treats in mystery fiction.

The best choice may even change from week to week. Reach for a cozy when you want clever company, a sense of place, and a mystery that lets warmth share the page with wrongdoing. Choose a thriller when you want urgency, uncertainty, and a story that keeps the lights on a little later than planned.

There is no rule saying a reader must pick one side of the bookshelf. Follow the mood you have, the comfort you need, and the kind of clues that make your own tail wag. A good mystery should leave you pleased you stayed for the answer.

“All men dream: but not equally. Those who dream by night in the dusty recesses of their minds wake in the day to find that it was vanity: but the dreamers of the day are dangerous men, for they may act their dream with open eyes, to make it possible.”

- T.E. Lawrence

Thomas Edward Lawrence (1888–1935), famously known as Lawrence of Arabia, was a British soldier, archaeologist, and writer whose influence extended far beyond the battlefield. Born in Tremadog, Wales, he grew up in Oxford and developed a passion for history and archaeology. Before World War I, he participated in excavations at Carchemish along the Euphrates River. When war broke out, he became a British intelligence officer and worked closely with Arab forces led by Prince Faisal during the Arab Revolt against the Ottoman Empire. His experiences in the desert would profoundly shape his life and literary legacy.

Lawrence was also an accomplished author, known for his introspective, poetic, and deeply personal writing style. His most celebrated work, Seven Pillars of Wisdom, published in a limited edition in 1926, documented his experiences during the Arab Revolt while exploring the psychological burdens of war. An abridged version, Revolt in the Desert, followed in 1927. He also translated Homer’s Odyssey in 1932, while his memoir The Mint, describing his experiences in the Royal Air Force, was published after his death in 1955. Throughout his writing, Lawrence frequently examined the conflict between personal ideals, political realities, and the struggle to understand one’s identity.

Despite his military achievements and growing international fame, Lawrence remained a complicated and often conflicted figure. His accounts revealed the emotional toll of warfare, the difficult political compromises that followed victory, and his own uncertainty about the role he had played in history. While many admired his strategic brilliance and literary talent, others questioned how much of his legendary reputation was shaped by his own storytelling.

Lawrence’s life ended tragically in 1935 when he died following a motorcycle accident in Dorset, England. Nearly a century later, his legacy continues to inspire debate among historians, military scholars, and readers. He remains both an admired wartime figure and a controversial historical personality whose actions and motivations are still examined.

Ultimately, Lawrence’s story is about more than military victories or personal fame. His writings offer a powerful exploration of ambition, identity, loyalty, and the lasting consequences of war. Through Seven Pillars of Wisdom and his other works, he left behind a deeply human portrait of a man caught between extraordinary historical events and his own internal struggles.

Hello everyone,

I’m Mojeeb.
Reintroducing myself to those who might be coming across my work for the first time.

I’m a product engineer, strategist, and founder of BlindspotLab, an independent product studio behind Arcapush, Revel, Whate, Dearly, and a few other products I’ve built and shipped.

For a long time, I’ve been bootstrapping everything myself.

From building and deploying products to paying for hosting, databases, APIs, and keeping the infrastructure running, most of this journey has been funded out of my own pocket.

And I’m grateful for how far I’ve come.

But I want to be vulnerable for a moment.

I’ve been reaching out to potential clients and businesses, pitching my work through cold emails, introducing what I’ve built, and looking for opportunities to make this journey financially sustainable.

So far, I haven’t received the responses I’ve been hoping for.

I won’t pretend the silence hasn’t been discouraging.

Some days, it gets to me. I’m human, after all.

But I don’t want that silence to break my spirit or stop me from doing what I genuinely love: building things.

Because building a product is one thing. Keeping it alive, reliable, and growing is another.

Take Arcapush, for example.

What started as an idea to make product discovery easier has grown into a platform indexing hundreds of products and helping builders get discovered.

But growth comes with responsibilities.

Some of the free infrastructure I’ve relied on has reached its limits, and there are implementations I’ve been planning to make Arcapush more reliable, scalable, and capable of onboarding more products.

I don’t want to wake up one morning worrying that something has broken simply because I couldn’t afford to keep the infrastructure running.

So, I’ve decided to launch a personal creator token on Robinhood Chain through @ponsdotfamily.

Not because I believe a token will magically solve everything, but because I want to explore another way for people who believe in my work to support what I’m building.

I’ll earn creator fees if the token generates eligible trading activity. Those fees will help support my product infrastructure, continued development, and personal living expenses.

I also hope to give back through community content initiatives, rewards, contests, and a few surprises. I’ll share the details and rules separately.

For transparency, I’ll be buying $10 worth of the token myself during deployment.

I’ll launch using mojeeb.eth, and I’ll share the official contract address once it’s deployed.

This isn’t a promise of financial returns. The token is speculative, and there’s no guarantee of trading activity or creator-fee income.

I’m just a builder trying to find a sustainable way to keep building.

To everyone who’s supported my work, shared my products, offered feedback, or simply encouraged me along the way, thank you.

I don’t take any of it for granted.

And if you’re discovering me today, welcome to my little corner of the internet.

I’m Mojeeb.

I’m still learning. Still building. Still figuring things out.

And I’m not giving up. ❤️

DYOR. NFA.

text:
🇾🇪🇸🇦|Strikes from Yemen Tighten the Noose: Saudi Arabia Holds a Useless Umbrella

Report: Sarah Obeid

October 23, 2026. Riyadh.

For decades, Saudi Arabia has spent hundreds of billions of dollars to purchase an "umbrella" the umbrella of "American protection." Its framework consists of Patriot missile batteries, THAAD systems, the U.S. Fifth Fleet, the CENTCOM chain of command, and a long series of security commitments.

Missiles from Yemen have struck this umbrella and it failed to provide any cover.

💥 Strike One: The Ministry of Defense Building

The Ministry of Defense building in Riyadh was struck directly by a ballistic missile. This was no mere border outpost or peripheral military base; it is the nerve center for Saudi military decision-making the very place where orders to bomb Yemen are issued and target lists are approved.

What kind of umbrella is it that cannot even protect its own Ministry of Defense?

🎯 Strike Two: King Fahd International Airport, Dammam

Dammam, the most critical aviation hub in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province was hit by a ballistic missile from Yemen. The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation confirmed two deaths; the initial report had cited only one. The figure was later revised because the second victim was not discovered immediately.

What kind of umbrella is it that cannot even protect its own international airport?

📜 Strike Three: Aramco Facilities in Yanbu

Yanbu, an oil export terminal on the Red Sea coast and the terminus of the East-West Pipeline serves as Saudi Arabia’s sole route to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. It was struck by a missile from Yemen, sparking a fire.

What kind of umbrella is it that cannot even protect its own oil export terminal?

⚔️ Strike Four: Abha International Airport

Abha, located in southwestern Saudi Arabia near the Yemeni border, was struck directly by a missile from Yemen.

Four targets the Ministry of Defense, Dammam Airport, the Aramco facilities in Yanbu, and Abha Airport encompassing four vital functions: military command, aviation logistics, oil exports, and civil aviation.  In the span of 48 hours, the Yemeni armed forces striking four specific sets of coordinates exposed every single flaw in this "umbrella."

💥 What is the "umbrella" supplier doing?

The United States has withdrawn non-essential government personnel and their families from Saudi Arabia. The U.S. State Department issued an order for such personnel to depart, and U.S. government employees are now required to obtain special authorization to use Saudi airports.

The supplier of the "umbrella" is pulling its people out, while the buyer remains exactly where they were.

The United Kingdom has announced the deployment of Royal Air Force Typhoon fighter jets to Saudi Arabia, ostensibly for the "defensive" protection of Saudi cities and critical infrastructure. British warplanes are now patrolling the very skies that the Saudi air defense system failed to secure.

The umbrella is torn. The supplier has sent a few aircraft to patch it up yet Yemeni missiles continue to fly.

🎯 Why is this umbrella useless?

The U.S. military presence in Saudi Arabia is built on the assumption that Iran is "afraid," afraid of U.S. aircraft carriers, afraid of U.S. sanctions, and afraid of U.S. strikes.

But Saudi Arabia is not facing Iran; it is facing Yemen, a nation that has endured eleven years of bombardment, eleven years of blockade, and the starvation-induced deaths of hundreds of thousands of its people. It is a nation that has brought the war back into the Saudi heartland using domestically manufactured missiles, drones, and naval mines.

A nation that does not fear U.S. aircraft carriers is not going to fear the "umbrella" that the United States has extended over Saudi Arabia.

The umbrella provided to Saudi Arabia was designed for a conventional war: Patriot systems to intercept ballistic missiles, THAAD systems to counter medium-range missiles, and the Fifth Fleet to safeguard maritime shipping lanes.

However, this umbrella was never designed for:

Yemen’s "dive-bombing" drones, locally produced air-defense missiles, oil tankers striking mines after disabling their tracking devices, naval mines in the Strait of Hormuz, the blockade of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait or an adversary that simply does not fear.

📜 Saudi Arabia’s alternative: Another useless umbrella

Saudi Arabia is now searching for alternatives.

Enter Israeli intelligence. Israel is providing intelligence on Yemen to Saudi Arabia, with U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) serving as the coordinating hub.  Following major military setbacks in Yemen, Saudi Arabia urgently requested intelligence assistance from Israel.

Israeli technology: Saudi Arabia’s F-15SA fighter jets are equipped with Israeli-made combat helmets. Elbit Systems and Israel Aerospace Industries have sold advanced weapons systems to the Saudis.

Israeli air defense: Saudi Arabia and Israel coordinate air defense efforts under the auspices of CENTCOM. Israel’s "Arrow" system and the U.S.-made THAAD system have seen operational coordination in the context of the ongoing conflict.

Yet, this "Israeli umbrella" is a useless one. In southern Lebanon, Israeli defenses are breached daily by Hezbollah’s drones; Israel’s northern defensive line is failing. The Israeli economy is buckling under the strain of war, while its Prime Minister campaigns for office even as he faces trial for corruption.

How can an umbrella that cannot even protect its own holder offer protection to anyone else?

⚔️ The Noose in Yemen

A statement from the Yemeni Armed Forces puts it clearly: "A siege for a siege; an escalation for an escalation."

Saudi Arabia has blockaded Yemen’s ports; Yemen has shut down Saudi airports. Saudi Arabia has bombed Yemen’s markets, hospitals, schools, weddings, and funerals; Yemen has struck Saudi Arabia’s Ministry of Defense, airports, and oil facilities.

This is not mere "retaliation"—it is an "equation."

Saudi Arabia spent hundreds of billions of dollars to purchase an "umbrella." Yemen, using domestically manufactured weaponry, has proven that this umbrella is made of nothing but paper.

The noose is tightening. The umbrella is tearing. And yet, Saudi Arabia continues to search for yet another umbrella.

But the next one will be just as useless. The problem does not lie with the umbrella; it lies with the one holding it. A nation that outsources its national security to foreign powers will never find an umbrella capable of truly shielding it from the storm.

Long live Yemen. Long live Ansar Allah. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

text:
State Farm Arena is publicly owned, not private property.

It is owned by the Atlanta Fulton County Recreation Authority (also called the City of Atlanta and Fulton County Recreation Authority), a public corporation and political subdivision of the State of Georgia created by state law in 1960 to acquire, construct, and operate athletic and recreational facilities. The authority holds the title on behalf of the City of Atlanta and Fulton County.

The arena is operated by the Atlanta Hawks (whose ownership group is private), under a lease/operating agreement. Naming rights are held by State Farm (a private company), but that does not confer ownership.

This public-ownership / private-operation structure is common for many major sports venues. For practical day-to-day control of events, entry, and security, the operator (Hawks/arena management) sets the rules, which is why officials in the Enes Freedom incident described the premises in terms similar to a private establishment. Legally, however, the underlying ownership is public.

Public ownership makes a First Amendment claim more plausible than it would be on purely private property, but success is far from automatic.

Key legal points for the Enes Freedom incident:

First Amendment applicability*: The First Amendment restricts *government action. Because State Farm Arena is owned by a public authority (Atlanta Fulton County Recreation Authority), restrictions on entry or speech can potentially be challenged as state action. This is stronger than on fully private property. Atlanta police involvement further strengthens the state-action argument for the physical blocking and denial of entry.

Forum classification: Sports arenas are generally treated as **nonpublic forums (or limited public forums). In these spaces, the government or its agents may impose reasonable restrictions that are viewpoint-neutral. Content-based rules (e.g., limiting certain messages on clothing) can be allowed if they are reasonable given the venue’s purpose (a ticketed sporting event focused on the game, safety, and order). Strict scrutiny does not automatically apply the way it would on a sidewalk or park.

How the facts fit**: Officials cited safety concerns that Freedom himself had raised with authorities and the league. They offered an alternative (a private suite with extra security) rather than a total ban based solely on the “What is a Woman?” shirt. He refused and was then denied entry. A bona fide safety/order rationale plus an offered alternative is a stronger defense for the arena than a pure viewpoint-based exclusion. Whether the safety claim was genuine or pretextual would be a central factual dispute in any lawsuit.

Private operator / team role**: The arena is operated by the Atlanta Hawks (private ownership) and the event was hosted by the Atlanta Dream. Courts do not automatically treat private operators of public venues as state actors; it depends on the degree of government entanglement, joint action, or public function. Outcomes in similar cases vary and are highly fact-specific.

This is similar to Freedom’s pending lawsuit against the Chicago Sky over his August ejection and ban from Wintrust Arena (also publicly owned, by the Metropolitan Pier and Exposition Authority). In that case, the Sky argues the removal was for conduct (approaching the court and gesturing), not the shirt. The same legal gray areas apply here.

In short: Public ownership opens the door to a First Amendment challenge that would not exist on purely private property, especially with police involvement.

text:
DOJ announces $1.8 BILLION healthcare fraud crackdown in California, says rehab clinics drugged patients to keep billing insurers | The Post Millennial

Federal prosecutors announced charges Thursday against 15 defendants, including six medical professionals, in a Los Angeles health care fraud takedown involving more than $1.8 billion in allegedly fraudulent claims. Fraud targeted in the takedown includes a massive addiction treatment operation accused of luring vulnerable Americans with drugs, cash, and free flights, then preventing some from leaving so their insurance could continue to be billed.

The Justice Department described the alleged substance abuse treatment scheme as the largest of its kind it has ever prosecuted, with $1.6 billion being billed. Other cases in the takedown involved unnecessary invasive arterial procedures that allegedly harmed patients, and hospice providers accused of billing Medicare for people who were not terminally ill.

Eight defendants were arrested Thursday, with six expected to appear in federal court in Los Angeles and two in Texas.

“These charges include the largest sober home fraud scheme the Department has ever prosecuted, and a scheme involving unnecessary invasive procedures detected through data analytics,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the DOJ’s National Fraud Enforcement Division. “Our message is simple: if you steal health care dollars from the American taxpayer or abuse your position to harm patients, we are coming for you – and the data will lead us to wherever you are.”

At the center of the addiction treatment case are father and son David Young, 71, and Nathan Young, 39, both of Los Angeles. Prosecutors allege they controlled dozens of purported treatment companies and used patient recruiters, including Honey Phipps, 42, and Cody Phipps, 36, of Greenville, Texas, to bring people to their facilities.

The recruiters allegedly targeted homeless individuals, people living in poverty, and attendees at substance abuse support groups. Prospective patients were offered money, apartments, hotel stays, cars, gift cards, marijuana, cigarettes, illegal drugs, and prescription medications.

Prosecutors say the defendants sought patients whose insurance offered the highest reimbursements and sometimes fraudulently enrolled people in policies for which they were ineligible.

Patients were then allegedly divided according to their insurance coverage. Some with lucrative policies received private apartments, hotel accommodations, and dinners, while others were housed in cramped, unsanitary properties described as “trap houses.”

According to the indictment, the Youngs cycled patients through facilities regardless of whether treatment was necessary or provided. When patients tried to leave, the Youngs allegedly directed staff to medicate them “to knock the client out.”

Prosecutors also allege patients were offered drugs, cut off from family communication, denied access to their belongings, and physically blocked from leaving.

Employees allegedly coached patients to fabricate symptoms, and some patients were encouraged to consume drugs or alcohol to qualify for detoxification. Subsequent “therapy” sometimes consisted of Zoom sessions with more than 100 attendees, during which patients merely had to activate their cameras.

Nicholas Moore, 33, of North Myrtle Beach, South Carolina, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit health care fraud and wire fraud in connection with the operation. Moore, who managed several facilities, admitted helping submit $199 million in fraudulent insurance claims.

A separate indictment charges cardiothoracic surgeon Dr. Harold Tabaie, 78, and chiropractor Hany Malek, 61, with a roughly $135 million scheme involving unnecessary arterial procedures.

Malek allegedly posed as a medical doctor and diagnosed patients with arterial disease. Tabaie then performed atherectomies, procedures using a bladed catheter to remove arterial plaque, on patients who allegedly did not have the disease. Some experienced extreme pain and discomfort. The DOJ said data analysis identified Tabaie as an extreme national outlier in billing for the procedures.

Three hospice cases involved more than $138 million in allegedly fraudulent Medicare claims. Prosecutors say beneficiaries who were not terminally ill were enrolled in hospice, sometimes without their knowledge, while providers billed for unnecessary or nonexistent services.

In one case, Geoffrey Jimenez, 60, allegedly recruited seniors at community centers with offers of free medical services and kickbacks. Some beneficiaries learned they had been placed in hospice only after Medicare or their regular medical providers contacted them.

The announcement also included separate charges against two doctors accused of accepting kickbacks for unnecessary genetic testing and a physician accused of illegally selling prescription drug samples, including Ozempic and Mounjaro.

Additionally, prosecutors announced an indictment against Christina Mareik, 61, who was previously charged by complaint in a separate nearly $270 million Medi-Cal pharmacy fraud case. Authorities allege the scheme generated approximately $269 million in fraudulent claims, of which California’s Medicaid program paid approximately $179 million.

1SG, AWP DAILY ORDER — October 23, 2026
Promise #296 • HIS SPIRIT DWELLS IN YOU

Today’s 365Promises promise: “I have given you My Spirit, so your body could be My temple.” 

“your body is the temple of the Holy Spirit who is in you, whom you have from God”
— 1 Corinthians 6:19, NKJV, excerpt. 

1 — THE ORDER

Honor Christ with the body and life that belong to Him.

Battle Line: I belong to Christ. His Spirit dwells in me. My next action will honor Him.

2 — THE TRAINING

Warrior Doctrine — God’s presence reaches into ordinary life.

Paul gives this teaching within a direct call to flee sexual immorality. Christ purchased you, and His Spirit dwells in you; what you do with your body matters to God. Read 1 Corinthians 6:18–20 for the full context.

This also shapes everyday stewardship: how you speak, what you watch, how you rest, and how you treat the person in front of you. You do not leave God’s presence behind when you leave your place of prayer.

Armor Fit

Helmet of Salvation: Remember whose you are before deciding what to do.
Belt of Truth: Test your impulse against Scripture.
Breastplate of Righteousness: Use your body to serve and turn from sin.
Boots of Peace: Enter each encounter ready to listen and offer care.

Dependence drill: Pause. Remember His presence. Choose obedience.

You can involve Jesus in the smallest decision without becoming afraid of making a mistake. Dependence is a relationship of trust. An ordinary setback does not prove you excluded Him, and a strong feeling does not automatically establish His instruction. Return to Scripture, pray, and take the next faithful step.

Cross-reference training — NKJV

John 14:16–17: The Spirit’s abiding presence.
Romans 12:1: Offer your body to God.
Galatians 5:22–23: Recognize the Spirit’s fruit in your conduct.
Colossians 3:17: Honor Jesus through words and deeds.

3 — THE EXECUTION

Commander’s Orders

Begin with gratitude: “Lord Jesus, I belong to You. Help me honor You today.”
Before one routine decision, pause and consider what agrees with His Word.
Practice bodily stewardship through appropriate rest, nourishment, or stepping away from temptation.
Give one person your full attention. Listen, ask what would help, and offer one practical kindness.
Tonight, identify one obedient response and one area to confess and surrender.

Daily Mission:
I belong to Christ, and I will care for the people He places in my path.

Prayer of Deployment

Father, thank You for giving me Your Holy Spirit through Christ. Teach me to honor You with my body, thoughts, words, and actions. Keep me mindful of Your presence in ordinary moments. Give me discernment through Your Word, strength to turn from sin, and patience to care for others. When I stumble, lead me to confession and renewed obedience. Lord Jesus, govern my next step. Amen.

Iran threatens to strike oil and AI facilities across Gulf if US and Israel renew attacks

Iran’s security chiefs say there will be ‘zero red lines’ if Trump and Netanyahu attack again

Iran will strike oil facilities, undersea cables, datacentres and AI facilities across as many as seven countries in the Gulf in the event of a fresh US-Israeli attack, Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s supreme national security council, has said.

Mehdi Mohammadi, an adviser to Mohammad Ghalibaf, the hardliner who led Iran’s negotiations with the US to end the conflict between the two countries, said Donald Trump and Benjamin Netanyahu had agreed in principle on an attack, but could not guarantee a successful outcome.

He added: “We see the next conflict as an existential threat. The third war in two years means a threat to existence. Our strategy is ‘zero red lines’.”

Mohammadi said: “We break the temporal and spatial dimensions of the conflict. The war will continue longer and in a wider geographical area than the enemy anticipates.”

Iran’s ability to mount such operations, including any unofficial help it receives from China or Russia, will be a key factor in any American decision to restart the war.

Iranian media reported that Rezaei had declared: “In the event of a war, cables, datacentres and artificial intelligence facilities could also be targeted. If the conflict breaks out again, we will have a broader plan.

“There can be no arrangement in which Iran’s economic lifelines come under attack while the economic architecture enabling those attacks is considered untouched and immune.”

According to recent reports in US media, US military advisers have drawn up a detailed list of targets for a fresh joint US-Israel assault on Iran to be implemented after the US midterm elections on 3 November.

Foreign ministers from three European countries, as well as Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Egypt, will meet in Istanbul on Friday to establish agreed policies on the linked Iranian, Yemini and Palestinian crises.

There is alarm that a further war is now the working assumption in Tehran and Washington.

The naval services of Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps (IRGC) claimed to have simultaneously struck four commercial ships seeking to navigate through the strait of Hormuz on Wednesday.

The ships were said to be transferring oil from ship to ship.

The IRGC claimed a further three ships had been struck when they hit mines in the strait.

There was no independent verification that this number of ships were hit, but Brent crude oil was trading at $113.4 a barrel, a recent high, propelled by US reports of the imminent renewed joint Israeli-US assault on Iran.

Trump has backed away from striking Iran again seven times in the past four months. However, a deadlock in diplomatic negotiations has led US government officials to brief about a potential new military campaign that would target missile sites, oil installations and nuclear sites.

The sabre-rattling by both sides has coincided with extended joint-training manoeuvres by the US and Israel, including practice runs over Iraq. Dozens of Israeli planes also flew close to the Iranian border earlier this week, according to the news site Axios.

A big fire at a large aluminium factory in Arak in central Iran suggests sabotage operations may be under way inside the country.

Netanyahu met the US secretary of defence, Pete Hegseth, in Israel on Monday to discuss the timing and purpose of a joint attack, including the possible political implications for Netanyahu’s chances of re-election.

Netanyahu would prefer it if Iran attacked first, he reportedly told Hegseth.

A US military buildup is due to be completed by early November, before a possible newly Democrat-inclined Congress or Senate take their seats in January.

Trump intends to have stationed three aircraft carriers, thousands of marines, fighter jets and special operations forces in the Middle East by November.

Reza Nasri, an international lawyer close to the Iranian foreign ministry, said: “A third wave of war would not stay contained.

Power grids, desalination plants, refineries and ports across the region would burn.

Tens of millions would be left without water or electricity, and a massive wave of refugees would move from Arab countries towards Europe.

“Hormuz would close completely, oil would spike, and the global economy would tip into recession.

Israel’s economy, already bled by mobilisation and missile fire, would not survive a prolonged war of attrition.

And Trump would be trapped in a crisis that consumes the rest of his presidency and leaves a wreck for his successors,” Nasri said.

Fars news agency, which is close to the IRGC, said Iran had issued directives to its various military and operational units “stipulating that in the event of a new widespread war, involving the assassination of Iranian officials and the killing of civilians, the Iranian response will not be limited to military targets, but will also include political targets”.

Mediators from Iran and Pakistan this week again explored familiar if reconfigured options for a ceasefire, including proposals that Iran receive billions in frozen assets in return for lifting its blockade of the strait, allowing UN weapons inspectors to view its bombed nuclear sites and to export its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country.

Iran has offered to end the Hormuz blockade within seven days and start talks on its nuclear file, but only if preconditions are first met, including lifting US sanctions.

Today my second book is published: Everyday Crypto. An Everyday Guide to Cryptocurrency, managing your crypto wealth and protecting yourself and your family.

Crypto has stopped being exotic. A quarter of Americans, and one in twelve British adults, now own some, and most of them bought it on their phone in a few minutes. Nobody told them how to keep it, who really holds it, or what happens to it when they are gone. Everyday Crypto is the plain guide to owning it well.

It answers the questions people ask me most often and rarely get a straight answer to. Is it too late to buy, and how much is a sensible amount? The app says my crypto could be earning, so where does the yield come from? My coins are on an exchange: do I own them, or does it? I bought a hardware wallet, am I safe now? A text from my bank, a call from my son: how do I know it’s real? And the one that started the whole series: what happens to my crypto when I die, and who can my family call?

The book is built from true stories rather than theory. The exchange that failed with the customers’ money inside. The hardware wallet whose faulty dice cost its owners their coins five years later. The text message that opens a months-long con. Each one shows what went wrong, why, and the calm habits that would have stopped it.

Then it changes register. For the holder of real wealth, and for the wealth managers who have spent years forbidden from touching this asset, it sets out custody that survives an audit, the concentrated position, crypto philanthropy, and inheritance that works on the day. The regulators and legislators in Washington and Westminster who are, at last, writing rules that let banks and advisors offer this safely get a chapter of their own, because that is where crypto goes next: into the ordinary bank account.

Five questions run through every chapter: how much, who holds it, in what form, what the tax authority needs, and who inherits it. They are the same questions at fifty dollars a month and at fifty million. Only the zeros change.

It is the second of The Everyday Guides, following Who Holds the Key?, and like that book it assumes nothing beyond the ability to use a phone. You don’t need to become a security expert. But by the time you finish this book, you will know how to protect yourself and your family.

text:
🇦🇱|RAMA THREATENS TO BAN PROTESTING STUDENTS FROM TAKING THE TRAIN. STUDENTS ASK: DOES THIS COUNTRY EVEN HAVE TRAINS?

October twenty three, twenty twenty six, Tirana. Day one hundred forty six of the Flamingo Revolution.

Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama has announced that students participating in the protests will be barred from using the railways.

The issue here is not just whether this infringes upon their rights. It is that the premise itself is false.

Albanias railway system is among the oldest, most dilapidated, and least reliable in Europe. The national network spans roughly four hundred twenty kilometers, mostly built during the communist era, featuring aging infrastructure, obsolete signaling systems, and train speeds that consistently fall below European standards. Many lines have lacked passenger service for years. The route from Tirana to Durres, in theory, exists. In reality, it is a project that has been repeatedly promised, repeatedly delayed, and repeatedly inaugurated with ceremonial ribbon cuttings.

So when Rama threatened to ban students from taking the train, the students response was spot on: Does this country even have trains?

Two Layers to the Threat

The first layer is the threat itself. Faced with student protests entering their one hundred forty sixth day, the Prime Ministers chosen new tool is to deny them access to a public transport service, rather than addressing their demands, increasing education funding, or repairing leaking classrooms. Instead, he opts to strip away their right to travel.

The second layer is the absurdity of the threat. The service he claims to be taking away, for the most part, does not exist. Rama is not punishing the students. He is punishing a phantom railway system.

A government that deploys armored vehicles, stun grenades, and water cannons against students, while also lowering the age of criminal responsibility, can in the end think of no further punishment than to ban them from a transport service that is not even there.

Why the Students Remark Lands Like a Slap in the Face

Does this country even have trains, you—

This remark is not just an insult. It is an act of gathering evidence.

It reframes Ramas threat, shifting it from an exercise of power to a delusion of power. A genuine ruler threatens to take away what you actually possess. A ruler who has lost all legitimacy threatens to take away what you do not even have.

Every threat he issues exposes what is missing in the nation under his rule. By banning students from taking trains, he reveals that there are no trains. By deploying armored vehicles, he reveals that the police cannot control the streets. By lowering the age of criminal responsibility, he reveals his inability to address public demands through policy.

Every punishment is, in effect, a self incriminating confession.

Day One Hundred Forty Six: What Does He Have Left?

Day one hundred forty six. A Prime Minister who has set out empty chairs, placed pillows, written the word dialogue, only to be rebuffed by students three times.

What remains in his arsenal? Police, armored vehicles, surveillance networks, loans from Abu Dhabi, technology from Israel, equipment from Turkey, and the tacit approval of Washington. And of course, a threat to ban the use of trains.

A Prime Minister who commands all these resources finds that his ultimate tool is to prohibit the use of something that does not even exist.

The Mirror

Rama says: I will ban students from taking trains.

The students ask: Does this country even have trains?

Taken together, these two statements offer a complete diagnosis of the current situation in Albania.

A Prime Minister who has consigned the national railway to the last century, handed over the coastline to Kushner, outsourced surveillance to Abu Dhabi, awarded defense contracts to Israeli businessmen, and diverted the education budget toward police and armored vehicles, now threatens to take away the railways.

But the railways do not exist. Just like the European Union membership he promised. Just like the dialogue he pledged. Just like the European future he guaranteed.

Everything he promised is non existent. Everything he threatens to take away is also non existent. The only things that are truly real are the leaking classrooms, the fifteen year old struck by a stun grenade, the Turkish insignia on the armored vehicles, and the people who, on this one hundred forty sixth day, have yet to return home from the streets.

Friedrich #Merz went to 🇲🇪 with a clear message: as far as he is concerned, the era of 🇪🇺-Western #Balkans summits where leaders from the region arrive to complain, that they have already delivered, or that they would deliver if only the EU put a real offer on the table, is over.

As Merz put it: the 🇪🇺 has delivered; now the region must deliver.

He set this against the moment Europe is in: an ever more aggressive and dangerous 🇷🇺 to the east, and shifting Western engagement, including from the 🇺🇸 and other global players. The 🇪🇺 needs this region, and Merz does not want it to become (!) a place of competition, or one the 🇪🇺 loses.

Merz's thinking: since June 2026, when he and #Macron tabled their joint 🇫🇷🇩🇪 paper, both the European Commission and the European Council have moved forward and taken on board their ideas. The result is an offer that works on two levels.

1️⃣ For front-runners like 🇲🇪, a credible path to finalise accession and join, with the door then kept open for the others too, provided they do the reforms.

2️⃣ For all, enhanced gradual integration is on the table: deeper institutional socialisation, integration into 🇪🇺 programmes and projects, and partial access to the single market.

Whether this holds and the 🇪🇺 keeps/regains its foothold in the Western Balkans depends on 4️⃣ sets of questions:

1️⃣ Will Merz's words be taken seriously in the region? The election campaign in 🇷🇸 and the results in 🇧🇦 give little ground for optimism. Key political stakeholders still look to other global centres, from #Moscow and #Beijing to #Washington, as the places where attractive and credible offers come from. In Merz's own words: in key countries of the region Western Balkans have already become a place of competition, and 🇪🇺 is losing.

2️⃣ What really happens with 🇲🇪? Will Merz's words survive a crowded European electoral calendar, from 🇪🇸, 🇫🇷 and 🇵🇱 to 🇩🇪 regional elections next year, as well as 🇭🇷's bilateral interests?

3️⃣ What will happen with the 🇪🇺's internal reforms and the safeguards for Montenegro set out in the Commission's October 2026 paper? And will what is agreed be enough to convince majorities in member states, not just for 🇲🇪, but for the other candidates in line?

4️⃣ How quickly and how clearly will the Commission move on #gradual #integration? There is a lot of talk, but all anyone comes back to is #energy (offered two decades ago), #transport (offered a decade ago), and targeted initiatives like #roamathome (discussed for years). There is also serious doubt about how clear, achievable and legally and politically sound the gradual-integration offers and the process for achieving them, set out in the October paper, really are.

For now in 🇧🇦's daily newspaper #DnevniAvaz

text:
In a fair housing case, a plaintiff can claim a violation of 42 U.S.C. § 1983 if they can prove that a person acting under color of state law deprived them of a right guaranteed by the U.S. Constitution or specific federal housing statutes.
While the Fair Housing Act (FHA) is the primary federal law used to combat housing discrimination, Section 1983 serves as a procedural vehicle to sue state or local government actors for constitutional violations (like Equal Protection or Due Process) or concurrent federal statutory violations related to housing.

Core Elements Required for a Section 1983 Fair Housing Claim

To successfully bring a Section 1983 claim in a housing context, the plaintiff must establish the following framework:

ElementRequirementApplication in Housing Cases
Color of State LawThe defendant must be a state, county, or municipal actor, or a private entity acting in concert with the government.Local zoning boards, municipal housing authorities, city councils, or building inspectors.
Deprivation of RightsThe action must violate a federal constitutional right or a specific federal statutory right.Discriminatory zoning (Equal Protection), arbitrary denial of housing permits (Due Process), or FHA violations by a public entity.
CausationThe defendant's official policy, custom, or direct action must have proximately caused the housing deprivation.A city passing an ordinance specifically designed to block affordable housing in a racially motivated manner.

How It Intersects with Fair Housing

Plaintiffs often pair Section 1983 claims alongside standard FHA claims when dealing with government defendants. The layout below details the primary constitutional pathways used in these lawsuits:

Constitutional BasisLegal TheoryExample
Fourteenth Amendment: Equal ProtectionThe government intentionally discriminated against a protected class regarding housing opportunities.A city council denies a zoning variance for an apartment complex because the residents will be predominantly minorities.
Fourteenth Amendment: Substantive Due ProcessThe government's housing or zoning decision was arbitrary, capricious, and lacked any rational basis.A local board denies a housing permit based purely on personal animus or political hostility rather than zoning codes.
First Amendment: RetaliationThe government penalized the plaintiff for exercising their right to free speech or advocating for fair housing.A municipality revokes a developer's existing permits because the developer publicly criticized local housing discrimination.

Advantages of Including a Section 1983 Claim

If the defendant is a government entity, adding a Section 1983 claim alongside an FHA claim offers specific legal advantages:
• No Cap on Punitive Damages: While the FHA has specific remedies, Section 1983 allows for robust punitive damages against individual officials acting in their personal capacities to punish egregious misconduct.
• Attorney's Fees: Under 42 U.S.C. § 1988, a prevailing plaintiff in a Section 1983 case is generally entitled to recover reasonable attorney's fees, lowering the financial barrier to bringing a lawsuit.
• Bypassing Administrative Requirements: Unlike some housing claims that require exhausting local administrative remedies first, a plaintiff can generally file a Section 1983 action directly in federal court.

The programme equipped young people with practical skills in audio-visual content production, digital storytelling and responsible communication, while opening avenues for their participation in India’s growing creative economy.

Speaking on the initiative, Shri Santosh Ajmera, Vice-Chancellor, SRFTI, said:

“The creative economy offers immense opportunities for our youth, and audio-visual storytelling can be a powerful instrument for livelihood opportunities and nation-building. By equipping young people with the skills to create credible, engaging digital content that reflects local realities and perspectives, we can strengthen the flow of authentic information, promote media literacy and bring local developmental stories to the forefront. This is particularly important in regions where responsible communication and an understanding of local realities are vital.

SRFTI is committed to taking its expertise in film, television and media education beyond the traditional classroom. I encourage other institutions, government organisations and stakeholders to institute similar skill-development programmes for young people. SRFTI would be happy to serve as a technical partner, extending its expertise in audio-visual production, digital storytelling and media training to support such initiatives and strengthen India’s creative ecosystem.”

✨ Students of Mass Communication and Journalism from St. Joseph University, Patkai Christian College and Tetso College participated in the programme. The initiative recognises the growing importance of skilled local youth in creating credible, context-sensitive and engaging audio-visual content. By strengthening their ability to document local realities, verify information and communicate responsibly, the programme seeks to counter misinformation, promote authentic local narratives, and document local development initiatives, community experiences and success stories for wider audiences in support of the vision of Viksit Bharat.

BIRTHING OF A NATION
Faith • Family • Freedom

DAILY SCRIPTURE

FRIDAY, OCTOBER 23, 2026

WHEN GOD SEES THE BROKENHEARTED

📖 Psalm 34:18 (NLT)

“The LORD is close to the brokenhearted; he rescues those whose spirits are crushed.”

🔥 TODAY’S MESSAGE — GOD HAS NOT WALKED AWAY

Have you ever reached a place where you’ve prayed, believed, stood faithfully, and yet everything around you seems to be falling apart?

You look at your circumstances and wonder, Lord, where are You in all of this?

Sometimes the greatest battles aren’t the ones people can see. They’re the silent struggles carried by those who keep smiling, keep working, keep encouraging others, and keep pressing forward when their own hearts are hurting.

Think about the disciples after Jesus was crucified.

They had walked with Him, witnessed His miracles, heard His promises, and believed He was the answer they had been waiting for.

Then came the cross.

Their hopes appeared shattered. Their expectations were overturned. The One they trusted had been laid in a tomb.

But here’s what they couldn’t see.

While they were grieving on earth, God was accomplishing something greater than they could possibly imagine.

The cross wasn’t the end of the story. Resurrection morning was coming!

And perhaps that’s where someone reading this finds themselves today.

You’ve experienced disappointment. You’ve lost something precious. You’ve been waiting for an answer that hasn’t come. Maybe you’ve even wondered whether God has forgotten you.

But listen carefully.

A broken heart does not mean an absent God.

Psalm 34 doesn’t promise that believers will never experience sorrow. It promises something far more personal: the Lord draws near to those whose hearts are broken.

Jesus understands rejection. He understands betrayal, loneliness, suffering, and tears.

And He is still the same Saviour today.

Don’t allow yesterday’s disappointment to convince you that tomorrow holds no hope.

The God who raised Jesus from the dead is able to bring life into situations that appear hopeless.

Your circumstances may not change overnight, but His presence can sustain you while you wait.

You may be walking through a valley, but you are not walking through it alone.

🔥 TODAY’S MISSION

Look for someone who may be struggling silently today. Send a message, make a phone call, offer encouragement, or take a moment to pray with them.

Sometimes God answers someone’s prayer through the compassion of another believer.

And if you’re the one struggling, don’t isolate yourself. Bring your burdens to Jesus and reach out to someone you trust.

🙏 TODAY’S PRAYER

Heavenly Father, thank You that You never abandon Your children in their darkest moments. Draw close to every broken heart today. Strengthen those who are weary, comfort those who are grieving, and restore hope to those who feel defeated. Help us become vessels of Your love and encouragement. In the mighty name of Jesus Christ, Amen.

FAITH • FAMILY • FREEDOM

text:
Podcast Summary | Candace: Candace Owens x Baron Coleman: The Real UVU Review. | Ep 407

Overview
Nearly a year after the Tyler Robinson case began, a trial date is expected soon, and this review reconstructs the timeline while challenging the official federal narrative as implausible and internally inconsistent. The central argument is that the prosecution's case rests on shaky foundations: a convoluted movement map, missing surveillance footage, unresolved questions about the rifle, contested DNA and fingerprint evidence, and text messages treated as decisive without proper authentication. The hosts contend that absent a year of media messaging, the preliminary hearing would read to most observers as a weak case, and that Turning Point USA's conduct around the courthouse has fueled rather than dispelled distrust.

Key Themes
- The official movement map is unnecessarily convoluted: the route through Chick-fil-A, the woods, the Gunther building housing UVU police, and other buildings seems far less direct than a simple path to the Losi Center, which sits only 10 to 20 feet from the Chick-fil-A.
- Key surveillance footage was never shown at the preliminary hearing despite a long investigation period, raising doubts about the evidence actually presented.
- The rifle narrative has unexplained gaps: no evidence was presented that the weapon was reassembled on the rooftop, and no explanation was offered for how the scope could be zeroed without test firing.
- The neck wound drives skepticism: critics argue it does not look like an entry wound, that no exit wound through a few inches of neck tissue is implausible for a .30-06, and that Charlie did not move backward as expected from such force.
- DNA and fingerprint results did not place Robinson on the rooftop, leaving the screwdriver—whose reported location shifted from near the gun to the woods to the rooftop—as essentially the only item placing him there.
- The text messages are described as containing essentially every element needed to convict, seen as unusually complete and self-incriminating, and are treated as central to the case—without them, the hosts argue there is no viable path to conviction.
- Turning Point USA's removal of camera footage, a staffer's rapid declaration of death and self-filming, and shifting public accounts are cited as early signals that something was wrong.
- The hosts argue the preliminary hearing produced no concrete DNA or physical evidence connecting Robinson, the gun, and the bullet, and that nothing shown there is guaranteed to appear at trial.

Detailed Summary
The review centers on reconstructing September 10th. The official narrative says Robinson woke around 4 to 5 a.m., arrived at UVU around 8:30 in a maroon shirt, light shorts, a black hat with a white logo, and light shoes. He allegedly lingered at the top of the parking structure for 7 to 8 minutes before moving to a lower level. The federal narrative claims he asked a Turning Point USA employee whether the event was there—yet TPUSA staff did not arrive until about 9:00 a.m. and were initially in the parking lot, not the amphitheater. The hosts treat the claim that he visited UVU just to ask that question as implausible.

He allegedly left the parking structure around 9:33 a.m., was caught on neighborhood cameras before 10:00, then returned to campus. He allegedly bought and ate Chick-fil-A at the Sorenson building around 10:10. The map then shows him dropping a backpack in a wooded area, passing the Gunther building that houses UVU police, moving through the computer science building, and reaching the Losi Center railing. The hosts note the Chick-fil-A is only about 10 to 20 feet from the Losi building, making the longer route suspicious.

He allegedly left campus just before 11:00 and submitted his Wordle score at 11:28—an odd detail the hosts find inconsistent with the official story. TMZ footage at 11:49 shows him in a black long-sleeve shirt with an American flag, walking with a limp. The limp is questioned as possibly performative or explained by the weapon. At 12:15, he allegedly reached the top of stairs near the Losi rooftop, looked over a short concrete wall for about 70 seconds, then hopped over and ducked down. No evidence was presented that he reassembled the rifle there, and the hosts question how the scope would be zeroed without test firing. The jump is described as athletic but not impossible; the person is characterized as very athletic and healthy. The government's pleading called the suspect reckless for reassembling the rifle and jostling the scope.

The neck wound is the central point of skepticism. Speakers argue it does not look like an entry wound, that no exit wound through roughly 3 to 4 inches of tissue is implausible given the expected 1,500 pounds of force, and that Charlie only slumped slightly rather than moving backward. The early assumption that the bullet passed through shaped public narratives—people reasoned it looked like an exit wound and speculated about an entrance from behind—so the claim that there was no back wound upended the official story.

Terrell Farnsworth is described as running to a wall, filming a selfie, and being the first to pronounce Charlie dead within about a minute, then flipping the camera to show Charlie being dragged away. The narrator says Farnsworth called nervous, gave inconsistent explanations for removing footage, and claimed not to know how to send a file despite running an audiovisual company. The narrator says they had recorded a FaceTime conversation with Farnsworth and that feds were in contact with TPUSA about whether it was recorded. Andrew Kolvet's tweet about a "Superman neck" miracle is said to remain unretracted, and the narrator says they did not believe Erica's account that Andrew went rogue and that a surgeon separately violated HIPAA to speak to a PR agent. Owens recalls a phone call with "Terl" around September 19th and says she reported it the next day, the day of Charlie Kirk's private funeral. She says Justin Strife called her husband asking about a recording, which she cites as evidence people were panicking. A September 14 press conference with Cash Patel and Governor Cox is referenced as presenting a reviewed-footage narrative.

Official accounts changed repeatedly: claims about the shooter changing clothes on the rooftop, being suicidal, and his father turning him in were later dropped. Bill Ackman's $1 million offer tied to Tyler Robinson's father was, according to Owens, directed to the feds—she says this was not public before and views the dropped father-turned-him-in story as a narrative that was set and then abandoned. Owens says she spoke with Ackman directly and did not view it as a threat at the time, but later saw him as personally vindictive toward her and promoting threads about her. Owens says her reporting was initially meant to help clear someone's name, but she stumbled onto a larger story, which she says made her a target.

Investigators initially claimed a screwdriver was found near the gun, then Fox News and legal sources reported it was in the woods; about five to six days later Kash Patel said it was found on the rooftop—a relocation the speakers call suspicious. DNA and fingerprint results did not place Robinson on the rooftop; DNA was indeterminate and the fingerprint could not be identified. The Discord narrative originated from the probable cause affidavit: a roommate allegedly showed investigators Robinson's Discord messages and allowed photos of the screen; after Discord said the conversations did not take place there, the narrative shifted to text messages and was dropped. The affidavit and statement of facts are characterized as hearsay-based documents meant to justify holding the suspect, not something a jury will see.

Officer Christopher Bagley was deemed unconvincing: his body camera allegedly died exactly when he discovered the screwdriver, and he said he did not know or remember the plainclothes officer who accompanied him onto the rooftop. Bagley was the first to suggest the shot came from the Losi rooftop and went up with Utah State University officer Alan Robertson. Speakers note Axon body cameras give a warning before dying and turn red, and say Bagley appears on photo or video shortly before going to the Losi Center with no red ring on his camera. Agent David Hull is described as the SBI co-lead investigator who presented the notorious video 12.1 purportedly showing Robinson on campus; speakers say his presentation was out of order, skipped around, included mirrored footage, and jumped ahead without explanation.

The testimony's attempt to place Robinson on campus is criticized as disjointed. One described sequence shows a person in black at the top of a stairwell while testimony discusses a person in maroon walking around campus. The maroon person leaves and another returns dressed differently head to toe, with a different backpack, hat, shirt, and pants; faces and hair also look different to the speakers. The stated basis for treating them as the same person includes matching Converse sneakers and a shared tunnel route, which the speakers treat as insufficient. They argue investigators should rely on stronger evidence such as cell phone signal data. The handling of the crime scene—paving over dirt—is treated as a major red flag suggesting someone above the lead investigator authorized it.

Forensic examiner Amanda Baker's testimony is framed as undermining public claims about DNA. She said DNA on an item does not prove someone touched or used it, and degraded DNA on the screwdriver cannot establish contact by Robinson or Lance Twiggs. Baker, described as an FBI forensic examiner from Quantico with 10 years there, was requested by the state of Utah to test the towel and screwdriver. She testified DNA turnaround normally takes 90 to 200 days, but this case was sped up due to its high-profile nature, with instructions to work around the clock. Her September 13 notes are cited: she spoke with an FBI special agent and with David Hull, who asked whether Robinson's DNA could not be excluded and told her no additional comparisons were needed at that time. Baker testified she could not have told them Robinson's DNA was on the towel or screwdriver, contradicting a public claim attributed to Cash Patel. She testified DNA can persist indefinitely and degrade over time, citing recoveries from items 40 or 50 years old. The screwdriver samples were described as tremendously degraded.

The towel narrative is treated as unverified: the hosts claim authorities never said the towel was on the roof, and that the public assumed it from a swinging object visible when someone jumped down. The hosts say that swinging object is now described as a gun, which they dispute because guns do not move that way. They argue a towel is an implausible choice for concealing a gun on a college campus, where a bag would be less conspicuous. Sergeant Brian Davis is described as the co-agent who assembled the probable cause case and discussed why Lance received use immunity; a lawyer on the show says use immunity is unsurprising if a witness lived with the suspect and touched evidence. Davis reportedly admitted text messages were not published in their entirety, only relevant portions for probable cause.

The hosts question the authenticity of the text messages, arguing they are too detailed and precise—containing everything needed to convict—and have not been properly technologically authenticated. They argue the messages seem implausible on common sense grounds: Tyler allegedly sent detailed messages when he could have spoken face-to-face later that night. A photo of a broken phone shows a green dead cell running top to bottom, and the hosts note text content appears over that area. They suggest the messages could have originated from another device or an already-logged-in account, citing search warrants listing many devices. Lance Twigs's account is treated as highly suspicious: he allegedly found a confession letter, photographed it, but the letter was later burned, making it untestable. Twigs testified their narrative is an LGBTQ crime, but said he never really thought about it and it never came up. He and Tyler met in 2023, became roommates, and began dating three months later. Twigs said he saw Tyler on the morning of the 11th, who confessed and said he regretted it. Twigs's family reportedly was surprised police questioned him only a couple of hours before releasing him.

Fingerprints collected by Lisa Farmer were tested and reportedly did not belong to Robinson. FBI Sergeant Jennifer Fuina testified that fingerprints found where the suspect climbed down did not belong to Robinson, and that the recovered gun had one fired round and three unfired rounds with engravings still on them. An abandoned backpack found near the Fulton Library bus stop, on the alleged shooter's route, contained a jacket, gloves, and possibly a mask; testing reportedly stopped after a phone call said it belonged to someone on Charlie's detail. The hosts question who on the detail would abandon a backpack at a bus stop and note gloves in September when it was 91 degrees as suspicious.

Seven fragments were reportedly removed from Charlie's body, but only four were sent to examiner Samantha Carner; three were too small to use. Carner sought to connect the gun to one bullet jacket fragment. She testified she had taken only one bullet proficiency test, in 2023, and that test had a high error rate; her conclusion in the case was inconclusive, which she called appropriate. A live demonstration is described in which the examiner repeatedly declined to conclude a match from bullet striation photos; the host says all three were fired from different weapons. The critics characterize bullet striation, DNA, and fingerprint analysis as dependent on subjective human eyeballing, undermining claims of overwhelming evidence. Caitlyn Oliver, described as an ATF forensic biologist, testified about prints on the gun; four or five sets were found, Matt Robinson was named, and the hosts say Tyler Robinson's prints were the most degraded while Matt Robinson's were stronger. The hosts criticize the defense attorney as knowledgeable but poor at communicating quickly.

The hosts argue that, absent the year-long media operation, the preliminary hearing would read to most observers as a weak prosecution case. They contend TPUSA's conduct—especially involving influencers around the courthouse—suggests an organization acting like it has something to hide. A recurring criticism is that TPUSA repeatedly makes PR blunders and never apologizes or shows humility, even when caught being wrong. They claim TPUSA is increasingly relying on less credible people because the good people Charlie Kirk surrounded himself with are unwilling to cooperate. One host offers a three-step turnaround plan: radical transparency, issuing statements only through official channels, and not attacking people.

text:
A Solar Storm Supposedly Delayed a Train in 1841. But the Railway Didn’t Exist Yet | Tudor Tarita, ZME Science

For more than 150 years, scientists believed it was the earliest documented example of a solar storm interfering with human technology. There was just one glaring problem. The Victorian railway hadn’t even been built yet.

The story appeared in the prestigious scientific journal Nature in 1871. According to the account, an intense magnetic storm on October 18, 1841, scrambled telegraph signals along the South Devon Railway. Unable to confirm that the tracks ahead were clear, railway officials held the 10:05 p.m. express at Exeter for 16 minutes.

The superintendent reportedly suspected “some one was playing tricks with the instruments,” according to the original Nature article.

Now, an international team of researchers has uncovered the mistake and traced the incident to a much more plausible date. Their new study also reshuffles the history of humanity’s first encounters with a technological threat from the Sun.

The 10:05 Train

The story returned to scientific attention in 2013, when Baylor University space-weather researcher William “Trey” Cade III rediscovered the 1871 account and suggested it might describe the earliest known example of space weather disrupting technology.

But there was a problem with the date. The South Devon Railway, where the incident supposedly happened in 1841, didn’t open until 1846. The train simply couldn’t have been there.

“You don’t have to talk to many railway enthusiasts before someone points out that the line didn’t open until 1846!” James Wild, a space physicist at Lancaster University who led the new investigation, told Earth.

Wild and his colleagues suspected that the incident might have happened several years later. Cade himself joined the investigation, helping to correct the historical account he had brought to light.

To find out, they turned to old railway timetables. The original account mentioned a very specific departure time: 10:05 p.m.

That proved to be the breakthrough. The researchers discovered that a train matching this description ran from Exeter between March 1848 and July 1849. They focused on October 18, 1848, exactly 7 years after the date published in Nature.

Then came the most convincing evidence.

Records from the Greenwich Observatory showed that a powerful magnetic storm swept over Britain that very evening, right around the train’s scheduled departure. Newspapers reported spectacular northern lights across England, including an unusually brilliant display near Leeds, while an astronomer’s drawing from the following morning showed a large group of sunspots, another sign of intense solar activity.c

Suddenly, the pieces fit together. The railway existed, the train was scheduled to depart at the right time, and a magnetic storm was underway that could have interfered with its telegraph signals. The researchers also found no comparable evidence of intense geomagnetic activity in England on October 18, 1841.

The researchers believe someone probably made a simple typographical error in the 1871 Nature article, turning 1848 into 1841.

They even tried to identify the article’s anonymous author, finding clues pointing to Victorian electrical engineer Nathaniel John Holmes. But they couldn’t locate the original manuscript or a contemporary report of the train delay.

So while the evidence strongly favors 1848, the precise circumstances of the incident remain unconfirmed. What researchers can say with certainty is that it couldn’t have happened in 1841.

The Sun’s Technology Disrupting History

Correcting the date means the Exeter incident loses its place as the earliest credible recorded technological disruption caused by space weather. That distinction now belongs to March 19, 1847, when a brilliant aurora coincided with strange electrical disturbances on the Midland Railway near Derby.

Railway engineer William Henry Barlow documented unexplained currents flowing through telegraph wires. He presented his findings to the Royal Society in 1848, and they appeared in an 1849 scientific paper.

The underlying physics is straightforward. Powerful solar eruptions can disturb Earth’s magnetic field. As that field changes, it can induce electric fields at Earth’s surface, driving unwanted currents through long conductors such as telegraph wires. Those currents can confuse electrical signaling equipment.

In Exeter’s case, the reported problem was specifically the inability to establish whether the track ahead, near the village of Starcross, was clear.

The timing was particularly consequential. Better batteries had made long-distance telegraphy practical during the 1840s, just as solar activity began rising. An emerging technology was encountering an environmental hazard its inventors had barely anticipated. These incidents preceded the famous Carrington Event of 1859, an enormous solar storm that disrupted telegraph networks across continents.

The vulnerability hasn’t disappeared. A 2023 modeling study found that geomagnetic disturbances could still cause malfunctions in modern railway signaling systems.

The historical correction also offers a broader lesson. A single erroneous date survived in the scientific literature for generations, until researchers checked it against evidence as mundane as a train timetable.

And there may be more surprises buried in the archives. The 1847 incident is only the earliest credible example researchers have identified so far, not necessarily the first time the Sun interfered with human technology.

Steve Hilton’s plan for California is no state income tax on the first $150,000 of earnings. The graphic’s conclusion is that the state cannot afford another four years of Democratic control. The tax change is a campaign proposal. It is not enacted law and it carries no guaranteed savings figure.

California’s high taxes, housing costs, and outward migration are the backdrop. Hilton is offering a concrete threshold: the first $150,000 stays untaxed at the state level. That structure would leave more money with middle-income households and change the incentive to leave. The broader claim is that continued one-party governance produces the conditions that make the tax cut necessary. Four more years, in this framing, means four more years of the same trajectory.

Voters can weigh the proposal against the record. No state income tax on the first $150,000 is the specific offer. The judgment that California cannot absorb another Democratic term is the political conclusion attached to it. Neither claim has been tested by passage or by an election result yet.
