text:
Is sanctuary a dead end for dogs?

Duke doesn’t think so. Look at that happy boy! 

But it’s a question worth asking, particularly in an animal welfare world where success is so often measured by adoption numbers, length of stay, and how quickly an animal moves through the system.

But what happens to the animals who don’t fit that model?

The dogs with significant behavioral challenges, bite histories, the elderly, the medically complicated. The animals who, for one reason or another, are considered unadoptable.

Does their inability to find a traditional forever home make their lives any less worth saving?

At LHRR we believe the answer is unequivocally no.

Over our five years in rescue, we have successfully adopted out a significant number of dogs. Perhaps not as many as some traditional adoption based rescues, but our mission has always been different.

We are a sanctuary. Sanctuary does not mean adoption is off the table but it means we offer life long care when adoption isn’t an option. 

In fact, we have three upcoming adoptions that we are incredibly excited about!

When one of our animals is ready for adoption and we find a home that can safely and appropriately meet their needs, we celebrate. But for the animals who may never have that opportunity, our commitment remains exactly the same.

Because adoption is one measure of success in animal rescue. It is not the only measure of a life well lived. 

The majority of the animals who come into our care are not considered adoptable. Many have behavioral or medical needs that make placement in a traditional home difficult, and sometimes impossible.

These are often the animals who have exhausted their options. And we believe they deserve more than simply being kept alive.

They deserve to live.

To feel the sunshine on their faces. To roll in the grass. To have favorite toys, comfortable beds, familiar routines, and people who know them as individuals. For us they are adopted, they have found their family, with us. 

They deserve affection, enrichment, companionship, and the opportunity to experience happiness.

They deserve a home, even if that home happens to be a sanctuary.

Our animals are not simply residents of a rescue facility. They are members of our family. We spend our days with them, learning their personalities, understanding their needs, building their trust, and giving them the stability that so many have never experienced.

And we believe sanctuary comes with an extraordinary responsibility.

It is not enough to provide food, water, shelter, and medical care. Those are necessities, not the entirety of a meaningful life.

True sanctuary requires individualized care, enrichment, attention to physical and emotional well being, and an ongoing commitment to ensuring that the lives we are preserving are lives worth living.

And that brings us to $5 Friday. 

If you believe that sanctuaries have an important place in animal welfare, that animals who cannot be adopted still deserve love, dignity, and a fulfilling life, and that sanctuary is not a dead end but a life line we hope you’ll consider supporting our work today.

Your donation helps us provide lifelong care, veterinary treatment, enrichment, and the safe, comfortable homes our animals deserve.

Whether you can give $5, less than $5, or more, every contribution matters.

Because not every animal will find a traditional forever home. But every animal deserves the chance to have one.

And sometimes, that forever home is a sanctuary.

Please donate and help us continue being that home.

text:
Conor McGregor Getting Sued Again And This Time the Legal Web Is Getting Harder to Escape
The roar of the crowd had long faded by the time Conor McGregor’s name stopped echoing through arenas and started echoing through Irish courtrooms. By July 2025, when three judges at the Dublin Court of Appeal dismissed his appeal in full, it was clear that the fighter’s legal chapter would outlast his time in the octagon. He had not competed in MMA since breaking his leg against Dustin Poirier at UFC 264 in 2021. The courts had taken over.
At the center of the original case was Nikita Hand. She alleged that McGregor sexually assaulted her in a Dublin hotel in December 2018. In November 2024, a High Court jury found him civilly liable and awarded her roughly €248,000 (about $257,000), plus substantial legal costs. McGregor denied the allegations throughout.
He appealed. His legal team argued, among other points, that the jury had been asked an imprecise question. The Court of Appeal rejected the arguments as unpersuasive, calling the suggestion that the jury had been confused “simply unreal.” The Irish Supreme Court later refused a further appeal, finding no issue of public importance. It could have ended there. It did not.
Nikita Hand, along with Samantha O’Reilly and Steven Cummins, has now filed a separate civil lawsuit against McGregor alleging malicious abuse of court process. The claim centers on affidavits O’Reilly and Cummins submitted in support of McGregor’s appeal—affidavits that were later withdrawn before the hearing. The Court of Appeal found the withdrawal so striking that it referred the matter to prosecutors. In September 2026, O’Reilly and Cummins were charged with perjury, appeared in Dublin District Court, and were granted strict bail. A trial is expected to begin in November. The pair, who lived next door to Hand and her then-partner at the time of the 2018 incident, had offered an alternative account of her injuries. Once those statements were pulled without explanation, the court’s concerns triggered a criminal investigation.
From the outside, the sequence is striking: a civil appeal that introduced new witnesses, saw those witnesses abruptly retract their testimony, and produced perjury charges. Even setting aside the original findings, it is a notable chain of events.
Across the Atlantic, a different case closed. A 49-year-old business executive had sued McGregor in Florida, alleging sexual assault in a restroom at Miami’s Kaseya Center during an NBA Finals game in June 2023. No criminal charges were brought by the Florida State Attorney’s Office. In December 2025 the plaintiff voluntarily dismissed the suit with prejudice, permanently closing it. McGregor denied those allegations as well.

text:
The 1947 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was announced on this day. It went to two labs that had each been told to stop.

Half went to Carl and Gerty Cori, for working out how the body stores sugar as glycogen and spends it again. In Buffalo she was told to stop publishing with her husband or leave, and at a later job interview she was told it was "un-American" for a married couple to work together. She didn't stop. When Washington University hired Carl, nepotism rules meant Gerty came on as a research associate at about a tenth of his salary. She wasn't made a full professor until 1947, sixteen years later. With this prize she became the first American woman to win a science Nobel, and only the third woman to win any science Nobel. A few months earlier, on a climbing trip in the Rockies, she had learned she had myelofibrosis, the bone-marrow disease that killed her ten years later. She worked through nearly all of it.

The other half went to Bernardo Houssay in Buenos Aires, who showed that the pituitary pushes blood sugar up, against insulin. In 1943 Argentina's military government fired him for calling for democratic elections. He had offers from abroad and stayed, keeping his lab going on private money, and that's where the Nobel news found him. He was the first Latin American scientist to win.

Luis Leloir, whose Nobel anniversary is Tuesday, trained with Houssay and also passed through the Coris' lab.

All three are in The Molecule Hunters: https://t.co/JWQInfY0Ao

text:
$RCI Q3 2026 earnings: Rogers cash flow rises, but wireless sales and sign-ups fall

Rogers Communications, the Canadian telecom and media group, generated higher cash flow even as its core wireless business shrank. Total service revenue edged up 1% now that last year's buyout of Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment sits in both periods, while wireless service revenue fell 1% and new postpaid phone additions dropped to 6,000. Free cash flow rose 65% to $1.4 billion, but by our math the unchanged full-year outlook implies service revenue will fall about 2% in the fourth quarter.

• Total service revenue: $𝟒,𝟕𝟖𝟎𝐌 (+0.9% from a year ago)
• Wireless service revenue: $𝟐,𝟎𝟑𝟑𝐌 (-1.3% from a year ago)
• Free cash flow: $𝟏,𝟑𝟕𝟎𝐌 (+65% from a year ago ($274M from asset sales))
• Full-year 2026 outlook: 𝐔𝐧𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝 (middle of the range: 4% service revenue growth)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: 🔴 Bearish

The story got worse because wireless service revenue contracted while the promised capital spending cut still leaned heavily on selling assets. Deducting $274 million of network and property sales accounted for more than half of the third-quarter capital spending drop by our math, and borrowing $4.35 billion on October 1 to buy the rest of MLSE pushes debt leverage back above 4 times. The bright spot: Media revenue grew 9% on strong Blue Jays attendance.

The question now is whether Rogers can sell a minority stake in its combined sports empire in the first half of 2027 at a price that pays off its new short-term bank debt. Bulls point to 100% ownership of MLSE and rising sports revenue, while sceptics point to the company's new warning that league approvals and valuation are not guaranteed. A signed sports stake deal by mid-2027 will settle it.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢 𝐌𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐚 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐒𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐬 𝐆𝐫𝐞𝐰 𝟗% 𝐖𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐀𝐜𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐇𝐞𝐥𝐩
Rogers took control of Maple Leaf Sports & Entertainment (MLSE), the owner of the Toronto Maple Leafs and Toronto Raptors, on July 1, 2025. That made the third quarter the first period where the Media division's year-over-year comparison included MLSE in both years. Revenue still rose 9% to $821 million, and Media profit before interest, taxes, depreciation and one-offs (adjusted EBITDA) grew 12% to $84 million.

The Toronto Blue Jays baseball team drew over 3.3 million fans this season, its highest attendance since 2016, while the National Hockey League season started in September this year and Warner Bros. Discovery channels brought in more subscriber money. Because those gains came from operations rather than buying a business, they show the sports portfolio can grow on its own, though higher player salaries and programming costs pushed Media operating expenses up 9% to $737 million.

What to watch: fourth-quarter Media revenue and adjusted EBITDA. That period compares against last year's Blue Jays World Series run, when Media earned $221 million in adjusted EBITDA, so a sharp drop would show that sports earnings remain tied to playoff schedules.

🟢 𝐏𝐡𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐔𝐩𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐂𝐮𝐭𝐬 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐒𝐞𝐠𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐬
Rogers aims to protect profitability in its Wireless and Cable divisions by avoiding deep price discounts and cutting operating expenses. In the third quarter, Wireless adjusted EBITDA rose 1% to $1,383 million, lifting its margin on service revenue by 1.3 percentage points to 68.0%, while Cable adjusted EBITDA rose 1% to $1,164 million and its margin gained 0.4 percentage points to 58.6%.

Wireless equipment revenue grew 9% to $655 million while the cost of buying those phones rose only 2% to $579 million, because existing customers upgraded to pricier phones and Rogers kept pricing firm. Cable operating costs fell 1% to $823 million as productivity initiatives outweighed higher content licensing costs, though consolidated adjusted EBITDA margin still dipped 0.4 percentage points to 46.6% because the lower-margin Media unit grew fastest and raised Media operating costs by 0.9 percentage points of total revenue by our math.

What to watch: fourth-quarter Wireless equipment margin during the holiday shopping season. If rivals discount phones heavily in November and December, Rogers will have to choose between giving back its hardware margin gains or losing more subscribers.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐀𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐒𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐃𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐇𝐚𝐥𝐟 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐂𝐮𝐭
Rogers lowered its full-year capital spending target in April 2026 because of "ongoing impacts from heightened competitive intensity and recent regulatory decisions". Reported capital expenditures fell 46% from a year ago to $524 million this quarter, pushing capital intensity — capital spending as a share of revenue — down 8.4 percentage points to 9.6% and lifting free cash flow 65% to $1,370 million.

• Reported net capital spending: $524 million, down $440 million from a year ago
• Proceeds from selling network and property assets deducted from capital spending: $274 million, up from $13 million a year ago by our math
• Gross capital spending before asset sales: $798 million, down 18% from $977 million a year ago by our math
• Free cash flow before asset-sale deductions: $1,096 million by our math

Because Rogers defines capital expenditures net of asset disposal proceeds, selling $133 million of wireless network assets, $86 million of cable assets from "under-construction rural fibre network projects we have deprioritized in the current environment", and $55 million of real estate accounted for 62% of the reported spending drop by our math. Gross network spending did fall this quarter after staying flat in the second quarter, but free cash flow is still leaning on one-time property and project sales.

What to watch: fourth-quarter asset-sale proceeds deducted from capital expenditures. If gross spending stays near $800 million without more asset sales, Rogers will miss the $573 million fourth-quarter net spending pace implied by the middle of its full-year outlook.

🔴🔴 𝐖𝐢𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐒𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐒𝐮𝐛𝐬𝐜𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐅𝐞𝐥𝐥
Wireless is the largest profit engine at Rogers, and its service revenue depends on how many customers it adds and what each pays per month. In the third quarter, Wireless service revenue shrank 1% from a year ago to $2,033 million, worsening from a flat first half as the company cited "promotional discipline and lower overall market activity in Canada".

• Monthly mobile phone revenue per user (ARPU): $55.22, down $1.48 or 2.6% from a year ago
• Postpaid mobile phone net additions (customers on monthly bills): 6,000, down from 62,000 a year ago
• Prepaid mobile phone net additions (pay-in-advance customers): 11,000, down from 49,000 a year ago
• Prepaid monthly customer cancellation rate (churn): 4.77%, up from 2.86% a year ago

Holding back on price promotions protected equipment margins, but it cost Rogers subscriber growth: total mobile net additions dropped by 94,000 from a year ago to just 17,000 by our math, while postpaid monthly churn still ticked up 0.04 percentage points to 1.03%. Because the subscriber base is now growing less than 1% a year while monthly revenue per user falls 2.6%, wireless service revenue cannot grow until one of those trends reverses.

What to watch: fourth-quarter mobile phone ARPU and postpaid net additions. Another drop in ARPU above 2.5% alongside weak subscriber additions would show that regulatory fee bans and past price cuts are still outweighing price discipline.

🔴🔴 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐌𝐋𝐒𝐄 𝐏𝐮𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐬 𝐃𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐁𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐔𝐩
On October 1, 2026 — one day after the third quarter closed — Rogers paid $4.35 billion in cash to Kilmer Sports Inc. for the remaining 25% of MLSE, giving the telecom group 100% ownership. Management argues that owning all of MLSE lets it sell a minority stake in its combined sports and media business (Rogers Sports) by the first half of 2027 to unlock "significant unrecognized value in our sports assets" and pay down debt.

To pay Kilmer on October 1, the Canadian carrier drew US$3,077 million ($4,367 million) on four new one-year bank credit facilities maturing in September 2027. While reported debt leverage — adjusted net debt divided by trailing 12-month adjusted EBITDA — fell to 3.7 times at September 30 from 4.0 times at the end of 2025, adding the $4.35 billion October 1 borrowing raises debt leverage back to about 4.2 times by our math.

The company also expanded its risk disclosures this quarter, warning there is no guarantee it will complete a Rogers Sports stake sale "whether at the expected investment amount, within the anticipated timing, or at all", and noting that sports leagues must approve any buyer. What to watch: a signed deal to sell a minority stake in Rogers Sports by the second quarter of 2027, because a delay or lower price would leave short-term bank debt maturing with leverage above 4 times.

🔴 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐓𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦 𝐑𝐮𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐂𝐮𝐭 𝐅𝐞𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐀𝐝𝐝 𝐍𝐞𝐭𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤
Canada's telecom regulator, the CRTC, banned phone and Internet activation and plan-switching fees starting June 12, 2026. The third quarter was the first full period under that rule, and Rogers said lower fee revenue contributed to the 1% drop in wireless service revenue. On June 30, the CRTC also ordered Rogers and its rivals to justify other remaining fees, and on September 10 it mandated peak-hour Internet speed guarantees starting March 2027.

Meanwhile, Rogers has transferred construction of certain government-subsidized rural broadband lots to outside builders as part of its capital spending cuts, but disclosed this quarter that it remains legally responsible to the Canadian and Ontario governments if those builders fail to finish on time. What to watch: the CRTC's ruling on the June 30 fee inquiry, because banning more fees would cut high-margin service revenue directly.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐖𝐢𝐥𝐝𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐞 𝐑𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐞𝐟 𝐓𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐒𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐞 𝐒𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞
Rogers offered its Rogers Satellite service — which connects mobile phones directly to satellites where cell towers do not reach — free to all wireless customers in British Columbia during wildfire emergencies this quarter. While the deployment showcased network reliability, the company still did not disclose how many paying customers use the service, and noted only that satellite operating costs increased Wireless expenses.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐂𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐮𝐛𝐬𝐜𝐫𝐢𝐛𝐞𝐫𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏,𝟗𝟖𝟕 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
Cable revenue was essentially unchanged from $1,981 million a year ago, or up about 1% by our math after excluding the customer-facing data centre business sold in late 2025. Retail Internet net additions slowed to 10,000 from 29,000 a year ago, and total customer relationships shrank by 2,000 as video and home phone cancellations outweighed Internet gains.

𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐞, 𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐧𝐞-𝐨𝐟𝐟𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟏.𝟐𝟗  ⇘ decelerating
Diluted earnings per share excluding one-offs fell 5.8% from $1.37 a year ago, after rising 0.9% in the second quarter and 2.0% in the first quarter. Higher adjusted EBITDA was outweighed by an 8.9% rise in adjusted finance costs to $585 million and $119 million in cash payouts to the minority investors in its wireless backhaul subsidiary.

𝐀𝐜𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐜𝐭 𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟑): $𝟓,𝟖𝟏𝟓 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
Accounts receivable — money owed by customers — fell 4.8% from December 31, 2025 due to seasonal billing patterns, while long-term financing receivables for phone payment plans dropped 9.8% to $1,080 million. Contract liabilities — cash collected upfront for subscriptions and sports tickets — fell 7.5% from year-end to $1,031 million as Rogers recognized revenue across the sports calendar.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐓𝐨𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡: +𝟑% 𝐭𝐨 +𝟓%  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from +3% to +5%
Unchanged. The full-year plan still calls for service revenue to grow 4% at the middle of the range over 2025's $19,104 million. Because service revenue grew 6% across the first nine months, by our math the middle of the range implies fourth-quarter service revenue will fall about 2.5% from a year ago as the company compares against last year's Blue Jays World Series run.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡: +𝟏% 𝐭𝐨 +𝟑%  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from +1% to +3%
Unchanged. The telecom group still expects full-year adjusted EBITDA to rise 2% at the middle of the range from $9,820 million in 2025. After 3% growth in the first nine months, by our math the middle of the range leaves fourth-quarter adjusted EBITDA down about 0.5% from last year's $2,689 million, reflecting flat wireless profit and the tough baseball playoff comparison.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐬: $𝟐,𝟓𝟎𝟎–𝟐,𝟕𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇒ stable
🠆 unchanged from $2,500–2,700 million
Unchanged. Management kept the full-year capital spending target it lowered by $800 million in April 2026. With $2,027 million spent in the first nine months, by our math the middle of the range leaves $573 million for the fourth quarter, down 39% from $934 million in the fourth quarter of 2025.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐅𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰: $𝟒,𝟏𝟎𝟎–𝟒,𝟑𝟎𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇘ decelerating
🠆 unchanged from $4,100–4,300 million
Unchanged. The outlook still points to $4,200 million of free cash flow at the middle of the range, up 25% from 2025 after the April raise. Because Rogers generated $3,128 million in the first nine months, by our math the middle of the range requires $1,072 million in the fourth quarter, up 5.5% from $1,016 million a year ago.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡-𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐜𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐨𝐧 𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬?
Proceeds from selling network assets and property reduced reported third-quarter capital spending by $274 million, or 62% of the year-over-year drop by our math. Investors need to know what gross spending level sits behind the $573 million fourth-quarter implied target.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐫𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐉𝐮𝐧𝐞 𝐂𝐑𝐓𝐂 𝐟𝐞𝐞 𝐛𝐚𝐧 𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐨𝐯𝐞?
Wireless service revenue fell 1% in the first full quarter under the CRTC's ban on activation and plan-switching fees, and the regulator is now challenging other fees. Management has not disclosed the annual dollar drag from these rules.

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐌𝐋𝐒𝐄 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧 𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐨𝐰𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫?
Media revenue grew 9% and adjusted EBITDA rose 12% in the first quarter with MLSE in both periods of the comparison, but Rogers combines MLSE with the Blue Jays and Sportsnet. Standalone figures would show how the $4.35 billion buyout is performing.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐥𝐨𝐧𝐠 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐭 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐭𝐨𝐥𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝟒.𝟐𝐱 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞?
Drawing $4.35 billion on short-term bank lines on October 1 to buy the rest of MLSE pushes pro forma debt leverage back to about 4.2 times by our math, while S&P carries a negative outlook on Rogers' BBB- rating ahead of the 2027 sports sale.

text:
@mjkeenan @JohnCleese @StephenKing @elonmusk @DaveSFoley 

I thought there was a weird Ledbetter thing regarding ban-the-box?

Ban-the-Box laws are fair-chance employment policies that prohibit employers from asking about a job applicant's criminal history on initial application forms, shifting those inquiries to later in the hiring process. [1] (https://t.co/dFq72aPRup), [2] (https://t.co/qK3TfS4CeA), [3] (https://t.co/wrX12XZH3d)

How Ban-the-Box Works

• Removal of Initial Questions: Employers must remove check boxes or questions about criminal records, arrests, or convictions from initial job applications. [1] (https://t.co/duD3t0omgB), [2] (https://t.co/wrX12XZH3d)
• Delayed Background Checks: Criminal background checks and conviction inquiries are delayed until later in the hiring process—typically after an initial interview or once a conditional job offer has been extended. [1] (https://t.co/8jCjJGIZJU), [2] (https://t.co/wrX12XZH3d)
• Focus on Qualifications: The policy ensures applicants are first evaluated based on their skills, experience, and qualifications rather than immediate disqualification due to a past record. [1] (https://t.co/tQuX12pMX2), [2] (https://t.co/qK3TfS4CeA)
• Individualized Assessment: If a background check reveals a criminal history, many jurisdictions require employers to conduct an individualized assessment (considering factors like the nature and age of the offense and its relevance to the job) before withdrawing an offer. [1] (https://t.co/GB5d0VJMJ8), [2] (https://t.co/tQuX12pMX2), [3] (https://t.co/wrX12XZH3d)

Scope and Coverage in the U.S. and Minnesota

• National Reach: Over 35 to 37 states, Washington, D.C., and more than 150 cities and counties have enacted fair-chance hiring policies. While many jurisdictions initially applied these rules only to public-sector employers, a growing number have extended them to private employers and government contractors. [1] (https://t.co/i6Wxg1CXct), [2] (https://t.co/yUW87NTIZz), [3] (https://t.co/tQuX12pMX2)
• Minnesota Law (Minn. Stat. § 364.021): Effective January 1, 2014, Minnesota’s Ban-the-Box law applies to both public and private employers in the state.
• Employers cannot ask about criminal history on the initial application.
• Inquiries or background checks must wait until the applicant has been selected for an interview or, if no interview is conducted, after a conditional job offer is made.
• Exemptions apply where background checks are legally mandated (such as for certain teachers or commercial drivers).
• Violations can result in employer fines ranging from $500 to $2,000 depending on company size. You can review compliance guidelines via the Minnesota Department of Human Rights. [1] (https://t.co/JBH4soTIDT), [2] (https://t.co/oWfo70sibG), [3] (https://t.co/bBUi0MjuaK)
If you'd like, let me know:
• Are you looking at this from an employer compliance perspective or as a job seeker?
• Which specific city or state are you located in?

2. $FICO — Fair Isaac
FICO provides credit scoring models used to assess creditworthiness.
These models are deeply integrated into financial processes, making them difficult to replace quickly.

Banks and other institutions rely on these scores to make critical lending decisions, creating high barriers to entry for potential rivals.

3. $MCO — Moody’s
Moody’s provides credit ratings, research, and financial analysis.
The company has built a strong reputation, established proven methodologies, and maintained a market presence over decades.
Its deep integration into financial systems—combined with the high level of trust it has earned—makes it nearly impossible for a new entrant to replicate its credibility.

4. $MELI — MercadoLibre
MercadoLibre operates an ecosystem in Latin America encompassing e-commerce, logistics, and financial services.

Its ecosystem connects buyers, sellers, and payment users, while its logistics infrastructure requires significant capital investment and deep local expertise.

These factors create a strong competitive moat against online rivals.

5. $CP — Canadian Pacific Kansas City (CPKC)
CPKC operates an extensive railway network connecting Canada, the United States, and Mexico.

Building such infrastructure requires massive capital investment, complex regulatory permits, and extensive labor.

This vast physical network presents an insurmountable barrier for any new competitor.

6. $VRSK — Verisk Analytics

Verisk provides data and analytical tools that help insurance companies assess risk and make informed decisions.

Its specialized expertise and the deep integration of its products into client business processes make switching to a different provider a complex and difficult undertaking.

Its core strength lies not just in collecting data, but in transforming that data into actionable insights for critical decision-making.

7. $INTU — Intuit

Intuit develops financial and accounting software for individuals and small businesses, with products including TurboTax and QuickBooks. Sustainable waste management and comprehensive services for collection, processing, and disposal.

The ecosystem is non-negotiable; it serves as a platform designed to drive cost-effectiveness and operational efficiency.

8. $RSG — Republic Services

Republic Services provides collection, processing, and disposal services for residential, commercial, and municipal clients.

The business operates within a framework of strict regulations, permits, licensing requirements, and regulatory oversight.

While perhaps not the most "glamorous" sector, it is a capital-intensive business that requires extensive local infrastructure, ongoing upgrades, and years of operational execution.

9. $SPOT — Spotify

Spotify allows millions of users to listen to music and podcasts.

It offers a highly personalized, enduring user experience—a platform that has evolved over time to achieve global scale.

Its competitive advantage lies in its user experience, distribution capabilities, and ability to monetize its audience.

CHRIST THE REDEEMER TOWERS ABOVE THE CLOUDS A LASTING SYMBOL OF CHRISTIAN STRENGTH

The image of Christ the Redeemer standing high above the clouds in Brazil is more than a striking photo. It is a clear statement that faith still stands taller than the confusion and disorder of the modern world. While cities below struggle with secular pressures and cultural drift, the statue remains fixed on the mountain, arms open, looking over the land.

This is not soft symbolism. It is a concrete reminder that Western civilization was built on Christian foundations and that those foundations have not disappeared. The figure of Christ rising above the clouds shows order above chaos and permanence above the temporary storms that pass beneath it. Ave Christus Rex is not a slogan. It is a recognition that authority and truth do not bend to the shifting moods of any age.

Brazil still carries this Christian inheritance in plain sight. The statue does not apologize for its message. It simply stands. In a time when many institutions avoid clear statements about faith, heritage, and order, the sight of Christ the Redeemer above the clouds offers a direct counterpoint. The image does not negotiate. It declares that something higher remains in place.

The video makes the point without commentary. Clouds gather and move, yet the statue holds its ground. That is the statement: faith endures, the Christian West still has visible monuments, and some symbols refuse to sink into the fog.

She had already dedicated part of her life to serving her country. Even after her life ended, she found a way to continue helping others.

Ivy Unruh proudly served as a United States Marine, earning the respect of friends and fellow service members through her strength, discipline, and selflessness. Those who knew her remembered someone who cared deeply about others and carried herself with quiet determination.

Then tragedy struck.

At just 25 years old, Ivy lost her life in a case that devastated those who loved her. Authorities later charged her estranged husband with first-degree murder in connection with her death.

Her family and friends were left mourning a daughter, a friend, and a Marine whose future had been cut tragically short.

But Ivy had made a decision long before that heartbreaking day. She had chosen to become an organ donor.

That single decision would go on to bring hope to others.

According to accounts shared by those close to her, Ivy's donated organs saved six lives, giving six people another opportunity to spend time with their families, celebrate birthdays, make memories, and experience moments they might otherwise have lost.

For the families who received that extraordinary gift, her legacy became something deeply personal. In the middle of their grief, Ivy's loved ones could find some comfort in knowing that her final act had helped others continue living.

One friend recalled that Ivy had always wanted to help people. Even after her passing, that desire to make a difference became part of her lasting legacy.

Her military service reflected a commitment to something greater than herself, and her decision to become an organ donor offered another expression of that same spirit of giving.

Heroes are often remembered for the battles they fight, the sacrifices they make, and the people they protect. But sometimes, a person's legacy continues in a different way, through the lives they help save and the families they give more time together.

Ivy Unruh's final act of service did not take place on a battlefield. It began with a personal decision she made long before anyone knew how much it would mean.

She could not see the futures her donation would help make possible. But six people were given another chance at life, and that gift continues to represent the difference one decision can make.

Though her own story ended far too soon, the lives she helped save became part of her enduring legacy.

May Ivy Unruh be remembered for her service, her generosity, and the lives that continued because of her final gift.

text:
The governor put a price on his head, so this pirate put a bigger one on the governor’s. In the early 1800s, Jean Lafitte and his brother Pierre ran one of the boldest smuggling operations in American history. From their hideout in the swamps of Barataria Bay, south of New Orleans, they captured ships and sold their cargo at cut-rate prices to eager buyers in the city. Everyone knew what they were doing, and plenty of locals loved them for it.

Louisiana Governor William C.C. Claiborne was not one of them. In November 1813, fed up with Lafitte openly breaking the law, he posted notices all over New Orleans offering $500 for the pirate’s arrest. Lafitte didn’t run. He didn’t hide. According to the legend, he strolled into the city and went about his business like nothing had happened. 

Then, days later, New Orleans woke up to brand-new posters hanging right next to the governor’s. Lafitte had copied the language almost word for word, except now he was offering $5,000 to anyone who would capture Governor Claiborne and deliver him to Barataria. The city loved it. The governor did not.

But the story has an even bigger twist. Just a year later, during the War of 1812, the British tried to recruit Lafitte to help them take New Orleans. He refused, warned the Americans, and offered his men and supplies to General Andrew Jackson. Lafitte and his fighters helped win the Battle of New Orleans, and President James Madison granted them a pardon. The pirate the governor wanted locked up ended up helping save his city.

text:
Pentagon warning puts insider-information risk at center of prediction markets

The most consequential development for prediction-market participants is the Pentagon’s new directive barring military personnel from using classified or other nonpublic information to trade on platforms including Polymarket and Kalshi. AP reports that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth issued the instruction, putting a sharp institutional line around a concern that grows as event-contract markets reach further into politics, economics and geopolitics.

Pentagon draws a compliance boundary

The directive does not change the mechanics of trading, but it underscores the reputational and regulatory stakes around information advantages. Prediction markets are often promoted as aggregators of public expectations; their credibility depends on participants not turning privileged access into a trading edge. For followers of Polymarket and Kalshi, the warning is a reminder that expansion into sensitive real-world events brings scrutiny well beyond traditional gambling enforcement.

Political donations meet regulatory pressure

Reuters reports that Kalshi, Polymarket and their founders have donated at least $5 million to political groups during the current election cycle while the firms face heightened state and federal scrutiny. That pairing is likely to intensify attention on how prediction-market companies seek influence while arguing for their legal and regulatory frameworks.

The issue matters because policy outcomes increasingly shape the industry’s operating environment: what contracts are permitted, which agencies claim oversight, and whether states can impose their own restrictions. Political engagement may become a larger part of the sector’s public story as legal questions move from niche disputes to broader regulatory debates.

Utah escalates its case against Kalshi

Axios reports that Utah has sued Kalshi, alleging it offered illegal gambling and seeking fees, profits and punitive damages connected to wagers by Utah users. The suit adds a concrete state-level challenge to the industry’s push for broader availability.

For market watchers, the key question is not simply one platform’s exposure in Utah. The case could help clarify—or complicate—the boundary between federally regulated event contracts and state gambling law. A patchwork of state actions would make nationwide expansion more costly and uncertain, even as platforms broaden their offerings.

Growth brings a wider audience—and more pressure

The Atlantic describes the rapid expansion of prediction markets led by Kalshi and Polymarket, citing rising valuations, expanding offerings and growing appeal among younger bettors. That momentum is visible alongside a busy market backdrop: Polymarket’s October Fed decision event led 24-hour volume, ahead of the 2026 midterm balance-of-power market.

Why it matters

Prediction markets are becoming more mainstream precisely as their legal, ethical and political boundaries are being tested. For participants, the story is increasingly about market access and platform legitimacy—not just the next contract’s implied odds.

Northwest Bio Partners With King’s College Hospital And King’s College London For Programs In Europe - Northwest Biotherapeutics
Programs Include Both Clinical Trial and Compassionate Use Bethesda, Maryland, April 12, 2012 – Northwest Biotherapeutics (OTC Bulletin Board: NWBO) (NW Bio) announced today that it is partnering with King’s Health Partners to both manufacture and deliver a new treatment for patients with brain cancer as part of its ongoing 240-patient clinical trial for Glioblastoma multiforme (GBM), the most lethal form of brain cancer. Specialists at King’s College London will manufacture NW Bio’s immune therapy treatment, DCVax®, for the clinical trial which will take place and involve brain cancer patients at King’s College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust. Both institutions are part of King’s Health Partners, a pioneering collaboration which brings together one of the world’s leading research-led universities with three of London’s most successful NHS Foundation Trusts to reduce the time it takes for research discoveries to become routine clinical practice. The collaboration with King’s College Hospital includes two important dimensions. One such dimension is enabling the Hospital to join NW Bio’s ongoing, 240-patient randomized, controlled clinical trial for GBM brain cancer, which is currently under way at more than 30 clinical trial sites across the U.S. A second important dimension involves treatment of patients on a compassionate use basis, for those who do not fully meet the criteria to enroll on the clinical trial, but may benefit from the treatment. This compassionate use dimension will enable treatment of such patients to proceed while the clinical trial is ongoing. The collaboration with King’s College London involves support from the College for the manufacturing of NW Bio’s DCVax® immune therapy. King’s has a specialized “cGMP” (clean room) facility for processing of cell therapy products, and specialized scientific staff already experienced in working with such cell products. Under the collaboration, King’s will make available its cGMP facility and experienced personnel to support the production of NW Bio’s DCVax® products. The necessary regulatory permits are already in place for the production of DCVax® products at the facility, and Cognate BioServices, Inc., NW Bio’s contract manufacturer, is conducting technology transfer and training in the proprietary DCVax® production processes. 2 Cognate will manage and oversee the processing at King’s (in addition to the production at Fraunhofer in Germany) on an ongoing basis, to ensure consistency and coordination. This collaboration with the College brings important additional manufacturing capacity and flexibility for NW Bio’s DCVax® products, without the need for any capital investment by NW Bio. Overall, this partnering with King’s College Hospital and King’s College London, as part of King’s Health Partners, provides another solid foundation for NW Bio’s programs in Europe, in parallel with NW Bio’s partnership with the Fraunhofer Institute in Germany that was announced last year. “We are pleased to be leading the way in bringing these novel immune therapies to patients in the UK,” commented Dr. Keyoumars Ashkan, Consultant (i.e., Specialist) Neurosurgeon, Reader (Associate Professor) in Neurosurgery and Lead for Neuro-Oncology at King’s College Hospital. “Brain cancers are some of the most lethal cancers, and there is a great need for new and better treatments. The positive data from the Phase I clinical trials in the U.S. were very encouraging in delaying disease progression and extending survival times, without significant toxic side effects. October 22, 2026 | The Bullish MHRA Approval Thesis

1. Why the Sequence Matters: August–October 2026
The developments following the August Commission on Human Medicines (CHM) meeting may represent a coordinated progression toward DCVax-L marketing authorization rather than isolated corporate announcements.

The bullish interpretation: NWBO may have resolved the significant CHM objections during September, with October representing the transition toward final regulatory processing and commercialization readiness.

2. Why NHSBT's Public Involvement Is the Strongest Operational Signal

The October NHS Blood and Transplant announcement is particularly significant because NHSBT confirmed that its teams were already supporting DCVax-L production.

Therapeutic Apheresis Services (TAS) performs leukapheresis to collect the patient's immune-cell starting material.

Cellular and Molecular Therapies (CMT) provides specialized cell processing and handling.

Advent/Sawston provides the established DCVax-L manufacturing infrastructure.

Leeds and Oxford are the initial NHSBT locations, with phased expansion to additional English locations being explored.

Crucially, NWBO described the collaboration as the culmination of months of joint work.

The bullish hypothesis is that this work may have supplied the contractual, quality-control, traceability and operational documentation needed to address some of CHM's August concerns.

If the remaining objections related to manufacturing logistics or control of patient-specific starting materials, the NHSBT arrangement could have been particularly relevant.

3. Why Another CHM Meeting May Not Be Required

MHRA's National Assessment Procedure, Section 2.6, explains that following written or oral representations, the MHRA considers CHM's final advice and proceeds toward granting or refusing marketing authorization.

The published procedure does not require another routine CHM meeting after final advice has been delivered.

Therefore, if NWBO completed oral representations at the September 24–25 meeting and CHM was satisfied, the next stage could be the MHRA's internal assessment, final compliance checks, product documentation and licensing decision.

An additional information request remains possible, but another CHM meeting is not automatically required.
This supports the hypothesis that October's “under assessment” wording may refer to final regulatory processing rather than another scientific hearing.

4. Why GZ's Reported October 14 Email Matters

Why would NWBO investor relations even mention the upcoming quarterly filing as a possible decision milestone if management believed the application still faced an extended, unresolved scientific hearing process?

If George Zavoico's reported hope for an announcement before the third-quarter 10-Q is accurately quoted, it deserves consideration alongside the other developments.

A mid-November horizon is unusually near-term for a regulatory process that has already lasted almost three years.

My most bullish interpretation is that management may believe the substantive regulatory issues are substantially behind it, leaving the timing of the final MHRA decision outside its control.

That is not equivalent to formal approval guidance, and the complete October 14 email has not been independently authenticated.

5. My Most Bullish Reconstruction of What Happened Behind Closed Doors

August: CHM identifies unresolved concerns and recommends oral representations.
Early September: NWBO and Advent finalize critical manufacturing and quality arrangements, potentially including NHSBT collection and processing responsibilities. The September 7 and 15 manufacturing authorizations document continuing regulatory oversight of those activities.

Late September: Under this hypothesis, NWBO presents its clinical evidence, manufacturing documentation and operational arrangements to CHM. The Commission is satisfied and delivers final advice.

Early October: MHRA continues the application assessment, potentially undertaking final compliance, legal and licensing work. NHSBT publicly confirms the operational collaboration.

Mid-October: NWBO investor relations reportedly expresses hope for a near-term regulatory announcement.

The combined sequence suggests the possibility that NWBO has moved from answering major regulatory objections to awaiting a final licensing determination.

6. My Most Aggressive Scenario — October 22, 2026
October 22 – November 16, 2026

A plausible near-term UK marketing authorization window if the September CHM objections were resolved.

In this scenario, no additional CHM meeting is necessary because final advice has already been provided. MHRA completes its remaining regulatory procedures and communicates its decision.

This is an intentionally aggressive bullish scenario, not a confirmed MHRA schedule.

7. Stress Test

Three unanswered questions could materially change this interpretation:
Did the September oral hearing occur, and was CHM satisfied? Its occurrence and outcome remain unconfirmed.

Were the NHSBT agreements part of the regulatory response? NHSBT's operational involvement is verified, but its direct role in resolving CHM objections has not been established.

Were the outstanding objections primarily manufacturing-related? If CHM's remaining concerns involved unresolved clinical efficacy or comparator bias, manufacturing agreements alone would not settle them.

The September licences also do not themselves constitute DCVax-L marketing authorization, and the NHSBT announcement confirms initial operational locations rather than a fully deployed national treatment network.

My Conclusion

If I adopt the September-hearing hypothesis, the most coherent bullish explanation is that NWBO has already completed the consequential scientific and operational responses, and the MHRA is now finishing the authorization process.

The concentrated progression from August CHM objections to September manufacturing authorizations, a possible September oral hearing, October's NHSBT announcement and reported management optimism is consistent with an advanced regulatory process.
The strongest implication is not that approval is guaranteed, but that the next significant announcement could plausibly be the marketing authorization decision itself rather than another scientific presentation.
The pieces may already be in place. What remains is the MHRA's decision.

Europe in Flames, India on Edge: The Gen-Z Revolt

Europe is witnessing a wave of youth unrest, with demonstrations, clashes, looting and, in some places, curfews. From France to Belgium, Spain, Portugal, Italy and Greece, Generation Z is taking to the streets. India, too, has witnessed youth protests in New Delhi. But the demands are different, hence what do these young people really want?

In Europe, economic frustration is the common thread. High rents, housing shortages, rising living costs, inflation, tuition fees and inadequate education funding have left many young people feeling that a decent future is slipping beyond their reach.

In France, what began with grievances over classroom shortages broadened into a much larger political confrontation. Trade unions and left-wing groups joined the demonstrations, adding their own demands. What began as protest became, in some places, disorder and violence.

President Trump would offer a different explanation: uncontrolled Muslim immigration. Muslims account for roughly 10% of France’s population, and immigration has become a contentious issue involving integration, public services and competing cultural values. But blaming immigration alone for the unrest would be simplistic. Housing costs, economic pressures and political discontent are independent grievances that cannot be dismissed.

Elsewhere in Europe, many youth protests have focused on affordable housing, education and the cost of living. Some have involved peaceful encampments and grassroots fundraising; others have escalated into clashes. It is important to distinguish legitimate demonstrations from violence rather than treating every protest as part of a single conspiracy.

India’s protests, however, have taken on a more overtly political character. Social media helped mobilise young demonstrators in New Delhi, while questions arose over political backing and funding. Their demands centred on the Chief Election Commissioner and the removal of allegedly illegal voters from electoral rolls.

The controversy reflects a deeper political struggle. Opposition parties in India have accused the government and election authorities of wrongdoing, while supporters of voter-roll revisions argue that electoral lists must be revised and accurate, preventing illegals to vote. 

Large gatherings of energetic young people can quickly become difficult to control. Allegations of police brutality, like claims of deliberate provocation, deserve independent scrutiny. Arrests, releases and heightened surveillance may contain immediate unrest, but they do not resolve the underlying grievances.

Political leaders across the spectrum in India have supported youth protests when doing so advances their own interests. Yet the young demonstrators deserve to be heard in their own right, not merely used as instruments in a larger political contest.

The lesson for governments in Europe and India is clear: young people cannot be silenced indefinitely when they see their economic prospects shrinking or their political voice ignored. Governments may restore order through force, but lasting stability requires action on housing, employment, education, fairness and public accountability.

Generation Z has demonstrated its ability to mobilise. The real test is whether governments respond with meaningful reforms—or simply wait for the next eruption.

Podcast Summary | The Shawn Ryan Show: #350 Mike Hayes - The Navy SEAL in Obama’s Situation Room During the Captain Phillips Rescue

Overview
Mike Hayes’s story is less about heroics than about preparation, restraint, and the moral weight of command. A retired Navy SEAL commander who served in the White House during the Captain Phillips hijacking and later led a 2,000-person special operations task force in Afghanistan, Hayes frames elite performance as trainable calm, deliberate judgment, and loyalty to the person next to you. His near-hostage experience in Peru, his refusal to abandon a teammate, and his leadership choices in Kosovo and Afghanistan converge on one idea: character is revealed in how you carry risk for others, and it is built long before the crisis arrives.

Key Themes
- Survival under captivity came from composure and de-escalation, not force: staying unarmed and appearing non-threatening removed the captors’ reason to kill.
- Loyalty to a swim buddy overrode an easy escape; Hayes chose a shared fate over personal safety and frames that choice as identity, not calculation.
- Elite teams execute through implicit coordination built in debriefs, where teammates learn how each other thinks rather than merely what to do.
- Leadership means slowing down to explain hard calls in person, especially when a decision protects lives at the cost of mission optics.
- Military service is a family sacrifice, and leaders who understand that make service easier for others rather than harder.
- Resilience is largely trainable: repeated exposure to discomfort makes operating outside a comfort zone familiar, though innate calm still matters.
- Restraint in the field—not firing when firing was possible—repeatedly proved decisive in surviving ambiguous, high-risk situations.
- Giving back is treated as an obligation: book profits, speaking fees, and quiet initiative are directed toward Gold Star families and recognition of the fallen.

Detailed Summary
Hayes’s career spanned South America, Kosovo, Iraq, and Afghanistan, along with White House work under Presidents Bush and Obama, including START treaty negotiations with Russia and the response to the Captain Phillips hijacking. He commanded a 2,000-person special operations task force in Afghanistan and served as deputy commander for special operations in Anbar Province, Iraq. After the military he worked at Bridgewater, became COO of VMware, and is a managing director at Insight Partners. He wrote Never Enough and Missiondriven, and donates all book profits and speaking fees to his charity, which has paid off 12 Gold Star widow mortgages.

The Peru incident anchors the conversation. Traveling with another SEAL, Ken, Hayes stayed back in Lima while their squad flew to Iquitos. Unarmed and in an SUV, the two were pinned in by cars, and armed men dressed as police forced them into their own vehicle. Fluent in Spanish, Hayes told the captors they were economists and desk workers at the embassy. They were driven around for about an hour while the captors threatened torture and execution. When the vehicle slowed to roughly 20 to 25 miles per hour, Hayes had a real chance to jump. He did not take it, because he could not live with himself if Ken were killed.

Instead he translated for Ken so his friend could comply with the captors, and he used the translation to slip coded English information, including a real embassy switchboard number, gambling that the captors did not understand English. Eventually they were let out at gunpoint in a dark neighborhood. They walked fast, hid behind a tree, and the captors drove off with the vehicle. Hayes attributes survival to the captors concluding the two were not actually training Navy SEALs; the same captors later killed another woman on the same streets who panicked. He notes that being unarmed likely saved them, since weapons would have given the captors reason to kill—despite his disagreement with the embassy policy against riding around armed.

Throughout the ordeal he thought about his fiancée and immediate family, and he invokes a St. Christopher medal she gave him reading safe in my heart always. He offers no tidy answer for why they were released. His mindset during the escape was that the longer the shot, the greater the chance of injury rather than instant death, and that it was either going to be now or never. He stresses the lesson to be missed: in a pre-cellphone era, no one would have known where they were for about 48 hours. After the hijacking he felt almost invincible for two or three weeks, a feeling echoed by a sister-platoon member who survived a helicopter crash and shared the same if that did not get me, nothing will sensation.

On resilience, Hayes argues training repeatedly stretches limits until operating outside a comfort zone becomes familiar, though some innate ability to stay calm and weigh options matters. He distinguishes doers, who keep generating contingency plans until a problem is solved, from people who shut down or cancel days and weeks when crisis hits. He cites a Christian Craig Head interview in which a saved victim described shutting down and calling a crisis hotline, calling that response the majority of humanity while noting that guys like us do not shut down. Calm is treated as a deliberate value: calm breeds calm, excitement breeds excitement. In business crises such as departures, lawsuits, and advertisers leaving, he cannot sleep until he has roughly 10 different plans and works through them one by one.

A core leadership principle runs through the conversation: never confuse outcomes with activity, and define what success looks like in a crisis before choosing actions—beware of fast trains to the wrong station. He cites pre-cellphone contingency planning with rally points around the city in case of separation. An Iraq anecdote illustrates trained reflex: during a houseborne IED alarm in a house with roughly 14 people, Hayes and Josh Cox dove out a second-floor stairwell window, felt no pain, and their hell-week whistle-drill training kicked in; they laughed once the house did not explode.

His path into the SEALs came through family and exposure. His grandfather was Naval Academy class of 1940, a career naval officer present at Pearl Harbor on the USS Maryland who later commanded a 35-plane bomber squadron. His father was a career naval supply officer whose first duty was on a submarine. Hayes entered ROTC at Holy Cross in 1989, partly motivated by the scholarship so his siblings could attend college, and first encountered the SEAL community at a 1989 campus ceremony honoring John Connors, a SEAL killed on the runway in Panama, reinforced by a Reader’s Digest article titled The Measure of a Man. He chose the man-versus-man challenge of SEAL training over the man-versus-machine appeal of being a pilot after flying off an aircraft carrier, and he was one of 19 graduates from a class of 120. Pre-9/11 officer career paths allowed only two operational deployments, so he deliberately took a staff tour in Germany to become a better platoon commander.

In Kosovo, his platoon photographed illegal Russian arms transfers to Kosovo Serb forces during a special reconnaissance mission. A major ordered the team to continue mission despite compromise concerns; Hayes consulted his five teammates, and they collectively decided to continue because the perceived risk was not extremely high. Soon after, they counted 19 armed men actively hunting them. The team fired no shots, which Hayes credits for their survival, and the intelligence reached the presidential daily briefing the next morning. Chad Wilkinson and Adam Nubold rapidly plotted enemy force locations from an OH-58 Kiowa link arranged by Jimmy Graham, helping extract the team. He was denied leave to attend his daughter’s birth during that deployment, a decision that shaped his leadership philosophy: never let people around him miss their child’s birth, and make service easier for others rather than harder.

After 9/11, his task unit deployed to Germany expecting to enter northern Iraq through Turkey, but Turkey refused passage for US forces, leaving the unit ready for war but unused and deeply demoralized. Hayes called a Pentagon staff officer listed on a deployment order to get his task force inserted; the message was corrected and reissued about four hours later, but senior commanders confronted him and the deployment ultimately did not lead to action. He applied for the Paul Mill Fellowship, two years of fully funded graduate school with one Navy officer selected per year, while in Germany, and was the first SEAL ever selected, attending Harvard Kennedy School from 2003 to 2005.

After the June 28, 2005 helicopter loss known as Red Wings, in which 11 SEALs and eight Nightstalkers were killed, he was assigned to SEAL Team 10 and tasked with reconstituting the force and supporting survivors. He made chaplain and psychologist support mandatory for all SEALs involved, breaking cultural ground in special operations mental health care, and the chaplain and psychologist originally scheduled for three or four days stayed about a month. He emphasizes maintaining mission readiness while on deployment and, without judging the operational call, references the adage that a compromised team should assume compromise and exfiltrate.

As SEAL Team 2 commander in Afghanistan in 2012, he canceled a special recon mission targeting roughly 40 Taliban because two Taliban were moving up the hill toward the small unit. He prioritized the lives of the SEALs and Green Berets over potential gains, and though the team saw him as risk-averse, he flew out to explain his reasoning in person, drawing on the Kosovo lesson. He describes a principle-based debrief approach separating data, logic, and conclusion, teaching SEALs how to think rather than what to think, and admitting when he was wrong. Risk versus reward has no formulaic answer; special operators aim to never fight fair, ethically and legally, and stack odds in their favor.

He recalls meeting Brian Woullette as a new guy at SEAL Team 4 in 1994, initially clashing, then building mutual respect before Woullette was killed in action by an IED in a Humvee along with three others. Hayes cold-emailed Boston Globe reporter Shaughnessy to dedicate a Red Sox game to Brian, arranging roughly 50 donated tickets so the family could take over a section near the end of a sold-out season. The family was brought onto the mound at Fenway Park, Brian’s picture appeared on the big screen, and about 35,000 fans gave a roughly four-minute standing ovation. His mother later tied the 2004 World Series win to the dedication and related omens. Hayes pauses at the Waltham square named after Brian to say a prayer, and he deliberately acknowledges people memorialized in road or place names, especially service members.

Elite performance, he argues, is speed, agility, precision, and especially the ability to execute without communicating—knowing teammates so well you can anticipate their actions, built through repeated debriefs and learning how teammates think. That principle applies to sports teams as well as military teams. Deployment sacrifice extends to spouses and children; on a bus returning from the airfield, he broke down realizing he was back in America and no longer had to worry about roads blowing up. His daughter once made a deployment box for a friend’s daughter with about 300 note cards, one for each day of a 10-month deployment, including prompts like wearing her dad’s t-shirt as a pretend hug. Service is a family unit effort, and Hayes wishes more Americans understood its depth.

text:
Why Did El-Sayed Hide With AOC in the U.P.?
While El-Sayed went leaf peeping Up North, Rogers got on like a house on fire with Detroit voters

By Jay Murray @Stainless31 

The trajectory of Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate campaign last week sends mixed messages about his comfort level as the 2026 midterm elections enter the home stretch.

Spending over a week in Northern Michigan, including a day in the sparsely populated Upper Peninsula, the good “doctor” would appear content with where he stands in Metro Detroit with black and Jewish voters—two essential demographics El-Sayed has struggled to win.

Sensing potential blood in the water, Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers has aggressively campaigned in Detroit like no Republican has in decades—possibly ever—in an attempt to reach black voters, shocking pundits and activists across the political spectrum.

In an off-the-cuff remark about Rogers’ intensive campaigning in Detroit, prominent Detroit political activist Sam Riddle stated, “I’ve never seen a Republican do this in Detroit, ever.”

Republican strategists closely watching the race between Rogers and El-Sayed offered several theories as to why the latter decided to escape Metro Detroit so close to Election Day.

“He thinks he’s already won, and he’s getting out of sight for a few days to avoid adversarial media and tough questions about Hasan Piker and Iran,” said one consultant.

“He promised to campaign with AOC, but he doesn’t want to drag her around chasing working-class voters [in Metro Detroit] who find her repugnant,” said another Republican politico.

Democratic voters I spoke with in western Wayne County were quick to pounce on those theories, citing the idea that he’s fighting for every last Michigan resident, but given the minuscule number of low-propensity voters spread out over 300 square miles of rural Michigan, it’s hard to buy into that idea while Rogers continued to pound pavement in urban Democratic enclaves.

Adding fuel (and scrutiny) to the idea that El-Sayed is making unforced errors down the final base path is the last-minute transfer of $1 million into his campaign from AOC, pouring additional cold water on his promise not to accept money from big donors while running ads promoting the idea of keeping money out of politics.

Now back downstate, the good doctor appears stuck in a pickle as a now-fired field organizer was caught on hidden camera claiming El-Sayed has accepted campaign funding from foreign sources.

Meanwhile, on the same day, film of Mike Rogers working behind the counter of a popular Detroit bar playing grab-ass with black voters showed a more comfortable image of an outsider actually enjoying himself with people not traditionally tied to conservative politics.

What does all this mean for a Senate race with every eye in the nation watching?

In polling commissioned by the Enjoyer last month, Republican enthusiasm was in the gutter, and all trends appeared to favor Democrats across the state, including El-Sayed. But with absentee ballots showing tepid returns thus far, Democrats might be feeling anxiety about their own chances.

El-Sayed’s fumbling of easy geopolitical questions on Israel didn’t play well last week, and various Jewish Democrats for Rogers groups appear energized and actively hammering Metro Detroit with signs and social media ads.

The big guns are coming out. Both former President Obama and current President Donald Trump are coming to Metro Detroit for campaign stops on behalf of El-Sayed and Rogers, respectively.

But Trump is less popular than a virus, and the last time Obama stumped hard for anyone—Kamala in 2024—he ended up scolding black males and setting the former vice president’s campaign on fire with urban voters across the country.

Perhaps the secret weapon for Mike Rogers is his wife. Sparking a nuclear meltdown last Wednesday among prominent Democrats in Lansing, who degraded into Bluesky copium rage, Kristi Rogers handed out gas cards to Detroit voters.

The Enjoyer spoke with a retired Detroit male voter who met Ms. Rogers and stated, “sheeeit, that is a good-looking white lady.”

Pre-Market Update | Friday, October 23, 2026

Good morning, traders and investors!

Wall Street is heading into Friday on shaky ground following yesterday's sharp technology selloff. Stock futures are pointing lower, oil prices are climbing, and investors are becoming increasingly selective about where they're putting their money.

Here are the big stories I'm watching this morning and, more importantly, what they mean for our trading decisions.

 1. Technology Stocks Are Feeling the Pressure

The Nasdaq 100 plunged nearly 3% yesterday, its worst session since June, as concerns surrounding AI spending and valuations resurfaced.

Here's what's interesting: Investors aren't necessarily questioning the long-term potential of artificial intelligence. They're questioning how quickly these enormous investments will translate into profits.

My takeaway: A great company isn't automatically a great investment at any price. Watch the semiconductor sector and the Nasdaq closely. If the market can't hold a rebound, I'd be cautious about jumping into beaten-down technology stocks too early.

2. Oil Prices Are Becoming a Bigger Problem

Oil is back in the spotlight as escalating tensions in the Middle East threaten energy supplies. Brent crude briefly climbed above $114 a barrel.

Higher oil prices can put renewed pressure on inflation, corporate profit margins, and consumer spending.

My takeaway: Keep an eye on energy stocks, transportation companies, and Treasury yields. Sustained higher oil prices could complicate the Federal Reserve's next moves and create additional volatility across the market.

3. Strong Earnings Aren't Enough Anymore

Western Digital reported impressive revenue growth of 55%, yet its shares declined in pre-market trading. Meanwhile, investors continue to scrutinize the enormous spending commitments from companies such as Meta.

This tells us something important about the current environment: Expectations are extremely high, and even good results can disappoint when a stock is priced for perfection.

My takeaway: Pay attention to how stocks react to earnings, not just the earnings numbers themselves. Price action often tells us more about institutional sentiment than the headlines.

4. American Express Offers a Look at Consumer Strength

American Express raised its full-year earnings outlook, supported by continued spending among affluent consumers.

That's encouraging, but it also highlights the importance of looking beneath the surface of consumer spending. Different income groups can experience the same economy very differently.

My takeaway: Consumer-related earnings will be particularly valuable as we assess whether higher interest rates and energy costs are beginning to affect spending patterns.

5. Two Economic Reports Could Move Markets Today

We have two important releases coming after the opening bell:

- 9:45 AM ET: Flash Manufacturing and Services PMI
- 10:00 AM ET: University of Michigan Consumer Sentiment and Inflation Expectations

These reports could influence interest-rate expectations, Treasury yields, and the direction of equities heading into the weekend.

My Trading Game Plan

With technology under pressure, oil rising, and uncertainty surrounding interest rates, this isn't an environment where I want to chase stocks simply because they've pulled back.

I'll be watching SPY, QQQ, and DIA for signs of stabilization, paying particular attention to market breadth and whether buyers can sustain any early rebound.

Remember, we don't have to trade every day. Sometimes protecting capital and waiting for a higher-probability setup is the smartest trade we can make.

Trade the charts, manage your risk, and don't let the headlines dictate your decisions.

Have a great Friday, everyone!

Expert Report Must Be Admissible or it Will be Excluded

No Breach of Contract no Bad Faith

Post 4568
Posted on October 23, 2026 by Barry Zalma

A Party Cannot Designate One Witness While Submitting An Undifferentiated Product Of That Witness And An Undesignated Collaborator.

Post 4568

In Dustin Cain; Amanda Cain v. State Farm Fire and Casualty Company, No. 25-60442, United States Court of Appeals, Fifth Circuit (October 16, 2026) Dustin and Amanda Cain sought homeowners’ insurance benefits after a tree fell on their Mississippi home on August 27, 2022. State Farm concluded that the tree caused only a roof puncture and that other damage resulted from excluded long-term conditions. It paid $10,042.90 and later an additional $3,130.08.

The Cains relied on an engineering report and contractor estimate asserting substantially greater damage, sued for breach of contract and related relief, and designated Sean Fee as their sole expert. Fee’s report and a later repair estimate were jointly authored with Jim Irmiter, but neither document identified which opinions, work, or reasoning belonged to Fee.

The repair estimate was also served on the discovery deadline, months after the expert-designation deadline and without prior leave.

The district court struck the expert materials, entered summary judgment for State Farm because the Cains lacked admissible proof of causation and damages, and denied post-judgment relief.

LAW

The US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit reviews exclusion of expert testimony and denial of Rule 59(e) relief for abuse of discretion, but reviews summary judgment de novo.

Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 26(a)(2)(B)(i) requires a retained expert’s report to state completely the opinions that the witness will express and the bases and reasons for them. The expert must offer an independent opinion rather than serve as another person’s mouthpiece. A joint report may be permissible when each contributing expert is designated and the report clearly attributes opinions to each witness.

Under Mississippi law a bad-faith claim cannot survive without an underlying breach of the insurance contract.

DISCUSSION

The Cains argued that Fee and Irmiter had jointly reached a unified opinion and that any uncertainty concerned weight rather than admissibility. The Fifth Circuit rejected that position. The reports merely said both men contributed to, reviewed, and concurred in the contents; they did not reveal what work Fee performed, which conclusions were his, or the bases for his conclusions.

The problem was heightened because Irmiter was not designated as an expert. Without attribution, State Farm and the court could not meaningfully test Fee’s methodology or reliability. Once the expert evidence was excluded, the Cains conceded they could not prove the claimed damages. Their extra-contractual claims also failed because Mississippi bad-faith liability requires a viable underlying contract claim.

ANALYSIS

The decision turns on expert attribution, not a categorical ban on collaborative work. Its practical rule is that a party cannot designate one witness while submitting an undifferentiated product of that witness and an undesignated collaborator. Clear attribution is necessary to satisfy disclosure duties, permit effective deposition and cross-examination, and allow the trial court to perform its reliability-screening role.

The evidentiary ruling was dispositive because causation and repair costs were technical issues outside ordinary lay knowledge. The case also illustrates that the compounding risk of late expert supplementation. The appellate holding rests principally on the reports’ failure to identify Fee’s own opinions, waiting until the discovery deadline left little opportunity to cure the defect.

CONCLUSIONS

The Fifth Circuit affirmed. Before expert testimony may be subjected to the adversarial process, it must first be admissible. Here, the admissibility of the proposed expert reports was the issue, not their weight. Because the Johnsons' breach of contract claim fails, their bad faith claim necessarily fails. The district court correctly granted summary judgment dismissing all of the Cains' claims after it struck their proposed expert testimony and report.

ZALMA OPINION

In Federal Practice a designated expert must identify which opinions, work, or reasoning belonged to the designated expert. When the parties submitted an expert report in the name of a single expert when a second expert admittedly participated in the creation of the report but did not identify who did what to the report. Since it was filed late, could not be corrected, and did not identify who did what to the report. That failure caused the report and estimate to be rejected by the court and the plaintiff unable to prove their damages.

text:
“Sir” Allen Stanford offered a $20 million prize for one cricket match in 2008. less than four years later he was sentenced to 110 years in prison for a $7 billion fraud.

the match was played in Antigua on November 1, 2008. England faced the Stanford Superstars, a team led by Chris Gayle, with $20 million going to the winners. the Superstars won and England were all out for 99. it was part of a $100 million, five year cricket deal, and that June he had landed a helicopter at Lord’s with fake dollar notes on board.

Antigua and Barbuda had knighted him in 2006, and he went by Sir Allen. Forbes put his wealth at about $2 billion in 2008. according to the Justice Department he owned six private planes and a 112 foot yacht with support vessels.

the money came from depositors. his bank in Antigua sold certificates of deposit at premium rates, and prosecutors said only 10 to 15% of the assets were invested as promised. the rest went to his own businesses through undisclosed loans, while new deposits paid the people who wanted out. by 2008 depositors were owed more than $8 billion.

a jury convicted him on 13 of 14 counts in March 2012. on June 14 the judge sentenced him to 110 years and a $5.9 billion money judgment. Antigua had already taken the knighthood back.

after the collapse a receiver sold the contents of his Miami offices, about 25 truckloads valued at around $2 million. one buyer paid $1,500 for a leather chair, a cherry wood desk and a credenza.

in the video below, CNBC asks Sir Allen how his firm avoided the subprime crisis. he says they never understood the risk, so they did not take it. then he is asked if it is fun being a billionaire. he says yes three times.

who was really carrying the risk: Stanford or his depositors?
