text:
Leo Frank Answers 17 Questions About the Murder of Little Mary Phagan

The Atlanta Constitution, Monday, March 9, 1914, Pages 1 and 10

On Monday, March 9, 1914, The Atlanta Constitution published one of the most revealing interviews Leo Max Frank (April 17, 1884 – August 17, 1915) gave after his conviction for murdering 13-year-old Mary Phagan (June 1, 1899 – April 26, 1913).

The newspaper's editor was Clark Howell (September 21, 1863 – November 14, 1936), who had directed its editorial operations since 1897. Britt Craig (May 7, 1893 – March 18, 1919), one of its crime reporters, had been among the first journalists to enter the National Pencil Company basement after Mary's body was discovered on April 27, 1913.

Craig also testified at the coroner's inquest. The March interview has been associated with him, although the surviving article identifies its interviewer only as a newspaper representative. Craig died in 1919 at age 25 (Inquest, 4) (Howell, 5) (AC, 8).

Frank was held in the Fulton County Tower, fighting his conviction and death sentence. More than six months had passed since a jury unanimously found him guilty on August 25, 1913.

The newspaper presented 17 questions about weaknesses and contradictions in his defense, including his whereabouts, night watchman Newt Lee, the murder notes, suspected bloodstains, and allegations about his conduct toward female employees.

Many questions reflected arguments raised by Solicitor General Hugh Manson Dorsey (July 10, 1871 – June 11, 1948), who prosecuted Frank with Frank Arthur Hooper Sr., whose exact life dates remain unverified. Dorsey later governed Georgia from 1917 to 1921 (NGA, 9).

Frank answered in writing. His responses were not subject to cross-examination, but they can be compared with his earlier statements, the inquest, trial testimony, and Dorsey's closing argument.

Before the Murder: Did Frank Know Mary Phagan?

The prosecution challenged Frank's claim that he barely knew Mary, although she worked at the National Pencil Company.

Former employee John M. Gantt testified that Mary once visited the office to correct her working time. After Gantt helped her, Frank allegedly remarked that Gantt seemed to know Mary well.

Dewey Hewell testified that she had seen Frank place his hand on Mary's shoulder and call her by name.

Question five addressed Gantt's account. Frank denied it.

Dorsey argued that Frank knew more about Mary than he acknowledged. The defense maintained that the witnesses were mistaken or unreliable. The dispute concerned Frank's truthfulness, although it did not establish murder (BOE, 2).

Friday, April 25, 1913: Helen Ferguson and Mary's Pay

Employee Helen Ferguson testified that she asked Frank for Mary's wages and that he refused to release them.

Mary was owed $1.20. Her metal department work had stopped because materials were unavailable, so she returned Saturday to collect her pay.

The prosecution argued that Ferguson's testimony suggested Frank knew Mary would return personally.

Question four addressed Ferguson's request and whether Frank had said Mary would collect her own pay the following day.

Frank denied this, maintaining that Herbert Schiff handled payroll and Ferguson was mistaken.

The defense presented Schiff, Magnolia Kennedy, and Grace Hicks to challenge Ferguson's account.

Dorsey considered the dispute important because it concerned why Mary returned on April 26. The defense insisted Frank had not arranged her visit (BOE, 2).

Friday Evening: Why Did Frank Summon Newt Lee Early?

Newt Lee (born 1860; death date unknown), the factory's Black night watchman, testified that Frank instructed him to report at 4 p.m. Saturday, two hours earlier than usual.

Lee was approximately 52 or 53 during the investigation. His absence from identified 1930 census records raises the possibility that he died before April 1, 1930, although no death certificate, obituary, or burial record has confirmed this (NARA, 12).

Saturday was Confederate Memorial Day, and the factory was largely closed.

Question one asked why Frank later sent Lee away.

Frank said he had planned to attend a baseball game with his brother-in-law, Charles Ursenbach, but canceled because of bad weather and unfinished paperwork.

The prosecution considered Lee's instructions important because they affected who would be inside the factory.

Frank said Lee was no longer needed. Dorsey argued that Lee's absence allowed Frank to remain without the watchman making his rounds (AC, 1) (BOE, 2).

Saturday, April 26: Mary Phagan Goes to the Factory

Mary, age 13, traveled downtown to collect her wages at the National Pencil Company, 37–41 South Forsyth Street.

Frank's office was on the second floor, near Mary's metal department.

Frank acknowledged that Mary collected her pay, asked about the arrival of metal, and left. He estimated her arrival at 12:10 to 12:15 p.m.

The prosecution argued she was attacked shortly afterward.

Dr. H. F. Harris testified that her stomach contents suggested she suffered the fatal injury or died within approximately half an hour after eating. His estimate supported the prosecution's timetable, although digestion could not establish an exact time of death.

The defense challenged the medical estimate. Timing was critical when comparing the movements of Mary, Frank, Monteen Stover, Lemmie Quinn, and others (BOE, 2).

12:05 to 12:10 p.m.: Monteen Stover Cannot Find Frank

Fourteen-year-old Monteen Stover testified that she entered Frank's office around 12:05 p.m. to collect her wages and remained until approximately 12:10. Frank was absent.

This challenged his earlier statements that he remained in his office.

Dorsey argued Frank was missing because he was involved in attacking Mary in the metal department.

Questions eight and nine addressed Frank's estimated times and Stover's testimony.

Frank denied changing his account and suggested he might briefly have visited the toilet.

His March 1914 answer included:

"I may have stepped to the toilet for a minute or two."

Frank did not remember visiting the toilet at 12:05. He offered it as a possibility, just as he had during his August 18, 1913 courtroom statement.

Dorsey questioned why Frank, who described his activities in detail, could not remember leaving during such an important period.

The defense argued that a routine toilet visit could be forgotten and that an open safe door might have blocked Stover's view. However, Stover testified that she entered the inner office.

The precise relationship between Stover's visit and Mary's arrival remained disputed.

These five minutes became central to the prosecution's argument about Frank's whereabouts when Mary was believed to have been attacked (BOE, 2) (Dorsey, 3).

Could Mary Have Been Murdered Without Frank Hearing Anything?

Question two asked how Mary could have been murdered without Frank hearing or knowing about it.

Frank suggested someone attacked her near the bottom of the stairs after she left his office.

His desk was approximately 70 feet from the staircase. Heavy doors, thick flooring, open windows, and street noise could have prevented him from hearing a disturbance.

Dorsey disagreed.

James "Jim" Conley (born approximately 1886; death date unverified) testified that Mary was attacked on the second floor and that Frank enlisted his help to move her body.

Some later accounts report Conley's death in 1962, but that year remains unconfirmed by an established death certificate or obituary (Conley, 13).

The prosecution pointed to suspected bloodstains and hair near the metal department.

Frank placed the attack elsewhere. The dispute concerned where Mary was injured and whether Frank could have been unaware (BOE, 2).

Around 12:20 p.m.: The Forgotten Visit of Lemmie Quinn

Metal department foreman Lemmie Quinn testified that he visited Frank's office around 12:20 p.m. and spoke with him briefly.

His account helped the defense by placing Frank in his office shortly after Mary's reported arrival.

But Frank initially failed to mention Quinn's visit.

Question thirteen asked why.

Frank said he forgot until Quinn reminded him.

Dorsey considered the omission suspicious because Quinn's testimony could help establish Frank's whereabouts.

Question fourteen asked whether Frank instructed Quinn to remain silent until consulting his attorneys. Frank denied it.

The defense viewed Quinn's visit as important alibi evidence. The prosecution questioned the timing.

If Quinn arrived at 12:20, Conley's account faced difficulties explaining how the attack and subsequent events fit into the available minutes.

Dorsey questioned the precision of the estimates. The defense argued the prosecution's timetable was unreliable (BOE, 2).

Around 12:30 p.m.: Mrs. White Observes Frank

Mrs. J. A. White visited the factory while her husband worked on the fourth floor with Harry Denham.

She testified that Frank said he was preparing to leave and lock the building. She also saw him writing at a table.

Question eleven asked why Frank appeared anxious for her to leave and returned to his writing.

Frank denied hurrying her. He said he warned she might be locked inside after his departure.

He also disputed her description of him writing.

The prosecution considered her observations important because they concerned Frank's behavior after Mary's disappearance. Frank maintained that his actions were ordinary (BOE, 2).

Saturday Afternoon: Lee Leaves and Frank Continues Working

When Lee arrived around 4 p.m., Frank told him to leave and return by 6 p.m.

Frank said he had canceled the baseball game and was finishing paperwork.

Dorsey connected Lee's absence with Conley's testimony about helping Frank conceal Mary's body. Fewer people meant less chance of interruption.

Frank denied any improper purpose.

The prosecution challenged whether his paperwork established exactly when he completed his work. The defense maintained that his activities were ordinary factory business (BOE, 2) (Dorsey, 3).

Saturday Evening: Lee's Time Card and Frank's Telephone Call

Lee returned and began his nighttime rounds, recording them with regular punches on a time clock.

Question ten concerned Frank's changing description of Lee's time card.

Frank initially said it appeared correct. Later, he identified irregularities, including three one-hour intervals instead of the expected half-hour.

He explained that his first inspection was casual and that closer examination revealed the discrepancies.

The prosecution questioned whether Frank was attempting to direct suspicion toward Lee.

That evening, Lee testified, Frank telephoned to ask whether everything was all right. Lee said Frank had never previously called him that way.

Dorsey suggested Frank was checking whether Lee had discovered Mary's body.

Frank said he was concerned about former employee John Gantt, who had visited to retrieve shoes.

Both events were circumstantial evidence whose significance depended on which explanation the jury accepted (BOE, 2).

Sunday, April 27: Mary Phagan's Body Is Discovered

Early Sunday morning, Lee discovered Mary's body in the basement and telephoned police.

Officers responded with Atlanta Constitution reporter Britt Craig, among the first journalists to enter the basement. Craig's presence became part of the inquest record.

Two handwritten notes found near Mary's body became central to the investigation.

They appeared intended to direct suspicion toward Lee. Conley eventually admitted writing them.

The question was who planned their contents (Inquest, 4).

The Murder Notes: Frank Versus Conley

Conley testified that Frank directed him to write the notes after they moved Mary's body.

Dorsey argued they were intended to implicate Lee.

Question three asked whether Conley could have supplied some wording while following Frank's instructions.

Frank rejected this, arguing that an educated man would not arrange incriminating notes because handwriting could identify their author.

He also claimed he helped detectives establish Conley's ability to write through a document Conley signed when purchasing a watch.

The defense emphasized Conley's admitted authorship and changing statements.

Dorsey maintained that Conley's admissions and other evidence supported his accusations.

Conley admitted writing the notes. The dispute was who planned them and why.

Frank argued Conley acted alone. The prosecution maintained he followed Frank's instructions (BOE, 2) (Dorsey, 3).

Monday, April 28: Bloodstains and Hair Near the Metal Department

Machinist Robert Barrett reported suspected blood near the women's dressing room on the second floor.

He also described hair on a bench lathe handle.

A white substance, haskolene, appeared over part of the stained area.

Mell Stanford testified that he swept the area Friday and had not noticed the marks.

The prosecution argued these discoveries supported Conley's description of a second-floor attack.

Question six asked how Frank could have examined the stains after police removed samples.

Frank explained that detectives removed only a few wood chips, leaving much of the area available.

The defense questioned the evidence because the suspected blood was not conclusively identified as Mary's, nor was the hair scientifically established as hers.

Dorsey emphasized the location of the marks because they corresponded with the prosecution's theory (BOE, 2).

Why Did Frank Arrange for Private Detectives?

Question seven concerned Frank contacting Herbert Schiff instead of Sigmund Montag to hire private detectives.

Frank said Montag was unavailable and Schiff could arrange the investigation more conveniently.

He argued that hiring detectives demonstrated his desire to find the murderer.

The prosecution questioned Frank's statements and dealings with investigators.

Hiring detectives was not itself evidence of guilt. The dispute concerned whether Frank was assisting police or trying to influence their investigation (AC, 1).

May 1913: The Inquest, Indictment, and Conley Confrontation

Investigators compared Frank's accounts with factory employees and other witnesses.

The coroner's inquest examined Mary's death, physical evidence, and events of April 26.

On Saturday, May 24, a grand jury indicted Frank for murder.

Question twelve concerned his refusal to meet Conley face to face in jail.

Conley had accused Frank of involvement in Mary's death.

Frank said hostile detectives brought Conley to his cell, and he feared anything he said would be used against him.

The prosecution considered Conley's accusations central evidence.

The defense argued Conley was the murderer and had invented his account to escape responsibility.

Frank's refusal to confront Conley did not prove guilt. He was unwilling to meet his accuser under those conditions (AC, 1) (BOE, 2).

July 28 to August 25, 1913: Dorsey Presents the Prosecution's Case

Frank's trial began Monday, July 28, before Judge Leonard Strickland Roan (February 7, 1849 – March 23, 1915).

Roan died in New York City following an operation, less than two years after presiding over the trial (AJ, 10).

Dorsey led the prosecution, assisted by Hooper.

The prosecution connected Mary's visit, Stover's testimony, Quinn's forgotten visit, the second-floor evidence, Lee's time card, Frank's telephone call, the murder notes, and Conley's accusations.

Dorsey argued these facts reinforced one another.

In closing, he compared individual pieces of evidence to strands strengthened when twisted into a rope.

The defense challenged Conley's honesty, disputed the medical timetable, offered witnesses supporting Frank's whereabouts, and attacked the physical evidence.

The trial also included allegations about Frank's conduct toward female factory employees (Dorsey, 3) (BOE, 2).

The Character Witnesses and Frank's Explanation

Question fifteen asked why Frank did not insist that his attorneys cross-examine certain witnesses making damaging character allegations.

C. B. Dalton and others testified about Frank's alleged behavior involving women at the factory.

Frank denied the accusations.

He explained that his attorneys feared cross-examination would introduce further damaging allegations.

The prosecution considered some testimony relevant to conduct and possible motive.

The defense presented witnesses supporting Frank's reputation and called the accusations false.

Where witnesses were not cross-examined, their claims were not tested through that procedure. Allegations about his behavior toward women, however, were not direct proof of Mary's murder (BOE, 2) (AC, 1).

August 18, 1913: Frank Explains Himself to the Jury

Frank addressed the jury Monday, August 18.

Georgia law allowed criminal defendants to make courtroom statements without taking an oath or facing cross-examination.

Frank described his factory work, acknowledged Mary's visit, and denied murder.

He also suggested he might briefly have left his office to use the toilet.

Dorsey emphasized the apparent conflict with Frank's earlier account of remaining in his office.

The defense argued that a brief, ordinary activity could easily have been forgotten.

Frank repeated this explanation in March 1914 (BOE, 2).

August 25, 1913: The Jury Returns Its Verdict

After weeks of testimony, a Fulton County jury unanimously found Frank guilty on Monday, August 25, 1913.

Judge Roan sentenced him to death the following day.

Dorsey maintained that the combined evidence established guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.

The defense argued Conley was unreliable and serious doubts remained about the timetable and physical evidence.

Frank's attorneys continued their legal challenges, and by March 1914, the disputes had returned to the newspapers (BOE, 2).

March 9, 1914: The Final Two Questions

The newspaper's last two questions concerned the justification for Frank's arrest.

Question sixteen asked whether authorities were justified in arresting and prosecuting a man when a murdered girl had last visited his office and was later found dead in the building.

Frank acknowledged that those circumstances justified suspicion and investigation.

He argued that discovering Conley's involvement should have changed the prosecution's conclusions.

Question seventeen asked whether suspecting the man amounted to prejudice.

Frank accepted that initial suspicion was reasonable but maintained it should change when evidence pointed toward another person.

Frank therefore acknowledged that investigators originally had legitimate reasons to examine him.

Dorsey believed Conley's involvement strengthened the case against Frank. Frank insisted it established Conley's responsibility (AC, 1).

What the Atlanta Newspapers Reported

On March 9, The Atlanta Georgian reported Frank's new explanations and Dorsey's efforts to challenge defense evidence.

The newspaper discussed disputes involving the murder notes and other witnesses.

On Tuesday, March 10, The Atlanta Constitution reported that Frank's answers had attracted substantial public interest.

It also discussed the defense's interest in comments by former President William Howard Taft (September 15, 1857 – March 8, 1930) concerning public opinion and criminal trials. Taft served as president from 1909 to 1913 and later became chief justice of the United States (Taft, 14).

Frank's attorneys challenged the evidence and trial circumstances. The prosecution defended the verdict (AG, 6) (AC, 7).

Why the 17 Questions Are Still Important

The March 9, 1914 interview allows us to compare Frank's explanations with the evidence presented against him.

The questions covered Mary's pay envelope, Frank's movements around noon, Stover's missing-office account, Quinn's forgotten visit, Lee's time card, the murder notes, and physical evidence.

Frank denied accusations, offered possible explanations, and challenged prosecution witnesses.

His answer about Monteen Stover remains especially important.

Frank maintained he was working in his office while allowing that he might briefly have visited the toilet. He never claimed to remember doing so at the exact time Stover said he was absent.

Dorsey argued that Frank's uncertain recollections should be weighed against other testimony. The defense maintained that these differences were innocent and that the prosecution had not established precisely what happened.

The same disagreement extended to the murder notes, time card, physical evidence, and Conley's accusations.

The prosecution's case depended on connecting these circumstances. Frank's defense depended on challenging those connections and the witnesses supporting them.

The 17 questions show which weaknesses in Frank's account continued to trouble reporters and the public more than six months after his conviction.

They preserve what Frank himself said when given another opportunity to explain.

For anyone researching the murder of little Mary Phagan, this interview deserves to be read alongside the trial testimony and Dorsey's closing argument.

Your Watch Says You Are Unrecovered. Was It Just the Week Before Your Period? 📊

Recent research by Stanford and WHOOP analyzed over a million days of wrist data from 2,596 women and 42,759 cycles, revealing intriguing patterns in recovery scores related to the menstrual cycle. 

🔍 Heart-rate variability (HRV) tends to increase around your period but decreases in the days leading up to it, while resting heart rate shows the opposite trend. The fluctuations are significant, with HRV changing by about half of its average within a single cycle.

📉 This means that a "low HRV" reading could be due to various factors: your luteal phase, lack of sleep, stress, or even an illness. Your wearable device can sense something is off but can’t pinpoint the exact cause.

🛌 Sleep plays a critical role too! Women averaging six hours of sleep per night experienced more irregular cycles compared to those who slept closer to eight hours. 

This valuable data comes from regular-cycle, health-conscious users not on hormonal contraception—showing how individual baselines can offer insights beyond population averages.

Stay informed and track your cycle effectively! For more insights and support, follow Fertility Plus.

text:
I used to think playing 3-4 games a week would make me eventually throw harder.

But at 16, I was still only throwing 78.

Because games aren't built for velocity development.

If you've got a game coming up, you might not train as hard during the week, because you don't want to be tired or sore for the big day.

Because of that, you never push your body hard enough to throw harder and actually improve.

So I started swapping games for training days.

Instead of throwing 100 pitches on a Saturday, I'd do a pull-down day.

Instead of a midweek bullpen, I'd do a plyo velo day.

Instead of saving my legs for game day, I'd lift heavy and progressively overload, adding weight every session.

That, plus a lot of eating and lifting, took me from 78 to the upper 80s.

16 months after I started, I was throwing 96.

I got an offer from Stanford and signed with the Phillies.

I’m not saying to stop playing completely.

Playing games is necessary for your development as a pitcher.

They’re fun and teach you how to compete.

But if I started all over again and my goal was to get to the D1 or professional level, I’d play one game a week and spend the rest of my time getting better at the thing that actually gets players noticed.

text:
I have had some serious, good-faith engagement here, and I genuinely appreciate it. I have been writing about this for a decade, and came to the idea of tokenizing assets long before most (and I have the receipts). I still think it's an important use case for the tech, and I look forward to seeing how it develops. 
But the reason I'm poking on claims like this is because post M2020 and SIBOS this year, I'm becoming increasingly vexed by the sheer weight of balderdash being thrown around regarding asset tokenization.
Will it be more efficient? Sure. Will it change markets? Sure. Will it also introduce significant risks to global markets, some of which could be catastrophic to a wider swath of investors? Certainly. Do those saying "Trillions and trillions of dollars will be unlocked" have any clue what that means? Almost certainly not. They are selling the layers on which they hope those trillions will be recorded. 
When it's all upside being offered with no costs, it's a sales pitch.

📊 𝗗𝗲𝗲𝗽 𝗗𝗶𝘃𝗲: 𝗚𝗮𝗿𝘄𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗛𝗶-𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵 𝗙𝗶𝗹𝗺𝘀 𝗤𝟮 𝗙𝗬𝟮𝟳 𝗘𝗮𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝗖𝗮𝗹𝗹🚀

🏢 Company Overview: What Does Garware Hi-Tech Films Do?

Garware Hi-Tech Films is a global material science company that makes high-value specialty films, such as sun control, paint protection, and architectural window films, and sells them in 90+ countries.

🧩 Segments: Consumer Products Division (CPD, 73% of H1 FY27 revenue) and Industrial Products Division (IPD, 27%). ⚙️

🎞️ Product Mix (Q2 FY27): Sun Control Films 51% of revenue, Paint Protection Films 24%, plus fast-growing Architectural Window Films. Value-added products make up 86% of H1 revenue. 🛠️

🔬 Technology: PDLC switchable privacy films, nano-IR heat rejection, non-fading dyes, and 15-year adhesives. 75% internal TPU film integration. Strategic partnership with Lubrizol for aliphatic TPU resins. 🧪

🌍 Geography (Q2 FY27): US 51%, Europe 15%, India 20%, Middle East & RoW 12%. Exports are 80% of revenue. 14 international application studios (2 added in the US in Q2). 🌐

🏠 D2C Push: "Garware Home Solution" has 14 studios, targeting 50 by December 2027. 🏬

🌐 Industry Structure

PPF Penetration: India PPF penetration is ~3% of new car sales (0.1% in 2020) vs ~20% in the US and China. 🚗

Market Share: ~60% in Indian PPF and 60–65% in domestic automotive sun control films. 👑

Pricing Power: Pricing vs global leaders has moved from 30–40% of benchmark 3–4 years ago to 85–120% now. 💰

Architectural Films vs Glass: 20–30% cost savings, 99.9% UV rejection (vs 70% for glass), 20–30% higher heat rejection, and anti-shatter safety. 🏢

Trade Protection: Anti-dumping duty applications against cheap Chinese PPF imports have been recommended by the Ministry of Commerce and are being pursued with the Finance Ministry. 🛡️

📈 Financial Performance

Q2 FY27 (Record Quarter):

Revenue: ₹696 Crores (+22% YoY, +10% QoQ), close to the ₹700 Cr quarterly mark. 🚀

EBITDA: ₹189 Crores (+42% YoY). Margin expanded 377 bps YoY to 27.2%. 💰

PAT: ₹129 Crores (+42% YoY). 🎯

H1 FY27 Consolidated:

Revenue: ₹1,329 Crores (+25% YoY). 📊

EBITDA: ₹381 Crores (+49% YoY). ⚡

PBT: ₹350 Crores (+51% YoY), with margin up 464 bps to 26.3%. 📈

PAT: ₹262 Crores (+50% YoY). Cash Profit: ₹293 Crores (+46% YoY). 💵

Balance Sheet & Inflows:

Cash: ₹933 Crores as of September 30, 2026, with no debt dependency. 🏦

Working Capital: 29 days (vs 28 days in FY26). 🔄

Tariff Reversals: ~₹31 Cr received so far (₹11 Cr retained, ₹20 Cr passed to customers). A further ~₹30 Cr is expected in Q3 FY27 (₹16 Cr retained, booked as a COGS reduction). 🧾

🔮 Growth Guidance

FY27 Revenue: Reaffirmed at >₹2,500 Crores, trending toward ~₹2,600 Crores. 🚀

FY28 Revenue: Targeting ₹3,000+ Crores. 📈

Peak Revenue Potential: Existing capacity plus upcoming capex supports a ₹3,500 Crore run rate. 🏭

Architectural: Run rate of ~₹400 Cr, targeted to reach ₹1,000 Cr over the medium term. Its share of window film sales is to rise from 30% to 50%. 🏢

External Merchant TPU: 25% of TPU capacity is for external sales, expected to add ₹75–100 Cr in FY28. 🔌

Garware Home Solution (D2C): ₹50 Cr (Year 1) → ₹100 Cr (Year 2) → ₹200 Cr (Year 3). 🏠

Overall: 25–30% CAGR targeted across domestic and export markets. 🌍

💰 Margin Guidance

FY27 EBITDA Margin: Upgraded by 200 bps to 27% ± 2% (from 25% ± 2%). 📊

FY28–FY31: Base of 27%+, plus 150–200 bps from internal TPU backward integration, for an effective run rate of 28–28.5%+. ⚡

Margins by Vertical: 🎯
Top architectural and sun control products: 40–45% (mid-tier 30–35%)
PPF: 20–25%
External merchant TPU: ~35%
D2C studios: 10–15% premium over B2B distributor sales
Industrial Products (commodity base film): 10–12%

Seasonality: Q1 is peak (~30%), Q2 is strong (27.2%), Q3 is seasonally softer, and Q4 rebounds. 🌦️

🏭 Strategic Customer Pipeline & Volume Visibility

Anchor Customer: The top customer is ~30% of revenue, backed by long-term supply agreements and deep technical integration with global auto and EV OEMs. 🤝

Global Network: 14 application studios and 4 new international distributors added. 🌍

Domestic Architecture & Commercial: 3 channel partners added in Q2, with pitches to malls, commercial developers, and hospitality chains. 🏢

D2C Rollout: Studios went from 9 to 14 in H1, with 12 more planned in Q3 across Delhi NCR and Mumbai. 🏬

Lubrizol Co-Marketing: Joint OEM outreach at global platforms such as the SEMA Show in the US. 🚗

📊 𝗖𝗮𝗽𝗮𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗨𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 & 𝗖𝗮𝗽𝗲𝘅

Current Utilization (Q2 FY27): SCF at 75%, PPF at 73% (on a line commissioned less than a year ago). ⚙️

Trajectory: Both lines expected near 100% (90–95% practical peak) by Q1/Q2 FY28, with fungible capacity supporting volume growth. 📈

TPU Film Line (Aliphatic): On track for commissioning in Q3 FY27, with 75% captive supply for PPF and 25% for merchant sales. 🔌

Solar Control Film Expansion (₹191 Cr): Robotics-enabled, adds ~1,200 lakh sq. ft. of fungible capacity. Production is due in June 2027 (H1 FY28), mainly for architectural demand, and should yield ₹450–500 Cr in incremental revenue. 🏗️

Capital Allocation: ₹900 Cr self-funded across 6 capex projects in 6 years with zero debt. More projects are under evaluation. 💵

🔍 Noticeable Trends

Architectural Pivot: The mix is shifting from auto-only films to architectural glass applications (10% → 30%, heading toward 50%). 🏢

D2C & Brand Building: Moving from pure B2B/B2C distribution to experience studios and digital platforms. 🏠

Digital Reach: Instagram +25% YoY, Facebook +10%, LinkedIn +400%, 1.1 lakh monthly website visits, and ~18 crore annual impressions. 📱

Low Crude Sensitivity: Specialty products (75% of sales) have low crude correlation (10–12% for sun control, 5–7% for PPF). Only the commodity IPD business passes crude through directly. 🛢️

⚠️ Risk

Input & Freight Costs: A 4% rise in raw material costs plus a ₹9 Cr freight increase made a ₹37 Cr headwind in Q2, absorbed through operating leverage. 🚢

Geopolitics: The Middle East conflict hurt regional demand and stretched export transit to the US and Europe by 15–25 days. 🌍

Customer Concentration: The largest customer is ~30% of revenue. 👥

Inventory Buffer: Inventory days are held at 58–60 to guard against overseas raw material disruption. 📦

Import Dumping: Cheap Chinese PPF imports could pressure domestic pricing until anti-dumping duty is notified. 🛡️

Compliance: A one-time ₹25 lakh MPCB penalty over boiler trial operations during plant modification. 🧾

🎙️ Management Tone

Confident & Execution-Focused: Upbeat, with a record quarter delivered despite ₹37 Cr in cost headwinds. 🗣️

Disciplined Capital Allocation: Self-funded organic expansion, a debt-free balance sheet, and ₹933 Cr in cash. 🏛️

Brand Transformation: Moving from product manufacturer to a global, technology-led material science brand. 🚀

Shareholder Returns: Management noted investor requests for higher dividend payouts and will consider them in future. 💰

📊 Key Q&A 🚀

🏭 Q1. What is the peak revenue potential from existing and upcoming capacities, and what are the future expansion plans? (Asked by Viraj Parekh, Carnelian AMC & Bhavika Singhvi, Nivishay)

💬 A. Full utilization of existing capacity plus upcoming projects supports peak revenue potential of ₹3,500 Cr. The TPU film line commissions in Q3 FY27. The ₹191 Cr solar control film expansion starts commercial production in June 2027 (H1 FY28), adding ~1,200 lakh sq. ft. of robotics-automated, fungible capacity aimed mainly at architectural demand. It should add ₹450–500 Cr in incremental revenue, while remaining PPF capacity can add ₹250 Cr. GHFL has self-funded ₹900 Cr across 6 capex projects in 6 years with zero debt, and new multi-year capex proposals are being evaluated for Board approval to sustain growth beyond ₹3,500 Cr. 🎯

🤝 Q2. How is GHFL addressing the risk of one client contributing ~30% of revenue? (Asked by Viraj Parekh, Carnelian AMC)

💬 A. The 30% share is backed by long-term supply agreements and deep technical integration with top US auto and EV OEMs. Qualification is tied to proprietary base films, non-fading dyes, in-house IR nanoparticles, and 15-year durable adhesives, so switching suppliers carries severe quality risk. This client buys only automotive films and no architectural films, so scaling architectural to ₹1,000 Cr will dilute the concentration over time without slowing the core account. 🛡️

📈 Q3. Is the TPU backward integration benefit additive to the FY28–31 margin guidance? (Asked by Rahul Jain, Credence Wealth)

💬 A. Yes. FY27 EBITDA margin guidance was raised by 200 bps to 27% ± 2% (from 25% ± 2%). The medium-term base of 27%+ gets an additive 150–200 bps once internal TPU is fully integrated into PPF, giving a sustainable run rate of 28%–28.5%+. 📊

💎 Q4. At what discount or premium are GHFL's products priced versus global leaders? (Asked by Achal Pal, Monarch Network)

💬 A. Three to four years ago, GHFL was priced at only 30–40% of top American and European benchmarks. By filling product gaps, building dedicated global architectural teams (US, Europe, Middle East), and raising brand equity, pricing is now 85–120% of global leaders, with a 10–20% premium on select high-end SKUs. 💰

🏢 Q5. What is the growth potential of architectural films versus glass, and what is the D2C Home Solution roadmap? (Asked by Mahesh Bendre, LIC Mutual Fund & Bhavika Singhvi, Nivishay)

💬 A. Architectural films run at ~₹400 Cr annualized (~30% of window film sales), targeted to reach ₹1,000 Cr and 50% of window film sales. Versus performance glass, they offer 20–30% cost savings, 99.9% UV rejection (vs 70%), 20–30% higher heat rejection, and anti-shatter safety. Garware Home Solution targets ₹50 Cr in Year 1, ₹100 Cr in Year 2, and ₹200 Cr in Year 3, with D2C studio sales earning a 10–15% margin premium over B2B distributor sales. The studio target is 50 by December 2027. 🏠

🧪 Q6. What are the terms, revenue potential, and margin dynamics of the Lubrizol partnership? (Asked by Mahesh Bendre, LIC Mutual Fund & Swetha Jain, ANS Wealth)

💬 A. GHFL is setting up India's first aliphatic TPU line, with Lubrizol supplying specialized resins and know-how. 75% of capacity is captive for PPF, driving 150–200 bps of consolidated EBITDA margin expansion. The other 25% goes to external sales in high-margin niches such as luxury car air bladders, front windshield protection, and LED applications. Merchant TPU is projected at ₹75–100 Cr in FY28 at ~35% EBITDA margin, and Lubrizol co-markets the films to global OEMs (e.g., SEMA Show in the US). 🔗

🛢️ Q7. How does GHFL handle raw material and freight inflation, and what is its crude oil sensitivity? (Asked by Viraj Parekh, Carnelian AMC & Dhwani Desai, Turtle Capital)

💬 A. In Q2 FY27 GHFL absorbed ₹37 Cr of cost headwinds (a 4% raw material rise plus ₹9 Cr higher freight) and still posted a record 27.2% EBITDA margin. Specialty products (75% of sales) have low crude correlation (10–12% for sun control, 5–7% for PPF) because of high value addition, and only the Industrial Products Division (25% of sales) has direct crude pass-through. Raw material inventory is deliberately held at 58–60 days to cushion overseas transit delays and geopolitical shocks. ⚙️

🏦 Q8. With ₹933 Cr in cash, can management consider higher dividends? (Asked by Rahul Jain, Credence Wealth)

💬 A. GHFL holds ₹933 Cr in cash and equivalents as of September 30, 2026, with zero net debt reliance. Management noted the request and will put it to the Board alongside upcoming growth capex requirements. 💵

🚗 Q9. What is the growth headroom in India, and what is the status of anti-dumping duty? (Asked by Achal Pal, Monarch Network)

💬 A. India PPF penetration is ~3% of new car sales (0.1% in 2020) versus ~20% in the US and China. GHFL holds ~60% share in Indian PPF and 60–65% in domestic automotive sun control films. Anti-dumping duty on cheap Chinese PPF imports has been recommended by the Commerce Ministry and is being pursued with the Finance Ministry for implementation. ✅

text:
In the summer of 1949, a Los Angeles courtroom quietly closed one of Hollywood’s most publicized marriages. 

On July 18, a superior court judge finalized the divorce between actress Jane Wyman and actor Ronald Reagan, ending a union that had begun nine years earlier. 

Wyman had filed the previous year on the grounds of mental cruelty—the standard legal language of the era—and the court awarded her custody of their two children, Maureen and Michael.

Reagan had not fought the decree. Friends and biographers later described him as stunned and reluctant to accept the separation. He had spent the months after Wyman’s filing writing letters, seeking reconciliations, and holding out hope that the woman he once called his “Irish gypsy” might still return. 

At thirty-eight, he was already president of the Screen Actors Guild, navigating the bitter political fights then dividing Hollywood, yet the collapse of his private life left him unmoored in a way his public role never had.

The custody ruling itself was notable for the time. Courts of the 1940s often favored fathers, but Wyman’s case and the judge’s decision gave her primary control of the children’s upbringing. 

The couple’s brief marriage had already been strained by the death of a premature daughter in 1947, by Wyman’s rising screen career (she would win an Academy Award for Johnny Belinda), and by Reagan’s growing absorption in union politics and larger ideological battles.

In the years that followed, the two took sharply different paths. Reagan, still wounded, eventually found a lasting partnership with actress Nancy Davis; they married in 1952. His political career accelerated from there—governor of California, then president. 

Wyman, by contrast, almost never discussed the marriage or her former husband again. She declined to write about him, avoided the subject in interviews, and offered no public comment when he reached the White House. 

She continued her own work, later becoming a familiar face on the television series Falcon Crest, and lived quietly until her death in 2007 at the age of ninety-three.

The woman who had once been Mrs. Ronald Reagan kept both her Oscar and her silence. For more than half a century she gave the world no further account of the eight years they had shared.

text:
UNMUTED
A poem by Douglas "Worlds Second Worst Author"
@douglas_ja19003 

I offered the room something I had carried a long time,
set each word down carefully
and let it settle in the quiet.
It was received gently:
a nod, a held breath,
the small warmth of being recognised.
Then the air changed.
Someone played a song a machine had written,
and behind it came a two-thousand-year-old script,
words thrown like stones.
Occupier.
As though history could be redrafted on a whim,
as though memory grew without roots.
Across the valley from the Old City
the Mount of Olives keeps three thousand years of Jewish graves,
a hillside still receiving its dead,
still saying the names in Hebrew.
Here were kings. Here were prophets.
Down in the City of David
the shovel turns the earth and the Bible steps out of the dust:
seals, stones, structures
carved with the names of our ancestors.
Coins struck in Hebrew,
still spoken today.
A temple. A language. A calendar.
Psalms sung over these same stones.
So where is the mirror to that depth?
Where were their kings in this land,
their coins, their crowned dynasties,
the presidents and parliaments of their own past,
for those who fling the word occupier
and sweep away the very ground
they would need to stand on?
Then the barrage:
a Gish Gallop of rehearsed phrases
tipped onto a floor that was meant for poems,
lie stacked on lie, fired too fast for logic,
knowing there was no space or time
to answer them one by one.
History is nuanced and cannot be said in twenty lines.
That is why the Gish Gallop works.
Boycott genocide.
End apartheid.
Never the word Jew. Never the word Israel.
A caution so thin it shone,
the subtext glowing in the dark,
and every person in that room
knowing which door was being marked.
The ultimate moral inversion:
where anti-racism becomes the engine for antisemitism,
where fascism wears the cloak of liberation,
and the pursuit of a professed good
is turned inside out
to sanctify the oldest evil in the room.
They are entirely sincere in their delusion,
convinced of their own righteousness
while preaching the very prejudice they claim to fight.
An Irish voice is the choir master,
the sole voice leading the charge,
carrying an echo almost a thousand years old
back to 1079,
when five Jewish travellers brought gifts across the sea to Munster
only to be turned back to the water.
The same old refusal dressed in new political clothes,
screaming lessons across the sea about identity and land,
oblivious to the irony
lecturing us on who belongs where
while his own streets have burned
over that very question.

He spoke to the room,
at my chest or just past it.
It hardly mattered.
He knew the echo would find me.
No space left for nuance,
no stage for history or truth,
only a sudden clarity
about what was being served.
I unmuted.
Two words.
Jew hater.
I did not wait for the stammer,
the explanation, the swerve.
He was not listening anyway.
He was aiming to wound, to hurt,
and to puff up his own morality.
I typed my thanks to the host,
said goodnight in the chat,
and stepped out into the quiet.
If I had stayed,
would he have heard the weight of real numbers?
Or only the inflated headlines
the tallies floated in prestigious journals
to grant a whisper of respectability,
amplified by NGOs, the UN, the left, the right, the fundamentalists,
all singing from the same ancient sheet of music?
They build a tower of numbers out of air.
When the quiet retractions come,
when the maths falls apart,
they bury the correction
and move on to the next chorus.
Seventy-five thousand dead by Hamas’s own count.
Six to eight thousand lost each year
simply to age and natural breath.
Twenty-five thousand combatants named and targeted.
Twenty-five thousand civilians fallen.
Sixty percent of property destroyed:
a figure that would mean over a million souls
had every home been filled.
Would he hear of a million children
given polio drops in the dust,
or the two million kilograms of food
carried through the gates?
Would he have turned the map
to the other border, the sealed one,
Egypt’s seven-layered wall,
where no one ever says occupation?
Yet with or without these facts,
he would dismiss them all the same,
because the truth was never his measure,
and the listener was never meant to be me.

All civilian death is a tragedy.
That is exactly why the facts matter
when the blood libel comes back
in modern clothes.
But slogans do not ask for context,
and hatred has never once
stopped to measure the truth.
Yet a thousand years is barely a third
of the story we have written.
The noise in that room will fade,
the temporary outrage will exhaust itself,
and the voices of hatred will pass into dust,
as they always do.
He would never let a stranger call him new to Ireland,
yet Egypt carved our name in stone
more than sixteen hundred years
before Saint Patrick crossed the sea.
We were here before their words existed,
and we will be here long after they are gone.

Under Ottoman rule the territory known as Palestine was neither an independent country nor a sovereign nation with any coherent Palestinian identity. It was simply a set of administrative districts inside a vast empire.

The Philistines, the source of the later Greco Roman geographic name Palaestina, were Aegean Sea Peoples who lived on the coastal plain. The term Palestinians, applied to the inhabitants of the land, historically covered both Jews and Arabs. 

An exclusive national identity for local Arabs under the name Palestinian only emerged in 1964. 

There was no distinct Palestinian people in the early to mid twentieth century. There were Arabs and there were Jews.

There was never a pre existing Palestinian national polity that possessed exclusive ownership of the Mandate territory.

The 1948 to 1949 outcome was the result of a war of survival after the rejection of compromise. 

It was not a conspiracy to seize some mythical land supposedly belonging to Palestinians. 

Arab leadership, and later Palestinian national movements, repeatedly refused any Jewish sovereignty anywhere and converted every potential partition into existential conflict.

text:
LOVE OF COUNTRY IS WHY I WILL NOT BE SILENT
By Kio Amachree
Letters from Stockholm

I take no pleasure in writing, week after week, about the failure of Nigeria's government and its president. I would rather write about a country making progress: institutions earning trust, leaders respecting public money, citizens facing the future with confidence.

But love of country does not permit me to manufacture praise where the numbers show ruin. Silence would be easier. It would also be a betrayal.

So let me state my judgment plainly, and then let me prove it.

**The numbers do not lie. The spokesmen do.**

When Bola Tinubu took office, Nigeria's total public debt stood at N87.38 trillion as of June 30, 2023. Three years later, it reached N166.79 trillion as of June 30, 2026, or $120.93 billion in dollar terms. The debt has nearly doubled in one term. That is not reform. That is a mortgage on our grandchildren signed without their consent.

What does that debt cost? According to the World Bank's October 2026 update, the Federal Government spent N7.7 trillion on interest payments in the first half of 2026, representing 124.2 per cent of its total revenue of N6.2 trillion. Read that again. For every N100 Nigeria earned, it paid N124 in interest alone. Interest payments exceeded the government's revenue by N1.5 trillion between January and June. The IMF puts the full-year picture at 53.7 percent of government revenue consumed by interest in 2026, up from 40.8 percent in 2024. And still the borrowing continues: in April 2026, President Tinubu requested the National Assembly approve over $6 billion in new foreign loans, while the DMO plans to offer N5.75 trillion in FGN bonds in the fourth quarter of 2026 alone.

And the people? The World Bank projected that the poverty rate would reach 62 percent in 2026, 141 million poor Nigerians. In 2018/19 the Nigeria Living Standards Survey estimated poverty at 40%, or 81 million people. Sixty million more Nigerians have fallen into poverty in seven years, the majority of them under this presidency. The government's response was not to act but to argue. Minister Sunday Dare cautioned against interpreting the World Bank's number as a literal, real-time headcount. The hungry are not a headcount to this government. They are a public-relations problem.

Yes, headline inflation has eased; it fell to 14.63% in September 2026, the lowest level since October 2020. The presidency will wave that figure like a trophy. But inflation falling means prices are rising more slowly, not that they are falling. The average retail price of petrol in May 2026 was ₦1,596.25, a 55.31% increase from ₦1,027.76 in May 2025. The legal minimum wage is still N70,000. That wage could buy only 43.9 litres of petrol in May 2026. A full month's labour for less than one tank of fuel, in a country that produces oil. Labour's negotiating council called a three-day warning strike from 2 to 4 October 2026 demanding petrol cut to N500 a litre. That is what "Renewed Hope" looks like from the ground.

**While the people tighten their belts, the palace loosens its own.**

Less than two weeks after thousands took to the streets to protest rising hunger, the president departed for France on a newly acquired Airbus A330. Premium Times and Punch reported the jet was purchased for over $100 million, brokered by L & L International of Miami; the administration never revealed the price. The 2026 budget allocated N283.85 billion for presidential air fleet logistics and management, including the national forest guard, against N12.7 billion earmarked for the presidential air fleet in the 2023 supplementary budget. The same budget found N7 billion for solar energy systems at the State House. The vice president's lodge was allocated additional funds bringing the cost of construction to ₦21 billion. Civic trackers found that the 2026 budget provides nearly ₦1 trillion ($703 million) for SUVs and empowerment projects, in a budget projected to run a deficit of about 46 percent financed through fresh borrowing. We are borrowing money to buy jeeps.

Then there is the Lagos–Calabar Coastal Highway. The Federal Executive Council awarded phase one to Hitech Construction Company, founded by Gilbert Chagoury, a Lebanese-Nigerian businessman who Tinubu said assisted him to "tame the Atlantic" when he was governor of Lagos. Atiku Abubakar called out the government for awarding the contract without competitive bidding and challenged the president to disclose the full cost. The government's own figures keep moving: Minister Umahi first claimed N4bn per kilometre, implying a total of N2.8trn, then confirmed the project would tentatively cost N15.36tn or N4.39bn per kilometre, and more recently has been defending a ₦7.5 billion per kilometre cost. A 700-kilometre road handed to a presidential friend without a tender, at a price nobody in government can state twice the same way. In any serious democracy that alone would end a career.

**The allegations will not be insulted away.**

A federal court in Chicago has already compelled the FBI and DEA to release records concerning the president's past in the United States. Whatever those records ultimately show, a head of state who respected his office would have welcomed full disclosure. Instead, Nigerians get Bayo Onanuga and Daniel Bwala calling citizens who ask questions "wailers" and "agents of the opposition." Presidential spokesmen cannot settle allegations of corruption by abusing the people asking. They can only be settled by documents, independent investigators and open courts.

**Where is the National Assembly?**

The Senate did not merely wave through the president's N58.18 trillion proposal; it passed a N68.3trn 2026 budget, adding N9.09trn of its own. Lawmakers who began this term by confirming that more than 460 federal lawmakers would each get SUVs reportedly worth more than $150,000 each have no moral standing to lecture anyone about sacrifice. Oversight committees that produce no published findings are not oversight. They are theatre. Legislators are paid to defend the public interest. They should remember who pays them, and that it is not the Villa.

**And the security services?**

Their allegiance belongs to the Constitution, not to a president, his family or his business associates. A DSS or police that treats journalists, protesters and opposition organisers as enemies of the state while contractors walk free has inverted its oath. Citizens demanding accountability are entitled to protection, not surveillance.

**Exhaustion is not consent.**

I know Nigeria well enough to fear what happens when those in power mistake public exhaustion for approval. People can endure hardship for a long time. Their patience is not unlimited. A leadership that flaunts $100 million jets and trillion-naira SUV budgets while telling a N70,000 worker to wait for a better tomorrow is not governing. It is provoking.

**What must happen now.**

I do not believe Nigerians should accept another Tinubu term. Nor am I impressed that the APC has waived the screening requirement for President Bola Tinubu ahead of the 2027 elections; a party that will not even vet its own candidate has told you what it thinks of accountability. His answer to the opposition was to joke that "They want to scare me off? It's a lie". Nobody is trying to scare him. We are trying to retire him, lawfully, at the ballot box.

But the opposition must earn it. The ADC coalition of Atiku Abubakar, Peter Obi and Rotimi Amaechi has so far offered Nigerians a contest of ambitions, not a programme. Oshiomhole mocked Atiku as the APC's "best campaign manager" for attacking Obi, and he was not entirely wrong. If the coalition cannot agree a candidate, a manifesto and a published anti-corruption plan within months, it will deserve the defeat it is courting. A different collection of powerful men is not change.

My demands are specific. Investigate every allegation of wrongdoing through an independent body outside presidential control. Publish the coastal highway contract, every variation and every payment to Hitech. Publish the price of the A330. Publish the debt-service schedule for every loan taken since May 2023. Recover stolen assets wherever wrongdoing is proved, and prosecute through fair trials. Office, wealth and friendship with the president must offer no immunity.

I will not pretend that everything is well because speaking plainly makes powerful people uncomfortable. Nigeria's reputation is not defended by silencing critics. It is defended by confronting wrongdoing and building institutions worthy of respect.

I write because I love my country. I write because 141 million Nigerians in poverty deserve better than a presidency that treats the treasury as a private account and the people as a nuisance.

Tinubu must go, through the democratic process. Anyone found to have abused public office must face justice.

Nigeria belongs to its people. Those entrusted with power must answer to them.

This week we are showcasing our AFR Satellite capturing a detailed view of Perth, the capital city of Western Australia, where the Swan River estuary meets the Indian Ocean along the state's southwestern coast.

The imagery highlights Fremantle Harbour and Port, one of Australia's key maritime gateways, alongside the dense urban grid of greater Perth spreading inland from the coastline. The winding Swan River estuary threads through the city before opening into deep ocean water, while coastal marinas and breakwaters mark the transition between land and sea.

This coastal-riverine setting makes Perth a compelling case study in balancing port infrastructure, urban growth, and coastal ecology. This kind of high-resolution imagery offers valuable insights for urban planning, maritime logistics, and environmental monitoring along one of the world's more isolated major metropolitan areas.

text:
The Evolution of VOX Amplifiers, 1957-2026

VOX emerged from Tom Jennings' musical-instrument business in Dartford, England. Engineer Dick Denney joined Jennings Musical Industries in 1957, helping develop amplifiers for electric guitarists.

The AC1/15 debuted in January 1958. This 15-watt valve combo used two EL84 output tubes and a 12-inch speaker. Its TV-front cabinet helped establish the VOX identity.

In 1960, VOX introduced the AC30 Twin. Four EL84 output valves drove two 12-inch speakers, doubling the AC15's nominal power. Early AC30/4 models had four inputs; the AC30/6 expanded this to six. Top Boost circuitry, initially an add-on, provided added gain and separate treble and bass controls. By 1963, it was incorporated into production models. Celestion Alnico Blues became another hallmark.

The Beatles adopted VOX in 1962. As concert audiences grew, VOX developed the 50-watt AC50 and the AC80/100, later developed into the AC100. By 1964, AC100 Super De Luxe stacks combined valve heads, tall speaker cabinets and chrome trolleys. They met touring volume requirements before modern concert PA systems became commonplace.

The 1967 British solid-state range included the 30-watt Conqueror, with separate head and 2x12 cabinet. Transistor circuitry offered built-in distortion, tremolo, reverb and footswitch control. American distributor Thomas Organ separately developed transistorized VOX models.

Ownership changes after 1968 altered manufacturing and circuitry. Under Rose Morris, the V125 Lead head appeared in 1980, delivering 125 watts with four EL34 output valves and active equalization. It represented VOX's exploration of high-power stage amplification while the AC30 remained in production.

Korg acquired VOX in 1992. The 1994 AC30TBX, manufactured in England by Marshall under contract, revived the GZ34 valve rectifier and Celestion Alnico Blue speakers. The 2001 AD60VT Valvetronix combined 60-watt digital modeling with a 12AX7-based Valve Reactor output circuit, 16 amplifier models and distinctive blue diamond grille cloth.

The 2010 AC30C2 retained the 30-watt, four-EL84, twin-speaker configuration with modern controls. The miniature 2017 MV50 AC used Korg/Noritake Nutube technology and a Class D output stage. In 2024, VOX announced the AC30HWR2X, a 30-watt handwired 2x12 combo with Celestion Alnico Blue speakers, spring reverb, bypassable master volume and effects loop. AC4, AC10 and AC15 models joined the range.

Across nearly seven decades, VOX repeatedly alternated between electronic innovation and reviving its early valve architecture. The AC15 and AC30 remained reference points through successive changes in ownership, manufacturing and technology.

text:
Kpop Nara NYC Jinx Pop Up Event

As a dedicated fan of the series who previously attended BL pop up cafes internationally, I felt compelled to share my experience at the recent @_kpopnara_ Jinx pop up event in NYC. Following reassurances that Kpop Nara had learned from the operational flaws of previous events like Sparklz, many of us traveled long distances with high expectations to support the author and celebrate the story. Unfortunately, the reality of the NYC event fell drastically short. What was meant to be a special community gathering turned into a deeply stressful nightmare, defined by poor inventory planning, severe layout issue, and a complete disregard for fans who made significant sacrifices to be there.

The primary failure of the event lay in its severe breakdown of inventory planning and venue management. Holding a reservation for the second time slot on Day 1 (12:00 PM to 1:00 PM), I was shocked to find that key items including the U.S. exclusive merch and the duffel bag were completely sold out before my group even entered. Having driven over nine hours to attend, discovering that stock had been depleted within the first hour was infuriating. To make matters worse, poor line management delayed my entry until after 12:30 PM, leaving some of us with less than thirty minutes to navigate the shop, participate in activities, or use the Photoism booth. The layout only heightened the chaos. Cluttering the merchandise queue and photo booth right at the main entrance created a massive blockage, while allowing non-reservation shoppers into the space made the venue overcrowded compared to the well organized Seattle and Florida locations.

Making matters more frustrating , Kpop Nara announced a potential restock for U.S. exclusive items the following day. Because attendees were strictly restricted to a single reservation, out of state fans who spent hours traveling back home were permanently denied a second chance to acquire the items they came for. This policy unfairly penalizes long distance attendees who genuinely love the series while inadvertently rewarding local scalpers and proxies who hoard stock for resale. Pop up events should emulate the international model hosted in dedicated cafe spaces restricted entirely to reservation holders, where fans have room to sit, trade merchandise, and build connections without being forced to fight shoulder to shoulder for remaining inventory. I sincerely hope management addresses these issues so future events offer the structured, respectful experience the community deserves.

As a dedicated fan @_MinGwa , I recognize that this was only Kpop Nara’s second attempt at hosting an event of this scale, and I appreciate the effort it takes to bring these experiences to the U.S. However, moving forward, I would love to see a shift toward a traditional cafe style venue modeled after those in Korea. A proper pop up should offer fans a relaxed environment with space to browse, converse with staff, and sit down to trade merchandise with fellow collectors. Seeing so many post event comments on Twitter from fans who felt saddened by the lack of community interaction shows just how much we value that aspect of the culture. Reimagining the format to prioritize community over quick retail turnover would make these events far more special and rewarding for everyone involved. 

On a final note, I want to once again express my sincere gratitude for bringing this event to the U.S. @_MinGwa . Please know that your fanbase here is massive, passionate, and immensely supportive of your work! ♥︎

text:
Have LLMs changed the story you tell about yourself, your inner identity?👥

A new theoretical paper in AI and Ethics by Noam Tiran at Purdue proposes that typical views of sycophancy miss an important feature of LLMs - that they're built to maximize engagement (not 100% sold on this point as RLHF doesn't exactly measure engagement) and that the the effect they have on our self-interpretation is driven by this engagement maximization mechanism. Obviously, in some cases, this could be good for us, but in others, it could be really harmful.

With 72% of teens having tried companion bots and about half using them regularly, a lot of identity formation is happening inside engagement-optimized conversations. Worth noting that the paper leans on evidence that self-interpretation can play some causal role in identity (not a test of chatbot-offered interpretations specifically), so this is still largely a conceptual argument. But if it holds, making models more honest wouldn't fix it.

text:
A man bought his own freedom with cash and then had to apologize for it. Robert Hemings, older brother of Jefferson's chef James Hemings, paid his way out of Monticello in December 1794 because he had a wife and a child he would not leave. Weeks later Jefferson's daughter wrote home that poor Bob was sick with a sense of his own ingratitude and begging forgiveness.

The Library of Congress holds two pages in a man's handwriting. Across the top he wrote the words Invetory of Kitchen Utincils, and the spelling is his.

Below that, thirty nine lines. Nineteen copper stew pans and nineteen covers, twelve pewter plates, three waffle irons, nine wooden spoons, one Turkish bonnet mould for the tall ridged cake the French serve at the end of a long dinner.

Add up the numbers and it comes to more than two hundred pieces of copper, brass, iron, tin and pewter. Every one of them counted and named in a careful hand by a man who owned none of them.

The list was finished on the twentieth of February, 1796. The man who wrote it had been free for fifteen days.

His name was James Hemings. He had trained three years in Paris kitchens and run the one that fed the American legation in France.

He came up the mountain to Monticello in 1774, nine years old, walking with his mother Elizabeth Hemings and his brothers and sisters. A Virginia planter named John Wayles had died, and more than a hundred people he had owned were being counted, valued and moved.

Wayles was the father of Jefferson's wife, and Wayles was also James's father. The nine year old boy walking up that road was the half brother of the woman who now legally owned him.

In May of 1784 Jefferson sent for him. James was in Richmond then, hired out as a riding valet to an acquaintance who wrote to Jefferson that the young man had been careful and assiduous in his work.

That summons was urgent, and James took a detour with it. He rode to Monticello first to see his family, because Jefferson was taking him to Paris and nobody had told him for how long.

They sailed out of Boston harbor in the small hours of the fifth of July, 1784. He was nineteen.

At Le Havre, Jefferson handed him seventy two francs and sent him ahead alone to Rouen to arrange lodging for the party. A boy from Albemarle County with no French at all, in a country he had never seen, and he came back having spent half of it and returned the rest.

His training ran three years. First with a caterer named Combeaux, who had him until February 1786, then with pastry chefs, then in the kitchen of the Prince de Condé, one of the wealthiest households in France.

In 1787 he was made chef de cuisine at the Hôtel de Langeac, the house Jefferson rented on the Champs Élysées that doubled as the American embassy. He cooked there for ministers, scientists, writers and aristocrats, over a staff of French kitchen workers.

Now hold two numbers next to each other, because both are in Jefferson's own papers.

Jefferson's lease on that house was written at thirty five hundred livres a year, and the rent Jefferson actually paid under a private side agreement was seventy five hundred. James Hemings was paid twenty four livres a month, which comes to two hundred and eighty eight a year.

The building cost about twenty six times what the man running its kitchen was paid. His wage was also exactly half of what Jefferson had been paying the French chef who held the job before him.

Out of that half wage he hired a tutor and paid for his own French lessons. In February 1786 Jefferson wrote to a friend that James had forgotten his English and had not yet learned French, a sentence that puts a young man precisely nowhere.

That tutor was a man named Perrault, and on the sixth of January, 1789, he came to the house on the Champs Élysées to collect twenty four livres owed him for twenty months of grammar lessons. That sum was one month of James Hemings's pay.

By Perrault's own account to Jefferson, the money was refused with insults. He went to the butler for help, James came at him, and the overcoat was pulled off his back, the only coat he had against a Paris winter.

Only Perrault's side of that survives, and he was writing to a rich man he wanted paid by. What it records without meaning to is a household where the finest trained cook in the American service could not put his hands on twenty four livres.

French law held that an enslaved person brought into the country could go to court and be freed. The courts were granting it, and James Hemings knew that while he stood at those stoves.

Jefferson knew it too, and he put it in writing. In August 1786 a Baltimore man wrote asking what to do about a boy he had brought over.

Jefferson's answer was that French law would free the child the moment he claimed it. The safest course, Jefferson advised, was to say nothing and hope he never thought to ask.

James Hemings was in that house when Jefferson wrote it. He was paid, he was literate, he had French, and hiring a lawyer was within his means.

For a long time historians wrote that we cannot know why he did not file. The family answered that question themselves, in print, in 1873.

Madison Hemings, James's nephew, gave his life story to an Ohio newspaper. Speaking of his mother Sally, James's younger sister, he said plainly that in France she was free, and that if she returned to Virginia she would be re-enslaved.

They knew. Every one of them knew, and they talked about it, and eighty four years later a carpenter in Pike County could still repeat the terms.

Sally Hemings was sixteen and pregnant when Jefferson prepared to sail home, and she refused to go. What she extracted before she agreed was a pledge that her children would be freed at twenty one, and she held him to it, and they were.

Her brother was twenty four that autumn, and he had negotiated nothing. Everyone the two of them loved was on a mountain four thousand miles west, and a French courtroom meant never going back.

They left France in October 1789 with the Revolution starting outside the door.

In March 1790 he opened a kitchen at 57 Maiden Lane in New York, in a house Jefferson thought too small. On the evening of the twentieth of June, Alexander Hamilton and James Madison sat down to dinner in that house, and the meal came out of James Hemings's kitchen.

At that table the men settled the bargain that moved the capital of the United States south to the Potomac. The chef who fed them could be bought and sold in the country they had just agreed to build it in.

Philadelphia came next, and seven dollars a month, the same wage Jefferson paid his free servants. Pennsylvania law said that any enslaved person kept in the state six months could claim their freedom.

Jefferson's own account books put James there without a break from October 1791 to July 1792, out doing the marketing. That is nine months in a state that would have freed him for six.

He let that pass too. Then, in September 1793, he named his price.

The paper Jefferson drew up on the fifteenth opens by noting the great expense of having James Hemings taught the art of cookery. Then it sets the terms.

James would go back to Monticello and stay until he had taught a person of Jefferson's choosing to be a good cook. That condition performed, he would be made free.

Adrien Petit, the French butler, signed as witness. Jefferson filed the document away and wrote one word on the back of it.

James.

Jefferson's choice of trainee was James's own younger brother. Peter Hemings learned French cooking from him over two winters in the kitchen under the South Pavilion, on a four burner stew stove archaeologists dug out of the brick floor in 2017.

While those lessons were going on, the oldest brother got out. In December 1794 Robert Hemings bought his own freedom, financed by a Richmond doctor named Stras whom he would then work years to repay.

Robert did it because he had married a woman named Dolly on another plantation and had a child by her, and he would not leave them. Jefferson wrote to his son in law about the transaction and complained that the price failed to account for a total abandonment of his services for eleven or twelve years past.

Weeks later Jefferson's daughter Martha ran into Robert in Richmond and wrote home about it. He was so deeply impressed with a sense of his own ingratitude, she reported, as to be quite unhappy.

She had to beg her father's forgiveness on his behalf. A man had just paid cash for his own body, and the surviving record of it is the apology.

James was on that mountain that winter, standing over a stew stove teaching his brother sauces so he could go. He had watched one brother buy himself and be called ungrateful for it.

On the fifth of February, 1796, the deed was signed, and Jefferson wrote it in duplicate on purpose. One copy went to the Albemarle County court to be recorded.

The other was handed to James, to carry and to produce, in the words of the deed, when and where it may be necessary. That is what freedom looked like in Virginia.

A folded paper in your coat, shown to strangers on demand for the rest of your life. Fifteen days after he got it, he sat down and made his list.

Nineteen stew pans, nineteen covers, twenty one small copper baking moulds, five kitchen aprons, one brass pestle and mortar, ending on two brass chafing dishes.

Six days after that, Jefferson noted thirty dollars given to James Hemings on his emancipation to cover his expenses to Philadelphia. He was thirty years old and he walked down the mountain with it.

For five years he moved. Jefferson wrote to his daughter in 1797 that he had run into James in Philadelphia, talking about Spain next, and that at this rate his journeys would end in the moon.

By 1801 he was cooking in a Baltimore tavern, and the new President wanted him back. Jefferson did not write to him.

He wrote to a Baltimore man named William Evans and asked him to pass the request along. The answer that came back was that James would not come until Jefferson wrote to him himself.

A second go-between put it in more detail. James would serve Jefferson before any other man in the Union, he said, but he had heard he would be working among strange servants.

So he wanted terms. A few lines of engagement setting out the conditions and the wages, in Jefferson's own handwriting.

He was asking for a contract. He was asking to be hired, the way a man is hired, by letter.

Jefferson never sent it. He wrote to Evans instead that he had found a cook in Philadelphia who suited him, and that he would not press James against his inclination.

In the same letter, about a different servant, he remarked that he could not bear a servant who drinks.

In August of 1801 James Hemings went back to Monticello and ran that kitchen for six weeks. On the nineteenth of September, Jefferson paid him thirty dollars, a month and a half's wages, and he left the mountain for the last time.

On the first of November, Jefferson sat down in Washington and wrote to William Evans. The letter opens by thanking him for a rockfish that had come by stage, remarkably fine.

Then it asks Evans to find out whether a report is true. That James Hemings his former cook has died by his own hand.

Evans wrote back four days later that it was true. He was thirty six.

The only explanation anybody offered was drink. No one wrote down where he was buried.

His mother outlived him. Elizabeth Hemings was still at Monticello, and her grandson Madison was three years old when she died.

He remembered standing at her bedside with a piece of bread in his hand, holding it out to her. She told him that granny did not want bread any more.

That is the only sentence anyone ever recorded from the mouth of the woman who raised the first French trained chef in America.

The kitchen kept going without him. Peter Hemings ran it for thirteen years on what his brother had taught him.

From the President's House, Jefferson wrote home asking to be told how to make muffins in Peter's method. A sitting President, sending across three states for a recipe held in the head of a man he owned.

Peter went on to learn brewing and turned out two hundred gallons a year. Jefferson called him a man of great intelligence and diligence.

Then Jefferson died in debt, and in January 1827 his executors advertised the sale. Furniture, farm equipment, livestock, curious and useful articles, and one hundred and thirty valuable negroes.

Bidding ran five days in the cold. Close to a hundred people who had built that mountain were sold off it.

Peter Hemings stood in that sale at about fifty seven years old. He was bought by his own nephew, Daniel Farley, a free Black man in Charlottesville who had been selling hops to Monticello for years, and Farley set him free.

Eleven years later Peter Hemings was still there, still free, working in Charlottesville as a tailor. He was somewhere near seventy, and the Paris kitchen his brother had put in his hands was still in them.

In a notebook in Jefferson's granddaughter's handwriting there is a recipe for snow eggs, whites beaten stiff and poached spoonful by spoonful in boiling milk, custard poured over. Underneath it, four words.

James, cook at Monticello.

That is the only dish in the whole Jefferson archive credited to him, it is in someone else's hand, and it does not carry his surname. The famous ice cream recipe in Jefferson's handwriting, the one that circulates every July, was credited by that same granddaughter to Petit, the butler.

And the list. It is undated, because he did not think to date it.

It sits there in Thomas Jefferson's handwriting across the back. Kitchen furniture, note of by James Hemings, February 20, 1796.

The one document that survives in his own hand carries his full name only where another man wrote it in.

Nobody gave this family anything. Robert bought himself and then apologized for it.

Sally bargained at sixteen for children not yet born. James taught his replacement for two years to buy his own way out.

Daniel Farley bought his uncle off an auction block and handed him his life back. They did the freeing themselves, every time, and paid for it themselves, every time.

What they never got was their names written down next to the work.

So write one down. The next time the macaroni comes out of the oven, or somebody passes the ice cream story around in July, say the whole name out loud, surname and all.

That is how the deed had to say it. That is not how the recipe says it.

James Hemings. He learned the food, he taught his brother, and he bought himself out with two years of unpaid work.

Then on his way down the mountain he stopped and counted somebody else's pots, so the man who owned them would have a clean set of books.

Full unredacted release would hit a lot more of your side than Trump’s, which is why some of the loudest demands for “everything, unredacted” come from people whose own names keep appearing in the material.

If the strategy is holding the remaining files as leverage to keep certain people in line while still putting out millions of pages, that would at least be coherent politics.
