text:
DID YOU KNOW THAT WINNIE BYANYIMA WAS AMONG THOSE WHO FOUGHT IN THE LUWERO BUSH WAR?

Before becoming internationally known for her diplomatic work, human rights advocacy and leadership in global development, Winnie Byanyima was among the Ugandans who joined the armed struggle against Milton Obote’s government in the early 1980s.

She left her job as a flight engineer with Uganda Airlines and joined the guerrilla struggle that lasted from 1981 to 1986. Historical accounts describe her participation in the struggle in the Luwero Triangle, where she lived alongside fellow fighters under the difficult conditions of the bush.

Interestingly, although Byanyima participated in the struggle, she was not given a military rank. Nevertheless, her contribution reportedly extended beyond the battlefield. Drawing on her education and international connections, she helped mobilise support and resources abroad. She also served on the National Resistance Army (NRA) delegation during the 1985 Nairobi peace talks.

Her journey from flight engineer to guerrilla fighter, diplomat and international leader offers an important perspective on Uganda’s liberation struggle. It reminds us that participation in a revolutionary movement did not always translate into formal military rank, even for those who took part in the struggle.

Uganda’s history is more complex than the titles, ranks and positions we remember. Sometimes, understanding that history means recognising the contributions of people whose roles did not fit neatly into the conventional military hierarchy.

text:
The View from the Office

I met up with Maya True Wasik for breakfast at Le Pain Quotidien at Columbus Circle. She had tea and an egg, cheddar and avocado sandwich. I had the yogurt parfait.

Maya is a senior at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill and an aspiring documentary filmmaker. We were introduced by a mutual friend, Ryan Cheah.

Maya is finishing her degree remotely from New York so she can work as an intern at NBC. She spent the past summer assisting the network’s documentary team. At the end of the summer, her internship was extended into the academic year. 

The incredible part of the job for Maya is getting to work with people who have decades of experience, at NBC and other outlets such as Vox and Vice Media.

On the side, she shoots photos and videos for restaurants, startups and events to generate revenue that keeps her afloat. At events, people often ask how she got the gig. “It’s actually the camera that keeps getting me connected,” she tells them.

She’s worked on documentaries covering the environment, arts and culture. She produced a short film, Buckets and Boots, about local recovery efforts in North Carolina after Hurricane Helene. The film placed fifth in the Hearst Journalism Awards Program’s Multimedia III Enterprise Story competition.

Maya grew up in North Carolina. Her mother is a professor at Elon University who wanted her children to be citizens of the world, so she sent Maya to a school where half the day was taught in Spanish, and later a year of high school in Costa Rica, and then United World College in New Mexico. Maya also lived in Hong Kong for a stretch.

We talked about how much journalism has changed and how different it is to try to land a job as a journalist. When I started at Bloomberg, people typically looked for an entry-level job at a news organization, where someone more experienced would teach them the ropes. 

Maya, by contrast, started making content, and job offers have followed.

You can connect with Maya via LinkedIn or DM me for a warm introduction.

Weak-kneed Republican figures like Iowa Senate candidate Ashley Hinson clutch their pearls, weeping over institutional decorum while the civilizational foundations burn. President Trump understands the tactical utility of the strike, even as we recognize that neither Ramaswamy nor his libertarian dogma offers a permanent home for the soul of the Folk. Politics is a zero-sum struggle between the architects of national decline and the defenders of the historic nation. Every candidate must choose a side. We reject the sterile abstractions of procedural democracy. We reject the weaklings who prioritize committee rules over the survival of the commonwealth. The health of a nation depends upon the integrity of the family, the sanctity of truth, and the ruthless exposure of imposters who seek dominion over the public trust. text:
Yakov Smirnoff: From the Soviet Union to a U.S. Ph.D. While Making Millions Laugh

Yakov Smirnoff’s remarkable journey took him from the Soviet Union to the United States, where he built a successful career in comedy, became an American citizen, and ultimately earned a doctorate, all while bringing laughter to millions.

Born in Odesa, then part of the Soviet Union and now in Ukraine, Smirnoff began his career as a stand-up comedian in the Soviet Union. In 1977, he immigrated to the United States to pursue his dream of a career in American show business, despite not yet knowing English.

On July 4, 1986, Smirnoff became a U.S. citizen. Following the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991, he continued to build his career in America. In 1993, he began performing year-round at his own 2,000-seat theater in Branson, Missouri. As of 2024, he continued to perform there on select dates while also touring internationally.

Beyond his achievements in entertainment, Smirnoff pursued an academic path in psychology and leadership. He earned a master’s degree in psychology from the University of Pennsylvania in 2006 and a doctorate in psychology and global leadership from Pepperdine University in 2019. His journey reflects a commitment to lifelong learning and personal growth that extends well beyond the stage.

America’s Heart: A Tribute to September 11

Following the terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001, Smirnoff created America’s Heart, a monumental 200-by-135-foot mural honoring the victims and commemorating the nation’s resilience in the face of profound loss.

Deeply affected by the tragedy and the helplessness he felt in its aftermath, Smirnoff began painting on the night of September 11, channeling his emotions into an expression of remembrance and solidarity.

He later invested $100,000 of his own money in an effort to have the mural displayed at Ground Zero. Through this deeply personal undertaking, Smirnoff sought to honor those who lost their lives, acknowledge the suffering of their families and loved ones, and pay tribute to the courage, compassion, and unity that emerged in the aftermath of the attacks.

America’s Heart represents one artist’s response to a national tragedy and his desire to preserve the memory of those who perished on September 11, 2001. It stands as a testament to the power of art to express grief, honor lives lost, and offer a message of hope in the face of profound sorrow.

From escaping the limitations of the Soviet Union to entertaining American audiences, earning advanced academic degrees, and creating a memorial tribute to September 11, Smirnoff’s life story encompasses humor, perseverance, education, and a deep appreciation for the country he chose to call home.

GAME OF THE WEEK PREVIEW: GAINESVILLE vs. MILTON

@RedElephant_FB will face off against a very talented @MiltonEagles_FB squad in what should be one of the best matchups in the state of Georgia this week!

Milton’s offense is led by QB @derrickbakerQb1, who is closing in on 2,000 passing yards this season. The rushing attack features @AtchisonSheldon, a physical back who runs extremely well behind his pads and possesses the explosiveness to turn any carry into a big play.

On the defensive side of the ball, Milton features the versatile @RomanTumminia, who lines up at both DL and LB. He’s been extremely productive this season, ranking second on the team in tackles behind Boston College commit @BlaizeBattaglia, another key playmaker for this Milton defense.

Now, let’s talk about this loaded Gainesville defense! 

@RedElephant_FB has talent at all three levels, starting with sophomore LB @ChanceDavis76, a true sideline-to-sideline playmaker who flies around the field, plays downhill, and consistently finds himself around the football.

The secondary might be one of the biggest strengths of this Gainesville defense, featuring 6’3” SS @TheJermiahproct alongside @Marcus__5 and @zachary3_ingram. A very talented group capable of making life difficult for opposing quarterbacks.

And we certainly can’t forget about @iiamjahh_, one of the most highly recruited defensive backs in the country, holding offers from programs all across the nation. A true difference-maker in coverage and NOT a guy opposing quarterbacks want to test! 

MY TAKE: This matchup will be a great test for both teams. Milton brings a balanced offensive attack with playmakers capable of changing the game at any moment, while Gainesville counters with an extremely talented defense that has speed, physicality, and playmakers at every level.

Something has to give.Can Milton’s offense find success against this loaded Gainesville defense, or will the Red Elephants’ defensive playmakers take control of this matchup?

Lord,

You have taught us 
the weight of kindness.
You have shown us how a soft word 
can turn away wrath, 
how a cup of cold water 
is not forgotten, 
how mercy can reach 
where force never will.

Yet You have also shown us 
the edges of the world.

There are places 
kindness cannot enter, 
doors it cannot open, 
chains it will not break.

There are times when gentleness 
is not the answer, 
only the companion 
of something sharper.

So we ask for both.

Keep our hearts soft 
toward the wounded and the weary.
And make our spirits steady 
when the moment calls 
for clarity, for courage, 
for the clean cut of truth.

Teach us when to offer flowers
and when to stand with a sword,
not in anger,
but in faithfulness.

Not everything yields to warmth.
Some things must be met 
with light that does not flinch.

Give us the wisdom 
to know the difference,
and the love to carry both.

text:
HFCL Ltd Concall Summary for Q2FY27

FINANCIAL PERFORMANCE
- Revenue reached ₹2,541.79 Cr, up 144% YoY.
- EBITDA rose 224% to ₹658 Cr.
- EBITDA margin expanded to 25.89%, up 640 bps.
- PAT surged 448% to ₹394.22 Cr.
- PBT increased 406% to ₹538.60 Cr.
- Export performance grew approximately 493% YoY.
- Management described this as its best-ever quarter.

MANAGEMENT GUIDANCE
- FY27 revenue growth guidance raised to at least 80%.
- Earlier growth aspirations were 20%, then 40%.
- ₹10,000 Cr revenue target may arrive before FY29.
- Management expects Q3 revenue to grow sequentially.
- FY28 guidance was not formally provided.
- Management expects revenue and profitability to improve.
- No significant preform supply constraints were reported.

ORDER BOOK AND DEMAND
- Total order book stands at approximately ₹28,900 Cr.
- Optical fibre and data-centre orders total ₹18,500 Cr.
- Management estimated around 70% of export orders from hyperscalers.
- Order book includes approximately ₹5,000 Cr of O&M contracts.
- Contracts range from months to four years.
- New customer programs could extend visibility further.
- Demand remains strong across AI, data centres and telecom.

OPTICAL FIBRE AND CONNECTIVITY
- Fibre capacity is expanding from 34 million to 43 million.
- Cable capacity is rising from 34 million to 63 million fibre-kilometres.
- Fibre capacity utilisation is effectively around 100%.
- Data-centre products command higher realisations than telecom products.
- Data-centre revenue share estimated at 65–75%.
- Telecom revenue share estimated at 25–35%.
- Connectivity solutions revenue may exceed ₹800 Cr in FY27.
- Management targets ₹2,000 Cr connectivity revenue next year.
- Higher-value products should support margins.
- Management expects margins to improve further.

CAPEX AND BACKWARD INTEGRATION
- Planned investment totals approximately ₹1,800 Cr.
- Investment covers optical fibre, cables and preform manufacturing.
- Preform capacity is planned at 600 tonnes.
- Commissioning target remains October 2028.
- Initial own-preform availability is expected earlier.
- Own preform could improve margins through backward integration.
- Around half of future preform requirements remain externally sourced.
- Germanium supplier discussions are underway.

DEFENCE AND AEROSPACE
- FY27 defence revenue aspiration stands at ₹500 Cr.
- Management discussed ₹500–600 Cr as its current-year ambition.
- FY28 defence revenue target is at least ₹2,000 Cr.
- Three-year defence revenue aspiration reaches ₹5,000 Cr.
- Aerospace acquisition carries an approximately ₹1,600–1,800 Cr order book.
- Acquisition completion was expected during November.
- Thermal weapon sights deliveries have commenced.
- Radar approvals could support additional revenue.
- Andhra Pradesh allotted 1,000 acres for ammunition manufacturing.
- Ammunition facility revenue may begin in approximately two years.
- Management sees defence as a second growth engine.

EPC BUSINESS AND DELEVERAGING
- EPC segment reported a quarterly loss.
- BharatNet billing delays contributed to reported losses.
- Management expects delayed milestone bills to be submitted.
- Next two quarters' combined losses may reach ₹75–100 Cr.
- EPC profitability is expected from Q1 next year.
- Army maintenance contract approval was nearing completion.
- EPC restructuring recommendations were under preparation.
- Management expects debt reduction to begin this year.
- Debt could decline substantially by March 2027–28.

INDIA DATA-CENTRE OPPORTUNITY
- Management cited India's current capacity near 1.6 GW.
- Industry capacity could reach 6 GW by 2030.
- Management believes capacity could potentially reach 10–12 GW.
- US capacity was cited at approximately 130 GW.
- Growth could expand across India, Europe and Asia.
- Telecom operators may increase fibre-network investments.
- Management sees no immediate slowdown from higher US rates.

KEY MONITORABLES
- Execution against the ₹28,900 Cr order book.
- Sustainability of elevated EBITDA margins.
- Hyperscaler order concentration and customer diversification.
- Fibre and cable capacity expansion timelines.
- Preform commissioning and raw-material availability.
- Connectivity revenue ramp-up toward ₹2,000 Cr.
- Defence revenue conversion against ambitious targets.
- Aerospace acquisition integration and order execution.
- EPC losses, billing recoveries and restructuring decisions.
- Debt reduction alongside substantial capital expenditure.

OVERALL TAKEAWAY
- HFCL has raised FY27 growth expectations significantly.
- Data-centre connectivity remains the key near-term growth driver.
- Defence offers a potential second growth engine.
- Margin improvement depends on product mix and integration.
- Execution, EPC losses and ambitious guidance remain crucial monitorables.

text:
Every new solar panel lowers what solar earns

Yesterday's chart was one day in Spain: free at noon, $260 at 7:45 p.m. Repeat that for years and solar ends up cannibalizing its own revenue. In 2019 a MWh of Spanish solar sold for slightly more than the average price for power from any source. In 2026 so far, it sells for half.

It's not just Spain. German solar earned about half the average price in 2025. In California it's under a third.

Every solar farm produces in the same hours. Once there is enough of it at noon, gas drops out and something cheaper sets the price: other solar, hydro, or an offer below zero. So solar sells most of its output into hours its own output made cheap.

Therefore, solar targets in MWh measure the wrong thing. They count how much energy solar makes, but the market pays for when it makes it.

text:
‡

Breeders' Cup Blast From the Past: Stung by a Poor Shoemaker Ride

In the mid/late 1980s I had begun to publish some of my work, but was still gambling fairly seriously, as well. In early November of 1987, I was in California to cover the Breeders' Cup at Hollywood Park, which turned out to be extraordinary, both as a group of races, and betting experience.

They offered a Pick-9 that day (yes, nine races), including what I recall as at least one allowance race after the seven Breeders' Cup races had been run (I can't locate a full set of charts). That allowance race, one of the two non-BC races in the pick-9, was won by a Fappiano filly (I think), which in retrospect made some sense as she was 1st Lasix. But given that it was a pick-9, and I did not want to invest a lot of money on the ticket, I couldn't go very deep at all, and had to single a few horses.

All four of my singles were in the BC races, and three of them won: Very Subtle (16/1 - Sprint), Miesque (7/2 - Mile), and Ferdinand (1/1 - Classic). I hit one of the two non-BC races, and the only single and BC race that I missed was the Juvenile Fillies, thanks to a bizarre, and wholly uncharacteristic ride by the great Bill Shoemaker.

The filly that I had singled in that race was named Jeanne Jones. She was trained by Charlie Whittingham, and was sent off as the second favorite (2.20/1) behind a four-horse Lukas entry. She was, oddly enough, and along with her trainer's star of the day, Ferdinand, by Nijinsky. Though a brilliant turf horse himself, and much more of a turf influence as a stallion, Nijinsky had remarkably gotten two horses that were good enough to have had big chances in Breeders' Cup dirt races on that particular day. 

Despite an obviously strong pace developing, for some inexplicable reason Shoemaker rode Jeanne Jones aggressively early, and she not only forced a :22 quarter, but had taken the lead by the half in :44 flat, and covered 6f. in 1:09 flat (see attached chart). I was shocked, and none too happy, but when she drew well clear into the stretch, it appeared that she might actually win in spite of it all. 

It wasn't to be. She shortened stride, was stopping badly late, and the late-running longshot Epitome nailed her on the wire (see video linked below). It was a painful wait before the photo finish result was announced, and a particularly painful "dirty nose" loss.

https://t.co/APtDKaXXtI

To make matters even worse, I happened to have been watching training with Gary Young during the week leading up to the BC, and we had both taken note of how well Epitome had been training. But as it would have radically increased the cost of my ticket, I never seriously considered using her.

The upshot of all of the above is that I ended up with seven out of nine winners, and I believe two or three times. I don't recall the exact amount, but it was well into the thousands. Yet despite that fairly juicy consolation, and my having done well otherwise during the day, I always wondered what the 8/9 payout would have been, had Shoemaker not decided to unveil his best Earlie Fires impression. 

To be fair, Whittingham subsequently came to believe that the filly also resented the whip, and you can see signs of it in the video as Shoemaker smacked her late in the race. So despite her early efforts, she probably would have won had she been hand-ridden home!

***
As a final note, it was, nevertheless, a fantastic day of racing, and undoubtedly one of the very best of the Breeders' Cups. Very Subtle was a sensational winner of the sprint; easily in the top five sprint performances of any that I have seen over ~50 years. Miesque was brilliant, as she was again at Churchill the following year. And the Ferdinand – Alysheba stretch battle ranked right up there with the Easy Goer – Sunday Silence, and Tiznow – Sakhee Classics.

Official summary (Congressional Research Service, Introduced in House):
Reversionary Interest Conveyance Act
This bill directs the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) to offer to sell the reversionary interest of the United States in approximately 8.43 acres of land in Sacramento, California, as generally depicted on a specified map dated November 7, 2022. Within two years of receiving a request from the owner of the land, the BLM must offer the reversionary interest and convey the reversionary interest to the buyer upon payment. The payment must be in an amount that is at least the fair market value of the reversionary interest. The buyer must also pay all costs related to the applicable conveyance of the reversionary interest, including all surveys, appraisals, and other administrative costs.
The bill subjects the conveyance to valid existing rights.
The proceeds from the sale must be deposited into Federal Land Disposal Account.

These letters to the WaPo Editors are well stated:

"The No Surprises Act is supposed to protect patients. Here’s how it hurts providers.
Reforming the No Surprise Act and AI standards, in readers' eyes.
October 22, 2026 at 4:29 p.m. EDT Yesterday at 4:29 p.m. EDT

Jackson Hammond and Brian Blase’s Oct. 18 op-ed, “A $17 billion surprise bill for Americans,” argued the No Surprises Act’s arbitration system is driving up health care costs, but they missed the root cause driving disputes.

I am a practicing emergency physician, and I’ve never met a colleague who said they view arbitration as a business model. But it becomes necessary when insurers terminate network contracts to make lowball payment offers to physicians who treat patients in emergencies, regardless of their ability to pay.

The op-ed, which detailed the new Paragon Health Institute analysis, argued that independent arbitrators side with providers in roughly 85 percent of disputes. But that statistic deserves context. In one study, which was backed by the Americans for Fair Health Care coalition, insurers’ qualifying payment amounts were set at $0 in more than 20,000 disputes, and in almost 1,000 others, they were set at less than $1.

Meanwhile, more than 20 percent of the time, insurers delayed paying arbitration awards or failed to participate, leaving physicians waiting to be paid for care they had already provided.

Paragon argues that physicians use arbitration to demand higher rates. My organization, TeamHealth, has seen awards below what insurers paid for the same services in 2019.

Health care systems would rather work under fair, stable in-network agreements, but persistent underpayments make it harder to recruit and retain clinicians and negotiate sustainable contracts, contributing to narrower networks and reduced access to emergency care.

Congress should preserve the No Surprises Act’s patient protections, require insurers to comply with arbitration decisions and address the payment practices that make arbitration necessary.

Jody Crane, Richmond
The writer is the chief medical officer for TeamHealth."

Letter #2:

"Every single day in America, someone experiences a life-threatening event that requires an air ambulance to keep them alive and get them to a hospital that can provide the appropriate level of care. Teams of dedicated medics, nurses and pilots are on duty 24/7 to respond to emergencies. But these services are critically undervalued by health insurance companies.

As important as the No Surprises Act is for protecting patients, it lacks the enforcement mechanisms needed to ensure emergency care providers are reimbursed.

Unfortunately, a growing number of payers are refusing to pay the outstanding claims that independent arbitrators have determined they owe — decisions which are legally binding and must be paid within 30 days. To date, insurers owe my company, PHI Health, more than $50 million in unpaid independent dispute resolution awards for emergency care already delivered.

This enormous burden has forced us to suspend operations at one base in rural California and threatens the future of air ambulance services. Insurers’ failure to respect the law could eventually leave many communities without air medical services, a situation Congress hardly intended.

The No Surprises Act needs more teeth to ensure that insurance companies follow the law and that claims owed are paid promptly.

Paul Julander, Tempe
The writer is co-president of PHI Health."

text:
In 1919 a man from Barbados wrote billiard table repairman in the occupation blank on his citizenship papers. Two years later, on the next form in the same process, Alexander McDonald Williams wrote manager, Central Baseball Park, because in between he had built the first Black-owned ballpark in Pittsburgh with money he did not really have.

Five years after that he had lost the team, the park and his house. The state of Pennsylvania has decided twice that this does not merit a sign.

On the fifteenth of July, 1919, a man in Pittsburgh sat down with a federal form and wrote his occupation in the blank.

Billiard table repairman.

Two years and two weeks later, in the same blank on the next form, he wrote something else.

Manager, Central Baseball Park.

Between those two lines, in his own handwriting, a man from Barbados built the first Black-owned ballpark in Pittsburgh. Twelve years later another man built one four blocks away and got the credit for all of it.

His name was Alexander McDonald Williams and he was born on the twenty-third of March, 1883. He left Bridgetown on the fifteenth of August, 1903, on a Leyland Line steamer, and came into New York ten days later at twenty years old.

He worked his way to Pittsburgh, married a woman named Margaret, and had two boys, Bailey in 1916 and McDonald in 1918. Around 1914 he opened a billiard hall in the basement of Burke's Theater, at the corner of Fullerton Street and Wylie Avenue.

He was not there alone. His brothers Charles and Stanley came out of Barbados behind him, and all three held a piece of that pool hall.

Stanley was the baby, born in 1900, and he landed in Pittsburgh at thirteen. A Courier profile years later said he had come to study dentistry at Pitt.

He never did. He racked balls for his brothers instead, and between 1926 and 1933 he waited tables.

The corner they were standing on would get a name after the war. People called Fullerton and Wylie the Crossroads of the World.

It held restaurants and nightclubs and theaters, and it held speakeasies and gambling houses and brothels. A man told a Courier columnist in 1954 that the crossing beat Seventh and T in Washington, because everything a night-lifer could want was standing on it.

Alexander watched Black Pittsburgh walk past his door every evening and pay other men to sit in other men's ballparks. His brother-in-law Arlis Bailey had managed a sandlot team since 1908, a club the janitors of the Frick Building put together downtown.

That is as close as the family has ever gotten to explaining where the baseball came from.

In 1920 Alexander rented two lots off Wylie Avenue and hired an architect named Louis Arnett Stuart Bellinger. Bellinger was one of roughly sixty Black registered architects in the whole United States, and this was the first thing he ever built in Pittsburgh.

They put a grandstand up on an old dump. Alexander called it Central Amusement Park, and people on the Hill called it the Chauncey Street park.

The first game was played there on the twenty-fourth of July, 1920, in a ballpark that was not finished. The lumber was still being delivered in August, and one of those delivery receipts, made out to Bellinger, is among the handful of papers that prove the place ever stood.

His first tenant was a club called Sell Hall's American Giants, who wore green and got called the Green Socks. In 1921 Alexander stopped renting his field to other men's teams and built his own, the Pittsburgh Keystones, with Dizzy Dismukes to manage and pitch.

That same year he and Stanley chartered a company to run it all, the Marathon Amusement Company, formed to promote indoor and outdoor athletic sports for public amusement. Alexander was president and Stanley was treasurer.

Two of the incorporators were Robert Vann and Ira Lewis of the Pittsburgh Courier. They would spend the next thirty years deciding what Black Pittsburgh read about itself.

In 1922 the Keystones went into the Negro National League. On the twenty-eighth of January that year, the owners of the league sat for a photograph at their annual meeting in Chicago, and Alexander Williams is standing in the back row of it.

Eight years earlier he had been repairing pool cues in a basement.

The Keystones finished seventh with ten wins and twenty-one losses, and then they folded. That one dismal summer was the only season of league baseball the Chauncey Street park ever saw.

Alexander lost his savings.

By 1924 the ballpark belonged to Sell Hall. In 1925 it was sold again and turned into a summer dancing pavilion.

William G. Nunn wrote its obituary in the Courier that June, under the heading of its passing. Where the shouts of the diamond fans had been, he wrote, the city would now hear jazz-crazed youth.

Alexander had come from Barbados with nothing and built a ballpark, and inside five years he had lost the team, the park, and the house.

He died in 1941.

Bellinger was thirty-four when the first thing he ever built for Black Pittsburgh came apart. He had been born in Sumter, South Carolina in 1891, the son of a carpenter, in a family of men who worked with their hands.

He took a degree in architecture from Howard in 1914 and taught mathematics in Ocala and then in Columbia. He registered for the draft in 1917 and came north to Pittsburgh in 1919.

The census caught him in 1920 renting a room on Chauncey Street, a short walk from the ballpark he had just drawn. He opened a downtown office in 1922 at 525 Fifth Avenue, across from the county courthouse.

In 1927 he designed the Pythian Temple on Centre Avenue. People know that building now as the New Granada.

In 1928 he built a house for himself and his wife Ethel and spent nineteen thousand dollars on it. When the Depression came for his practice he closed the office and sold the house.

Then in 1931 a numbers man came looking for somebody who could draw a ballpark.

Gus Greenlee was born the day after Christmas in 1895 in Marion, North Carolina. His father Samuel made his living as a brick and mason contractor.

Gus quit college in his second year and rode a freight car north to Pittsburgh in 1916. He shined shoes and drove for an undertaker before he bought his own taxi.

In 1917 he enlisted and went over as a machine gunner with the 367th Infantry. He fought at Verdun, took shrapnel in the left leg at St. Mihiel, and came home in 1919 to sell whiskey out of the back of his cab.

The Williams brothers already knew him, because everybody on that corner knew everybody. In 1924 the Courier carried advertisements for Greenlee's Paramount Inn on Wylie Avenue, listing Gus Greenlee and Tom Welch as the proprietors and Charles Williams as the manager.

Greenlee had also bought a pool hall in the basement of the M. J. Farrell Building. About five years later he sold that business to Stanley Williams.

One family lost a ballpark. The other one was buying their pool halls and hiring their brothers.

By the mid-twenties Greenlee was running the Hill District's illegal lottery, and at its height his organization was taking in as much as twenty-five thousand dollars a day across nearly a hundred clearing houses. That money mattered for a reason that had nothing to do with gambling.

Black Pittsburghers were routinely shut out of conventional credit, so the numbers bankers did the lending the established banks would not.

Greenlee paid people's rent and buried their dead, ran a soup line through the Depression, and staked new businesses on the Hill. In 1948 the neighborhood named him its businessman of the year.

He was one of the largest employers of Black people in western Pennsylvania. The money came from a game with odds of nine hundred and ninety-nine to one.

He bought the Crawfords in 1930 and started buying ballplayers. Oscar Charleston, Josh Gibson, Satchel Paige, Judy Johnson, Cool Papa Bell, and a seventeen-passenger Mack bus with real leather seats that the papers priced at ten thousand dollars.

What he did not have was a field. The Crawfords rented Ammon Field for ordinary games and leased Forbes Field for the big ones, and at Forbes his players were not allowed in the clubhouse.

So the son of a brick contractor went and bought a brickyard. The Entress Brick Company had a full city block on Bedford Avenue between Junilla and Watt, and the Depression had left its stockholders ready to sell.

The deed to that block never went into his name.

The company formed to hold the land was called the Bedford Land Company. Dr. Joseph Thoms, the white physician who held the brickyard deed, was president, and Joe Tito, the white Latrobe brewer who had been Greenlee's bootlegging partner since the taxicab days, was treasurer.

Gus Greenlee held twenty-five percent of the stock and no office at all.

John L. Clark, the Courier columnist who doubled as the Crawfords' own secretary, set it down in the paper in exactly those words. Ground broke on the twentieth of July, 1931.

Steam shovels cut twenty-one thousand cubic yards of earth out of a hillside. The finished park swallowed seventy-five tons of steel and fourteen railcars of cement.

On the eighth of August the city denied the zoning appeal outright. No one has ever found the paper that reversed it.

Opening day was Friday the twenty-ninth of April, 1932, and the schedule ran by the quarter hour. Batting practice at 3:45 and 4:15, team photographs at 4:45, workouts at 5:15 and 5:30, the flag at 5:45, and baseball at six.

Greenlee came through his own gate standing up inside a red Packard convertible in a white silk suit and white buck shoes. Four thousand people paid fifty cents for the grandstand and thirty-five for the bleachers.

Both teams walked out behind a band to the flagpole in deep center field. Robert Vann of the Courier made a short speech about the man who had built the place, and the whole crowd stood up for Greenlee.

Eleven years earlier Vann had put his name on the incorporation papers of Alexander Williams's amusement company. Nobody at that flagpole mentioned it.

Then Vann went to the mound and threw the first pitch, and it bounced on the way in.

The umpire called it a strike.

Satchel Paige started. Josh Gibson played left field instead of catching, because he was still healing from an appendix operation he had gone through at spring training in Hot Springs.

Paige struck out ten and gave up six hits. Jesse Hubbard of the New York Black Yankees gave up three.

In the top of the ninth, Orville Riggins singled, Ted Page reached on a fielder's choice, stole second, took third on a throwing error, and came home on a blooper. In the bottom of the ninth with two out, Gibson hit a ball to deep center and a man named Thomas ran it down.

They lost the first game in the finest Black ballpark in America, one to nothing.

Then June came, and there was no roof.

The grandstand had been left uncovered to save money, and people sat in open sun for two and a half hours at a stretch. Buck Leonard was still talking about fans broiling out there forty years later.

In the spring of 1934 Greenlee went to the stockholders of the ballpark with his name on it and asked for a simple awning over the seats. The decision belonged to the men holding the other three quarters.

They told him no.

In 1936 he tried to go around them, selling eight dollar season passes over the counter at the Crawford Grill and raffling a new Ford sedan with the drawing set for the Fourth of July. The Courier never printed who won the car, and the grandstand never got its roof.

Tito's brother Ralph held the concession stand, and a Tito relative was the groundskeeper. After Prohibition ended, a Latrobe Beer advertisement went up along the bottom of the scoreboard in left field.

The Hill watched white men from outside the neighborhood take nearly every paying job inside a ballpark built for Black Pittsburgh. It blamed the Black man whose name was over the door.

He owned a quarter of it and could not have hired anyone if he tried.

He could not get a sheet of canvas raised over four thousand seats. In 1933 he pulled together a new Negro National League, installed himself as president, and started the East West All Star Game, which became the biggest single date on the Black baseball calendar.

He put permanent lights on that field in September 1932, eight years before the Pittsburgh Pirates managed it at Forbes. To break the state law against Sunday baseball he scheduled the Crawfords against the Grays for one minute past midnight on a Monday, and three thousand people came out at that hour to watch.

Cool Papa Bell said the outfield gave him room to run. In 1933 Bellinger was hired by Greenlee one more time, to draw plans for remodeling a storeroom at the Crawford Grill.

In July 1938 the Pittsburgh Housing Authority came for the ground. The Hill's housing was falling apart, Washington had money for three projects, and the flattest full city block in the neighborhood happened to have a ballpark on it.

The Authority offered fifty thousand dollars, and the Courier reported that if the stockholders declined, the parcel would be taken by condemnation. After the deal was agreed the price was cut to thirty-eight thousand, and there was nothing anyone could do.

The Crawfords played their last home game on the third of September, 1938, against the Homestead Grays. It was the first of four scheduled that weekend, and the other three had been moved to parks in Ohio and West Virginia.

No newspaper on either side of the color line ever printed the score.

Wendell Smith wrote in the Courier that the place looked like a graveyard now. On the twentieth of November the floodlights went into the classified ads of the Pittsburgh Press, and on the fourth of December the steel beams followed them.

Next door, crews in masks began lifting about two hundred people out of Lincoln Memorial Cemetery with a steam shovel while families stood and watched. Most of those graves reached Woodlawn without the stones they came with.

On the nineteenth of December the groundbreaking for Bedford Dwellings went out live on KDKA radio. The three million dollar construction contract went to a firm in Minneapolis.

Louis Bellinger spent 1938 on the payroll of the City of Pittsburgh's Bureau of Building Inspection. He was working for the city the year the city took the second ballpark he had drawn and pulled it down.

He died of a cerebral hemorrhage on the third of February, 1946, and the Courier put his photograph on the front page. He is buried in Allegheny Cemetery, a little way up the hill from Josh Gibson, with the details of his brief army service cut into the stone.

Greenlee's nightclub burned in 1951 and was never rebuilt. He died at home after a stroke on the seventh of July, 1952, and went into the same cemetery, in the same section as Gibson.

By then Alexander Williams had been dead eleven years, and the Crossroads of the World was being measured for demolition.

Charles never saw any of that either. In 1949 he was working behind the bar in his younger brother's club when a customer shot him.

Teenie Harris was at the memorial with a camera. The photograph he took is of Stanley Williams standing on a bridge, throwing flowers down into the Monongahela.

Stanley was the one who lasted. He opened his nightclub in 1933, in the space he had bought from Gus Greenlee, and by 1930 he had already thrown his wife Syvella a birthday party with an orchestra and handed her a two-tone brown Packard sedan.

Two men on that corner, two Packards, and only one of them is in the history books.

In 1950 Stanley wrote a letter to the editor of the Courier and described himself the way his brother once described himself on a government form. He was a native of Barbados, he wrote, and he had come here for economic advancement.

Urban renewal cleared him off Fullerton and Wylie in 1956. He opened again in July 1958 at 7403 Frankstown Avenue in Homewood, and he ran it until he died in 1977 at seventy-seven.

The family sold the place the following year.

The Courier had already tried to fix the record. On the twenty-fourth of February, 1962, it printed that the first man to put his own money into Black baseball in the form of an actual physical plant was Alexander Williams, who thought Pittsburgh was ready and put a ballpark on an old dump off Wylie.

That was sixty-four years ago and nobody moved.

In 2009 Pennsylvania set a marker on Bedford Avenue, standing exactly where the arched entryways of Greenlee Field had been. It calls that ballpark the first African American owned stadium in the Negro Leagues.

It was the last one.

Giants Park opened in St. Louis in 1919, and Central Amusement Park opened in Pittsburgh in 1920. Lewis Park opened in Memphis in 1922.

The historian Gary Ashwill went and checked the claim instead of repeating it. Greenlee Field, he found, was not the first of its kind but the last.

Mark Fatla, who spent years on Pittsburgh's old ballparks, put it flatter than that. The idea that Greenlee built the first Black-owned ballpark, he said, is not true.

In 2011 a retired English professor named McDonald Williams, then in his nineties, applied to the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission for a marker on the site of his father's ballpark. He was the baby born in November 1918, the one who was not yet two when the grandstand went up.

He sent them a history of the park, the stories his father had told him, a ballplayer's contract, and the receipts for the wood.

The commission denied it.

The state kept his paperwork for three years and destroyed it in 2015, along with the rest of the applications it had turned down. When the public historian David Rotenstein asked why the marker was refused, the agency told him the file was gone and withheld the internal records under a privilege that covers its own deliberations.

He appealed and won. What the state finally handed over in November 2022 was a screen capture of an internal list, with no reviewer named and no reason given.

McDonald Williams died in 2017 at a hundred and one.

His daughter Donna told Rotenstein that the record needs setting straight, and that she wants her granddaughters to understand whose shoulders they are standing on.

There is one photograph of the ballpark. Nobody knew that until the summer of 2022, when a conversation among researchers online finally put a name to a grandstand that had been sitting unidentified in the record the whole time.

The evidence was never really missing, and neither were the men.

Alexander Williams built it, Louis Bellinger drew it, and a state commission decided it was not worth a sign. The family is preparing to file again.

Go and read the name out loud once before somebody has to ask a state agency for permission to put it on a post.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter.
If you'd like to support the work, here's the link:
https://t.co/Vm6JEQyFTo
Every coffee helps me keep creating

https://t.co/2MFYz6LVg8 𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀 𝗕𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝘁 𝗖𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝗿, 𝗪𝗵𝘆 𝗗𝗼 𝗪𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗻 𝗡𝗲𝗲𝗱 𝗧𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗼𝗻𝗲 ? Five years ago, Peggy felt a nodule in the right breast and brought it to medical attention. Image guided needle biopsy confirmed it was breast cancer, and Peggy underwent right lumpectomy. The pathology report showed infiltrating ductal carcinoma, an invasive cell type. Surgical margins were good, and no additional treatment was offered. Peggy did well for two years at which time she had a recurrence. The breast cancer returned with a new mass in the right breast and palpable nodes in the right axilla. In addition, CAT scan showed multiple metastatic nodules in the lungs. Her doctors offered her chemotherapy which Peggy declined. Instead she did her own research and found a doctor in Ohio, Rebecca Glaser MD, who treats breast cancer with testosterone. Peggy went to Dr. Glaser’s Clinic, and started Dr. Glaser’s protocol. A testosterone pellet was implanted, and letrozole started. Letrozole is an aromatase inhibitor drug which prevents conversion of testosterone to estrogen. Over time, the breast mass and axillary nodes gradually decreased in size and disappeared. A follow up CAT scan one year later showed the lungs were clear. Peggy was in complete remission from breast cancer using Dr. Rebecca Glaser’s testosterone/ letrozole protocol. I was impressed with this, as using testosterone for treatment of breast cancer was new to me.

Testosterone: 39% Reduction in Breast Cancer

In 2013 and 2019, Drs. Rebecca Glaser,York and Constantine Dimitrakis studied the incidence of breast cancer in a 10-year prospective cohort study of 1,267 pre and postmenopausal women receiving at least two testosterone pellet insertions. The 10 year follow up data showed 39 percent reduction for invasive breast cancer in women treated with testosterone compared with the ‘‘age-matched’’ population.

Second Study : Testosterone Prevents Breast Cancer

In 2021, Dr. Gary Donovitz conducted a retrospective observational study over 10 years of 2,377 pre- and post-menopausal women treated with Testosterone pellets, alone or combined with Estradiol. This study showed 35-50% reduction in the incidence of breast cancer for testosterone treated women, thus confirming the earlier findings of Dr. Rebecca Glaser.(1-2)

Second Study : Testosterone Prevents Breast Cancer

text:
The problem with Fr. Rooney here isn’t that the intuition is bad; it is that the terminology is completely defective, which causes him to unknowingly set himself in complete opposition to texts like this (which Gemini did not send him for some reason): “punishment is required after faults are forgiven for two reasons, namely, to resolve a debt and to offer a remedy... in the penitential forum punishment must be reckoned for both reasons... But the punishment of purgatory is only for paying the debt, for at that point there is no further room for sinning.” (In IV Sent. d. 20, q. 1, a. 2, qc. 1)

For St. Thomas, there are not two forms of punishment (“vindictive” and “medicinal”); there are four forms of punishment (poena simpliciter/proper punishment, satisfactory, purgatorial, and medicinal). 

He lays out three of them in ST I-II, q. 87, a. 8: satisfactory punishment, which is voluntarily assumed and can be borne for another; punishment “inasmuch as it has the nature of punishment,” which is only ever for one’s own sin; and punishment “which has the nature of medicine.” The fourth is named in SCG: the punishment God inflicts on one who does not exact it of himself “will not be called satisfactory, since it was not from the choice of the sufferer, but purgatorial” (SCG III, c. 158). It is closely related to satisfactory punishment vis-a-vis the end and voluntarity, but is slightly different as to the origin. This is why they are sometimes identified. 

This is exactly what the Counter-Reformation theologians said to the Protestants, who conceded castigatio but denied poena. This is exactly how Catholic theologians refuted the moral arguments against satisfaction given by the Socinian heretics. This is how theologians responded to the various shades of modernist theologians and liberals throughout the 19th and 20th centuries who had a similar problem due to their complete acceptance of contemporary juridical notions that accepted punishment as merely medicinal.

After guilt is forgiven, it is fine to say that there is no vindictive punishment properly speaking (although certain theologians keep the terminology insofar as vindication touches the order of justice rather than the person... which is why it is often said that satisfaction is offered to the vindictive justice of God). St. Thomas himself says exactly this, and then separates the two aspects Fr. Rooney confuses: “Satisfaction is both punitive, inasmuch as it is an act of vindicative justice, and medicinal, inasmuch as it is a kind of sacramental. An indulgence therefore takes the place of satisfaction inasmuch as it is punitive, because the punishment another bore is imputed to this man as if he had borne it, and so the debt of punishment is removed; but it does not take the place of satisfaction inasmuch as it is medicinal, because the pronenesses to sin remain... But for the dying such preservation is not necessary, but only liberation from the debt of punishment.” (Quodl. II, q. 8, a. 2, ad 3) 

One of the strongest points for the traditional account (as one can see from the countless indulgence bulls from the Roman Pontiffs) is how bound up it is with Catholic praxis. Indulgences really do not make any sense under a purely 'medicinal' view of the matter...this gets especially obvious when you spend a few minutes thinking about the fact that the baptized have no debt of temporal punishment (which I will explain below). 

Theologians clarify that the liability to temporal punishment is no longer a liability to punishment simply speaking, but to satisfactory punishment (ST I-II, q. 87, a. 6): the debt remains, but it is paid voluntarily, insofar as we have violated the order of justice and inflicted injury upon the rights of God, and understand the moral obligation to restore this (note: closely related to this is the purgatorial punishment, which differs slightly from the satisfactory). All you need to do to understand what he means by these matters is simply to read his articles on satisfactory punishment. It is quite easy, actually! 

The faithful, by charity, are zealous to restore the right honor of God and voluntarily receive penal afflictions so as to restore this honor (which is exactly the context of the passages where St. Thomas and others require charity for satisfaction when they are wrested from their context). 

By the way, this is, in my opinion, why many are so uncomfortable with the notion. Satisfaction cannot be explained by some sort of necessity or (primarily) as some good of man; it has to be explained in terms of the rights and honor of God. St. Thomas requires that in satisfaction “something be subtracted from the sinner which redounds to the honor of God” (In IV Sent. d. 15, q. 1, a. 4, qc. 1), and adopts Anselm’s definition, “to render to God the honor owed” (Suppl. q. 12, a. 3). To justify a doctrine as primarily for the honor of God and to vindicate his rights makes many uncomfortable! It also supposes an objective order of justice (which Fr. Rooney derides as “abstract”), which is a mockery to contemporary jurists and does not correspond too well to modern notions: “it is not that the deficiency is always healed by the punishment in the one in whom it is, as is clear in the damned and in a thief who is hanged, but rather that the punishment compensates for the deficiency in the state of the universe or the republic due to the order of justice that appears in the punishment.” (In II Sent., d. 42, q. 1, a. 2) 

We should simply adopt St. Paul VI's description that these punishments are imposed “for the purification of souls, for the defense of the sanctity of the moral order, and for the restoration of the glory of God to its full majesty” (Indulgentiarum doctrina, n. 2). 

To reduce the satisfactory punishment to the “medicinal” is completely false. As briefly mentioned above, it makes mincemeat of quite a few fundamental doctrines and practices in Catholicism. To consider just one example among many... the newly baptized adult who has many habitual attachments to sin has no debt of temporal punishment and, upon death, immediately goes to heaven (“no satisfactory punishment is imposed on the baptized, because they are wholly freed by the satisfaction of Christ,” ST III, q. 49, a. 3, ad 2; cf. Florence, DS 1316); on the other hand, the man who has been Catholic for decades, living in a spirit of penance and far more holy than the newly baptized, suffers in purgatory. That is quite a surprise, isn't it!

This is also why Fr. Rooney’s recent words on the Passion are so defective. It is true that Christ did not suffer vindictive punishments inflicted upon him by God; yet he did suffer satisfactory punishments insofar as he voluntarily suffered penal afflictions, offered to the vindictive justice of God (note: not inflicted by the vindictive justice of God, but offered to the vindictive justice of God...an important consideration). “Christ bore a satisfactory punishment, not for his own sins but for ours” (ST I-II, q. 87, a. 7, ad 3). This was suffered to restore the rights of God, which we creatures have so grievously injured.

text:
I asked Grok about the story since you can't read it without subscribing. Here's the answer:

📷📷62 sources Here are the primary links to the story::

More Than 18,000 Children Injected With Vaccines Under Anesthesia or Sedation at Colorado Hospital Since 2020, Including Neurologically Vulnerable Kids
Original source it cites (AAP News, March 9, 2026):
How to make immunizations part of pediatric surgical, procedural care process
by Caroline A. Pasquariello, M.D., FAAP (Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia) and Kim M. Strupp, M.D., FAAP (Children’s Hospital Colorado).

The AAP piece states that Children’s Hospital Colorado (CHCO) has offered the influenza vaccine under general anesthesia to eligible patients since 2020, with “more than 18,000 patients” vaccinated since then. It also notes: “Additional vaccinations are administered at the request of the primary care clinician, particularly for children with neurocognitive conditions who are unable to tolerate vaccination without sedation.”This program began earlier; 2021 reports describe a “best practice alert” system at CHCO that sharply increased flu vaccinations given under anesthesia (e.g., from roughly 30 in a prior period to over 1,000 in the intervention period). Related coverage includes:Healio (Nov. 2021)
News-Medical (Oct. 2021)

The story has circulated widely on X via the Substack link and related posts. The AAP frames the practice as a way to increase vaccination rates (especially for kids with needle phobia or behavioral/neurocognitive challenges) during existing procedures involving sedation or anesthesia.

Question: For children, did the parents consent?

Thought for 13s
Yes, the program requires parental (or guardian) consent.

According to descriptions of the Children’s Hospital Colorado (CHCO) process (including a 2022 Anesthesiology paper on their influenza vaccination program and related reports):

Staff use a best-practice alert during preoperative registration/check-in to check vaccination status and eligibility.

They discuss the vaccine with the parent/guardian, provide information (including the required Vaccine Information Statement/VIS), and obtain parental consent (and patient assent when applicable).

Only after consent is obtained is a standing order placed and the vaccine administered under anesthesia/sedation during the procedure.

Families can and do decline. Common reasons noted include that the child was already vaccinated that season or the family has a longstanding preference to avoid the vaccine.

This is consistent with standard pediatric practice and CHCO’s general policies, which require informed consent from a parent or legally authorized representative for treatments and procedures. Federal rules also require providing the VIS before administering covered vaccines.

In short, the vaccines are not given automatically or without permission—the process is structured as an offer with explicit consent obtained beforehand. The AAP News article (March 2026) describing the >18,000 figure frames it the same way: the vaccine is offered to eligible patients.

text:
The Lipka Tatars - Muslim horsemen who lived in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth since the 14th Century—played a vital role in defending Poland against the Ottoman Empire, most famously helping King Jan III Sobieski lift the Siege of Vienna in 1683...

"Our Tatars are entertaining themselves with falcons they have brought with them; they are guarding the prisoners, and are proving to be loyal and trustworthy".

- Jan III Sobieski, Letters to Marysieńka

The saviors of Christendom, many remember King Jan Sobieski of Poland and his army, particularly the Wing Hussars, as the heroes of the Battle of Vienna of 1683, and rightly so. However, the heroic Polish warriors were only part of a much larger force which it seems popular history has forgotten. Some of the battles participants have been marginalized (such as Duke Charles of Lorraine), others such as Emperor Leopold I have been demonized with nationalistic vehemence. Still others have been simply forgotten by the popular imagination, as is the case of the Lipka Tatars.

Originating in the White Horde, a subdivision of the Mongol-led Golden Horde, in 1397 after a war against the Amir Timur the Tatar Khan Tokhtamysh settled with the remnants of his people as vassals of the Duke of Lithuania, Vytautas the Great. The Muslim Tatars soon become an integral unit of Lithuanian military forces and continued in this role during the time of the various unions of the Kingdom of Poland and Grand Duchy of Lithuania, which culminated in the Union of Lublin in 1569. They continued to serve their common fatherland faithfully, adopting the Civilization of Christendom and many elements of the Polish and Lithuanian Catholic culture, until the disastrous Second Polish–Ottoman War, and the Lipka rebellion in 1672.

Around 3,000 soldiers of the Tatar cavalry rebelled and joined the Ottoman Turks under the leadership of rotmistrz Aleksander Kryczyński. Made Bey of the fortress of Bar, Kryczyński was killed by the Tatars under his command rioting against their subjugation by the Turkish Sultan. In 1674 the fortress of Bar was besieged by Jan Sobieski, then Grand Hetman of the Polish Army, who wisely offered to restore to any Tatars who would rejoin the Commonwealth the ancient rights of the Tatar people. Earlier during the Swedish Deluge of Poland, 2,000 Tatars served directly under Sobieski’s command, and this offer of amnesty effectively ended the rebellion.

Elected King in the same year and crowned in 1676, Jan III Sobieski made good his promise and through the Sejm restored the ancient rights of the Tatars, and gave them holdings from his personal lands. In 1683, honoring his alliance with Holy Roman Emperor Leopold I, King Jan set out to relieve the Kaiserstadt Vienna with a force of 27,000 Poles, including several regiments of Lipka Tatars, who wore sprigs of straw upon their helmets to differentiate them from their Turkish allied co-nationals. Joining the 47,000 strong Imperial force under Duke Charles of Lorraine, the Poles and Tatars charged from the Kahlenberg, and the relief army won the field against the Turks, Crimean Tatars, and Protestant Hungarian rebels under Imre Thököly. As the campaign continued, the Polish army was overwhelmed by the retreating Turkish army at Párkány in the Kingdom of Hungary, and King Jan was cut off from his soldiers. His life was saved by the daring of the Muslim Tatar Lieutenant Samuel Mirza Krzeczowski, a participant in the battle of Vienna, who was promoted to the rank of colonel and rewarded with the estate of Kruszyniany.

text:
The Left has changed. Have Jews noticed?
October 7th exposed a political transformation that has been underway for years. What’s happening in Europe makes it impossible to ignore.
JOSHUA HOFFMAN
Since October 7th, I have come to believe there are three types of voters on the Left:
Far-Left radicals disguising themselves as “progressives”
Those who are making their way toward the Center and Right
Those who remain in denial about what the Left has become
Jews cannot afford to ignore the questions raised by that third category, especially not after October 7th, and even more so after what we have witnessed across Europe over the past week.
A political culture has taken shape on the Left in which some movements that claim to champion justice have become remarkably comfortable excusing intolerance, disorder, extremism, and even terrorism whenever they appear to serve a supposedly righteous cause.
Look at France, where demonstrations over education and living costs have descended into riots, looting, and attacks on public property. Belgium has experienced its own violent confrontations. The unrest has exposed uncomfortable questions about the ideologies, political movements, and institutions shaping much of modern Europe.
For me, as a Jew, this is part of a much bigger story, because what is happening in Europe reminds me of something that became impossible to ignore on October 7, 2023: The people who speak most loudly about tolerance are not necessarily the people most willing to practice it.
In 2025, French authorities recorded 1,320 antisemitic incidents, a historically high number. Antisemitic incidents accounted for 53 percent of all anti-religious acts recorded in the country, even though Jews represent only a small minority of France’s population.
Those figures do not mean that the Left is responsible for every antisemitic attack. Antisemitism comes from the Far Right, Islamist extremists, and elsewhere, too. But the Left has a particular problem because it claims a particular moral authority. It presents itself as the champion of minorities, tolerance, pluralism, and equality. And increasingly, that claim deserves scrutiny.
There is a contradiction at the heart of today’s “progressive” politics: Jews are embraced as victims but become objects of suspicion when they are successful. Suddenly, Jewish achievement is interpreted through the language of “privilege,” “oppression,” “colonialism,” and “capitalism.”
Jews should not have to apologize for our successes, and Israelis should not be expected to apologize for their achievements. Generations of Jewish perseverance, education, entrepreneurship, innovation, and communal responsibility have produced extraordinary results, often in the face of persecution and discrimination. The State of Israel’s accomplishments are similarly remarkable, particularly given the geopolitical challenges the country has confronted since its founding in 1948.
Yet an increasingly prominent strain of leftist politics, what I call the “New Left,” seems more interested in interrogating success. Through this worldview, achievement becomes evidence of privilege, prosperity becomes a source suspicion, and inequality of outcomes becomes proof of injustice. The distinction between creating opportunity and guaranteeing equal results begins to disappear.
There is nothing wrong with fighting poverty, confronting discrimination, or expanding opportunity. These are worthy goals. But there is something profoundly wrong with treating success itself as a moral offense. The answer to inequality should be to help more people succeed, not to diminish those who already have. That is not meritocracy. It is the politics of resentment masquerading as the pursuit of justice.
When this worldview is applied to Jews and Israel, the implications are especially troubling. Jewish achievement becomes evidence of “disproportionate power.” Israel’s technological, economic, and military successes become grounds for suspicion rather than accomplishments that can be examined on their merits.
Consider a recent statement by Michigan’s Democratic Senate nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, who declared on national television this week: “I think it’s time for us to realize that Israel is actually not our friend.”
Never mind that El-Sayed might have personal and family connections to the Muslim Brotherhood, which has made Israel one of its primary targets. And forget about the fact that El-Sayed is said to be receiving donations from people living outside the United States and cannot publicly distance himself from Hamas, an Islamist terrorist organization, without risking the support of some of his voters.
His statement is extraordinary given the depth of America’s relationship with Israel. At a time when NATO faces deep disagreements, Europe is grappling with instability, and the Middle East is caught between competing visions of confrontation and modernization, Israel remains one of America’s most consequential strategic partners.
Israel provides intelligence cooperation, develops cutting-edge technologies, contributes to missile defense and cybersecurity, and works with the United States against common regional threats. One can debate American foreign policy, foreign aid, and particular Israeli decisions without dismissing the strategic value of this relationship.
But that is the point: Increasingly, Israel is discussed in Left-wing circles not as an ally whose policies are open to criticism, but as a country whose legitimacy and accomplishments are themselves suspect.
El-Sayed at a campaign event at Michigan Technological University in 2025 (photo: Conlan Houston/Wikipedia)
The same ideological divide shapes the discussion of Gaza. Israel has severely weakened Hamas’ military capabilities following the October 7th massacre, while the civilian death toll and allegations of genocide remain subjects of profound dispute. Allegations of wrongdoing deserve serious examination, not wholesale acceptance. Yet too much of the political discussion seems incapable of distinguishing between legitimate criticism of Israel’s conduct and hostility toward the very idea of Jewish national success.
Former U.S. President Barack Obama, himself the “progressive” of all “progressives,” recently offered another example of how Israel’s history is presented. Speaking in Belfast, he claimed that Israel “took land off people and they were excessive,” and added that the Palestinians understandably reacted by saying, “This is injustice, and I want my land back.”
The Jewish return to the Land of Israel (our indigenous homeland) involved immigration, land purchases, national revival, and an internationally contested struggle for self-determination. In 1947, Jewish leaders accepted the United Nations partition proposal, while Arab leaders rejected it. Violence followed, and after Israel declared independence in May 1948, armies from neighboring Arab states invaded.
The war resulted in the displacement of hundreds of thousands of local Arabs through fighting, flight, and expulsions. Others stayed and became citizens of the State of Israel. The vast majority of their children and grandchildren will tell you that there is no other place in the Middle East they would rather live.
Those who were displaced became refugees, as millions of people have throughout history when wars have erupted. Their suffering was real, but so was the war that produced it. The displacement cannot be understood without acknowledging the rejection of partition and the invasion of the newly established Jewish state by neighboring Arab armies.
And therein lies the contradiction: If the Left is so appalled by the human consequences of war, why does it so often struggle to confront the Palestinian factions that have repeatedly chosen terrorism and war over coexistence? Why condemn the consequences of war while minimizing the decisions that helped bring those consequences about?
And why is Israel expected to bear the burden of history while those who have repeatedly sought its destruction are so often excused from responsibility for their choices?
The same problem appears in Left-wing narratives about Gaza that begin with Israel’s military response but minimize the Hamas-led massacre and kidnappings of October 7th. Context matters. So does the order in which events occurred.
This is one of my greatest concerns about the New Left: the temptation to cherry-pick and rewrite history until it conforms to an ideological narrative steeped in certainty but lacking in nuance, context, and intellectual honesty.
In fact, “Palestine” has become an omnicause on the New Left — a political symbol attached to issues that have little direct relationship to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. Gaza has nothing to do with the quality of public schools in France or housing costs in New York City. Yet anti-Israel slogans have become familiar features of Left-wing demonstrations and political movements organized around entirely different grievances, across the West.
For some, anti-Israel politics appears to provide a convenient language through which broader resentments about power, wealth, capitalism, and Western society can be expressed. At times, familiar antisemitic assumptions about Jewish influence and collective guilt are repackaged as political criticism — all leading to a troubling expectation in certain corners of the New Left that Jews can continue to be accepted, provided we edit Israel out of Judaism.
Jewish holidays are acceptable. Jewish food is acceptable. Jewish humor, Jewish traditions, and Jewish contributions to society can all be celebrated. But Jewish peoplehood, Jewish history, and our connection to our ancestral homeland are suddenly treated as political liabilities. In other words, some people seem perfectly comfortable celebrating Jewish culture while rejecting essential parts (i.e., Israel) of the Jewish story.
What kind of tolerance welcomes a minority only after it has edited out the parts of its identity that make others uncomfortable? What kind of diversity celebrates Jewish culture while treating Jewish national self-determination as inherently objectionable?
The irony is difficult to ignore. A political movement that prides itself on celebrating minority identities can end up telling Jews which expressions of Jewish identity are acceptable. And there is little meaning in telling people to be proud of who they are, only to demand that they become someone else.
a large group of people holding signs and flags
photo: Tristan Sosteric/Unsplash
There is another aspect of this story that deserves attention: the assumption that because a political movement stood on the right side of history yesterday, it must still be standing there today. History does not work that way.
Political parties change. Ideologies evolve. Coalitions form around new interests, new constituencies, and new priorities. The principles that once defined a movement can gradually become subordinate to the pursuit of power.
For many people who grew up on the Left, politics was never simply about taxes, immigration, or foreign policy. It was about identity. It was about being compassionate, tolerant, open-minded, and standing up for those who could not stand up for themselves. To question the movement, therefore, can feel like questioning one’s own morality.
But compassion does not belong to the Left. Neither does tolerance, equality, decency, or the pursuit of justice. These are human values, not political property. There is a crucial difference between abandoning your principles and discovering that your political affiliations no longer reflect them. The former can be a compromise of conscience. The latter can be an expression of it.
And that is what intellectual courage looks like: not blindly following a movement because it has always felt like home, not defending behavior you would condemn if it came from your opponents, and not confusing loyalty with integrity.
Leaving the New Left does not inherently make someone a bad person, just as remaining on the Left does not inherently make someone a good one. What matters is whether the decision is grounded in conscience, intellectual honesty, and a consistent set of principles.
Changing one’s political identity does not necessarily mean changing one’s values. Sometimes it means refusing to let a political identity define them.
The Right, of course, has its own history of antisemitism, including movements that have glorified fascism and revived some of Europe’s most poisonous conspiracy theories. It would be absurd to trade blindness toward one political extreme for blindness toward another. But that does not absolve the Left of its particular failures. In fact, it makes those failures more disturbing.
When a movement that openly embraces intolerance behaves intolerantly, we are witnessing the fulfillment of its ideology. When a movement built around opposing intolerance behaves intolerantly, we are witnessing the corruption of its ideology. And that deserves an entirely different kind of scrutiny.
For too long, political movements have been allowed to substitute the language of virtue for the practice of virtue. Call yourself “progressive,” and people assume your intentions are good. Speak about “equality,” and people assume you believe in equal treatment. Campaign against “hatred,” and people assume you oppose hatred wherever it appears.
October 7th exposed how dangerous those assumptions can be.
There is a difference between standing for principles and standing for the people who happen to share your politics. The former is liberalism. The latter is tribalism. And some of what passes for progressivism today appears increasingly unable to distinguish between the two.
I do not believe the most important divide in Western politics is necessarily between Left and Right. I believe it is between those who remain committed to the fundamental principles of liberal democracy and those who consider those principles negotiable whenever they interfere with a preferred political outcome. The tragedy is that some of the people undermining these principles continue to imagine themselves as their greatest defenders.
For decades, the Left’s greatest claim to legitimacy was that it stood against the prejudices and authoritarian impulses of the past. Today, some of its most vocal factions have become disturbingly comfortable reproducing them.
The most unsettling possibility is not simply that parts of the Left have abandoned their ideals. It is that they have become so convinced of their own righteousness that they can no longer recognize when they are betraying those ideals.

text:
Javadhu Powder or Javadhu Attar
Javadhu Powder or Javadhu Attar : Siddha Fragrance for Body Balance & Spiritual Purity
Javadhu (ஜவ்வாது) is a traditional South Indian aromatic powder rooted in Siddha medicine. Made mainly from sandalwood and herbs, it works as a natural fragrance, cooling body powder, and spiritual aid used for centuries in Tamil Nadu temples and homes.
What Is Javadhu?
Javadhu is a fine herbal powder or its extract is used externally. It is applied on the body, offered to deities, or used during pooja and meditation. Its soft, woody, slightly camphoraceous, and floral aroma creates a pure, temple-like atmosphere without overpowering the senses.
Siddha Roots & History
Javadhu belongs to the Siddha tradition and is mentioned in Sangam literature. Tradition links its refinement to Bhogar Siddhar, one of the 18 Siddhars associated with the Palani Murugan temple. He is said to have prepared this blend as an offering to Lord Muruga, who is still called Javadu Priyan (the one who loves Javadhu).
Spiritual Importance
Used in pooja, archana, and abhishekam
Applied on deities or mixed with sandal paste
Helps calm the mind before prayer and meditation
Believed to purify the space and invite positive energy
Traditional Ingredients
Core ingredients include:
Sandalwood powder (main base)
Pachakarpooram (natural/edible camphor)
Lotus stems, dried gooseberry, and arugampul (in traditional recipes)
Floral extracts (rose, jasmine, lotus)
Occasional additions: vetiver, saffron, or mild spices
Authentic versions are plant-based. Recipes vary slightly by region and maker.
Benefits for Body & Mind
Cools the body (sandalwood base)
Acts as a gentle natural deodorant without blocking sweat
Soothes the skin
Calms mental restlessness and supports focus
Creates a clean, sattvic atmosphere
How to Use
Personal use: Mix a small pinch with a drop of water or rose water and apply to the neck or wrists. Or lightly dust on clothes after bathing.
Pooja use: Mix with sandal paste for the deity or keep a little in the pooja room.
Use sparingly; a little is enough. And attar: rub it on your pulse points or, like any other attar, on your wrist and back of ear
Conclusion
Javadhu is a simple yet powerful link between Siddha herbal knowledge and spiritual practice. It offers cooling comfort, pure fragrance, and a calm atmosphere that supports both body balance and devotion. SHOP @ https://t.co/vWuqjCyDaG
