text:
Christ Woven Through Every Page: The Bible's Greatest Evidence of Divine Inspiration

Beyond the manuscript, historical, archaeological, and scientific evidence supporting the integrity of the Old and New Testaments, one of the most compelling evidences of the Bible's divine inspiration, in my view, is its extraordinary internal witness and unity.

Written by dozens of authors over roughly fifteen centuries, across different languages, cultures, and historical settings, Scripture nevertheless unfolds a single, coherent redemptive narrative from Genesis to Revelation. The deeper one studies its themes, structures, typology, prophecies, and interconnected patterns, the more the Bible resembles a unified masterpiece with one divine Author behind many human authors.

As we explore the principal themes of covenant, Christology, soteriology, kingdom, and eschatology, we discover that each is organically connected to subsidiary themes that permeate the entire canon. Among the most prominent are the Temple/Tabernacle/Household motif, representing God's dwelling with man, and the Garden/Land/Mountain motif, representing God's kingdom inheritance and sanctuary presence. Similarly, the themes of sonship, kingship, priesthood, sacrifice, inheritance, exile, and restoration are interwoven throughout Scripture, converging in the person and work of Christ.

Consider the remarkable typological framework embedded within biblical history. Adam foreshadows Christ, the Last Adam (Romans 5:14; 1 Corinthians 15:45). Noah's ark prefigures salvation through judgment. Abraham's offering of Isaac anticipates the Father giving His beloved Son. The Passover lamb points to Christ, our Passover Lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7). The bronze serpent lifted in the wilderness foreshadows Christ being lifted up on the cross (John 3:14-15). The Exodus itself becomes a paradigm of redemption fulfilled in Christ. The priesthood, sacrifices, Day of Atonement (Leviticus), and tabernacle all find their ultimate fulfillment in Christ's once-for-all atoning work (Hebrews 9-10).

The Messianic prophecies are equally striking. The promised Seed of the woman who would crush the serpent (Genesis 3:15), Abraham's Seed through whom all nations would be blessed (Genesis 22:18), the Prophet like Moses (Deuteronomy 18:15), David's greater Son and eternal King (2 Samuel 7:12-16), the virgin-born Immanuel (Isaiah 7:14), the Mighty God and Prince of Peace (Isaiah 9:6), the suffering Servant who would bear the sins of many (Isaiah 53), the ruler born in Bethlehem whose goings forth are from everlasting (Micah 5:2), and the Son of Man receiving an everlasting dominion (Daniel 7:13-14) all converge upon Jesus Christ.

The mountain theme further demonstrates this extraordinary unity. Eden itself appears as the original garden-temple mountain where heaven and earth meet. Abraham offers Isaac upon Mount Moriah, the future site of the temple. God descends upon Mount Sinai in fire, cloud, and glory. Zion becomes God's chosen dwelling place and kingdom mountain. Isaiah and Micah foresee the nations streaming to the mountain of the Lord in the latter days (Isaiah 2:2-3; Micah 4:1-2). In the New Testament, Christ is transfigured upon a mountain, crucified outside Jerusalem, ascends into heaven, and gathers His people to the heavenly Mount Zion (Hebrews 12:22). The biblical storyline culminates in the New Jerusalem, the consummate garden-city-temple where God dwells with His people forever (Revelation 21-22).

The death, resurrection, ascension, and exaltation of Christ form the central axis from which all these themes derive their meaning. Christ is the better Adam, the true Son of God, Son of Man, Prophet, Priest, King, Judge, Temple, Sacrifice, and Redeemer. Through His atoning death and victorious resurrection, righteousness is imputed to believers, God's justice is satisfied, and His people are united to Him by faith.

As a consequence of this union, believers participate in Christ's offices and inheritance. They become sons in the Father's household, priests in God's living temple, kings sharing in Christ's kingdom, and heirs of the renewed creation. Just as Adam once dwelt in Eden, so believers ultimately inherit the greater Eden of the New Creation through the Second Adam.

The household, garden, temple, kingdom, and mountain themes therefore do not terminate in themselves. They all point beyond themselves to Christ and His people. The church becomes God's household, His temple, His holy priesthood, and the firstfruits of the coming kingdom.

Finally, this eschatological garden-temple is situated upon the mountain of God. Mount Sinai and Mount Zion become representative of two covenantal realities. Sinai represents the Mosaic administration, characterized by law and the earthly shadows of redemption (Exodus 19; Galatians 4:24-25). Zion represents the heavenly Jerusalem, the Covenant of Promise fulfilled in Christ, where believers have already come by faith (Hebrews 12:22-24). Thus Scripture traces one grand movement from Eden to Sinai, from Sinai to Zion, from shadow to fulfilment, and from the first creation to the New Creation.

For me, this intricate and multi-layered unity is one of the strongest evidences for the Bible's divine inspiration. The convergence of types, shadows, prophecies, covenants, institutions, ceremonies, historical events, mountain motifs, temple imagery, kingdom themes, and Messianic expectations, all culminating in Christ, is exceedingly difficult to explain as the product of mere human authorship. The Bible does not read like sixty-six disconnected books; it reads like one unfolding story, authored by God Himself, with Christ woven into every page for those with eyes to see.

text:
Temple of Poseidon at Cape Sounio

Few places combine ancient history and coastal scenery quite like the Temple of Poseidon at Cape Sounio. Perched on a rocky headland at the southern tip of Attica, the temple overlooks the Aegean Sea and offers one of the most memorable settings for an archaeological visit near Athens.

The sanctuary was dedicated to Poseidon, the ancient Greek god of the sea, whose protection was especially important to a civilisation closely connected with sailing and maritime trade. Its position above the water made it a significant landmark for those travelling along this stretch of coastline.

The temple that visitors see today dates to the fifth century BC. Although only part of the original structure remains, its tall marble columns still create an impressive silhouette against the sea. The surrounding landscape adds to the experience, with rocky cliffs, open horizons and views that seem to stretch endlessly across the Aegean.

There is plenty to enjoy during a visit:
•  Explore the temple remains: Walk around the surviving columns and learn about the sanctuary's role in ancient Greek religion.
•  Take in the sea views: The headland offers sweeping panoramas of the coastline and surrounding islands on clear days.
•  Visit near sunset: The changing light creates a beautiful backdrop for the temple, although this is also a popular time to visit.
•  Discover the mythology: Poseidon's association with the sea adds another layer of meaning to a monument overlooking such an important maritime route.
•  Enjoy the coastal journey: The drive from Athens passes seaside areas and offers opportunities to stop along the way, depending on your route and schedule.

Cape Sounio is an excellent excursion from Athens, whether you are interested in archaeology, photography or simply experiencing one of Attica's most dramatic landscapes. Many visitors combine the temple with a drive along the coast and a meal at a nearby seaside restaurant.

If sunset is your goal, check the site's closing time before setting out, as access to the archaeological area may end before the sun disappears below the horizon. Arriving with enough time to explore means you can appreciate the temple itself rather than rushing straight to a viewpoint.

As you stand above the water, it is easy to understand why the ancient Greeks chose this headland for a sanctuary to Poseidon. The temple seems perfectly placed between land, sky and sea, making Sounio an unforgettable final stop on a journey through the history and landscapes of Greece.

text:
"The core biblical critique of treating holy relics, crosses, artifacts, or rituals as objects of focused devotion or mediation is rooted in Christ’s teaching and the New Testament’s emphasis on the finished, spiritual nature of redemption—not merely later Protestant reaction.

Key principles drawn directly from Scripture:

1. The Kingdom is not located or advanced by pointing to external places, objects, or observable signs (“here it is” or “there it is”).  
In Luke 17:20–21, when asked when the Kingdom of God would come, Jesus replies that it “does not come with observation,” nor will people say “Look here!” or “There!” because the Kingdom is “within you” / “in your midst” (present in the person and reign of the King, not a visible political or material structure). External markers—whether temple sites, sacred objects, or ritual locations—do not define or advance it. This undercuts any system that elevates particular artifacts, shrines, or “holy” material things as the means or locus of encountering the Kingdom. Nature itself (birds of the air, fish of the sea, lilies of the field in Matthew 6 / Luke 12) is cited by Jesus to illustrate trust in the Father’s provision without human accumulation or external control; the point is radical dependence on God rather than material intermediaries or storehouses of sacred things.

2. True worship is in spirit and truth, not tied to physical places, forms, or objects.  
John 4:21–24 is decisive: the hour has come when worship is neither on “this mountain” nor in Jerusalem. God is spirit, so true worshipers must worship “in spirit and truth.” The external geography, temple, and associated rituals of the old order are superseded. Heart, spirit, and alignment with revealed truth replace dependence on physical sites or material aids as the essential medium. This is the same trajectory that treats external religious apparatus as secondary at best.

3. Christ’s work is finished—once for all—rendering ongoing physical or ritual mediation unnecessary for access or atonement.  
John 19:30 (“It is finished,” tetelestai) announces the completion of the redemptive work the Father gave him. Hebrews 10:11–18 makes the contrast explicit: Old Covenant priests stood daily offering repeated sacrifices that could never take away sins; Christ, having offered one sacrifice for sins forever, sat down at the right hand of God. By that single offering he has perfected forever those being sanctified. “Where there is forgiveness of these, there is no longer any offering for sin.” Colossians 2:16–17 calls the old external regulations (food, festivals, sabbaths, etc.) a “shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ.” Self-imposed worship, rituals, or severity to the body have “no value in restraining the flesh” once the substance has arrived (Colossians 2:20–23). The cross itself is the instrument of the finished work; it is not an ongoing object requiring veneration as a source of grace.

4. The prohibition on graven images targets worship and service of the created thing in place of (or alongside) the Creator.  
Exodus 20:4–5 forbids making and then bowing down to / serving images or likenesses. The danger is diversion of ultimate trust, devotion, or mediation onto the material representation. New Testament continuity appears in the insistence that God is not served by human hands as though he needed anything (Acts 17:24–25) and that worship must be spiritual. When any artifact (cross, relic, statue, medal) becomes a focus of repeated ritual attention, pilgrimage, or perceived spiritual efficacy beyond simple remembrance, it risks functioning in the role the commandment and the New Testament reject—turning a created thing into a channel or object of religious devotion.

text:
The US Space Force recently tried to book launches for three future satellite missions. SpaceX declined to offer its services and no other company bid, according to Politico. Two of the missions belong to the Space Development Agency, which is building hundreds of military satellites in low Earth orbit for data relay and missile tracking.

Yesterday I wrote about SpaceX winding down Falcon 9.

The buying rules make the gap wider. A new rocket cannot bid on a Space Force launch until it has flown successfully. Commercial satellite operators have no such rule, and they are already booking early flights on rockets that have never flown. Some satellite builders cannot get a Falcon 9 slot after 2028.

Brigadier General Eric Zarybnisky, the acting head of launch acquisition, said he is not worried about any mission finding a ride. An industry representative told Politico the service needs to start buying capacity now "before it's too late".

The Space Force waits for new rockets to prove themselves while commercial customers book them first. Unless Congress lets it reserve flights on unproven rockets, it will keep depending on SpaceX's business choices.

With the November 3 midterms 11 days away, political anxiety is peaking and investors are tempted to sit in cash until the dust settles.

Look at what the S&P 500 has actually done from the close of every midterm election day through June 30 of the following year since 1950:

• 1950: +8.3%
• 1954: +29.1%
• 1958: +13.4%
• 1962: +18.9%
• 1966: +12.3%
• 1970: +26.7%
• 1974: +9.7%
• 1978: +22.3%
• 1982: +23.5%
• 1986: +19.1%
• 1990: +17.0%
• 1994: +23.6%
• 1998: +6.5%
• 2002: +8.7%
• 2006: +10.7%
• 2010: +2.5%
• 2014: +6.8%
• 2018: +16.3% (11/6/2018 to 6/30/2019; 2022 cycle also +16.3%)

Every single bar is green. 19 for 19.

The average S&P 500 gain across that eight-month window after the vote is +15.5%.

Why does the tape rally so consistently once the ballots are counted: 
Because markets hate policy uncertainty far more than they hate any political party. Before the vote, capital sits on its hands hedging tail risks. Once the election is over, the legislative rules of the road are locked in, gridlock usually caps extreme policy risk, and capital goes back to work.

Waiting for post-election calm has historically meant missing the exact window where stocks reprice higher.

Keep your near-term spending insulated in short-duration liquidity, keep your political opinions separate from your capital allocation, and let high-quality businesses compound.

text:
It's not too hard to think of some antitrust claims against a joint agreement between the B1G and SEC that have a solid chance of surviving motions to dismiss and real chance at trial.

Let me help you out:

Sherman Act, Section 1: Group Boycott / Concerted Refusal to Deal

The SEC and Big Ten are horizontally conspiring to lock down their non-conference schedules exclusively for one another. By design, this joint framework denies the Big 12 and ACC access to high-revenue, premier matchups. This concerted refusal to deal artificially depresses the competitors' strength-of-schedule (SOS) metrics, directly jeopardizing their access to the 24-team College Football Playoff.

Sherman Act, Section 1: Horizontal Market Allocation

The two dominant market forces are coordinating to horizontally allocate the premium collegiate regular-season broadcast market. By pooling their top brands into exclusive, guaranteed matchups, they are systematically dividing and monopolizing the highest-value television windows (e.g., FOX's Big Noon, CBS's 3:30 PM, ABC's Saturday Night Football), starving competitors of necessary broadcast oxygen and advertiser dollars.

Sherman Act, Section 2: Conspiracy to Monopolize

The SEC and Big Ten are utilizing their combined control over 80% of college football's elite brands to transform a competitive multi-conference ecosystem into an exclusionary duopoly. Through joint scheduling coordination and downstream television market manipulation, they demonstrate a specific intent to achieve total, unchecked monopoly power over the top tier of collegiate athletics.

Clayton Act, Section 3: De Facto Exclusive Dealing

The alliance functions as a de facto exclusive dealing arrangement with the market's primary broadcast gatekeepers (ESPN and FOX). By leveraging their massive market share to offer a consolidated block of premium inventory, the SEC and Big Ten coerce networks into prioritizing their content, effectively foreclosing the ACC and Big 12 from competing for prime-time network distribution.

text:
Pitt is going back to Holden Geriner on Saturday in Miami.

And honestly, I think this makes sense. I kind of saw it coming.

Matt Zenitz reported the news, but after watching Kade Bell’s comments earlier this week, I had a feeling this was where Pitt was headed.

Bell talked about how the coaching staff now knows what it has at quarterback.

He also emphasized that Corey Dailey is still a true freshman with a lot of development ahead of him. He’s talented, but he needs more time to grow physically and develop within the program.

Reading between the lines, it sounded to me like Pitt had seen what Dailey could offer right now and decided Geriner was the better option.

And I don’t think that means the coaching staff has lost confidence in Dailey.

I think he has a lot of potential and could develop into a really good quarterback.

But for now, it appears Pitt is turning back to the fifth-year senior.

And frankly, I wouldn’t be surprised if Geriner remains the starter for the rest of the season.

I wasn’t particularly confident about Pitt’s chances against Miami regardless of who started at quarterback, so I don’t know that this changes much.

But perhaps Geriner’s experience, familiarity with a larger portion of the playbook, and ability to manage the offense will give Pitt its best chance to be competitive.

We’ll see what happens Saturday in Miami.

Hi friend 👋🏼

Markets gave investors plenty to worry about this week, but the most interesting stories were really about trust: trust in economic signals, institutional forecasts, asset provenance and the people selling us valuable things.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐖𝐞𝐞𝐤𝐥𝐲 𝐅𝐮𝐧 𝐅𝐚𝐜𝐭 🤔

𝐀 $𝟔 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐋𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐧 𝐀𝐫𝐭 𝐀𝐮𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧

A Miami art dealer has been sentenced to 46 months in federal prison after admitting his role in a scheme involving forged Andy Warhol artworks.

Leslie Roberts allegedly used fraudulent invoices, fabricated authentication documents, counterfeit stamps and false identification numbers to make the works appear genuine. A family claimed in a 2024 lawsuit that it had spent $6 million on supposed Warhols sold through his gallery, including works depicting Marilyn Monroe and Debbie Harry.

One particularly revealing detail was hidden in the email addresses. The buyers had reportedly communicated with accounts ending in https://t.co/XzMYlTbXlI, despite the actual Andy Warhol Foundation using a .org domain.

The dealer maintained that the works had been authenticated by the foundation. There was one rather large problem: the foundation disbanded its authentication board in 2011.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐞 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐰𝐬 𝐡𝐨𝐰 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐛𝐞 𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐮𝐟𝐚𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐝 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐲 𝐰𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐛𝐮𝐲𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐨𝐧 𝐝𝐨𝐜𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬, 𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐦𝐩𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐢𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐰𝐢𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐥𝐲 𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐜𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐥𝐲𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐬𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐜𝐞.

Roberts had already served a previous prison sentence connected to fake Romero Britto and Peter Max paintings. In the latest case, federal reporting confirmed a 46-month sentence and the forfeiture of approximately $2.58 million in proceeds.

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐚𝐧 𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐫𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡 𝐩𝐚𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐜𝐞𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐬, 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐚𝐬𝐞𝐬 𝐨𝐫 𝐛𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐤𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐨𝐤𝐞𝐧𝐬, 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐫𝐝 𝐢𝐬 𝐨𝐧𝐥𝐲 𝐯𝐚𝐥𝐮𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐢𝐟 𝐢𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐧𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐨 𝐚 𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐢𝐧𝐞 𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐮𝐩𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 𝐫𝐞𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧.

Tokenization can make ownership records easier to track and transfer, but it cannot transform a forgery into a Warhol. Good technology strengthens provenance. It does not replace due diligence.

🔴 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐄𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤-𝐎𝐟𝐟 𝐓𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲 📉

The market’s condition deteriorated sharply, even though the underlying economy has not yet followed it down.

The Milk Road Macro Index fell from -0.93 to -1.51, pushing the indicator deeper into risk-off territory. Almost the entire decline came from market momentum, which dropped from -0.68 to -1.26.

Volatility also caught up with the nervousness already visible in bond markets. The VIX rose from 14.84 to 19.99, with official Cboe data confirming the latter reading.

Inflation added another layer of pressure. September produced a second consecutive 0.3% monthly increase in core CPI, weakening the recent disinflation narrative and raising expectations that interest rates could remain higher for longer.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐢𝐦𝐦𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐚𝐭𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐦 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐛𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐢𝐧 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭𝐬 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐫𝐨𝐚𝐝𝐞𝐫 𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐨𝐦𝐲, 𝐛𝐮𝐭 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐜𝐚𝐧 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐜𝐡 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐞𝐬, 𝐞𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐮𝐦𝐞𝐫 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠.

AI-related debt is one area to watch. Heavy investment in data centres, chips and infrastructure has created interconnected financing arrangements across the technology sector. If credit spreads continue to widen, forced selling could spread beyond the most speculative positions.

The next important test is the Federal Reserve meeting scheduled for October 27 and 28. Investors will be looking for any indication that inflation has not yet justified another rate increase in December.

Crypto has been comparatively resilient, with Bitcoin remaining above $80,000 at the time of the original report. One possible explanation is that much of the forced deleveraging has been concentrated in AI and semiconductor equities rather than digital assets.

𝐂𝐫𝐲𝐩𝐭𝐨 𝐦𝐚𝐲 𝐛𝐞 𝐚𝐛𝐬𝐨𝐫𝐛𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐜𝐤 𝐛𝐞𝐭𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐬𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐞𝐪𝐮𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐬𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐬, 𝐛𝐮𝐭 𝐚 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐥𝐨𝐧𝐠𝐞𝐝 𝐭𝐢𝐠𝐡𝐭𝐞𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐨𝐟 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐰𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐮𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐟𝐟𝐢𝐜𝐮𝐥𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐚𝐥𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐲 𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐤 𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐢𝐠𝐧𝐨𝐫𝐞.

🟡 𝐂𝐫𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐅𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬 𝐌𝐞𝐞𝐭 𝐚 𝐑𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐂𝐡𝐞𝐜𝐤 ⚖️

The calendar offered an irresistible comparison: October 19, 2026 fell on a Monday, just as October 19, 1987 did when Black Monday wiped more than 20% from the Dow Jones Industrial Average in a single session.

There were also some uncomfortable similarities. Investors faced rising rates, renewed inflation concerns, a strong dollar, expensive growth companies, geopolitical tension and pressure on technology stocks.

But the comparison quickly becomes less convincing when the starting conditions are examined.

The S&P 500 was reportedly only around 2% below its all-time high and remained up approximately 12% for the year. By contrast, the market had already fallen roughly 17% from its high before the 1987 crash.

The market also operates differently today. Circuit breakers can temporarily halt trading during extreme declines, reducing the risk that automated selling and panic feed continuously into each other.

𝐀 𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐦𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐬 𝐚 𝐦𝐚𝐫𝐤𝐞𝐭 𝐚𝐥𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐲 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐬𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦𝐢𝐜 𝐟𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐮𝐫𝐞.

Positioning may even create room for an upside reversal. The surge in crash predictions coincided with exceptionally high put-option activity, suggesting that a significant number of investors were already prepared for further declines.

If prices rise instead, market makers may need to buy back shares previously sold to hedge those options. That can add momentum to a rebound.

None of this guarantees that markets are safe. Inflation, rates, energy prices and AI-related credit risks remain genuine concerns.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐛𝐚𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞𝐝 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐬 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐨𝐧𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐛𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐮𝐬, 𝐛𝐮𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐯𝐚𝐢𝐥𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐞𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐝𝐨𝐞𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐦𝐚𝐤𝐞 𝐚 𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐞𝐚𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐁𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐤 𝐌𝐨𝐧𝐝𝐚𝐲 𝐢𝐧𝐞𝐯𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐨𝐫 𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐥𝐢𝐤𝐞𝐥𝐲 𝐨𝐮𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐞.

🟢 𝐁𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧 𝐄𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐉𝐏𝐌𝐨𝐫𝐠𝐚𝐧’𝐬 𝐋𝐨𝐧𝐠-𝐓𝐞𝐫𝐦 𝐎𝐮𝐭𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐤 ₿

For the first time, Bitcoin has reportedly appeared in J.P. Morgan Asset Management’s Long-Term Capital Market Assumptions, the projections used by institutional investors to build portfolios over periods of 10 to 15 years.

The headline number is a projected annual compound return of approximately 10%, placing Bitcoin above the other asset classes in the table. A traditional portfolio holding 60% equities and 40% bonds was projected to return around 7% annually.

If Bitcoin compounded at 10% from approximately $82,000, it would mathematically reach around $213,000 after 10 years and $343,000 after 15 years.

That distinction matters. The $343,000 figure is a compound-growth calculation based on the return assumption, not a formal JPMorgan Bitcoin price target.

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐥𝐨𝐩𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐟𝐮𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐞. 𝐈𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐁𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧’𝐬 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐧 𝐚 𝐟𝐫𝐚𝐦𝐞𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐮𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐛𝐲 𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬, 𝐰𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐡 𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐨𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐢𝐧𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐭𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐬.

There is also a substantial limitation. JPMorgan has not added Bitcoin to its model portfolios, partly because it assumes annual volatility of approximately 55%, around three times the level associated with equities or gold.

Higher government bond yields make that volatility harder to justify. When investors can obtain meaningful returns from bonds with considerably smaller price movements, Bitcoin must offer a convincing additional reward for the risk.

Even so, institutional infrastructure continues to develop. The same week brought further activity involving blockchain-based bank deposits, while large financial institutions continued expanding access to digital assets.

𝐁𝐢𝐭𝐜𝐨𝐢𝐧 𝐦𝐚𝐲 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐲𝐞𝐭 𝐡𝐚𝐯𝐞 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐞𝐝 𝐚 𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐧𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐟𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐬, 𝐛𝐮𝐭 𝐢𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐢𝐧𝐜𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐲 𝐛𝐞𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐚𝐧𝐚𝐥𝐲𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐬 𝐚𝐧 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞 𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐭 𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐭𝐡𝐚𝐧 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐦𝐢𝐬𝐬𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐬 𝐚𝐧 𝐞𝐱𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐲.

That quiet shift may matter more over the long term than any single weekly price movement.

Ive been looking at the reaction to the reports that were around this morning about Steve Morrison being approached to become the new #TownTeamTogether manager. 

It does make me wonder what people genuinely expect from the owner/club.

We are a small EFL club that is lucky to have a 4k crowd most games. We clearly have an owner with money but I wouldnt say its a bottomless pitt by any means.

If you were an experienced EFL manager would you come to Crawley?

Ive seen people mention Karl Robinson, Matt Sadler, Stuart Maynard, Andy Woodman.

Why would they come? They have all been paid well previously and im sure they all got nice packages when they were sacked from their last job. Money isnt as big a factor as what I feel everyone thinks it is unless its a bigger payday.

So you have to offer a platform to be successful. Does a team who are 6 points adrift at the bottom of League 2 do that? Also a team that realistically has a ceiling of a League One relegation fight like the last time we were in League one?

I would love to see the club show "ambition" and go out and get the best available candidate but I get the feeling they dont have that option.

Do I think Morrision is a great choice? Probably not. Do I think we can get an experienced manager like the names I listed above? No. 

Why would they want it?

text:
Haha... 

So my Suzuki V-Strom had just been stolen from in front of my home. Insurance barely covered the value. A riding buddy pointed out this bike, a 1999 BMW R1100GS on ADV Rider. Almost everything I wanted in a motorcycle to do a Pittsburgh PA to Dead Horse AK ride.  Problem is, it was in Boston, a 10 hour drive. And I did not have a truck yet. 

We do have a company here in the US called Keyboard Movers, which transport bikes and pianos, and asked the seller if he had used them. He suggested that the bike was in excellent shape, and that I could fly in to Logan, he would pick me up, and ride home.  Cost to truck it: ~$600. Plane ticket one way: $200.  So we made plans for a few weeks later. My boss at the time was pretty cool, and when I shared the news, he found a project we were working on in Baltimore that needed my attention, and offered to pay for my mileage riding back ($0.53 a mile back then) if I made the detour and a stop. Since I had friends down there, didnt even need a hotel. 

I flew in one morning, my Shoei helmet was a "personal item" that I had to wear on takeoff because it didn't fit under the seat. Met the seller, who's crane rental biz was 10 min from Boston Logan. He showed me the bike, had a bunch of extras to go with, and told me to take my time and get familiar on his property before I headed out. 20 minutes later, I was bombing down back roads of Massachusetts, headed for New Haven, before dropping into New York and skirting by NYC headed to Jersey. 

Then I spent the next day discovering how much of New Jersey was farmland. I took the off highway route along the Atlantic coast for a while, because its simply more interesting. Caught a nap at a motel a few hours from Cape May, and the next day, took the ferry to Delaware, land of a thousand toll booths. Made my way to Baltimore after that delightful ferry ride.  Met up with my friend Chris and his 50lb tortoise Oscar, who did not like this new machine parked in his yard 😂. We worked on a patent project for a day, and then I rode home not much later, up scenic historic route 30. 

I rode that motorcycle up and down the east coast, on and off road, from South Carolina up to the Finger Lakes in NY, as far west as Kentucky. Easily have over 150,000 miles of riding since 2002 when I got my license. 

Unfortunately, the bike has sat for the last 6 years, Needs repairs and so does my body.

text:
Brad Pitt offered Angelina Jolie $54.5 million for her half of the château where they got married. She took $64 million from a Russian vodka billionaire instead.

In the video below, a year after the wedding, they sit side by side on TV and joke about what ten years of marriage will do to them. Less than a year later, she filed for divorce.

They bought Château Miraval in 2008 for $37.5 million. His company owned 60%, hers 40%.

A few months before the wedding, he gave her another 10%. Now they were equal partners.

He threw himself into the wine. By 2021 the business was bringing in more than $50 million a year.

Then came the divorce.

She had agreed to his $54.5 million. The deal died over one clause. She says he wanted her to sign something that would stop her from ever talking about his behaviour during the marriage. She refused.

So she sold to the Stoli vodka group, controlled by Russian-born billionaire Yuri Shefler. Pitt says he never got a say.

He says they had agreed neither would ever sell without the other's consent. His lawyers say she let a stranger into his home.

Her side hit back. They say he spent the winery's money on his own projects, a house, a pool, a recording studio, so that she would "never see a dime."

And one detail tells you how far it went.

Pitt went to a court in Luxembourg to take back the 10% he gave her before the wedding.

They said their vows in that chapel. Four years later, they're still fighting over who gets to keep the walls.

Did Jolie have every right to sell her half, or did she sell his home to hurt him?

text:
You have the SEC part backwards.  The SEC has reacted exclusively to the consequences caused by the Big Ten.

NOTE:  Until the late 2010s, I was as connected as you could get to realignment, & was a source for ESPN.  So this subject is my wheelhouse.  Even now, I have strong connections, but back then, they were top, top tier.  So if you'll permit, I'll give you the 411.

Dec 19, 2009 -- Jim Delaney (B1G Commish) called a surprise PC & announced the Big Ten had launched an expansion committee to identify 1 team in order to reach the NCAA minimum of 12 teams to host a lucrative conference championship game.  In that PC, he said they wouldn't be looking exclusively at non-AQ schools, that they'd vet Big 12, ACC, and SEC schools too.  Until that point in time, no P5 conference had ever poached from a fellow P5 conference.  All additions had been independent teams (a la Penn St, Florida St, S. Carolina) at the expense of lesser conferences (Big East, SWC, etc).

Instantly, Mizzou's Governor began politicking in the press for Mizzou to get the invitation.  Nebraska also announced their interest.  That PC launched realignment *AND* created the conference instability that exists still today.

The next month, newly hired Pac-10 Commissioner, Larry Scott, announced the Pac-10 had formed a search committee as well.  They then reached out to Texas, Oklahoma, & Colorado, who negotiated a deal to join w/ A&M, TX Tech, and OK State.  With UT & OU's blessing, Colorado jumped on the offer before the rest to prevent the TX legislature from forcing CU out of the deal in favor of Baylor.

The resulting fallout from losing Nebraska & Colorado made the Big 12 poorer & the Big Ten richer.  Prior to that moment in time, the Big 12, Pac-10, SEC, and ACC teams all earned within $2M - $4M of each other.  The B1G created the revenue gap.  The following year, the Big Ten poached Maryland from the ACC & Rutgers from the Big East.  That made the ACC poorer & killed off the Big East.

The SEC's addition of A&M and Mizzou would've never happened if not for the Big Ten launching realignment.  And had the Big Ten not launched realignment, the revenue gap between the Big Ten and a Big 12 with Texas, Oklahoma, A&M, Nebraska, and Colorado would've never materialized.  Meaning, Texas & Oklahoma wouldn't have fallen behind their Big Ten & SEC peers & needed to reach out to the SEC to find a way to close the $20M TV revenue gap.  The Big Ten adding USC & UCLA, then circling back around the next year to kill the Pac-12 by adding Oregon & Washington, wasn't a response to the SEC adding Texas & Oklahoma.  It was the consequence from the Big Ten launching realignment in Dec 2009 and creating the revenue gap between the Big Ten and Big 12/ACC that created the dominoe effect.

text:
**Trump just shrugged off press outrage over a mother’s attack ad on her daughter running for Ohio governor, noting the same press would have run it as lead story if Mary Trump had said it about him.**

### 1. The Frame
**What people think this is about:** A president casually endorsing a brutal family-attack ad in a Republican primary while dodging questions on Ukraine, Starlink, and DOJ settlements.

**What the machinery is actually doing:** The sitting president is using a gaggle to normalize “mother says daughter is a liar and unreliable” as fair campaign material, while flagging press coordination to shield one candidate and punish another, with side commentary on midterms leverage over legal payouts and selective media amplification.

### 2. Observations
- Trump repeatedly frames the Ramaswamy ad as protected speech because the source is the candidate’s own mother; he contrasts it with how the press would treat identical statements from his late mother Mary MacLeod Trump. (ASR: “if my mother said bad about me, it would be a major news story… if it were about you or about especially about me… you’d have it as your number one story.”)
- He calls out unified press behavior as partisan shielding: “the press has teamed up because he’s a Republican… the press has ganged up on a woman making a horrible statement about her daughter and I don’t know why she should be shielded.”
- On Ukraine/Putin/Zelensky strikes, Trump offers only “we’ll see how it works out. That’s been happening a lot” — classic non-committal while the questioner pushes the “nothing’s changed” line.
- He ties DOJ lawsuit settlements explicitly to midterm outcomes: “if the Republicans don’t do well, I would say that maybe they won’t get their money.”
- Ilhan Omar’s “not to my knowledge” answer on marrying her brother is highlighted as telling; Trump contrasts it with how he would answer the same question.
- Starlink/Ukraine: Trump refuses to confirm or deny calling Elon but notes the service was restored and his relationship with Musk remains “very good.”
- The gaggle ends with Trump reiterating that if the mother’s claims are “even a little bit true, you don’t want her as governor.”

### 3. Snapshot
On October 22, 2026, President Trump held an informal press gaggle outside the White House before departing. The exchange, captured on the official White House YouTube channel, centered on Vivek Ramaswamy’s campaign ad featuring statements from Amy Acton’s mother, with additional questions on Ukraine, Michigan politics, Ilhan Omar, Elon Musk/Starlink, and DOJ settlements. The transcript is YouTube ASR.

### 4. Timeline of material facts
- **Oct 22, 2026** — Trump gaggle recorded and uploaded (YouTube, 21:03 UTC). Primary ASR quotes above.
- **Recent context (per gaggle)** — Ramaswamy ad using Acton mother’s statements aired; press and some Republicans (Ashley Hinson cited) called for it to be pulled.
- **Background (gaggle references)** — Acton mother’s statements described as calling daughter “dirty liar,” “unreliable,” etc.; allegations of stepfather abuse from 1970s mentioned by reporters but not addressed in detail by Trump.

### 5. Sides
**Trump / Ramaswamy-aligned (IT/LT mix)**  
Steelman: Campaign speech from a family member is fair game; press applies inconsistent standards when the target is a Republican.  
Critique: LT — mother’s statements are public and being used; IT — press amplification patterns often favor one side in primaries. Trump’s “if it were my mother” hypothetical is directionally accurate on media incentives.

**Press / Acton-aligned (IT/LT mix)**  
Steelman: Family trauma and decades-old allegations should not be weaponized in ads; shielding victims from parental attacks is a norm.  
Critique: LT — the ad exists and uses the mother’s words; IT — selective outrage when the same tactic would be celebrated against a Trump or Ramaswamy family member.

### 6. Rumsfeld Matrix
**Known Knowns (LT/IT):** Trump defended the ad on consistency grounds; press pressed on shielding the daughter; Trump linked settlements to midterms; Starlink was restored.  
**Known Unknowns:** Exact wording and full context of the mother’s statements; whether Trump personally called Musk; precise status of any DOJ settlements.  
**Unknown Knowns:** Internal polling or ad-testing data showing the mother’s statements’ impact; full history of Acton family allegations.  
**Unknown Unknowns:** How similar family-sourced attacks will be treated in future cycles if norms shift.

### 7. Incentives map
- Trump/Ramaswamy: Win primary by normalizing aggressive family-sourced attacks; signal to base that “rules” are applied evenly.
- Press: Engagement via outrage framing; protect preferred candidate (Acton) while punishing Republican ad; maintain narrative of Trump/Ramaswamy as norm-breakers.
- Media attention stack favors the family-drama angle over Ukraine or midterms leverage.
- Bureaucratic angle: DOJ settlements become bargaining chip tied to congressional control.

### 8. Dueling AI advice
**Moral AI Advice:** Treat family-member statements as admissible campaign material unless proven false; apply the same standard regardless of party. Watch whether the press shields one side consistently.  
**Evil AI Advice:** Weaponize any parental quote that damages the opponent; coordinate coverage to bury it when it helps your side and amplify it when it hurts the other. Midterm control over DOJ payouts is leverage — use it.

### 9. Practical takeaway
- Watch the full  gaggle video directly rather than clips.
- Track whether Ramaswamy keeps or pulls the ad and how Ohio primary polling moves.
- Note any follow-up on Starlink/Ukraine or DOJ settlements tied to election results.
- Compare press treatment of this ad versus past family-attack ads from other candidates.
- Listen for whether Trump’s “if my mother said it” standard is applied symmetrically going forward.

### 10. What would falsify this read
- Discovery that the mother’s statements were fabricated or coerced.  
- Trump publicly calling for the ad’s removal.  
- Uniform press condemnation of identical tactics used against Democratic candidates.  
- Concrete evidence Trump personally directed Starlink restoration for Ukraine.

text:
Fired Organizer’s Tape Rocks El-Sayed Senate Bid

Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate campaign spent the day after an O’Keefe Media Group video in damage control. The undercover clip shows field organizer Abdoul Beckwith telling a person he believed was a volunteer that El-Sayed receives overseas donations through family members and other intermediaries. Beckwith admitted the practice is not allowed. He said everybody does it. The video also captured him saying El-Sayed cannot fully reject Hamas or he will lose the people who brought him up. He made a parallel comment about the Muslim Brotherhood.
The Michigan Democrat Party fired Beckwith the same day. The campaign issued a statement calling the remarks untrue, wildly misinformed, and not reflective of the campaign. It claimed full compliance with Federal Election Commission rules. No independent audit of the donor file has been offered. That is the gap.
Foreign nationals are barred from contributing to federal campaigns. Funneling money through U.S. persons to conceal the true source is illegal. Beckwith described exactly that method on tape. He thought he was speaking privately to another volunteer. He had no obvious reason to invent a scheme that could sink the candidate he worked for. Krassenstein argued Beckwith lacked finance knowledge and was making it up, then added that overseas money from American citizens is legal. The second sentence undercuts the first. If no overseas money exists, the legal-status hedge is unnecessary.
El-Sayed is the Democratic Senate candidate in Michigan. The tape does not prove he personally ordered illegal donations. It does show a paid organizer describing illegal overseas cash and careful language around Hamas and the Muslim Brotherhood. The party cut the organizer loose without an investigation. The campaign denied the claims and stopped there. Voters can demand the donor records. Allegations stay allegations until proven. Silence on an audit is its own answer. The tape is public. The cleanup is incomplete.

text:
🚨 @Sezzle BNPL, just applied for a US bank charter 🇺🇸

And it's part of a much bigger wave right now.

Sezzle has applied for a national trust bank charter with the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC).

If approved, the new bank would offer:
• Checking and savings accounts
• A broader set of banking products
• Built for "digitally native consumers" who skip traditional credit

But here's where it gets interesting:

Sezzle isn't alone.

Under the Trump administration, fintechs are rushing to apply for OCC charters:
• @Block
• @tryramp  (applied just last week)
• Avant
• @ModernTreasury  

And this application is a pivot.

Sezzle originally planned to get a Utah license as an industrial loan company (ILC).

Then the rules changed:
• New BNPL rules in New York, Illinois and Oregon
• Bank and consumer group pushback on the ILC structure

So Sezzle changed course.

The review by the OCC, the Federal Reserve and the FDIC is expected to take 12 to 18 months.

Meanwhile, rival @Affirm went the ILC route in Nevada, and @PayPal  filed for a Utah license back in December.

The race for US banking licenses is clearly heating up.

text:
Good news from the ocean today

Stanford researchers found that severely bleached corals can fully recover in just seven weeks simply by briefly touching healthy clones of the same colony.
The healthy coral transfers its beneficial algae through the point of contact. In some cases only five days of contact was enough to jump-start recovery — and the bleached coral kept healing even after the two were separated. Without that touch, the bleached pieces died.

It’s one of the fastest coral recoveries ever documented and offers a new angle of hope for reefs struggling with marine heatwaves.
A small contact, a big difference.

Isn’t that cool?

text:
🎯 Before he was Paladin on Have Gun – Will Travel, Richard Boone was a tail gunner in the Pacific.

He was born in Los Angeles in 1917. He dropped out of Stanford and worked as an oil rigger, a bartender, and a painter.

In 1941, he joined the Navy. He served on three ships in the Pacific and flew combat missions as a tail gunner in Grumman Avenger torpedo bombers, the most exposed seat on the plane.

After the war, he turned to acting. In 1957, Randolph Scott was offered the role of a gentleman gunfighter named Paladin. Scott turned it down and passed the script to Boone.

Have Gun – Will Travel ran six seasons and became one of TV’s most popular westerns.

The man in black with the business card had already seen the real thing.

Have Gun or Medic? Which one do you remember? 👇

text:
My experience with the Toyota Innova Hycross Hybrid ZX(O).

This is going to be a harsh review, but an honest one.

First, I understand it's a Toyota. Reliability, resale value, and peace of mind are all there. But the way people hype this car, especially its hybrid system, made me expect a lot more.

1/ Fuel efficiency

I was expecting 16–18 kmpl in mixed driving, considering the claimed mileage is above 20 kmpl. But I was getting around 11–13 kmpl in mixed city and highway conditions, with an average speed of 50–60 kmph and cruising at 80–90 kmph. My driving wasn't extremely aggressive either.

Can it return 17–19 kmpl? Yes, under favourable conditions and with a lighter foot. But don't buy it expecting that figure in every driving condition.

For a hybrid, the real-world efficiency disappointed me. The diesel Innova Crysta makes a strong case when you consider fuel economy and the overall ownership experience.

2/ The infotainment system

Honestly, one of the most disappointing infotainment experiences I've had in an expensive car.

The interface feels basic. Bluetooth, FM, Wired Android Auto and Apple CarPlay. That's it, there was nothing to play with. No extra apps like Spotify or Amazon music to play songs without Bluetooth. Literally 0 features in the infotainment.

What frustrated me even more was having to stop the car to connect my phone when I couldn't get it to connect while moving. A passenger couldn't easily do it either.

At this price, I expected a much more polished, modern experience. The Maruti Brezza's infotainment system feels better thought out to me.

And no, a bigger screen doesn't automatically mean better technology.

3/ The 360-degree camera

This is another major disappointment.

The camera quality and clarity felt poor for a car costing ₹40 lakh plus on road. Parking cameras are supposed to make life easier, especially in a big MPV. Here, I expected much better resolution and a more premium experience.

I've seen much better camera systems in significantly cheaper cars. Tata has shown that a good camera system doesn't have to be reserved for expensive vehicles.

Toyota needs to do better here. Period.

4/ Where the Hycross genuinely shines

Space. Comfort. Ride quality.

The second row Ottoman seats are excellent, the cabin is spacious, and the suspension does a very good job of keeping passengers comfortable.

This is where the Hycross makes the most sense. If you have a driver and want a comfortable family car for long journeys, it does the job brilliantly.

It's also quick. The hybrid powertrain delivers strong acceleration, but when you push hard, the petrol engine gets noticeably loud. The car gathers speed, but the engine noise makes it feel like it's working harder than you'd expect.

5/ Is it really a premium car?

This is where my opinion might be unpopular.

The Hycross is comfortable, spacious, feature loaded in some areas, and backed by Toyota's reputation. It has a sunroof, ventilated front seats, powered seats, ADAS and a capable hybrid powertrain.

But the premium experience isn't consistent across the car.

The infotainment, camera quality and overall tech experience don't feel worthy of the price to me.

Personally, I find the Tata Safari, Mahindra XUV700 and even the Kia Sorento more premium in certain aspects of their cabin and technology experience. I'm not saying they're better cars overall. They simply do some things better.

6/ Innova Crysta vs Hycross

The Crysta had its own strengths, especially its diesel engine and that familiar, robust character.

The Hycross feels more car-like, offers better passenger comfort in many respects, and brings modern features and hybrid technology to the table.

But the hybrid badge shouldn't make buyers assume they'll always get exceptional mileage. Your driving conditions matter, and the gap between claimed and actual efficiency can be significant.

🏀 GRIZZLIES @ WARRIORS — NBA PREVIEW

Golden State is favored by 4.5 despite a depleted rotation. Is Memphis being undervalued?

📊 FAIR MARKET
* Fair Spread: GSW -2.0 | Market: GSW -4.5
* Fair Total: 232.0 | Market: 237.5
* Fair ML: MEM +133 / GSW -133
* Projected Pace: ~102 possessions
* Confidence: 62/100

🎯 SCORE PREDICTION
Memphis 115 — Golden State 117

🧠 HOW THIS GAME PLAYS OUT
* Curry carries the offense. Golden State scored just 105 against the Lakers, with Steph accounting for 23. Without Butler, Moody and Porziņģis, secondary creation remains a concern.
* Memphis attacks inside. The Warriors’ depleted frontcourt creates opportunities for paint scoring, offensive rebounds and second-chance points.
* Don’t overreact to Ty Jerome. His 45-point opener powered Memphis past Utah 123–103. Expect regression, but his playmaking can still pressure Golden State.
* Competitive finish. Golden State’s home-court advantage and Curry’s late-game shotmaking give the Warriors the edge, but Memphis has enough offensive options to stay within one possession.

🔑 X-FACTOR: Golden State’s defensive rebounding. Can an undersized rotation consistently finish possessions?

⚠️ MARKET CHECK — SMALL BET
The Warriors moved from approximately -3.5 to -4.5. Our fair spread remains -2.0, while the market total sits 5.5 points above our projection.
The discrepancies fall below MIDP’s mandatory investigation thresholds. Podziemski, Bassey, Coward and Stewart remain availability concerns, limiting confidence.

💰 BETTING CARD
🔥 BEST BET: Under 237.5 (-115)
* Fair Probability: ~62%
* Fair Odds: -163
* Estimated EV: +15.9%
* Stake: 0.50u
* Classification: SMALL BET

✅ OTHER PLAYABLE: Memphis +4.5 (-108)

* Fair Odds: -138
* Estimated EV: +11.7%
* Stake: 0.50u
* Classification: SMALL BET

🟡 PASS: Memphis ML +150 offers theoretical value, but the spread provides more protection. No player props without independent minutes and usage projections.

🚨 WHAT COULD GO WRONG?
Memphis dictates a faster pace, both teams shoot efficiently from three, or late fouling pushes the total over. Final rotation news could also invalidate the assumptions.

👀 LIVE WATCHLIST
1. If an unusually hot first quarter pushes the live total to 246.5+, reassess for an under at -110 or better, provided updated possessions and efficiency still support fair value.
2. If Memphis trails early despite favorable paint and rebounding numbers, reassess MEM +9.5 at -110 or better after accounting for remaining possessions and rotations.
Neither is an automatic wager without a refreshed live projection.

🏁 FINAL VERDICT
🎯 Memphis 115 — Golden State 117

text:
$BE

Bloom Energy raised its 2026 guidance for the third time this year on Thursday night. The stock fell 8.7% during the day before the print and another ~10% today.

Q3:
• Revenue $1.24B, up 138% from a year ago and ~$170M above estimates

• Product revenue $1.07B, up 179%

• Non-GAAP gross margin 34.5%, up 4.1 points. CFO Simon Edwards laid out the path: 28.7% in 2024, 30.3% in 2025, 34.5% now

• Non-GAAP operating income $286M, a 23% margin, vs $46M a year ago. Edwards: "Operating income in this quarter alone exceeded operating income for all of last year"

• Adjusted EBITDA $299M vs $59M a year ago

• Non-GAAP EPS $0.94, more than 35% above estimates. GAAP net income $250M, or $0.78 a share, vs a loss a year ago

How the 2026 guide has moved:
• April: revenue $3.4-3.8B, non-GAAP EPS $1.85-2.25

• July: $3.9-4.2B and $2.55-2.85

• Now: $4.4-4.6B and $3.10-3.40, with non-GAAP operating income of $960M-1.03B

Bloom started the year guiding ~60% growth and now guides ~122%. The EPS midpoint is up ~58% since April. The new midpoints sit ~9% above consensus revenue of $4.12B and ~10% above consensus EPS of $2.94. Nine months are done at $3.05B, which puts Q4 at $1.35-1.55B. Edwards said "the timing of a small number of deliveries around year-end will determine where in the range we land."

Demand:
• KR Sridhar in the release: "What began with hyperscalers is rapidly moving across market segments because every business needs reliable power to grow"

• On the call: "our backlog is continuing to expand faster than our revenue." Exact figures come with Q4

• Capacity is approaching 5 GW a year, and he called that "just a milestone in a long journey"

• AEP and partners are putting ~$4B into a 702 MW Bloom fuel cell plant in Wyoming that sells power to Google under a 20-year PPA, fully running by the end of 2028, with carbon capture planned. Sridhar's pitch: "Combustion technologies do not offer an affordable and scalable pathway to carbon capture today"

• On Nebius's 300 MW site in New Jersey: "their first block is almost getting ready," and "We will not be the bottleneck to them turning on their data center, their entire 300 megawatts." Vineland's planning board approved the Bloom-powered plan 8-1 in August

• Oracle's Utah site got power in less than two months

• "We are in conversations with all the hyperscalers" on 800 VDC power

• Edwards: "pricing remains strong and the cost reductions we've been driving are showing up in the numbers"

The weak spot is cash. Operating cash flow was -$27M as inventory, contract assets and receivables built up, and free cash flow was -$181M in Q3, though still +$42M year to date. Capex was $153M in the quarter. Edwards: "this quarter we used cash from operations, but that's not the beginning of a trend." Contract assets turn into cash as billing milestones are hit, so Q4 cash flow is the number I'm watching. Bloom ended September with $2.49B of cash against $2.47B of recourse debt.

This morning Morgan Stanley raised its target to $335 from $310, kept Overweight and lifted its shipment forecasts to 2.1 GW in 2027 and 3.7 GW in 2028, from 1.8 GW and 3.1 GW. BTIG cut to $250 from $295 but kept its Buy, citing margin pressure from the capacity ramp and expedited customer timelines.

Bloom joined the S&P 500 in September. The stock closed at $217.77 Thursday, ~26% below its Oct 6 close of $295.78, and trades at $193 now. In those same weeks Bloom raised its numbers again and said the backlog keeps growing faster than revenue.

text:
If you bought the tech dip and got hit again, you weren’t alone. A published summary of JPMorgan’s latest Retail Radar shows tech ETFs recorded their second-highest weekly retail inflows on record. Meanwhile, Goldman’s figures show tech-focused hedge funds down roughly 10% in October through the 22nd. The professionals are feeling this too.

Now rewind to April 2025. Business Insider’s headline was: “Retail traders keep buying the dip — and they keep getting burned.” People were buying on the way down, watching their losses deepen, and questioning themselves. Then, on April 9, Trump announced a tariff pause and the Nasdaq surged 12.16% in a single session, recovering a huge chunk of the damage in hours. That’s the part I remember: how quickly a policy change turned seemingly relentless selling into a historic rally. The fear felt overwhelming right up until the direction changed.

Today, oil keeps climbing even as exports recover. Gulf shipments excluding Iran averaged 24.6 million barrels a day in the week ending October 18, above prewar levels, while Brent has pushed above $115. Shipping remains dangerous and inventories are depleted, but my view is that a substantial part of this price is an anxiety/frustration premium: another day without geopolitical de-escalation, another premium added for what might happen next. Current flows have improved, but the market keeps pricing the possibility of another disaster. That’s the dislocation—and the potential reversal—I’m watching.

Meanwhile, the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield is back around 5%. The familiar explanation is a “flight to safety” from tech. Some of that may be happening, but I care more about where yields are and what they mean for financing than the label attached to the move.

On the way up, we heard endless explanations about fiscal irresponsibility and debt. America’s fiscal problems haven’t magically disappeared. Yet yields have fallen. That’s why I pick apart these narratives: a plausible explanation for price action gets presented as the definitive explanation, then quietly changes when the market changes direction.

Calling the Treasury rally a flight from tech doesn’t cancel its potential benefit to tech. Money can leave technology stocks for Treasuries while lower Treasury yields simultaneously help reduce corporate borrowing costs. Both can happen.

And the latest corporate-bond figures show some relief already. Yesterday, investment-grade yields fell from 5.92% to 5.79%, while high-yield borrowing yields edged down from 8.17% to 8.14%. Spreads widened, but total yields declined. These are broad indexes, rather than the borrowing costs of every AI company, but if financing is Wall Street’s central concern, that improvement deserves attention.

My thesis is that credible de-escalation could accelerate that relief. I could see the 10-year moving toward 4.5% within weeks of a genuine resolution, potentially helped by short covering. Lower oil, less uncertainty and sustained lower borrowing costs would materially change the backdrop for AI financing.

Where I got this wrong was timing. I expected de-escalation a week or two ago. I thought giving American voters relief from energy prices before the midterms would take priority. My expectation was that Washington would ease the confrontation, allow oil to come down, and retain the option to apply pressure again afterward if negotiations went nowhere. That seemed like the logical political and economic calculation.

Instead, the administration appears willing to tolerate far more economic pain to maintain pressure on Iran than I expected. Maybe it believes a deal is close. Maybe it thinks maintaining pressure offers more than temporary relief before the election. I don’t know its internal calculation. But in my opinion, allowing this uncertainty to keep punishing global energy markets, businesses and households is an incredibly irresponsible trade-off. The economic damage extends far beyond the country being pressured

text:
South Carolina took away a man's vote for stealing and left it for murder.

That was the suffrage article of 1895, and it ran to twenty offences: larceny, bigamy, forgery, receiving stolen goods, and no murder anywhere on the list. Robert Smalls was in the chamber while it was written, and the reason you can read what he said about it is not the state of South Carolina.

South Carolina let Confederate veterans over fifty skip the tax that paid for schools.

Every other man in the state between twenty-one and sixty owed a dollar a year on his own head, and the receipt for it was one of the papers you had to produce before you were allowed to vote. That left the men who had fought for the Union paying for the schools ten years longer than the men who had fought to destroy it. Robert Smalls sat in the room where that clause was written, and spent three months trying to stop the rest of it.

The room was the chamber of the South Carolina House of Representatives, and nobody in it had been hired to write down what was said.

The convention opened on September 10, 1895, with one hundred and sixty delegates. One hundred and twelve of them belonged to Ben Tillman's faction, forty-two were conservative Democrats, and six were Black Republicans.

Five of the six came out of Beaufort County. They were Thomas E. Miller, William J. Whipper, James Wigg, Isaiah R. Reed and Robert Smalls. The sixth was Robert B. Anderson, a teacher from Georgetown.

Nobody had to guess what the meeting was for. Months before it opened, both white factions had announced in public that they intended to take the vote away from Black South Carolinians, and the referendum that authorized the whole thing had squeaked through in 1894 by 31,402 to 29,523.

The convention published a journal, and that journal carries the motions and the business of the floor. What survives of what Smalls said in that chamber survives because his daughter went into the state's own newspapers afterward, gathered his speeches out of them, and carried the result to a printer on King Street in Charleston.

Smalls was fifty-six years old and had served five terms in the United States House of Representatives.

He told the chamber how the rules of this convention had been arranged. Under the constitution South Carolina was still living under, any two members could demand that a vote be taken by name, so the journal would show who had voted which way, and the committee on rules at this convention had set the number at ten.

Ten was four above the number they had.

Six men could not put a single delegate on the record.

Smalls said it plainly on the floor. They could not put the members of that convention on record without the assistance of some of the white members.

He came with a plan of his own. It ran to eleven sections, and it gave the vote to every male citizen of twenty-one and over who met a residence requirement, without distinction of race, color or former condition.

The eighth section is the one that matters later. It said the legislature could never strip a citizen of the vote except for treason, murder, robbery or duelling. That had been the rule in South Carolina since 1868.

He carried the plan to the suffrage committee himself and argued it in front of them. The committee reported it unfavorably, the convention adopted the committee's report, and that was the end of it.

Then he stood up and did arithmetic at them.

The 1890 census had counted 132,949 Black men over twenty-one in South Carolina and 102,567 white men. That was a Black majority of 30,292, and it was the entire reason the convention had been called.

Of those men, 58,086 of the Black ones and 13,242 of the white ones could not read or write. Smalls put the consequence in front of the chamber himself: an honest educational test, applied to everybody, would leave 89,415 white voters against 74,851 Black ones.

His side would take that deal.

Any qualification they liked, a property test, an education test, so long as it fell the same way on every man in the state, and in his own words, all that we ask is that they be fair and honest and honorable.

He reminded them that they had already tried the eight-box law. They had worn it so thin, he said, that it could no longer survive either a courtroom or a newspaper.

Then he put the state's own economy in front of them. The rice fields and the cotton fields ran on Black labor, the phosphate mines that paid the interest on the state debt ran on Black labor, and the same legislature that talked about being rid of the Black population had put a heavy tax on any agent who came into South Carolina to recruit workers out of it.

He told them the worst shock of his life had come in that same chamber, when a lawyer from Barnwell offered a draft constitution copied out of the 1865 constitution and the black code of 1866. Those were the documents that had barred Black men from holding office in South Carolina, and Congress had thrown them out. Throwing them out is what produced the Reconstruction Acts, and the Reconstruction Acts are what produced the convention of 1868, which Smalls told the room had given the state the best constitution any Southern state had.

I live on the very spot on which I was born, he told them, and he said he would ask no one else for permission to stay there.

He asked for one thing at the end of it, and it was procedural. The attendance was thin that afternoon, so he asked that the suffrage vote be held over until Monday.

Then he asked the senator from Edgefield straight out whether he meant to force it through that day.

Tillman said he did.

What the convention adopted instead of the plan ran on a calendar. Until January 1, 1898, a man could register if he could read a section of the new constitution, or if the registration officer was satisfied that he understood it when it was read aloud to him, and everyone who got through that door stayed a voter for life.

After that date the door narrowed. An applicant had to read and write any section put in front of him, or show that he owned property assessed at three hundred dollars and had paid the year's taxes on it.

Three men appointed by the governor ran the registration in each county. Smalls pointed out that the state supreme court had lately split over the meaning of a single section of law, two justices reading it one way and the third reading it another, and asked how an ordinary man was supposed to explain a section to the satisfaction of an official who already knew which answer he wanted.

Then there was the list of crimes that cost a man his vote under the new article. It ran to twenty offences, among them burglary, arson, perjury, forgery, robbery, bribery, larceny, receiving stolen goods, breach of trust, wife-beating, bigamy and adultery.

Murder is not on that list.

The old constitution had taken the vote for murder, and Smalls' own plan would have kept it there. The document South Carolina adopted in 1895 took the ballot from a man convicted of larceny and left it with a man convicted of murder.

On October 2 the convention took up section 34, which made a marriage between a white person and a person of one eighth or more Black ancestry unlawful and void.

Smalls moved an amendment to it. If South Carolina was going to write about the races mixing, then any white man who lived with a Black woman should be barred from holding any office of trust or profit in the state, and the children of those households should carry the father's name and inherit from him as legitimate children.

He explained to the chamber why he had written it that way. He gave them the census count of 1,132,060 Americans of mixed ancestry, said that a careful reading of the record showed more than three quarters of the mothers behind that number were Black women, and asked the room who they supposed the fathers had been.

A delegate called him to order for reflecting on the convention.

Smalls answered that he meant no reflection on anybody, and that any man with clean hands could keep his seat. Then he said that if white men were held to the standard Black men were held to, this convention would have to adjourn for lack of a quorum.

The chamber laughed.

Then it killed the amendment. On November 23 the Charleston News and Courier, the leading Democratic paper in the state, wrote in its editorial columns that the convention had rejected the addition by the largest vote recorded recently, and that its action had been a mistake.

The room was not the only audience.

On September 30, five of the six Black delegates had signed an open letter to the New York World setting out what the convention had been called to do and how the suffrage plan would work in the hands of the men administering it. The Columbia papers reprinted it four days later.

The New York Press ran an editorial on October 5 calling the amendment fight the most brilliant moral victory by a parliamentary minority it could recall. A body of clergymen and laymen meeting in Boston wired him on October 16. A man in Liverpool wrote on October 6 to say the report had crossed the Atlantic, and to ask for the best published account of the debate, because he wanted the details in full.

None of it moved a vote.

In December the committee on order, style and revision finished the document, and the only thing left was for the members to put their names on it. They were called up by county delegation, with President Evans and Vice President Jones signing first as the officers present, then Abbeville, then the rest of them in order.

When Beaufort was called, Smalls asked to be excused from signing, because he would not put his name to a constitution carrying that article on suffrage. The convention excused him unanimously. He was the only member of the Beaufort delegation in the room.

Somebody sent up a resolution during the signing that any member who did not sign should not be paid. Smalls said he would walk home to Beaufort rather than sign the thing.

The resolution was never put to a vote.

The constitution was ratified on December 4, 1895, and it did what it had been built to do. Writing in Constitutional Commentary a century later, the legal scholar Richard Pildes puts the number of Black South Carolinians registered to vote by 1896 at 5,500, out of the 132,949 the census had counted as men of voting age six years before.

The article Smalls tried to amend stayed in the constitution for another hundred and three years. South Carolina's voters took it out on November 3, 1998, and the historian Damon Fordham puts the margin at sixty-two percent of the ballots cast.

The pamphlet came out in 1896.

It ran twenty-nine pages, set by the Enquirer Print at 425 King Street in Charleston, and it carried his suffrage plan, the article the convention passed instead, the speeches as the state's papers had printed them, the editorials, the Boston telegram, the letters and the account of the signing. On the third page his daughter explained why the speeches are not given whole. No stenographers were employed by the Convention, she wrote, so there was nothing to reprint but what the newspapers had caught.

She did not present the book as a record of a defeat. In her introduction she called the six of them a very small part of what time and education were bringing forward, in spite of the lynchings and the caste prejudice and every other method being used against them.

She was not the only woman doing it. Mary J. Miller, out of the same Beaufort circle, brought out a twenty-three page collection of the Black delegates' speeches at her own expense, with no printer, no place and no date anywhere on it.

That is where the quotations come from.

When a line of Robert Smalls from 1895 turns up in a book, a documentary or a post, it is almost certainly coming out of those twenty-nine pages, because there is no official text of the speech for it to come out of instead. Andrew Billingsley, who wrote the standard book on Smalls and his families, used the two pamphlets as his principal source for those speeches, and noted that what the two women had done was left to sit in obscurity.

So there is something worth doing here, and it costs about four seconds. The next time that quorum line goes past you with his name under it, put the name of the person who kept it underneath.

She was born on December 1, 1863, went to the Miner Normal School in Washington and then the Boston Conservatory of Music, married and moved to Colorado, and came back to Beaufort to look after her father. She taught music afterward at the state's Colored Normal, Industrial, Agricultural and Mechanical College. She died in 1920 and lies in the same Beaufort churchyard as the man whose words she saved.

Her name was Sarah Voorhees Smalls.

South Carolina is still governed by the constitution those men signed that December. The state kept the document and it kept the list of who signed it, and what was said against it in that chamber survives in a book his daughter had to publish herself.

In July 2022 a company carrying Usain Bolt's name went quiet in at least 8 American cities. It left behind locked e-bikes and scooters and nobody answering the phone.

Bolt Mobility launched out of Miami in 2018 with the sprinter as co-founder and the face of the brand. In late 2020 it bought Gotcha Mobility of Charleston and took over its city contracts.

Portland, St. Augustine, Richmond in Virginia, Richmond in California and three towns in Vermont were left with equipment they could not unlock. The vehicles only opened through the company's app.

Officials emailed. They called. The customer service line was not staffed, and CEO Ignacio Tzoumas could not be reached either.

"They've vanished, leaving equipment behind," a Vermont county transport planner told TechCrunch that week.

Richmond, California said the company went out of business with no notice and left its equipment where it stood. A separate firm later offered to unlock the abandoned fleet so the cities could use it themselves.

Three weeks later the company finally spoke. It said investors had failed to deliver expected fundraising and it had to scale back.

The clip below is him unveiling that scooter in Paris, before any of this.

Bolt was the name on the vehicles, not the man running them.

Three months after the scooters went dark, his retirement account in Kingston still showed $12,758,181.74.

text:
🇮🇷|THE PLAYBOOK: VERTICAL TO HORIZONTAL

October twenty three, two thousand twenty six. Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, Speaker of the Iranian Parliament, posted a message. The message was not commentary. The message was a deconstruction of an operational manual.

He wrote this: Their post awakening playbook is to shift protests from a vertical axis to a horizontal one, then shame you for having woken up. Hold the line. The signal is Epstein and Gaza and war in Iran and corruption, all stemming from the same elite cabal. The noise is locals versus outsiders. Do not let them change the subject to evade accountability.

What do vertical and horizontal mean

A vertical protest points upward. Your anger points at those above you. Those people decide the budget and sign the contracts and deploy the police and sell the coastline to foreign developers and block medicine at the border. The arrow of a vertical protest points toward power.

A horizontal protest points sideways. Your anger points at those on the same level as you. Your anger points at neighbors and immigrants and people of a different sect and a different ethnicity and some other outsider. The arrow of a horizontal protest points toward fellow subjects. Those fellow subjects suffer the same oppression as you.

The shift from vertical to horizontal means you forget who stands at the top and you focus only on those beside you.

Students in France demand that their classroom roof stop leaking. That demand is a vertical protest. Then someone says it is the Muslims. That claim is a horizontal protest. The students now look at their neighbors instead of the budget.

Students in Albania demand funding for education. That demand is a vertical protest. Then Edi Rama says it is Russian bot accounts and it is Iranian agitation. That claim is a horizontal protest. The students now look at foreign agents instead of the Prime Minister.

A horizontal protest can never succeed. The target of a horizontal protest holds no power. The target lives like you. The target pays bills and waits in line at hospitals and worries about tuition for children. Meanwhile the man who holds real power stands at the apex of the hierarchy and looks down at the chaos below and says look, they fight each other.

Shaming you for waking up

You wake up. You see things as they are. You ask questions. Then they say you are too naive and you do not understand geopolitics and you are being used and foreign powers incited you and you think you understand and in reality you know nothing.

That shaming is the second layer of the operation. The first layer steers the narrative in a different direction. The second layer shames you for shifting your perspective.

You wake up because you notice the roof in your classroom leaks. They say you woke up because Russian accounts duped you or Iranian propaganda fooled you. They say you woke up because you fail to grasp complexity.

The word complexity is a tool for humiliation. The tool makes your anger feel too simplistic and your questions too childish and your demands too unrealistic. The tool wants you to go home and keep your mouth shut and leave matters to those who understand.

A student who wants a ceiling that does not leak needs no complexity. The student needs a ceiling. Complexity cannot fix a ceiling.

Signals and noise

Ghalibaf identifies four signals. The signals are Epstein and Gaza and the war with Iran and corruption.

He argues that the four signals originate from the same elite group at the very top.

Epstein was a financier. He is now dead. His client list has never been fully disclosed. His name appears in flight logs beside Trump and Clinton and Prince Andrew and Barak and many others. The network trafficked across nations. The full list remains hidden.

Gaza has faced blockade for seventeen years and bombardment for two years. More than twenty one thousand children are dead. More than seventy four thousand people are dead in total. The question stands. Who supplies the bombs and who provides the targeting intelligence and who offers diplomatic cover.

The war in Iran has dragged for eight months. Hospitals were bombed. Pharmaceutical plants were destroyed. Scientists were assassinated. The question stands. Who wages the war and who funds it and who profits from it.

Corruption runs from the coastlines of Albania to privatizations in Greece and from oil contracts in Iraq to aid funds for Ukraine. The question stands. Who signs the documents and who receives payments and who launders the money.

Ghalibaf says the four issues are not four separate issues. The four issues are four facets of one problem. The problem bears the name the same elite at the top.

The noise is locals versus outsiders.

Do not look at the Epstein list. Look at immigrants instead. Do not look at the children in Gaza. Look at Muslims. Do not look at the war in Iran. Look at foreign powers. Do not look at corruption. Look at how they take your jobs.

The function of the noise is to exhaust you with horizontal and lateral anger and to make you forget who stands at the very top of the vertical hierarchy.

Hold the line

Hold the line. Do not let them shift the subject. Do not let them turn the question of who bombs Gaza into a debate about problems within the Muslim community. Do not let them turn the question of who sells the Albanian coastline into a story about Russian bot accounts. Do not let them turn the question of who sits on the Epstein list into a dismissal that you are naive.

The line is vertical. The line runs from your anger straight toward that elite at the top. Holding the line means you prevent the twisting of the line into a horizontal conflict. Holding the line means every time someone says it is the immigrants, you ask who let them in and who profits from their labor. Holding the line means every time someone says it is foreign powers, you ask who signs the contracts and who receives the loans.

Ghalibaf speaks not only to the people of Iran. He speaks to everyone who begins to wake up. He speaks to students in France and students in Albania and teachers in Greece and workers in Serbia and taxpayers in the United States and mothers in Gaza. He says do not let them shift the subject to evade accountability.

Accountability is vertical. Accountability points upward. Accountability never points sideways.

Every instance of horizontal and lateral anger serves as a gift to those at the very top. The elite know full well that a protest directed sideways will never reach them.

Long live the awakening. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.
