text:
Data and Power: Why Safaricom and Kenyan Energy Could Be the Next Gold Mine
AI runs on two things: data (networks, cables, data centres) and power (lots of electricity, ideally cheap and clean). Whoever controls these in a region gets paid as AI grows. In Kenya, Safaricom has much of the data side and KenGen has much of the power side.
1. Safaricom is turning into a tech company, not just a telco
In his CNN interview, CEO Peter Ndegwa said the plan is to move beyond telecoms into technology, financial services and AI. M-PESA will grow into savings, investments and insurance. AI already screens about 150 million transactions a day for fraud. It's also meant to personalise My OneApp. Safaricom spends $400–500 million a year on Kenyan infrastructure as data demand grows.
2. It owns the pipes AI needs
Cables: Daraja gives Safaricom its own landing station and a new route to the Middle East and Asia. Today it relies on third parties to connect to undersea cables, and its SEACOM agreements expire in June 2028.  (businessdailyafrica)  (techmoran)
Data centres: with iXAfrica, Safaricom offers East Africa's first AI-ready data centre services to enterprise and cloud clients, at a Nairobi campus with 22.5MW of design capacity, the region's largest. iXAfrica is building two more Nairobi facilities: an 18MW one and a 53MW campus.  (Safaricom, iXAfrica launch East Africa’s first AI-ready data centre +2)
Customers and data: Safaricom held 69.8% of Kenya's 88 million active mobile subscriptions. That's a huge base for AI-driven lending, insurance and payments.
3. The money is already showing
FY2026 dividends totalled KES 2.00 per share; the share price rose 50.3% over the year, and market cap reached KES 1.44 trillion before the AGM.
4. Power is the other half
Data centres use enormous amounts of electricity, and Kenya has an advantage few countries have: geothermal, which is clean and runs 24/7. KenGen produces up to 70% of Kenya's electricity and is Africa's largest geothermal producer, seventh in the world. Microsoft and G42 committed to a $1 billion data centre at KenGen's Green Energy Park in Naivasha, to run fully on Olkaria geothermal power. Every new data centre is a new long-term power buyer.

text:
Based on your prologue, timeline, and eulogy, I would write a foreword that frames the book not as a success story, but as a study in resilience, reinvention, and the cost of choosing one's own path.

Cauldron to Crucible 
Foreword

Most memoirs follow a familiar path.
A young person discovers a dream, overcomes obstacles, achieves success, and reflects upon the lessons learned. The trajectory is upward, orderly, and reassuring.
This is not that kind of story.
The life described in these pages often moved in the opposite direction. It rose, fell, recovered, stumbled, reinvented itself, and started over again. More than once.
At various times, the author was a small town Texas boy, a Baylor student, a naval officer, a CPA, a bank executive, a consultant, a forensic accountant, a telemarketer, a bookkeeper, an investigator, a caregiver, and, when circumstances demanded it, a survivor.
Titles came and went.
Fortunes rose and fell.
Careers flourished and collapsed.
New opportunities appeared where none seemed possible.
The conventional measure of a life would struggle to make sense of such a journey. Success and failure arrived too often and too unpredictably. The pattern refuses to fit neatly into a résumé or a formula.
Yet there is a thread running through every chapter.
The story is ultimately about freedom.
Not freedom in the political sense.
Freedom in the deeply personal sense: the determination to live a self-directed life, even when circumstances, institutions, expectations, responsibilities, or mistakes attempt to dictate another course.
The young man described in these pages was expected to follow a certain script. Many people do. Some embrace it. Others spend their lives quietly trapped within it.
The author chose another path.
Sometimes that choice led to achievement.
Sometimes it led to hardship.
Occasionally it led to both at the same time.
The reader will encounter ambition, humor, miscalculation, persistence, pride, disappointment, recovery, and more than a few moments that provoke the question, "What happens next?"
That uncertainty is not a flaw in the story.
It is the story.
The chapters that follow are not the account of a man who always won.
They are the account of a man who repeatedly got back up.
In an age that often celebrates certainty, this memoir offers something more valuable: an honest record of adaptation. It is the chronicle of a life lived without guarantees, where identity had to be rebuilt more than once and where resilience became a habit rather than an achievement.
The title Cauldron to Crucible is fitting.
A cauldron is a place of turbulence, heat, and constant motion. A crucible is a place where pressure and fire transform the material placed within it.
The story you are about to read contains plenty of both.
Whether you agree with every decision the author made is beside the point. What matters is that he made them himself, accepted their consequences, and continued forward.
At the end of a long life, that may be one of the rarest accomplishments of all.
Welcome to the journey.

209 years ago today, Britain ARMED an African king. 🇬🇧

Muskets. Gunpowder. Ten thousand gun flints. Four hundred red coats. 💂

British sergeants to train his army. A salary in gold and silver, every year. 💰

Britain wanted him to win. 👑

Valley after valley. Chief after chief. Until two-thirds of Madagascar was under his rule. 🗺️

On purpose. 👀

Why? 🤔

Because on that island, chiefs raided villages and sold the people. To French slave ships. To Arab dhows. To other African kingdoms. ⛓️

Then they bought guns with the money. To raid more villages. 🔥

Guns for people. People for guns. 🔁

Britain had banned its own slave trade in 1807. But it couldn’t guard every beach on an island nearly a thousand miles long. 🌊

So a sergeant from Cork travelled 28 days, by canoe and on foot, to reach the king. 🛶

For two months they bargained. Then he made an offer nobody had authorised. 🤝

Every gun the slave trade gave the king, Britain would give him free. If he stopped selling people. ✋

On 23 October 1817, the king signed. Selling his people abroad would be punished by death. ✍️

Then Britain helped him take the island. Port after port, every one closed to the slave ships. ⚓

They teach you Britain profited from slavery. 📚

They never teach you how we got them to stop selling their own people. 🤫

Britain armed an African king. On purpose. 🇬🇧

Be part of us. ☝️🇬🇧

Be Proud Of Us. 🙏🇬🇧

The first-ever Army-to-Army Staff Talks between Ethiopia and India concluded in Pune, marking another significant step in the growing strategic partnership between the two countries.

The discussions covered military capacity building, defense technology, innovation, and expanded cooperation. The Ethiopian delegation also toured Indian defense industries, gaining firsthand exposure to India’s indigenous manufacturing capabilities and defense start-up ecosystem.

For Ethiopia, India offers a valuable partner in diversifying defense relationships, strengthening technological capabilities, and developing a more self-reliant defense industry. For India, Ethiopia represents a strategic partner in the Horn of Africa, where the security of the Red Sea and Indian Ocean increasingly intersects with its national interests.

The talks build on the Strategic Partnership announced during PM Modi’s December 2025 visit to Addis Ababa, reflecting a relationship increasingly moving from diplomatic engagement toward practical military and defense-industrial cooperation.

text:
📍 Jerusalem | Rare footage of the Dome of the Rock, guarded by Muslim troops of the British Indian Army, filmed in 1917 during the First World War.

At the heart of Masjid al-Aqsa stands the Dome of the Rock (قبة الصخرة, Qubbat al-Sakhrah). Its dome, golden today, was then covered in lead and would have appeared dark grey; the gold-coloured covering was added only during restoration in the late 1950s and early 1960s

The film captures the open stone-paved courtyard, the building's distinctive octagonal structure and dome, its entrances, and people moving through the sacred precinct. It offers a rare glimpse of the site’s appearance and atmosphere more than a century ago.

🔹 Who are the men walking inside?
The Imperial War Museums catalogue identifies Indian infantry regiments changing guard at the shrine, one probably the 58th (Vaughan’s) Rifles. The original film caption states that the site was guarded by Muslim troops of the British Indian Army, showing how soldiers from the Indian subcontinent took part in guarding one of Islam’s most sacred places. Other individuals in the footage cannot be identified from the film alone.

🔹 Who ruled Jerusalem in 1917?
Jerusalem had been under Ottoman rule for around four centuries. During the First World War, the Ottoman Empire fought against Britain and its allies. British forces under General Sir Edmund Allenby captured the city in December 1917, and Allenby formally entered Jerusalem on 11 December. The city then came under British military administration, ending Ottoman rule.
🔹 A moment of transition
This footage records the Haram al-Sharif’s historic Islamic architecture and sacred spaces, with Muslim Indian soldiers on guard, at the close of the Ottoman era and the beginning of British military rule in Jerusalem.

📚 Source: Imperial War Museum

text: This painting is titled "The Passage of the Delaware." It was painted in 1819 by Thomas Sully.  In 1817 the state of NC commissioned Sully to paint a heroic portrait of George Washington in action for the Senate Hall in the NC State House. The final canvas was 17 x 12 ft. which was  too large for the NC Senate Hall. Sully offered to paint a smaller painting, but the NC legislature withdrew from the contract. Sully then send the painting on tour that started in Virginia and made its way up to Boston, hoping that it would prompt Congress to acquire it for the US Capitol rotonuda. When that didn't happen, Sully ended up selling it to John Doggett, a Boston frame maker, for $500.

text:
My freshman year of college I met these three people at a party who were going to drive to California over fall break but thought they weren’t going to be able to afford it because their fourth person had justdropped out, so I offered to go and they said yes.

My mom‘s boyfriend gave me $200 and I left with them like two days after we’d met.

We drove from St. Louis to north of San Francisco and then back through the Southwest and Texas in seven days.

The $200 covered my share of gas and whatever I ate. I don’t even remember ever thinking about food. There must’ve been many long stretches in which I didn’t eat.

They knew people in Nebraska and Boulder, where we stayed the night for free. And then we camped on “the beach” in California and in a state park in Texas. Those are the only places we slept. That means taking turns driving straight through from Denver to San Francisco and from San Francisco to Texas.

I brought a backpack with some clothes and a copy of On the Road.

I called a buddy of mine back home from a payphone in Death Valley. I don’t even really know why and I remember feeling kind of embarrassed to have done it.

I otherwise had no contact with anybody. No cell phone, etc.

This all seems completely crazy to me now. How could you do this on $200? How could you do that without stopping more often? 

But we did!

text:
Seven Navy officers took eighty minutes over lunch to convict fifty Black sailors of mutiny. That is about ninety-six seconds a man, and the Navy sentenced every one of them to fifteen years of hard labor, reduction in rank and a dishonorable discharge. A commander admitted on the stand that he could not identify one man he had ordered to load ammunition.

You have already spent longer than ninety-six seconds on this post.

At two-thirty on the afternoon of Sunday, August 7, 1966, three hundred and eighty-five people walked out of the plaza at Willow Pass and Grant in Concord, California, into ninety-degree heat. They were walking six miles to a Navy gate to try to stop trucks carrying napalm from getting through it.

By the time they reached the water they were about five hundred. Shirts and shoes had come off along the road, two women had fainted and been carried into cars, and a mile out of town roughly forty young men had been waiting at a drive-in called Waring's Frosty Freeze to shout at them as they went past.

The gate faced Suisun Bay. Across the road stood about twenty police officers and a hundred hecklers, with ten Marines posted inside the fence.

A man named Bob Meriwether called a meeting of the thirty or so people who had agreed to be arrested. Hecklers walked over and stood around the meeting, coughing and whistling and talking so that nobody could hear.

Then the first napalm truck came down the road, bombs stacked in open crates, and turned in through the gate. Nobody was in position.

The Marines had a loudspeaker and they ran it all night. It announced that a white line painted across the pavement marked the edge of the Concord Naval Weapons Station, and that crossing it without a legitimate purpose and a definite destination carried up to six months in jail and a five hundred dollar fine.

By midnight the crowd had thinned to about sixty. A line of never fewer than ten stood facing the waterfront gate until morning, holding signs and singing, six feet from a railroad track where a Southern Pacific brakeman woke them at four in the morning by telling them to get up.

At a quarter past three, three women were pulled out of the path of a truck by one deputy and put down hard on the pavement by another. One of them could not get up on her own and was told she would be arrested if she did not move.

Just after seven a truck marked Explosives came through and did not stop. It pushed the seated bodies slowly along the roadway toward the white line, and when they crossed it Marines dragged them onto the base and charged them with trespassing.

A man standing there said what all of them were thinking. Not one of those people had trespassed voluntarily.

Thirty-one arrests by Thursday morning, nearly all of them released on their own recognizance inside the week. Six months and five hundred dollars was the most the law could do to a person for stopping bombs at that gate.

Twenty-two years earlier, at that same water, fifty Black men were sent to prison for fifteen years for refusing to load them.

They had seen it coming and they had put it in writing. In 1943 a group of Black sailors at Port Chicago wrote to a local attorney to say that morale had dropped to an alarming depth, and they closed with a question about whether they were waiting for a new deal in vain.

Nothing came back.

They had enlisted expecting the sea. Many had passed rating exams as machinist's mates, gunner's mates, radiomen and storekeepers, and all of them were put to lifting bombs onto ships by hand.

Cyril Sheppard came out of gunnery school with the highest marks in his class and qualified as gunner's mate third class. He never wore the stripe.

The base ran on Jim Crow down to the plumbing. Black sailors were barred from the whites-only heads on the ships they were loading, so a man who needed a bathroom walked half a mile to find one he was allowed to use.

They were issued no gloves. The bombs came slick with grease and were lifted by hand, and the heavy ones were rolled along the dock.

When men asked whether the things could go off, officers told them the munitions carried no fuses or detonators and could not explode.

That was false.

The winches were in poor repair, with broken levers and valves and brakes, and crews were told to load past capacity to keep the pace up. The pace itself was chalked up where everyone could read it.

In April 1944 the officer in charge, Captain Merrill Kinne, started posting each division's tons per hour on a board in the dock office. He said later that he took the idea from gunnery target practice, where you write up the shots fired and the hits made.

Officers bet on the outcome. Junior officers who came up short heard about their lack of tonnage from above, and they passed it down to the men.

Joe Small was twenty-two, a winch operator born in Savannah and raised on a New Jersey farm, and one of the older hands the officers leaned on. He told Lieutenant Delucchi more than once that the base was going to blow sky high.

Delucchi's answer, as Small repeated it almost forty years later into a tape recorder, was that if it did, Small would not know anything about it. He told him not to worry.

At 10:18 on the night of July 17, 1944, the two ships at the pier went up seconds apart. Everyone within a thousand feet was killed where they stood.

Three hundred and twenty men died, two hundred and two of them Black sailors, and about three hundred and ninety more were hurt. The blast was heard in Nevada and registered on instruments in Berkeley.

Most of the survivors were in their barracks getting ready for bed. The roof came down and the windows came in on top of them.

Percy Robinson made it outside and found men calling for volunteers to go down to the docks. He said he wanted to go, and the man he said it to, his own squad leader, asked him whether he had seen Percy get out of the barracks.

There was so much blood on his face that his squad leader did not know who he was talking to.

Around two hundred Black sailors went to the water that night and worked the fires, including the ones burning beside boxcars still packed with explosives. The Navy later commended them for coolness and bravery and said they had carried on in the service's highest traditions.

Of the three hundred and twenty dead, fifty-one could be identified.

Navy practice after an ammunition accident was to move the survivors, change their duties and send them home for a while. The white officers at Port Chicago asked for survivor's leave and were granted thirty days.

The Black survivors were kept where they were and put to work gathering what was left of the men they had worked beside. Not one of them was given leave.

Four days after the explosion the Navy opened a court of inquiry. Three senior officers and a judge advocate questioned a hundred and twenty-five witnesses across five weeks, and five of those witnesses were Black sailors.

On the facts, the inquiry was brutal about the command. Leadership had failed to prepare for the volume of explosives coming through, failed to supply competent petty officers, failed to train the officers and the crews before putting them on the job, and had broken federal safety code and disregarded Coast Guard regulations.

Then came the opinions section, where officers were allowed to interpret their own findings. It proposed that if human error caused the explosion, the error was rough or careless handling by an individual, meaning one of the men already dead, and it offered in support the claim that Black sailors were neither temperamentally nor intellectually capable of handling high explosives.

That was the Navy's public position on these men. It was printed, repeated and believed, and it hung over everything that happened next.

In early August, the admiral commanding the Twelfth Naval District put a very different sentence into a document stamped confidential. The Negro divisions, it said, had turned in a satisfactory record loading ammunition, and their tons per man per day equalled what civilian stevedores in the area were doing.

Professional dockworkers. That was the Navy's private assessment of the same men, written within weeks of the public one, and the men themselves never saw it.

There was more in the file. On August 12, the day after the survivors came off a prison barge, Navy leadership told Mare Island command that no white units were doing this work and that pains had to be taken so nobody could conclude hazardous duty was being handed only to Black personnel.

White loading battalions were arranged for Port Chicago and Mare Island within days. Navy Secretary James Forrestal wrote to President Roosevelt about it, and the admission that no white enlisted men had been doing the work went in by hand in the margin.

The loading was integrated to protect a court case.

Two weeks later Walter White of the NAACP wrote to Forrestal about race-based assignments at both bases. The Navy wrote back that he was mistaken, that Negro and white personnel were used indiscriminately, and that the Department would never assign any race exclusively to hazardous duty.

The survivors were sent twenty-five miles to the ammunition depot at Mare Island in Vallejo, mixed in with new crews of inexperienced men, under the same officers, with the inquiry unfinished and nothing about the work changed. On the morning of August 9 three divisions were ordered to march to the pier and load a ship.

They marched. Partway there they stopped.

There was no shouting and no threat made to anyone. Of the three hundred and twenty-eight men, two hundred and fifty-eight said they would take any other duty, any transfer, combat overseas, anything at all except loading under those conditions.

Cyril Sheppard asked to be put on a ship and allowed to fight, and said he would take his chances out there. What he would not do was watch men die of somebody else's negligence.

The admiral who had commended them for bravery three weeks earlier told them that mutinous conduct in wartime carried a death sentence, and that a firing squad was a worse risk than the ammunition. Then he had two hundred and fifty-eight of them packed onto a prison barge for three days.

Percy Robinson thought about his mother, who had been raised in Mississippi and had taught him what a white man's threat was worth. He decided not to hand them a legal chance to shoot him, and he went back to work.

Jack Crittenden was taken out of the stockade in handcuffs to be questioned with a Marine standing outside the door holding a club. He read the statement they had written down for him, told them it was not what he had said, and was informed that he had no alternative but to sign it.

On the barge the waiting turned into arguments and a few fights. Joe Small called the men together and told them to cut out the horseplay, obey the guards and hold together.

The Navy entered that meeting as evidence of a conspiracy.

Two hundred and eight men went back to the pier and were court-martialed for the delay, losing three months of pay. Roosevelt wrote to Forrestal that those men had acted out of mass fear, that it was understandable, and that their punishment should be nominal.

Fifty did not go back. On September 4 the Navy charged them with conspiring to make a mutiny, which carried death, rather than insubordination, which did not.

The trial opened ten days later in San Francisco Bay and ran into late October. The Navy invited the national press, which is not something it normally does.

Replacements kept arriving while the court sat. A seventeen-year-old from Harlem named Harry Belafonte reached Port Chicago with the wreckage still uncleared, and by his own account the fifty men were being court-martialed as he came in.

He was put on the same job. None of them had any training for it, he wrote later, and every man there understood exactly why he had been picked, because this was the work the Navy kept for the sailors it treated as most expendable.

Thurgood Marshall sat through twelve days of it as a member of the public, because a civilian lawyer could not represent enlisted men in a military court. He asked for the Navy's own documents and was refused, and he told reporters this was not fifty men on trial but the Navy on trial for its whole policy toward Black men.

The defense was five naval lieutenants led by Gerald Veltmann, ten clients each, barred from raising working conditions, safety violations or racial discrimination. They argued that the men had been frightened, because it was the only door the Navy left open to them.

The charge was conspiracy, which meant proving an agreement among fifty men. Asked whether he could identify a single one of them he had ordered to load ammunition, a Navy commander said that he could not.

On October 24 the seven officers of the court withdrew and came back in eighty minutes, taken over lunch.

That is about ninety-six seconds a man.

All fifty were guilty. All fifty got fifteen years of hard labor, reduction in rank and a dishonorable discharge.

Cyril Sheppard was in the brig when they came in with machine guns and lined the men up to read it out. He said his knees nearly hit the ground.

Marshall appealed in April 1945, and the Navy conceded that hearsay had been admitted forty separate times. Admiral Osterhaus was ordered to reconvene his court and reconsider, sat five hours on June 12, and changed nothing.

The men were quietly released in January 1946 after sixteen months, then kept in uniform and shipped overseas to sweep and pick up trash. A letter inside the corrections system had recommended letting them go without allowing the NAACP or the Black press to take credit for it.

Marshall went looking afterward for the paperwork on how the case ended. The final disposition had never been entered, and the Navy Department held no record of it.

The following month, on February 27, 1946, the Bureau of Naval Personnel issued Circular Letter 48-46, making Black sailors eligible for every rating, activity and ship in the service. The convictions stayed on the fifty men.

In 1994 the Navy reviewed the case for two years. It conceded that racial discrimination had played a part in who was assigned to load ammunition, and concluded that no error or injustice had occurred.

One of the survivors said it was like saying it was raining everywhere but right here.

Pardons came up later and most of the men refused them. Joe Small said a pardon means you are guilty and forgiven, and what he wanted was the decision set aside and the pay returned.

Jack Crittenden would not ask forgiveness for something he had not done. Freddie Meeks took one from President Clinton in 1999, as one of the last three alive, because he wanted the country to finally hear what happened.

On July 17, 2024, eighty years to the day, the Secretary of the Navy exonerated all two hundred and fifty-six men court-martialed after the explosion and handed the first pen to Thurgood Marshall's son. Every one of the sailors was dead.

Carol Cherry stood at a new monument on Yerba Buena Island that year for her father, Cyril Sheppard. She had learned he was a convicted man only about fifteen years earlier, and from a relative, because the gunner's mate who never got to wear his stripe never told his own children.

The gate is still there under another name. The land is Military Ocean Terminal Concord now, run by the Army, and the memorial holding the three hundred and twenty names cut into granite stands near the ruined pilings of the pier.

You can go and stand at those names. You have to call two weeks ahead, give your full legal name, your date of birth and your government identification number, and be a United States citizen, so that the Army can run a background check and clear you to walk in.

A ranger drives you out on a shuttle and stays beside you the whole time.

The bill on these men is a small one now and it is still open. A phone call, a two-week wait, and the willingness to carry the true version instead of the short one, so the next person who hears the word mutiny hears what it actually was.

Two sentences about the same men sat in the same Navy's files in the same month of 1944. One called them incapable and went out to the public, where it was used to bury them, and the other called them the equals of professional stevedores and went into a drawer marked confidential.

All fifty went into the ground before their country would say out loud which of the two was true.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter.

📊 REIT Earnings Quick Takes

Rexford Industrial (REXR) - the fourth-largest industrial REIT with an exclusive focus on the Southern California market - rallied 5% today after reporting an improved leasing quarter, raising its full-year earnings and same-store NOI outlooks, and making substantial progress on its $2B portfolio realignment and deleveraging plan.

REXR raised its 2026 FFO growth outlook to 1.0% from 0.2% previously, while increasing cash same-store NOI guidance to 0.5% from a 0.3% decline. 

Operating trends improved meaningfully beneath the headline numbers, with 3.7M SF of leases signed, nearly 60% above the trailing quarterly average, while same-property occupancy increased 200 basis points sequentially to 96.9%.

Leasing economics remain the primary near-term challenge, although trends moved in the right direction, with cash leasing spreads improving to -3.0% from -11.3% in Q2. 

REXR expects spreads to remain negative in the low-to-mid teens on average over the next couple of years as leases signed near the 2022-2023 market peak roll over, but noted that the portfolio realignment has removed many of the assets facing the steepest rent resets. 

Encouragingly, Southern California market rents increased roughly 1% sequentially, marking the first quarterly increase since 2023, while the market posted a second consecutive quarter of positive absorption.

The bigger strategic story remains REXR's portfolio reset, with $1.5B of dispositions completed year-to-date, including a $1.2B portfolio sale at a 5.5% NOI yield. Proceeds have been redeployed into debt reduction and share repurchases, with roughly $709M of stock repurchased year-to-date while leverage fell to 3.8x. 

REXR noted that repurchases currently offer an implied yield in the mid-6% range, making them more attractive than acquisitions and providing a compelling arbitrage relative to the assets being sold.

The results reinforce the stabilization theme highlighted in our earnings preview, with recovering tenant demand, constrained new supply, and improving absorption beginning to translate into stronger occupancy. 

REXR noted that demand was particularly broad across advanced manufacturing and logistics users, while increasingly strong demand for high-quality Class A space is benefiting its repositioning and development pipeline.

text:
The number worth watching is who takes the money. BMW opened the scheme to administration and development staff in Germany, with production excluded. About 50,000 people can see a personal offer, and the €650,000 is the top of the range in one agreement Handelsblatt saw.

Two figures in the post are softer than they look. BMW has confirmed "several thousand" cuts by the end of 2027; the 8,000 comes from one unnamed person quoted by Reuters. The portal pause rests on German press reports.

The old worry with voluntary exits is that the best people leave first. A 1997 World Bank paper by Martín Rama put it bluntly: the best workers go and the worst stay. The evidence since is mixed. Pencavel's study of University of California buyouts found 10% more severance raised the odds of leaving by 7% to 8%, and who would leave was hard to predict. A 2012 Cornell study found the underpaid signed up most, with no sign the most productive left.

BMW is not alone. VW plans 35,000 German job cuts by 2030, Bosch 13,000 and ZF 11,000 to 14,000 by 2028. China sales, the cost of EVs and US tariffs are squeezing all of them.

From Kampala the contrast is stark. UBOS counts 89.2% of employed Ugandans as informal, so most workers here get no package at all. For formal jobs, the 2026 amendment to the Employment Act now sets severance at one month's salary per year worked.

For a founder who has to shrink a team:

1. Decide which roles you can lose before you decide the money.
2. Make the offer by invitation, role by role.
3. Keep a retention offer ready for the two or three people you cannot lose.

text:
Jesse Legree just announced he is staying at Oregon State through 2027.

The two men who run that program looked at him once before and passed.

JaMarcus Shephard and Eron Hodges were both on Alabama's staff in the fall of 2025. Legree was a 160 pound defensive back at Loyola Blakefield in Baltimore who had moved to receiver for his senior year, and moving cost him. Coaches saw an undersized defensive back. The programs with room at receiver had already filled it.

Pittsburgh looked. Temple thought about him at cornerback. A few FCS schools circled.

His high school coach at St. Frances Academy called the silence debilitating, and kept the Oregon State conversations quiet so the kid would not get his hopes up over nothing.

Then Shephard got the Oregon State job on the 28th of November in 2025. Hodges told him to go watch Legree immediately.

He became the first player they went after.

The scholarship offer came by text, late on Signing Day, while Legree was sitting in a film room.

Here is what he has said about the place he said yes to.

"I barely knew Oregon was a state."

On the sixth play of his first college game he caught one and ran 71 yards with it. The next week he put 240 yards and two touchdowns on Texas Tech.

He has been the Pac-12 freshman of the week seven straight times. He leads the entire country in receiving yards and receiving touchdowns, as a true freshman, at 5 foot 10.

Chad Johnson offered $2 million of his own money to help the Beavers keep him.

He told ESPN's Pete Thamel.

Now the part that complicates it. He has played six games. Plenty of freshmen have had a season like this and never had another one, and nothing about today promises anybody a 2028. Eron Hodges said out loud a few weeks ago that keeping him was going to be hard.

Today it was not.

And there is one more thing, which is the part that stays with me.

Basketball was his first sport. He only picked up football to stay in shape for it, and he stopped growing at 5 foot 10. His older brother Josiah plays point guard at UTSA.

His dad Jeffrey coaches junior varsity girls basketball. He also works with the football program at St. Frances on mental health and player development.

So when Jesse Legree gets asked what he wants to do once the football is finished, he does not say coach, and he does not say television.

He says he wants to be a therapist. He says he wants to help people.

The kid nobody would take at receiver is now the best one in the country. And what he says he wants when it is over is to sit in a room and listen.

Mid-States Cash Grain Today
Friday, October 23, 2026

Grain futures closed out Friday's session with a firm, late week bounce led by strength in corn and wheat futures, while soybean contracts pulled back slightly. Strong domestic processing demand, surging crude oil prices above $103/bbl, and steady interior basis supported cash grain bids across the central states as row-crop harvest activity moves through its second half.

USDA Crop Progress Update
The latest USDA Crop Progress report showed national corn harvest advancing to 44% complete nationwide, while soybean harvest reached 64% complete. Corn maturity reached 95% with condition ratings holding steady at 56% good to excellent. Winter wheat planting for the 2027 crop advanced to 63% complete, with 39% emerged across the Plains.

Wheat Market Volatility Wheat markets caught a bid into week-end trading, with December CBOT wheat settling up at $6.25 per bushel and December KCBT HRW wheat closing firmer at $6.64 per bushel. While seasonal harvest supply pressure has unwound, persistent Black Sea export delays and elevated ocean shipping costs continue to offer an underlying floor under interior country elevator basis.

Drought and Soil Moisture

Soil moisture profiles across the Mid-States remain sharply divided as harvest progresses. Mostly clear weather across Iowa, Illinois, and eastern Nebraska allowed steady field entry with manageable grain drying costs. However, persistent topsoil deficits across Kansas, South Dakota, and North Dakota continue to raise emergence concerns for newly seeded winter wheat ground.

Biofuel and Ethanol Support Surging WTI crude oil prices near $103.22 per barrel continue to expand renewable fuel blend margins for regional processors.

Midwest ethanol plants and soybean crush facilities are maintaining competitive cash bids for spot physical deliveries to satisfy operational pipeline requirements ahead of late-fall maintenance turnarounds.

text:
THE UNITED STATES IS AN APARTHEID OCCUPATION!

🪶 GA-BE-NAH-GEWN-WONCE — "Wrinkled Meat" — CHIEF JOHN SMITH 🪶 c. 1822-1826 to February 6, 1922 | Cass Lake, Minnesota | Ojibwe
THE MAN THEY TURNED INTO A SIDESHOW.
That face with a thousand wrinkles — you know it. Every postcard shop in Minnesota sold it in 1915 as "The 137-year-old Indian."
His grave at Cass Lake still says 1784-1922. 137 years old. It's a lie carved in stone.
THE CORRECTED AGE:
Smith himself never claimed 1784. White photographers and newspaper men did — because an impossibly old Indian sold more postcards.
What we know:
- Paul Peter Buffalo, an Ojibwe man who knew him, recorded Smith saying: "I was a boy when the stars fell." He meant the Great Leonid meteor storm of November 12-13, 1833 — the night the sky fell, remembered by every Native child alive then. If he was 8-10 in 1833, he was born 1822-1826. That makes him 96-100 when he died. Old, but humanly old.
- Federal census and annuity rolls for Cass Lake Chippewa: His name first appears as an adult in the 1870s-80s, not in 1810s rolls. If he was born in 1784, he would have been 80 before the Civil War and on every early treaty — he isn't.
- The 1784 date was invented around 1914 by promoter C. A. A. Smith who took him to the Minnesota State Fair and to Washington as a curiosity. Older = more money.
So: ~100 years old. Not 137. Still a man who lived through everything.
WHAT HE ACTUALLY LIVED THROUGH — NOT A MYTH, A HISTORY:
Born c. 1825 in the deep woods between Red Lake and Cass Lake — before Minnesota was a state, before reservations.
- 1837: Pine Treaty — Ojibwe cede land for white pine logging. He is a child, watches loggers come. - 1855-1867: Treaty of Washington, Treaty of Old Crossing — his band pushed onto Cass Lake Reservation. - 1862: Dakota War — just south, 38 Dakota hanged in Mankato, largest mass execution in U.S. history. Smith stays neutral, survives because Cass Lake Ojibwe are not Dakota. - 1890: Wounded Knee — he is 65, hearing about Ghost Dance and massacre. - 1890s-1910s: Cass Lake becomes a tourist lake. White sportsmen want a guide. Smith becomes the most photographed Ojibwe in America — fisherman, storyteller, knows every lake.
He had 8 wives in his lifetime (Ojibwe custom, widowed many times), no children survived him. Adopted a son, Tom Smith.
He never lived in a house. Lived in a wigwam at Cass Lake until 1922, even when offered a cabin.
He died of pneumonia February 6, 1922. At his funeral, the Catholic priest and the Midewiwin medicine man both prayed.
WHY THEY LIED ABOUT HIS AGE:
1900-1920 America loved two kinds of Indian: the dead savage and the ancient, wrinkled curiosity. A 100-year-old man who still paddles a birch bark canoe? Sell it.
Star Tribune, 1920: "Oldest man in America lives in Minnesota woods!" Postcards: "Chief John Smith, 137 years old, smoked for 100 years."
They made him smoke a pipe for tourists, though he barely smoked. They made him pose holding 1920 newspapers to "prove" his eyesight.
He played along because tourists paid 25 cents for a photo, and that was money for flour.
He was not a chief by heredity. "Chief" was what white people called any old Indian they could sell a picture of.
His real name: Ga-Be-Nah-Gewn-Wonce — Ka-be-nah-gwe-wence — "Wrinkled Meat" — given to him in old age because of his face. The name is a joke, and he owned it.
THE DARK TRUTH IN HIS WRINKLES:
Each wrinkle is not age. It's allotment. Logging. His forest — Cass Lake was white pine, 200 feet tall — cut down in 15 years by Weyerhaeuser. His lakes stocked with walleye for white tourists, his right to net fish called "illegal."
He watched Cass Lake go from Ojibwe food lake to Minnesota resort lake while he lived in a wigwam 100 yards from hotels that sold his postcard.
That is why he lived so long. He refused to leave.
Grave still says 1784-1922. If you go to Cass Lake Cemetery, you can still see it — a small white headstone, American flag, Ojibwe offerings.
Do not say he was 137. Say he was ~100, saw the stars fall in 1833, and survived every single attempt by America to erase his people — treaties, logging, tourism — by staying on his lake and telling stories.
That's more impressive than a fake number.
> Ga-Be-Nah-Gewn-Wonce — "Wrinkled Meat." Not 137. 100. Old enough to remember when the stars fell in 1833, old enough to see his entire forest cut down and sold as postcards of his own face. Cass Lake, Minnesota. He never left.

text:
Let me analyze this parlay 🤑🏆

1. 🏈 Duke vs. Virginia — Over 46.5 total points (-115)
✅ Advantages
The bet wins if both teams combine for 47 or more points.
A few scoring drives, turnovers leading to short fields, or special-teams scores could help.
You don't need either team to win; only the combined score matters.
⚠️ Risks
A slow first half or conservative offensive game plan could leave the total short.
Red-zone failures and missed field goals can be costly.
If one offense struggles to sustain drives, the other team may need to carry most of the scoring.
Verdict: 🟡 Moderate risk. The line is attainable, but I’d want to see recent scoring form and defensive performance before calling it a strong pick.
2. 🟥 Massachusetts +14.5 vs. Connecticut (-110)
✅ Advantages
Massachusetts can lose by as many as 14 points and still cover.
A large spread gives the underdog some protection if Connecticut wins comfortably but not decisively.
The market has UMass around +13.5 to +14.5, so your line is within the current range. ￼
⚠️ Risks
If Connecticut controls the game early and scores consistently, the margin could exceed 14 points.
UMass needs to remain competitive for four quarters; a late scoring run could break the spread.
A spread is not the same as picking the winner: UMass can lose the game and still cash, but it cannot lose by 15 or more.
Verdict: 🟡 Moderate risk. The cushion makes this more appealing than taking Massachusetts to win outright.
3. 🐺 NC State moneyline vs. Stanford (-260)
✅ Advantages
NC State only needs to win; there is no spread to cover.
Current market odds also favor NC State, broadly in the -239 to -282 range. 
At -260, the implied win probability is about 72.2%.
⚠️ Risks
NC State has several players listed out, according to the latest injury report. ￼
Stanford is playing at home, which adds uncertainty.
A favorite can still lose, and the moneyline price offers limited value if the game is closer than expected.
Verdict: 🟡 Moderate risk. NC State is the logical favorite, but the price isn't a guarantee.

text:
In 1998, Warren Buffett gave a 1-hour masterclass on how to never lose money investing.

Here are the 22 most valuable lessons from his lecture:

1. You only have to get rich once. If you have $100 million and can make 10% unleveraged or 20% leveraged, the difference between $110 million and $120 million at year-end means nothing to your life, your family, or anything. But the downside, especially with other people's money, is disgrace, humiliation, and facing the friends whose money you lost. The equation never makes sense.

2. To make money they did not need, they risked money they did have and needed. That is just plain foolish, Buffett says, regardless of your IQ. If you hand him a gun with a million chambers and one bullet and offer him any sum to put it to his temple and pull once, he will not do it. There is nothing on the upside that justifies the downside. People do this financially all the time without thinking.

3. The smartest people in finance went broke, and that is the most fascinating story Buffett knows. Long-term Capital Management had 16 people with possibly the highest average IQ of any business in the country, 350 to 400 combined years of experience, and most of their own net worth in the firm. They still went bankrupt. Buffett says if he ever wrote a book, it would be called why smart people do dumb things.

4. Beta and sigmas tell you nothing about the real risk of going broke. The LTCM team relied heavily on mathematics and believed a six- or seven-sigma event could not touch them. They were wrong. History does not tell you the probabilities of future financial events. The real risk is not volatility. It is a permanent, irreversible blind spot in something crucial, often caused by knowing a great deal about something else.

5. Invest only in businesses you can understand. That one rule narrows the field by about 90%, and that is fine. Buffett can understand Coca-Cola. he cannot value an internet company, and he says if a student handed him a valuation of one on a final exam, he would flunk them. People thought Enron was incredible because it had a good track record, but almost nobody understood how it made money. That was the signal to avoid it.

6. You want a business that is a castle with a wide moat around it. Inside the castle, you want an honest, able, hard-working duke. The moat can be low cost, like Geico in auto insurance, or brand, or patents, or location. But a wonderful castle will always be attacked, so the job of every manager Buffett owns is one thing: widen the moat. Throw crocodiles and sharks into it to keep competitors out.

7. Moats change slowly and invisibly, but they change. Thirty years ago, Kodak's moat was as wide as Coca-Cola's. They had share of mind; the little yellow box meant best in everyone's head. Then they let Fuji into the Olympics and narrowed their own moat. Coca-Cola's moat, by contrast, is wider now than 30 years ago. Every time infrastructure gets built in a country that is not yet profitable, the moat widens a little. You cannot see it day by day, but in 10 years, the difference is enormous.

8. Share of mind beats share of market. When you say Disney, every person in the room has something in their head. Say Universal Pictures or 20th Century Fox, and you have nothing. A mother with two kids will pick the $17.95 Disney video over the $16.95 alternative because she knows it will be fine and does not want to preview ten videos to decide. That little bit of certainty in the customer's mind is worth a fortune.

9. The best businesses have pricing power and require little capital. see's candy sold 16 million pounds at $1.95 when Buffett bought it for $25 million. The entire thesis was whether the price could go to $2.25 without hurting sales. It could, because nobody wants to hand their valentine a box of candy and say, "This year I took the low bid." Today, See's makes $60 million on the same formulas and still takes almost no capital. Compare that to GM, which had to reinvest every dollar into better factories and whose stock barely moved over 50 years.

10. The best businesses earn a royalty on other people's capital. Coca-Cola sells a formula and collects a royalty on every drink. American Express takes a few percent of every dollar you spend. You put up the capital, they take a cut. Low capital intensity is one of the most underrated qualities in a business and one of the surest paths to durable wealth.

11. Define your circle of competence and stay inside it. The size of the circle does not matter. Staying inside, it does. If you know which 30 companies out of thousands you actually understand, you are fine. Buffett understood H.H. brown shoes and Frank Rooney, so he closed that deal in five minutes. If you do not know enough to understand a business instantly, you will not understand it in a month either.

12. Ignore the macro entirely. Buffett has never bought or skipped a business because of a feeling about interest rates, the economy, or any macro forecast. If Alan Greenspan and Bob Rubin both whispered exactly what they would do for the next 12 months, it would not change what he pays for anything. You want to focus on what is important and knowable. The macro is important but not knowable, so you ignore it.

13. Inactivity is the strategy, not a flaw. Wall Street makes money on activity. You make money on inactivity. A broker is like a doctor paid by how often he changes your pills. If everyone in a room trades their portfolio with everyone else every day, they all end up broke, and the intermediary keeps the money. Buffett looks for one good idea a year and rides it to its full potential. He measures Berkshire by how little turnover there is, like a church where the same people fill the seats every Sunday.

14. If you understand businesses, diversification is a mistake. For the 99% who will not evaluate businesses, Buffett recommends a low-cost index fund and extreme diversification. But if you bring real intensity to evaluating companies, owning more than six is a terrible idea. Very few people got rich on their seventh best idea. A lot of people got rich on their best one. Buffett keeps about half his money in what he likes best.

15. Buffett's biggest mistakes are mistakes of omission, not commission. The times he understood a business well enough to act and instead sat there sucking his thumb. He passed on healthcare stocks during the Clinton plan and on Fannie Mae in the mid-eighties, each a multi-billion-dollar miss. Accounting never captures these. The $2,000 he put into a Sinclair service station as a young man, money he lost, has an opportunity cost of about $6 billion today.

16. Focus on what will happen, not when. Coca-Cola went public in 1919 at $40 a share and dropped to $19 within a year. There was always a reason not to buy: the great depression, world war, sugar rationing, thermonuclear weapons. But one share bought then and reinvested would be worth about $5 million. If you are right about the business, you will make a lot of money. The timing is the tricky part, so do not focus on it.

17. When hiring, look for integrity, intelligence, and energy. But if the person lacks the first one, you actually want them dumb and lazy. Because a person with intelligence and energy but no integrity will destroy you. Buffett borrowed this from Pete Kiewit. The trait everyone screens for last is the one that matters most.

18. Here is a thought experiment Buffett gives students. Imagine you could own 10% of one classmate for the rest of their life. You would not pick the highest IQ or the best grades. You would pick the person you respond to best, the one who is generous, honest, gives credit to others, and has leadership qualities. Now imagine you also had to short one classmate. You would pick the egotistical, greedy, slightly dishonest one. The qualities that decide both are not talent. They are character.

19. Every quality on the admirable side is achievable, and every quality on the repellent side is removable. The things that make you want to own 10% of someone are not the ability to throw a football or run fast; they are behavior, temperament, and character, all of which anyone can choose. Buffett's point: you already own 100% of yourself, so you might as well become the person worth betting on.

20. The chains of habit are too light to be felt until they are too heavy to be broken. Buffett sees people in their forties and fifties trapped by self-destructive patterns they can no longer change. At a young age, you can choose any habits you want. Ben Franklin and Ben Graham both did exactly this, looking at people they admired and simply deciding to behave like them. There was nothing impossible about it.

21. Take a job you would take if you were already independently wealthy. Buffett told a 28-year-old at Harvard who wanted a consulting job "to look good on his resume" that it was like saving up sex for your old age. There comes a time to just start doing what you love. Buffett offered to work for Ben Graham for free, was told he was overpriced, and kept pestering him for years. Take the job you would jump out of bed for. You cannot miss.

22. You won the ovarian lottery, and that should shape how you think. Buffett imagines a genie 24 hours before your birth letting you design the world's rules, with one catch: you do not know which of 5.8 billion balls you will draw. Born here or in Afghanistan, with an IQ of 130 or 70, male or female, able-bodied or not. If you could put your ball back and draw one of 100 random others, most people would not, because they are already in the luckiest 1%. Buffett knows he is perfectly wired for a market economy that pays him like crazy, while an equally good citizen leading scout troops and teaching Sunday school is not, purely by luck.

text:
From time to time, it is wise to ask yourself, “What is this frenzied pursuit that I’m on?”

Think about it: Where in your day-to-day life are you not encouraged to chase something? More money, a better body, a bigger home, supercharged productivity, enhanced attractiveness, and endless optimization. It seems innocuous, but perhaps that is only because the vast majority of people have not challenged it.

It seems and feels as though this state of being is birthed from a diminished perspective of how you see yourself.

Ancient wisdom and modern research may explain why.

There is a story of a temple that kept a great Buddha that appeared to be made of clay. Long ago, when an army was marching toward the village, the monks covered their most precious statue in plaster and mud so the invaders would pass it by. The temple was spared, but the monks who knew the secret did not survive, and for generations the Buddha sat plain and unremarkable. Then one day, as the statue was being moved, it slipped and cracked. That night a young monk came to check on it and saw a faint light glowing through the break. He picked up a chisel and began to chip away.

Beneath the clay, the Buddha was solid gold. It had been gold all along.

Modern science offers its own glimpse of the gold. In studies by psychologist Kiley Hamlin, babies as young as six months watched a puppet try to climb a hill while one character helped it and another pushed it down. Asked to choose, the babies overwhelmingly reached for the helper (Hamlin et al., 2007).

Before language, before culture, before anyone taught them, they leaned toward goodness.

One story ancient, one study modern, and both point to the same quiet truth. The belief that we are insufficient, that we are somehow lacking at our core, is the clay, not the statue. Yet we spend our lives chasing, as if wholeness must be built from scratch, when all along it was only buried.

The gold is already there. The work is not to add more, but to clear away what was never you.

References:

Hamlin, J. K., Wynn, K., & Bloom, P. (2007). Social evaluation by preverbal infants. Nature, 450(7169), 557–559.

text:
The Redeemer Who Brings His People Home

One of the most remarkable promises in Jeremiah is that the Lord’s work of gathering Israel would one day become so great that it would overshadow even the memory of the Exodus. After centuries in which Israel remembered the Lord’s deliverance from Egypt, the Lord declared:

“Therefore, behold, the days come, saith the Lord, that it shall no more be said, The Lord liveth, that brought up the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt; “But, The Lord liveth, that brought up the children of Israel from the land of the north, and from all the lands whither he had driven them: and I will bring them again into their land that I gave unto their fathers” (Jeremiah 16:14–15).

The Exodus was Israel’s defining story of deliverance. God had broken the power of their oppressors, led them out of bondage, and brought them into a covenant relationship with Him. Yet Jeremiah foresaw a future deliverance so significant that it would become another defining witness of the Lord’s power to save. Israel would be scattered among the nations, but the scattering would not be the end of the story. God would gather His people again.

This promise was not simply about returning people to a particular piece of land. The Lord’s purpose was to restore His people to Himself. Earlier, He had declared, “Return, ye backsliding children, saith the Lord; for I am married unto you: and I will take you one of a city, and two of a family, and I will bring you to Zion” (Jeremiah 3:14). The language is intimate. The Lord speaks as one who has been betrayed but has not abandoned His covenant people. He seeks their return because He desires a relationship with them.

That is the deeper purpose of the gathering of Israel in our day. As President Russell M. Nelson has taught, the gathering is the most important work taking place on earth. But its importance rests on more than bringing people into the Church or increasing the number of disciples. It is part of Heavenly Father’s work to bring His children to Jesus Christ and offer them the blessings of the covenant He established with Abraham. “The Gathering of Scattered Israel” (October 2006).

Elder Quentin L. Cook explained in “Safely Gathered Home” (April 2023) that the gathering is part of our Heavenly Father’s plan to bring His children safely home. Through the restored gospel, priesthood authority, sacred ordinances, and covenants, God offers His children a way to return to His presence. The gathering is therefore inseparable from the plan of salvation and the redeeming mission of Jesus Christ.

Jeremiah’s prophecy also reaches beyond those who are physically alive. The Lord declared that He would send “many fishers” and “many hunters” to find scattered Israel and bring them back (Jeremiah 16:16). In its original setting, this language described the Lord’s determination to locate and recover a scattered people. In our day, it also evokes the worldwide effort to share the gospel with those who have not yet received it. Missionaries and members invite people to come unto Christ, exercise faith in Him, repent, be baptized, and enter into covenants with God.

Yet the gathering would remain incomplete if it concerned only those who have the opportunity to hear the gospel during mortality. Millions have lived and died without receiving the restored gospel or its saving ordinances. The Lord’s desire to gather His children does not end at the grave. Through temple and family history work, we participate in extending the blessings of Jesus Christ’s Atonement to those who have died. They are not forced to accept the gospel, but they can receive the ordinances they were unable to receive in mortality and choose whether to embrace the blessings offered through Christ.

This is one reason the gathering of Israel is so closely connected to temple work. The temple points us toward the ultimate purpose of gathering: to bind God’s family together through sacred covenants and bring His children into the blessings made possible by the Savior. The work reaches in both directions, toward those who need to hear the gospel now and toward ancestors who lived before these blessings were available to them. In both cases, the answer is Jesus Christ. No one is redeemed by genealogy, missionary effort, or ordinances considered apart from Him. We are redeemed through His infinite Atonement, and the Lord has provided a covenant path through which His children can receive its blessings.

Jeremiah ends his prophecy with a striking declaration from the nations: “Surely our fathers have inherited lies, vanity, and things wherein there is no profit” (Jeremiah 16:19). The people recognize the inadequacy of what they once trusted and turn toward the Lord. Their gathering includes a recovery of truth, a recognition of who God is and where salvation can be found. The Lord promises, “They shall know that my name is The Lord” (Jeremiah 16:21).

The same spiritual recovery lies at the heart of our work today. We invite people to discover that Jesus Christ lives, that His Church has been restored, and that His Atonement offers forgiveness, healing, and eternal life. We help the living and the dead receive the blessings of His gospel because every soul matters to Him. As we share the gospel, minister to those around us, perform temple ordinances, and seek out our ancestors, we participate in the fulfillment of Jeremiah’s promise.

The gathering is not ultimately about numbers, records, or even the building of temples. It is about people, Heavenly Father’s children, each of whom has infinite worth and the opportunity to come unto Christ. The Lord who once led Israel out of Egypt has not ceased to deliver His people. Through Jesus Christ, He continues to free us from sin, restore us to His covenant, and lead us toward His presence. The gathering of Israel is the work of bringing His children home.

text:
RIP Sister Mary Benedict Chung, R.S.M. (born Rona Chung, 1932, Troy, Trelawny – d. Oct 2026). #Jamaican Roman Catholic nun, educator, and social worker renowned for her long service in central Kingston.

Of Chinese-Jamaican parentage (daughter of Frank Chung and Beryl, née Lai), she boarded at Mount Saint Joseph High School in Mandeville from age eleven. The Sisters of Mercy’s work among the poor, particularly at Alpha Boys’ School, inspired her vocation. Despite her father’s scepticism that she “won’t last an hour,” she entered the Sisters of Mercy on 2 Feb 1948 at age sixteen.

An honours graduate of St Joseph’s Teachers College, she taught at Alpha Boys’ and Girls’ schools before becoming principal of Holy Family Primary (All-Age) School on Laws Street in central Kingston, serving that community for more than fifty years. In the 1970s, amid political gang violence that prevented children from attending school, she mediated a truce between rival factions (whose leaders’ children were among her pupils). Then-Prime Minister Michael Manley later credited her with a “great breakthrough.” The gangs requested a bakery in return; this became a lasting community enterprise.

After Hurricane Gilbert in 1988, she founded the Laws Street Trade Training Centre and relocated there to live among those she served. The centre offered vocational training (initially sewing, later baking, catering, and other skills) that reached thousands, some of whom advanced to professional roles. Its bakery, employing local people, provided the principal steady income. Fortnightly it distributed grocery and toiletry packages to roughly 400 indigent residents, supported by local firms. Chung also served on the board of Food for the Poor.

Awarded the Commander of the Order of Distinction (CD) and widely called the “queen of Central Kingston,” she continued her work into her nineties, marking her seventy-fifth anniversary as a Sister of Mercy in 2023. Her ministry combined education, peacemaking, and practical charity for the poor of inner-city Kingston. #Jamaica #Caribbean

My prediction: Indiana 24, Michigan 20.

   I expect a tight, physical game. Indiana enters 6–1 and favored by about a touchdown, while Michigan gets the home crowd and a fresh start with Tommy Carr at quarterback. 

   The deciding matchup for me is Carr against Indiana’s defense. Carr offers some hope, but Indiana’s ability to generate pressure and interceptions makes this a tough first start. I think Michigan hangs around into the fourth quarter before one stalled drive makes the difference.

   Michigan’s path to the upset: protect Carr, avoid obvious passing downs, and manufacture a short field on defense or special teams. If Michigan wins the turnover battle by two, I could see that score flipping.

   *I give Michigan roughly a 35% chance to win—a real opportunity, but I lean Indiana.

A better sentiment headline. Persistent inflation worries underneath.

Today’s final University of Michigan consumer sentiment index came in at 48.0, revised up from October’s preliminary 46.3. Compared with September’s 48.1, sentiment was almost unchanged.

Meanwhile, year-ahead inflation expectations rose to 4.7% from 4.6%. Longer-run expectations increased to 3.5% from 3.4%. Both rose for a second consecutive month.

Our read: the upward sentiment revision offers some relief, but households still see pressure on purchasing power. That combination keeps the Federal Reserve’s growth-versus-inflation trade-off in focus.

For gold, Bitcoin and equities, the next question is how this feeds into interest-rate expectations and actual consumer spending.

What we’re watching: whether household inflation expectations ease, and whether spending holds up despite weak confidence.

text:
I agree. Aunt Jemimah was worth a ton of money, and had a huge following. I always chose products with her on the label above others. 

I don't know, maybe I am atypical, but my mom informed my choices in my values. She spent her teen years in a Jewish ghetto in Düsseldorf Germany watching the Nazis come to power, she loathed racism, and passed those beliefs on to us. 

When I was in my early teens we owned a small grocery in Laurel, Mississippi, this was during the civil rights era. One day the head of the Klan in Mississippi showed up at our store, I watched my mother take a broom to him chasing him out of our store. 

But more important I saw her treat every single other person who came to our store with respect. She offered store credit, but unlike every other store in town she charged no interest no matter the color of your skin. If she heard you were sick like as not she was coming by with Jewish penicillin (chicken noodle soup) and groceries, especially if you had kids. And color made no difference, most of those trips to drop off soup and groceries I accompanied her. There was a race riot a few weeks after she chased off that Klukker, and every store along the tracks was looted and burned out, except ours, those neighbors she took care of took care of her.

text:
There's a lot of not understanding going on in these replies I think. 

Another NC quarterback worth bringing into this conversation is Faizon Brandon from Grimsley in Greensboro.

ECU identified him early enough to be his FIRST scholarship offer, according to Joel’s own reporting. NC State, UNC, Charlotte, Duke and NC A&T also offered. NC State made his final four alongside Tennessee, Alabama and LSU, but Tennessee ultimately won. No in-state program landed him.

That matters because identifying a talented local quarterback and convincing him to stay home are two different challenges. ECU recognized Brandon’s talent early and still couldn’t land him.

Brandon then won Tennessee’s starting job as a true freshman this season. He has since been replaced by George MacIntyre after struggling and dealing with a shoulder injury. MacIntyre started the Arkansas and Alabama wins. That doesn’t close the book on Brandon’s potential - it shows how much development can still be ahead of even a five-star quarterback.

Meanwhile, Atkinson took a different path through Mercer and is now producing at Oregon State.

Recruiting is an art, not a science with an exact formula for predicting every kid’s future. Using the lower divisions and the portal - kids write their own future nowadays regardless of D1 recruiting.

text:
For those who think that universal healthcare or Medicare for all is the way to go, please read the following. Canada has what your asking for and it isn't a good thing.
This was a friend's experience.
Most of you know I spent 4 days in the hospital in Nova Scotia Canada and I wanted to share my experience with Universal Healthcare.
📷 an ambulance with two very nice paramedics met me on my cruise ship and escorted me to the hospital.  We entered into a very long hallway where there were approximately 25 other patients in gurneys waiting to be seen by an emergency room doctor. I thanked the paramedics for getting me to the ER as I assumed they would be dropping me off and be on to their next call! That’s how we do it in the USA anyway.  They politely explained to me that they would not be leaving my side until I was actually seen by a doctor, which could take several hours as they might be needed to administer any life saving measures in the meantime.  They explained that healthcare is “free” in Canada to Canadian Citizens and that they can’t recruit doctors to work for them due to the high taxes and the low pay.  They told me to prepare for a long night.  Okay…… I started to realize I wasn’t in Kansas anymore.
It was a cold and rainy night and it was absolutely freezing in that hallway. I’m so sick and miserable being strapped in that gurney.  The hallways were crowded with us 25 + patients and at least 50 paramedics all staying with their patients.  To pass the time, the paramedics spent most of their time laughing and visiting with the other paramedics.  The lead paramedic was looking over my medical chart from the ship doctor and saw that he suggested I needed a CT scan.  He looked at me and said “I just want to prepare you that you may not get a CT scan for 2 or 3 days!”  2 or 3 days? WTH! At that point I pulled out my phone to see how far away I was from the nearest U.S. hospital…. 8 hours by car! I didn’t think I could do it and I felt stuck.
At  3 a.m. I am finally seen by a doctor and was told they would be admitting me.  They take me to my room and I’m so thankful to be off that gurney!  I look around the small room and I don’t see a bathroom.  I know the nearest bathroom is a long ways down the hallway and I don’t think I can make it by walking.  I call the nurse for a wheelchair when she tells me if it’s an emergency I can use the one in the room.  She opens up a cabinet and pulls out a toilet.  Are you kidding me? Well when you gotta go…. Sitting there with absolutely no privacy some random guy walks in my room!  Ugh! Poor guy! 📷
The next morning the doctor told me I needed to see a Urologist and he was at another hospital so I would need to be transferred there.  Thank you God! I’m getting out of this 3rd world excuse for a hospital.
The outside of the building looks decent, maybe things are looking up!  As I’m being taken to the 7th floor I’m paying close attention.  The hallways are filled with cardboard boxes, random equipment and supplies and appears to be mostly used as storage.  I pass several patient rooms and I can see that each small room has 4 patients in each one, divided by 4 curtains.  My heart sinks.
As they take me to my room my attendant told me I was in luck and I would have a private room since I had insurance and was a “paying customer” Whew!  I look around the small room and see a bathroom!  Oh yay! 📷📷
They also inform me “DO NOT” drink the water, don’t brush your teeth with it and don’t shower in it.  I look in my bathroom and sure enough the shower parts  were pulled out of the wall.  Right now I could care less about a shower!
At this point things are becoming a blur.  I only had to wait a couple of days for my CT scan and was able to get to the operating room to get a stent put in that the Urologist says I needed right away. As I’m wheeled to the operating room, the sheet I’m sitting on falls partially on the floor and when I get there, I look down and see the white sheet is absolutely filthy dirty.  I don’t know how often they mop those floors, but it’s obviously not often.  Do I really want them doing anything to me?  Doesn’t seem very sterile. The interior of the hospital is in disrepair.  Drywall falling off the walls, broken tiles, and filthy dirty!
Get back to my room and it’s pleasant enough, at least I have a window!  There is not a T.V. and no internet, so the days were very long. Luckily a nice nurse brought in a recliner so Ed was able to stay with me in my room.  Good thing as there were very few hotel rooms available and they were in the $700 a night range!
The food was fair, and you were able to order from a menu.  The breakfast menu didn’t offer any eggs or meat.  French toast it is, served cold of course! The next morning I ordered a “high protein” banana smoothie, should be safe.  Wrong!  I don’t know what was in that 4 ounce smoothie, but I wasn’t trying it!
The nurses were nice enough, they didn’t bother you very much.  I usually saw them twice per day, during shift changes.  On day 3, I really need a bath and my linens changed.  I asked a nurse for help.  Lucky me, since I didn’t have an open wound, I could have a shower!  Yay me!  She led me down the hallway and opened what looked like a closet door.  She handed me a small plastic container that contained a couple of dingy, tattered wash cloths and a towel the size of a standard kitchen towel.  All well, I’ll take it.
My last day a cleaning lady came to “clean” my room.  I don’t know why she even bothered.  She didn’t empty the trash, which was a large container that was more than halfway full.  Had to be there long before I came in.  What really shocked me was the Haz Mat container.  The container was not enclosed and was full of used syringes, bloody equipment, etc.  I just about barfed every time I walked by it.
I am thankful for the care I received. The doctors seemed knowledgeable and I did get better.  They did not seem in a hurry to discharge me and I’m assuming that was partly due to my ability to pay.  I feel really sorry for the Canadian’s that have to deal with this.  We were told that a lot of them travel to the U.S. for their healthcare.  I can see why.
I also realize that we need some reform with our American healthcare, but trust me, Universal Healthcare run by red taped government bureaucrats is not the way to go!  I’m amazed by the number of Americans who want this!  Sounds good until you actually have to live it!  I’m so thankful that I’m not a Canadian, because I would probably still be there!
The next time I visit our Montrose Regional Hospital I’m going to kiss the walls!/Nina David/Farmington New Mexico

text:
this a fun scenario.  I was talking to a builder on one of their 3 million plus custom home build listings in North Carolina.  

because it's new construction, we can do a Forward commitment and buy the rate down outside of closings on a block of funds, and buy down into the low 5's. 

The scenario started with putting  down 25%, and the client wanting to put an offer in under list price. 

in this case, im going to use an example number of 5%. 

So with a forward commitment, the builder would keep the price the same, but use the concession toward buying the rate down.

The payment is substantially lower obviously with the lower rate. 
 
What was fun about it, is that even when you drop the down payment to 20% down, the payment at the lower rate is still lower than the scenario with putting down 25% and the discounted price. 

in this scenario that 5% difference in down payment kept over 100k extra in their pocket. 

and the client started talking about the multi family deal they were simultaneously working on and could use the extra funds to go towards that. 

if you want so see the full breakdown on the numbers, let me know, and i will send you the breakdown.

Environmental Health Tracking Data Updates

EHD Map Survey

We're collecting your feedback to improve the EHD Map Version 3.0 before it's finalized. You can submit comments through our online survey. The survey is open until October 31, 2026.

The EHD map is an interactive tool that shows where people in Washington are likely to have been exposed to the greatest harm from environmental impacts on their health.

We also encourage users to check out our updated resources and materials for the EHD Map Version 3.0.

EHD Map users can now access the materials in 10 languages, including English. If you have feedback on any EHD Map resources or materials, please share it in our online survey.

Do you have questions about the EHD map?

The WTN team hosts EHD Map Office Hours. During these office hours, we’ll show how to navigate the map, interpret data, apply it to your work, and address specific technical issues. Anyone with questions about the EHD map can drop in! We’re offering 2 sessions this November:

▪︎ Session 1: Occurs monthly every third Wednesday (9 a.m. – 10 a.m.) via Zoom

▪︎ Starting in December, we’ll offer one session a month every third Wednesday from 9 – 10 a.m. 

For questions or additional information, please email us at: EHDMap@doh.wa.gov

☆ Tribal Updates on the EHD Map
Centennial Accords 2026

In winter 2026, the Washington Tracking Network (WTN) and our partners released draft updates to the Environmental Health Disparities (EHD) Map Version 3.0. In addition to showing where people are most likely impacted by environmental justice, the EHD map also shows areas where Tribal lands are within census tracts. According to the HEAL Act and other environmental laws, areas with greater impacts are supposed to be prioritized through engagement and resources.

The map builds on previous Tribal and community engagement. This includes listening sessions and roundtables held from 2023 to 2026. We also participate in Tribal forums, such as the Centennial Accords, and anticipate increased offerings for Native communities.

WTN makes updates according to available data, capacity, and science, in addition to community and Tribal engagement. We do comprehensive reviews every 3 years. We plan to incorporate feedback beginning in winter 2027.

We are interested in further developing the map or discussing environmental and climate priorities with Tribal and Native community partners. If you are interested in learning more, please consider a demonstration, workshop, or partnership. We also encourage you to leave comments about the EHD Map in our online survey, if you prefer that method.

https://t.co/Leg6vkJDzz

For questions, please reach out to Tribal Social Justice Strategist, Pah-tu Pitt (Pah-tu.Pitt@doh.wa.gov).
