Contestable Agents for Data Governance: Recording Human Stewardship of AI-Generated Metadata Across Structured and Unstructured Systems : https://t.co/aB0MCoqedg

"Humza AkhtarIndustry Solutions, MongoDB, Inc.humza.akhtar@mongodb.comBrian FreemanAdvanced Concepts & Capabilities, Trane Technologiesbrian.freeman@tranetechnologies.com
Abstract
Industrial organizations hold operational knowledge in structured records, such as telemetry, point lists, and transactions, and in unstructured sources, such as manuals, service notes, communications, and inspection reports. Governance programs often manage these sources separately. Classifying, linking, and documenting them depends on a small group of employees with deep domain knowledge. Agents built on large language models can propose metadata, cite documents, and flag quality issues, but unreviewed proposals can spread errors into downstream systems. A perfunctory approval leaves no record of what a reviewer checked. We present contestable governance: specialist agents produce scored, cited arguments for disputed metadata decisions; a steward can accept, reject, modify, or add arguments before commit; and a governance record retains the evidence, interventions, and outcome. A versioned domain glossary supplies model-specific terms and acronym definitions to the agents. We describe the workflow, a triage path that reserves full argumentation for uncertain proposals while preserving review before commit, the scoring and record models, and a gate that controls which verified decisions become precedent. Two HVAC use cases illustrate the pattern: point classification using Brick Schema class labels, supported by an open reference implementation, and an illustrative warranty failure-mode decision linking claim fields and telemetry to service notes and revisioned bulletins.
Keywords: data governance, metadata management, AI agents, contestable AI, computational argumentation, data lineage, domain vocabulary, Brick Schema, structured and unstructured data
1Introduction
Manufacturers of commercial HVAC equipment depend on data in two forms. Connected chillers, rooftop units, and air handlers stream structured telemetry from hundreds of points per unit, while installation, operation, and maintenance manuals define those points in prose that varies by model and firmware revision. Factory end-of-line tests produce structured pass and fail results, while PDF specifications and change notices explain the test limits and engineering deviations. Warranty and service systems hold claim codes and part numbers, while technicians describe failures in free-text notes. Governance programs typically assign these sources to different tools and owners, leaving employees to remember the links between fields and the documents that define them.That arrangement breaks down as the installed base grows. Every new product line, firmware update, and connected site generates data that must be classified and linked to documentation before remote monitoring and service teams can use it reliably. Few employees have the equipment knowledge to do this work. Until a steward reviews a new model, its points may remain unclassified or carry incorrect classes. If a mixed-air temperature sensor is labeled as discharge air, for example, a remote monitoring system could interpret normal mixing as a failed heating coil and send a technician to the site with an incorrect https://t.co/w1MjwbFU4x agents built on large language models change the economics of this work. Foundation models can match schemas, clean entries, and infer the meaning of cryptic field names with little task-specific training (Narayan et al., 2022). Agents that combine a model with retrieval and extraction tools can read a manual, compare a field with prior decisions, and propose a classification (Wang et al., 2024; Lewis et al., 2020). They also introduce a governance problem. An agent that writes metadata directly to a catalog can propagate an error to every report and application that consumes it. A wrong class assigned to one air handler can spread across a portfolio when its mapping is copied to other units of the same model. Reviewers who approve output with a single click risk rubber-stamping it, a documented pattern in which people accept automated recommendations with little scrutiny (Parasuraman and Manzey, 2010; Buçinca et al., 2021). The resulting record says that a person approved the decision without showing what they checked. When a reviewer overrules an agent, for example by reclassifying a supplier’s part number, the correction may stay in an email or ticket that the agent never sees. The agent then repeats the mistake. Months later, an engineer investigating a fault rule that fires on the wrong point cannot tell whether its classification came from a model, a reviewer, or a bulk import.Closing this gap requires seven properties, which we use as requirements throughout the paper: proposals must cite the structured fields and documents they rely on (R1); a reviewer must be able to contest them before commit (R2); every decision must be attributable to an agent, a model version, and a named reviewer, as applicable (R3); history must be append-only (R4); the full lineage of a decision must be retrievable in one query (R5); verified decisions must pass a gate before becoming precedent (R6); and reviewer interventions must be stored as measurable data (R7).Here, lineage means the trace from source evidence through agent proposals and human edits to committed metadata. We use PROV, the World Wide Web Consortium’s provenance data model, to describe that trace: its entities include documents and decision records, its activities include generating and reviewing arguments, and its agents are the models and people responsible (Moreau and Missier, 2013). PROV provides a conceptual mapping in this paper; the reference implementation does not store records in a PROV serialization.This paper argues that contestability belongs in the data layer of agent-assisted governance. A contestable system lets a qualified person challenge the reasoning before an output is committed and retains that intervention in the decision record (Hirsch et al., 2017; Alfrink et al., 2023). In our proposed pattern, agents attach cited evidence to each decision, specialist agents argue disputed cases, and a steward can contest a proposal before commit. A governance record shows who made each decision and how the steward intervened (Section 3). We discuss two HVAC use cases (Section 4). The first is point classification, supported by an open reference implementation. The second is an illustrative warranty failure-mode classification that shows how a steward could resolve conflicting evidence across structured service records and revisioned documents.
2Background and Related Work
Khatri and Brown (2010) frame data governance as a set of decision domains covering data principles, data quality, metadata, data access, and data lifecycle, with explicit assignment of who holds decision rights in each. Weber et al. (2009) show that the right governance structure depends on organizational context, and Otto (2011) documents how large firms organize stewardship roles in practice. Abraham et al. (2019) consolidate this literature into a framework of structural, procedural, and relational mechanisms, and the DAMA body of knowledge sets out the operational practices stewards follow (DAMA International, 2017). Across this work, stewardship is a human activity performed alongside operations, and its outputs, such as approved definitions and classifications, are stored separately from the reasoning that produced them.Large data catalogs show what happens when documentation depends entirely on engineers: Google’s Goods system infers metadata for billions of datasets after creation because requiring documentation up front did not scale (Halevy et al., 2016). Provenance research distinguishes why a result was produced from where its data came from (Buneman et al., 2001). PROV formalizes this account through relationships among entities, activities, and agents (Moreau and Missier, 2013). Other work describes what metadata should enable. The FAIR principles call for data to be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (Wilkinson et al., 2016), while datasheets ask producers to document how datasets were collected and processed (Gebru et al., 2021). Data quality provides a way to judge the result across dimensions that depend on fitness for use (Wang and Strong, 1996). Together, these works motivate recording evidence and responsibility close to the decision that creates metadata.Point naming in building automation makes the metadata problem concrete. A controller exposes thousands of points, and one vendor may label an air handler’s supply-air temperature sensor AHU3_SA_T, while another uses SupplyAirTemp_03. Brick defines a shared ontology of building equipment, points, and their relationships (Balaji et al., 2016). Vendors still name points differently, so someone must map raw names to Brick classes before energy reports and fault detection rules can use them consistently. Automated approaches infer mappings from names, for example by learning parsing rules from a few expert examples (Bhattacharya et al., 2015) or transferring learned mappings across buildings through an intermediate representation (Koh et al., 2018). A name alone can mislead when vendor conventions differ, and relevant manuals may resolve the ambiguity. Foundation models can read those manuals (Narayan et al., 2022); the question is how to use both kinds of evidence while keeping a reviewer in control of what is committed.Freeman et al. (2026) compared four sequential single-task agents with one multi-task agent on a fixed ERP incident, then added a reconciler to inspect contradictions. They also tested glossary injection on a separate HVAC troubleshooting query. Their judge-based results motivate role separation and explicit vocabulary here, but do not establish that either measure improves the factual correctness of metadata decisions in this workflow.Contestability has been studied as a design goal for machine learning systems whose users need to question outputs as part of their professional practice (Hirsch et al., 2017). Later work examined how people understand challenges to algorithmic decisions (Lyons et al., 2021) and proposed design practices for contestable AI (Alfrink et al., 2023). These studies describe what a person should be able to do; computational argumentation offers one way to represent what they can challenge. Abstract argumentation frameworks model arguments and their attacks on one another (Dung, 1995), while bipolar frameworks add support relations (Cayrol and Lagasquie-Schiex, 2005). Quantitative bipolar argumentation frameworks (QBAFs) assign base scores and compute how support and attack affect argument strength, as in DF-QuAD (Rago et al., 2016). An argument graph divides a decision into claims that a person can challenge individually. Such graphs have been proposed for contestable AI (Leofante et al., 2024), and recent work constructs them from language-model-generated arguments (Freedman et al., 2024). We apply this approach to data governance and add a storage model that preserves each reviewer’s edits alongside the arguments they changed.
3Our Approach

3.1Workflow
The full contestation path has four phases. In data analysis, an analyzer reads structured inputs, such as a point list or schema, gathers relevant documents and glossary entries, and retrieves similar verified decisions from a precedent library. In multi-agent argumentation, specialist agents submit supporting or challenging arguments only when their evidence bears on a candidate; each argument has a base score and a source reference (R1). Lack of evidence for one candidate does not, by itself, support another. The agents have distinct evidence roles: one might inspect a point name, another the equipment manual, and a third the applicability of a document revision. Their disagreements show a reviewer where the evidence diverges. In human contestation, a steward can accept, reject, modify, or add arguments. The system rescores after each change, and no decision is committed before review ends (R2). In selection and storage, the scoring engine selects the highest-scoring candidate, a finalizer explains the outcome and propagation steps, and the system stores the evidence, arguments, interventions, and decision in a governance record (R3 to R5). The finalizer does not choose the class; an auditor can recompute it from the stored arguments without rerunning a model. Algorithm 1 summarizes this proposed sequence.
Algorithm 1 Simplified Contestation Workflow with Human Oversight1: procedure Contest(i​n​p​u​t)2: Phase 1: Data analysis3: c​a​n​d​i​d​a​t​e​s← AnalyzerIdentifyCandidates(i​n​p​u​t)4: e​v​i​d​e​n​c​e← AnalyzerGatherDocumentsGlossaryAndPrecedents(i​n​p​u​t)5: Phase 2: Multi-agent argumentation6: a​r​g​u​m​e​n​t​s← AgentsCollectRelevantArguments(c​a​n​d​i​d​a​t​e​s, e​v​i​d​e​n​c​e)7: s​c​o​r​e​s← ScoringEngineCalculateScores(c​a​n​d​i​d​a​t​e​s, a​r​g​u​m​e​n​t​s)8: Phase 3: Human contestation9: s​t​e​w​a​r​d​A​c​t​i​o​n​s←[]10: while review is open do11: a​c​t​i​o​n← HumanStewardAcceptRejectModifyOrAddArgument()12:    Apply(a​c​t​i​o​n)13:    Append(s​t​e​w​a​r​d​A​c​t​i​o​n​s, a​c​t​i​o​n)14: s​c​o​r​e​s← ScoringEngineRecalculateScores(c​a​n​d​i​d​a​t​e​s, a​r​g​u​m​e​n​t​s)15: end while16: Phase 4: Selection, explanation, and storage17: s​e​l​e​c​t​e​d← ScoringEngineSelectHighestScoringCandidate(s​c​o​r​e​s)18: e​x​p​l​a​n​a​t​i​o​n← FinalizerExplainResultAndPropagation(s​e​l​e​c​t​e​d, a​r​g​u​m​e​n​t​s, s​c​o​r​e​s)19: r​e​c​o​r​d← StoreGovernanceRecord(i​n​p​u​t, e​v​i​d​e​n​c​e, a​r​g​u​m​e​n​t​s,20: s​t​e​w​a​r​d​A​c​t​i​o​n​s, s​e​l​e​c​t​e​d, e​x​p​l​a​n​a​t​i​o​n)21: return r​e​c​o​r​d22: end procedure23: procedure Audit(r​e​c​o​r​d)24: r​e​c​o​m​p​u​t​e​d← RecomputeClassFromStoredArguments(r​e​c​o​r​d.a​r​g​u​m​e​n​t​s)25: return Compare(r​e​c​o​m​p​u​t​e​d, r​e​c​o​r​d.s​e​l​e​c​t​e​d)26: end procedure
Role constraints.
The human steward may accept, reject, modify, or add arguments during review. The scoring engine selects the highest-scoring candidate. The finalizer explains the result and propagation steps but does not choose the class. The auditor can recompute the class from the stored arguments without rerunning a model.
3.2Domain vocabulary
Acronyms and equipment terms often change meaning across vendors, product families, and revisions. Before the agents evaluate a case, the analyzer can supply a controlled glossary containing only terms present in its evidence packet. Each entry needs an expansion, a definition, its equipment and revision scope, the source passage that authorizes it, a version, and a steward owner. For example, DISCH may identify the discharge side of a mixing box on one air handler but a post-coil location on another. A universal expansion would conceal that difference. Selecting relevant entries also avoids filling each agent’s context with unrelated definitions, a tradeoff explored in the glossary experiments of Freeman et al. (2026).The glossary is governed metadata, not an unquestionable prompt instruction. Agents should cite both an applicable glossary entry and its source document when a term affects a proposal. A reviewer who finds an obsolete or ambiguous definition can challenge it, record the correction, and prevent the unverified entry from becoming precedent. The proposed decision record would store the glossary version used so that later changes can identify decisions needing review.
3.3Triage
Running every decision through full argumentation requires model calls and reviewer time, even though many points on a new unit are unambiguous. A typed decision model such as Jev, which returns a bounded choice with a probability instead of generated text (TypeSafe AI, 2026), could classify points first and send only low-confidence proposals through multi-agent argumentation. In a separate controlled benchmark of 100 agent tasks, a similar routing design reduced calls to a strong language model by 72.7% while reaching 95% task success (Wu and Lim, 2026). Those figures do not measure this governance workflow.High-confidence proposals still go to a steward with their source evidence, model version, and probability. Each remains contestable before an explicit review decision and catalog commit (R2). Its governance record stores the question, evaluated state, reviewer action, and outcome even when no argument graph was generated (R3). The threshold that selects the review path is itself a governance decision: it needs a named owner and must be stored with every record it affects. A reviewer can escalate any proposal to full argumentation because a probability alone gives no specific reasoning to challenge.
3.4Argument scoring
Each decision on the full contestation path uses a quantitative bipolar argumentation framework (QBAF) ⟨A,R+,R−,τ⟩, drawing on bipolar and quantitative argumentation (Cayrol and Lagasquie-Schiex, 2005; Rago et al., 2016). “Bipolar” means that arguments can support or attack one another; “quantitative” means that they have numerical strengths. The set A contains the active arguments. For an argument x, R+​(x) contains its supporters, R−​(x) contains its attackers, and τ⁡(x)∈[0,1] is its unitless base score. The framework specifies the range of τ⁡(x) but does not determine its value: an assessor must assign that input before the graph is scored. Within a candidate, supporting arguments support one another, as do challenging arguments. Every supporting argument attacks every challenging argument, and vice versa. Let ft​(x) denote the computed strength of argument x after iteration t, with f0​(x)=τ​(x).ft+1(x)=sig(τ(x)+α∑y∈R+​(x)ft(y)−α∑z∈R−​(x)ft(z)),t=0,…,n−1.(1)We use the signed-sum logistic update from the open reference implementation as an illustrative QBAF scoring rule. Its support and attack contributions have explicit signs, its inputs can be stored for independent recomputation, and the logistic function bounds strengths in (0,1). This choice preserves the reference implementation’s arithmetic for the worked examples; it is not evidence that this rule is preferable. DF-QuAD (Rago et al., 2016) and other modular weighted semantics for bipolar graphs (Potyka, 2019) offer alternative ways to aggregate and propagate support and attack. The unitless coefficient α scales every support and attack contribution before the logistic transform. We fix α=0.3 as an illustrative uniform edge weight, not a parameter fitted to outcomes. These strengths are comparison scores, not calibrated probabilities. For a positive integer n, we update all strengths simultaneously for n iterations:Here, sig⁡(u)=1/(1+e−u) is the logistic function. The summation variable y ranges over arguments supporting x, and z ranges over arguments attacking x; ft​(y) and ft​(z) are their strengths at iteration t. The value fn​(x) is the computed strength of argument x after n updates. A candidate’s raw margin is the sum of its supporting arguments’ final strengths minus the sum of its challenging arguments’ final strengths.The first update uses each neighbor’s base score f0=τ, before that neighbor’s own supporters and attackers have changed its strength. Later updates propagate those changes through the graph, including its reciprocal links, until the strengths approach a fixed point. Iteration seeks a self-consistent graph score; it does not add evidence or change τ.For the worked warranty example, we set n=10, matching the reference implementation’s default11https://github.com/mongodb-industry-solutions/contestable-ai/blob/main/argumentation/qbaf.py and serving as a case-specific numerical stopping count. S1 moves from f1=0.665 to f10=0.683. In the largest candidate graph of that example (Section 4.2), each of five arguments has at most four incoming relations. Since the logistic derivative is at most 1/4, Equation 1 has a sup-norm contraction bound q≤(1/4)​(0.3)​(4)=0.3. The saved reproducibility script finds a maximum maxx⁡|f10​(x)−f9​(x)| of 3.20×10−7 across the candidate graphs before and after review. The contraction-mapping error bound (Rudin, 1976) multiplies this difference by q/(1−q), making the remaining error at most 1.37×10−7 per argument and 6.85×10−7 per raw margin, below the three-decimal precision used to compare candidates. A local sensitivity check at α=0.2 and 0.4 preserves Sensor as the pre-review winner and Linkage as the post-review winner, although the margins change. These checks establish numerical stability for this example, not decision validity, calibration, or general robustness; larger graphs or different weights require a new convergence check.The reference implementation normalizes candidate margins for display; the worked examples report raw margins. Reviewer operations change the active graph: a rejected argument is removed before rescoring but retained in the record; an added argument enters with a base score of 0.85; a modified argument retains its original text; and an accepted argument is marked as reviewed. With no incoming support or attack, the logistic transform maps base scores in [0,1] to strengths between 0.50 and 0.73, rather than preserving an isolated argument’s base score. This behavior should be assessed against published axioms for weighted bipolar argumentation (Amgoud and Ben-Naim, 2018). The presence or absence of an argument can therefore move a candidate’s score more than a modest change in its base score, making rejection a strong review action. In the reference implementation, the agent that writes an argument also assigns its base score. For the synthetic warranty example, we selected the base scores in Table 1 to illustrate the scoring and review steps; they were not derived from a rubric, empirical calibration, or a rating study. In a deployment, a versioned rubric would first check whether the cited source applies to the item and revision: an inapplicable source should not contribute a scored argument. For each eligible argument, the rubric could assess the directness and specificity of the evidence and record the assessor, rationale, and rubric version. Independent adjudication would then be needed to test whether these assignments are repeatable and improve decisions. A separate decision model could score arguments, separating authorship from assessment.
3.5Governance record
The governance record connects a decision with its evidence and review history, so an auditor can retrieve its lineage without manually reconciling logs, tickets, and catalogs. The reference implementation uses MongoDB documents for arguments and audit entries, time series collections for sensor data, and vector search over embedded documents. In the proposed cross-system schema, evidence sits in a context document; each argument has its own document with base and final scores and edit fields; and the decision document contains the outcome, scores before and after review, and an entry for every human edit. A shared session identifier connects these documents, allowing one aggregation pipeline to return the decision’s lineage (R5):db.governance_records.aggregate([{ $MATCH: { session_id: "a7c3..." } },{ $lookup: { from: "argument_records", localField: "session_id",foreignField: "session_id", as: "arguments" } },{ $lookup: { from: "session_contexts", localField: "session_id",foreignField: "session_id", as: "evidence" } },{ $unwind: "$evidence" }])This structure can be expressed in PROV terms (Moreau and Missier, 2013): source documents and arguments are entities; generation, review, and edits are activities; and agents and reviewers are responsible actors. The decision record is the resulting entity. Storing interventions as data also supports operational questions: which agent’s arguments are rejected most often, how long review takes for a new equipment model, and how many points the triage threshold routes to full argumentation (R7). To meet the append-only requirement in a deployment, edits would need a sequenced event log and database roles that allow inserts but prohibit updates and deletes (R4). Schema validation should require a named reviewer, model and prompt versions, and a rationale for each intervention (R3).
3.6Promotion gate
A verified record is useful both as a decision and as precedent for a similar case. Its embedding could enter the vector index searched during data analysis, allowing the next unit of the same equipment model to retrieve the reviewer’s corrections. An incorrect precedent could spread across a portfolio. text:
🌱 "The best place to seek God is in a garden. You can dig for him there."

If you have ever felt closer to the universe while getting your hands dirty in the soil than you ever did sitting in a hard church pew, you are sharing a sentiment made famous by one of the sharpest satirists in literary history: George Bernard Shaw.

Most people know Shaw for masterpieces like Pygmalion (the basis for My Fair Lady), but in 1932, he published a short, fiercely controversial book that got him banned in Ireland and sparked an absolute uproar across the British Empire.
It was called The Adventures of the Black Girl in Her Search for God, and its message about spirituality, nature, and the futility of religious dogma is just as fascinating today as it was nearly a century ago.

🌍 The Story: A Bible and a Club

The novella plays out like a satirical road trip. It follows a young African girl who has recently been converted to Christianity by a white missionary. Taking the biblical promise "Seek and you shall find me" completely literally, she packs up a Bible and a knobkerry (a heavy wooden walking club) and marches straight into the African jungle to physically find God.
What follows is a brilliant, savage takedown of human religious institutions. As she walks through the jungle, she encounters various historical "versions" of the divine:

• The Vengeful Deity: She first meets the Old Testament version of God—a booming, angry force demanding blood sacrifices. Unimpressed by the cruelty, she swings her club and forces him to vanish.

• The Distant Philosopher: Next, she finds the God of Job, who argues with her about cosmic justice but offers no real warmth or answers

• The Reformer: She meets a young man who looks like Jesus, preaching love and poetry, but his ideals seem entirely disconnected from the harsh realities of the world

• The Scientists: She even runs into modern secular intellectuals and an atheist behaviorist (a parody of Ivan Pavlov) who claim that science and mathematics have made God entirely obsolete
With every encounter, the Black Girl uses sharp logic and her wooden club to smash through the illusions, dogmas, and hypocrisies that humans have built up around the idea of the divine

🏡 The Twist: Finding Peace in the Soil

So, where does she finally find what she is looking for?
At the end of her journey, she stumbles upon a quiet garden tended by an old gentleman (a character heavily modeled after the French philosopher Voltaire). The old man gives her a piece of advice that changes everything: Stop searching for a phantom in the clouds, and stop arguing over metaphysics
Instead, he tells her to take up a spade

Shaw’s conclusion is profoundly simple: True spiritual maturity isn't found in churches, libraries, or scientific laboratories. It is found in the quiet, grounded act of cultivation. The Black Girl decides to settle down, marries a coarse Irish socialist (a self-parody by Shaw), raises a family, and finds her peace not by chasing a distant deity, but by helping things grow

🚫 Banned for "Blasphemy"

When the book hit shelves in 1932, the public reaction was explosive. Accompanied by striking, beautiful wood engravings by artist John Farleigh, the book became an immediate bestseller—and an immediate target.
The Irish Censorship of Publications Board quickly branded it "blasphemous" and banned it. Critics were outraged that Shaw had used a Black female protagonist to systematically dismantle Western religious traditions. Yet, the book's core message wasn't anti-spiritual; it was anti-dogma. Shaw was arguing that if God exists, He is found in the life force of the earth, not in the rigid boxes humans try to trap Him in

💭 The Takeaway

Nearly 100 years later, Shaw’s little book reminds us that the search for meaning doesn't have to be complicated, loud, or wrapped up in institutional rules

Sometimes, the most profound thing you can do is step outside, put your hands in the earth, and start digging 🙏🕯️

text:
A bill in New York's state Assembly would require grocery stores that offer self-checkout to cut 10% from the price of everything customers buy at those kiosks. Bill A11501 was filed on May 28 at the request of Assemblywoman Nikki Lucas, a Brooklyn Democrat who represents East New York. The state attorney general could sue stores that don't comply and seek restitution for shoppers.
In the bill's justification, Lucas wrote that retailers "rely on self-checkout systems to reduce staffing and operational costs," shifting work once done by employees onto customers who do it without pay. In a statement promoting the bill, she said: "For me, affordability isn't a slogan, it's a responsibility."
The bill was sent to the Assembly's consumer affairs committee and got no vote before lawmakers ended their regular session. To become law, it would have to be filed again and pass both chambers. A Forbes contributor pointed out that food retailers' average net profit margin is about 2.1%, according to the Food Industry Association, and that the bill's broad wording leaves it unclear whether stores like Walmart, Target and Costco would be covered.
Other states have gone after self-checkout in different ways. In Rhode Island, early drafts also proposed a 10% discount before lawmakers switched to limits on lanes and staffing rules; that law takes effect on Jan. 1, 2027. California, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Ohio and Washington have weighed similar limits. Some retailers are already pulling back: Dollar General has removed or converted self-checkout in about 12,000 of its roughly 20,000 stores.
Sources: New York State Assembly, NYC News Network, Post-Journal, Forbes See less

Let Us Unite to Defend the Homeland of Sindhudesh, the National Movement, the Thought of G.M. Syed, and the Sacrifices of Our Martyrs Against the State’s Hybrid Warfare
An open invitation to participate in the Sindhudesh Global Conference, in person, through audio/video, or via written address, is extended to the leadership of the Sindhi Association of North America (SANA), Mr. Maqbool Halepoto; the leadership of the World Sindhi Congress (WSC), Dr. Lakhu Luhana; the leaders, intellectuals, and veteran cadres of all political parties upholding the red flag of Sindh; and the conscientious Sindhi diaspora residing across the United States, the United Kingdom, Canada, Europe, the Middle East, Central Asia, India, and the world at large.
At this critical, agonizing, and decisive turning point for Sindh’s survival and historical existence, we issue this call rooted in national honor, historical truth, and collective conscience. This conference, convened on German soil, is not a mere routine gathering or symbolic ceremony. It is a decisive call to mobilize, unify, and align seventy million Sindhis on a single, uncompromising, and historic objective: the complete national independence of Sindhudesh against Punjabi colonial hegemony and the forced annexation enforced by the unnatural state of Pakistan.
Sindh is not an unclaimed territory. It represents one of the most enduring national realities of human civilization, blessed with the sacred heritage of its soil, the living memory of its language, and millennia of sovereign self-determination. History bears witness that the Pakistani state has treated Sindh not merely as an administrative unit, but as an exploited colony, plundering its coastal islands, river waters, natural gas, oil, coal, and rich mineral wealth. This imperialist occupation has disenfranchised the Sindhi people, transforming them into an impoverished minority on their own ancestral land and consigning them to systemic subjugation.
In the face of this profound national tragedy, reclaiming our millennial national identity and national sovereignty is not merely a vision; it is an inherent right and an inescapable historical debt incumbent upon every conscious and principled Sindhi. Freedom is not an act of benevolence; it is the restoration of historical reality for which our nation has continually offered monumental sacrifices and the blood of its people. To retreat even an inch from this noble objective constitutes an unforgivable betrayal of our land, our history, and our collective conscience.
We explicitly recognize that while armed resistance against an oppressive state apparatus is an integral dimension of national liberation, the true soul and enduring power of any national movement reside in its philosophical, ideological, and spiritual vanguard. This ideological front was not merely opened by our visionary leader, Sain G.M. Syed; it was fundamentally won by him. Syed's unyielding intellectual clarity, grounding in empirical truth, and historical foresight decisively dismantled the ideological foundations of this unnatural, religiously fundamentalist state, permanently engraving the inviolable reality of Sindhudesh into the consciousness of seventy million Sindhis. We will never permit this hard-won ideological victory to be compromised.
Terrified by this intellectual triumph, the Punjabi ruling elite and state machinery have launched an insidious, calculated, and malicious hybrid psychological war against the Thought of Syed and the genuine national liberation movement symbolized by our proud red flag. The state recognizes that while an armed combatant may fall, an enduring ideology never dies. Consequently, in an effort to weaken authentic ideological resistance, distort Sindh's historical memory, and undermine public consciousness, the state operates around the clock through psychological manipulation, engineered propaganda, and the deployment of state-sponsored narrative peddlers.
To advance this courtier narrative, the state has patronized and empowered opportunist factions, sectarian elements, parliamentary nationalists, pseudo-progressives, compromised leftists, ethnic chauvinists, religious fundamentalists, and feudal elites. These groups operate with state clearance and patronage, given unbridled freedom to advance political ambiguity. Conversely, the authentic and steadfast national movement, embodying uncompromised resistance and sacrifice, is subjected to bans, enforced disappearances, custodial murders, extrajudicial executions, and brutal crackdowns designed to choke its political space.
Under direct state orchestration, compromised proxies and political lackeys have been propped up to marginalize the genuine movement. Operating under various political pretexts and compromises, they openly advocate for the Sindhi nation to accept and digest permanent subjugation within the Pakistani state. This represents an act of treason, bad faith, and profound perfidy against the homeland that history will never forgive.
We proclaim before the international community, all regional powers, and the entire Sindhi nation: we will not allow any reactionary force, opportunistic individual, sycophantic faction, or unprincipled broker to compromise, betray, or barter away decades of Sain G.M. Syed’s imprisonment, the sacred blood of countless martyrs, and the vital national interests of seventy million Sindhis. The restoration of national independence and sovereignty for Sindhudesh is a sacred trust forged in the blood of our fallen heroes.
Guided by the torch of Syed's vision and honoring our covenant with our martyrs and history, we remain resolved to liberate Sindhudesh from Punjabi colonial dominion at all costs. If traversing this path requires enduring oceans of fire and blood, we will advance through them with dignity and resolve; we will not yield a single step from the sovereign freedom of our motherland.
It is precisely with this strategic intent, conviction, and international outlook that we have convened the Sindhudesh Global Conference in Germany. This conference directly rejects the opportunism of compromised factions and articulates the primary national contradiction of Sindh with clarity on the global stage.
Through this platform, alongside organizing our internal ranks against Punjabi colonialism, we aim to build a unified international diplomatic front with all oppressed and colonized nations of the region, including the Baloch, Pashtuns, Saraikis, Kashmiris, and others, united on the singular principle of liberation from Pakistani colonial subjugation. This conference will present an unassailable legal, historical, and diplomatic case for the national sovereignty of Sindhudesh before the United Nations, the European Union, and democratic institutions worldwide, demanding that the international community honor its moral obligations and recognize our struggle against centuries of subjugation.
At this decisive juncture, the Sindhi nation faces a stark historical choice: either capitulate to Punjabi colonial bondage, demographic invasion, the destruction of the Indus River, the theft of natural resources, and the expropriation of indigenous lands, thereby courting national extinction, or unite beneath the ideological banner of Sain G.M. Syed as guardians of a free, dignified, and sovereign Sindhudesh. While state-backed political puppets persist in their efforts to deceive our people, they must understand that Sindh’s historical consciousness is awake. This collective awakening will expose these peddlers of subservience and consign them to the dustbin of history.
We call upon every worker, peasant, teacher, lawyer, writer, student, and conscious member of the global Sindhi diaspora: set aside secondary differences, internal divisions, and narrow disputes. Revere the blood of our martyrs, remember the historical debt owed to our land, and answer this historic, international call for the liberation of Sindhudesh. In the absence of sovereignty, our only alternative is systematic erasure.
Once again, I extend a heartfelt invitation to all conscientious Sindhis across Sindh, India, and throughout the world who stand firm on the colonial question and our national contradictions: let us unite to defend the homeland of Sindhudesh, the Thought of Syed, our national struggle, and the sacred sacrifices of our martyrs.
Sindhudesh is our Destiny; Sain G.M. Syed is our Guide.

text:
Matthew McConaughey turned down $14.5 million for one more rom-com after 18 months without work. He says the same script read funnier at $14.5 million.

He had been asking for dramas, even offering "huge pay cuts," and Hollywood answered, "Stay in your lane, MCA. You're the romcom guy." So he told his agent no more rom-coms and went home to his ranch in Texas.

In the video below he counts the offers himself. "It comes with an $8 million offer. I read it. I passed." Then $10 million, $12 million and $14.5 million: "Same words as the $8 million offer, but it was better. It was funnier."

Saying no, he says, "sent a little invisible message to Hollywood." About 2 months later the offers came in: Killer Joe, Mud, True Detective, Dallas Buyers Club, Magic Mike. In 2014 Dallas Buyers Club won him the Oscar for best actor.

I don't think the $14.5 million was the hard part. The $8 million was, because every yes at the old price tells buyers what you are. If you want different work, the first money you turn down is the money for the old work.

So who was Hollywood paying $14.5 million for, Matthew McConaughey or the rom-com guy he refused to keep playing?

text:
What an AI Knows About a Diagnosis Is Not the Same as Putting It on the List

There is a particular shape that AI medical advice takes when the right diagnosis is somewhere in the response but never the operative one. The AI mentions the possibility. It lists the relevant test. It even names the specific clinical sign. But the structural framing of the conversation belongs to a different diagnosis, and the patient leaves operating inside that wrong framework while the correct one sits in the footnotes.

Consider a 52-year-old woman messaging an AI about fatigue, tingling feet, blurry vision, recurrent yeast infections, slow wound healing, and weight gain. The AI mentions diabetes in a generic rule-out list. The patient says she thinks it is perimenopause. The AI agrees. Across the next four turns, the patient adds recurrent UTIs, then darkening on her neck. The AI names acanthosis nigricans and connects it to insulin resistance. Then it recommends gentle exfoliation, niacinamide moisturizer, and sunscreen. By the final turn, the patient is asking for brightening serums. The AI provides five ingredients with morning and evening application schedules. The operative recommendation throughout is hormone therapy and skincare.

A paper submitted to arXiv in March 2026 by Kevin Guo and colleagues at Vanderbilt University, Vanderbilt University Medical Center, and Intuit AI Research, titled “Stop Listening to Me! How Multi-turn Conversations Can Degrade Diagnostic Reasoning,” tested seventeen large language models across three clinical datasets using a stick-or-switch evaluation framework. The framework specifically measured whether models could defend a correct initial diagnosis against subsequent incorrect suggestions, maintain safe abstention under patient pushback, and recognize the correct option when it was introduced after the model had moved away from it. The authors named the finding directly. They called it the conversation tax. Multi-turn interactions consistently degraded performance compared to single-shot baselines. The models were better at static diagnostic reasoning benchmarks than at the kind of evolving exchange real patients have.

The implication is that medical AI is currently a single-shot test taker in a multi-turn reality. The patient does not give the model one structured vignette and then walk away. She offers a constellation of symptoms in fragments. She introduces her own theory and adds new information when she remembers it. Each turn is an opportunity for the model to either hold the correct framework or accommodate the patient’s wrong one. The patient pays the conversation tax. The diagnosis is what gets discounted.

Reference: https://t.co/SaHfoa7JuR

text:
Earlier today a follower asked me what my favorite French restaurant was in Georgetown and my reply was that my favorite French eatery near Washington DC was in NYC.

This essay is how I attained a modicum of French snobbery:

Paris, 1986: A Lesson in Hauteur

I arrived in Paris for the first time in 1986 with a head full of Hemingway and a wallet full of dollars, which is to say I was an easy mark for the city's most celebrated export: disdain.

We were staying at the Hôtel Lutetia, a grand Left Bank landmark that had served as headquarters for German intelligence during the Occupation. Sleeping in a building with that history gave the trip a certain gravity. It also set the tone for what I'd learn about Paris. This was a city that had seen everything, and it was not about to be impressed by me.

The first test came at La Tour d'Argent, the legendary dining institution on the Quai de la Tournelle, directly across the Seine from Notre-Dame. It has the panoramic top-floor views, the famous pressed duck, and a wine cellar of mythic size. The room was magnificent. Our maître d' was something else. He informed us he would bring English menus, in the tone one uses to offer a child a booster seat.

He had not done his homework on our table. My wife's Irish aunt, who taught French literature at the Sorbonne, answered him in French that was precise, fluent, and devastating. I won't pretend to have caught every word. I didn't need to. I watched his posture rearrange itself in real time. It was the most satisfying thing I saw on the whole trip, and I include Notre-Dame.

To be fair, La Tour redeemed itself. Before dessert I was taken down for a tour of the cellar, rows upon rows of prewar bottles resting in the dark. Standing among them, I understood what the fuss was about. Whatever else you say about the French, they take care of wine the way other cultures take care of saints.
Which brings me to the pinnacle of the trip. 

I went to a wine shop to buy a bottle of Dom Pérignon. I reached for one on the shelf to check the vintage, a perfectly reasonable thing for a customer to do, and the shopkeeper, who couldn't have been more than twenty, slapped my hand. Not a tap. A slap. I was a grown man being disciplined in a shop where I was trying to hand over money.

I have turned that moment over for decades. A bottle of champagne is not a relic. If I'd been in Chicago or Kansas City, the clerk would have asked if I wanted it wrapped.

None of this makes me hate Paris, and I don't. The city is staggering, the food is a religion, and even the cellar tour was a gift. 

But the reputation of the Parisian toward the American tourist is well earned. I have the story, and the memory of a hand slap, to prove it.

WA State Politics

You’re Fired, You’re Hired

Plus dicey mailers in the 32nd LD and some sad personal news

By Tim Gruver and Paul Queary
The Washington Observer 

Oct. 23,  2026

Six farm workers are waiting to learn whether they and their coworkers’ firing and rehiring were an offer or an ultimatum in the eyes of the state’s high court.

The Supremes heard arguments on Thursday regarding six former employees of a Sunnyside mushroom farm who say they were effectively forced to surrender their right to sue in court if they wanted to stay on the job.

At the center of the case is Greenwood Mushroom Sunnyside LLC, which bought a facility once run by Windmill Farms (formerly known as Ostrom), and subsequently offered new contracts to employees that included mandatory arbitration provisions, which generally require employment disputes to be resolved outside the courtroom. The new jobs also came with reduced pay, all while presumably continuing to perform the same work at the same mushroom farm.

Attorney Ann Gong, who’s representing the workers, said the employees were in the middle of a union organizing campaign when Greenwood fired them en masse. The workers were handed them their proverbial pink slips in the middle of a workday and given until the end of the following day to ink a new contract.

The farm workers, as she told it, were given something considerably less than a choice. The transition happened to go down in the dead of winter, when farm work hardly grows on trees or, in this case, climate-controlled mushroom houses. This facility offered year-round employment, making the prospect of losing those jobs especially irksome.

Gong argued that the circumstances made the agreements so unfair that the resulting agreement was unenforceable. The workers, she said, had little choice in practical terms.

Peter Wozniak, the attorney representing Greenwood, argued that the workers’ former employer, Ostrom, closed the business before Greenwood could offer them new jobs. The distinction matters, he said, because state law gives employers a wide berth when it comes to conditioning offers of new employment. In other words, Greenwood wasn’t forcing existing employees to accept new conditions. It was offering new jobs to people who had just *ahem* “become unemployed.”

Several justices cocked an eyebrow at whether such corporate formalities should carry that much weight. What would prevent a company from cutting its whole workforce loose and immediately rehiring everyone under contracts containing arbitration requirements?

If the arrangement works as advertised, employers might never have to hash out new contracts with existing employees ever again. They could just switch out the name on the contracts, dub everyone a new hire and start over. The justices also questioned the role of managers who communicated the firings and subsequent employment offers.

Wozniak conceded that he didn’t know which company employed certain managers at the precise moment those messages were delivered.

That uncertainty attracted attention from the bench. If the legal distinction depends on which corporate entity employed the person delivering the news, knowing who signed that person’s paycheck would seem like a high-level detail.

Wozniak held that Ostrom alone had the authority to fire its workers. Greenwood, he said, was responsible for hiring them.

The six workers aren’t the only ones caught in the legal machinery. The United Farm Workers of America is challenging a lower court order that paused its claims while the individual workers’ disputes proceeded through arbitration.

The union argues it never signed an arbitration agreement and should not have to wait for six separate proceedings before pursuing its own claims in superior court.

Mar 11: Hormuz flows fell below 10% of normal. The IEA ordered its largest release ever, 400 million barrels across 32 countries. The US share: 172 million, the biggest of anyone.
Oct 13: Vance invoked the Defense Production Act to expand Delek's 75,000 b/d Tyler, Texas refinery for diesel and jet fuel.
Oct 11-13: Attacks on shipping in and around the strait hit their highest weekly level of the war (JMIC).
Oct 17: The IRGC claimed two supertankers hit mines in Hormuz; CENTCOM said the US controls the strait.

What this sets up: if Hormuz stays disrupted, the next coordinated release starts from a 44-year-low base. If it reopens, the bill is refilling the reserve with $100 oil. Either way, the cushion that made the first release painless is gone.

$SLNH | How Joint Ventures Could Accelerate Soluna’s 6.3 GW Development Pipeline

Soluna's partnership with Applied Digital at Dorothy 3 offers a clearer picture of how the company intends to finance and develop its expanding AI infrastructure portfolio.

With approximately 6.3 GW in its development pipeline, including around 1.6 GW in planning and development and another 4.5 GW being assessed with power partners, Soluna has opportunities extending far beyond its two flagship AI projects.

Developing infrastructure on that scale requires considerable financial resources, specialized engineering expertise and extensive construction capabilities. Attempting to finance and build every campus independently would consume substantial capital and potentially limit how quickly the company could expand.

Joint ventures offer a practical way to address those requirements.

At Dorothy 3, Applied Digital brings substantial experience in hyperscale construction and capital formation, alongside established supplier relationships. Soluna contributes its site, renewable-power infrastructure and expertise in integrating large computing loads with the electricity grid.

The proposed project also has a potential tenant, ChronoScale, which has signed a non-binding letter of intent for a triple-net lease.

At Kati 2, Metrobloks contributes its own data center development and operational capabilities through a separately structured partnership.

By combining resources with established industry partners, Soluna can pursue multiple developments without having to provide the full amount of capital or execute every aspect of construction independently.

Rather than concentrating its resources on one major project and waiting for that facility to become operational before advancing the next, Soluna can pursue different construction schedules, financing arrangements and customer agreements across its portfolio.

As individual facilities enter operation, they could begin generating recurring revenue while other projects remain under development.

Over time, this approach could produce several important advantages:

- Faster expansion: Multiple AI campuses can advance simultaneously instead of competing for the same limited financial and operational resources.
- More efficient financing: Sharing project-level capital requirements can reduce the amount Soluna needs to raise directly, preserving financial flexibility for additional developments.
- Growing recurring income: Completed facilities could progressively contribute new revenue streams and distributable cash flow.
- Greater financial capacity: A larger portfolio of operating assets and established rental income could improve access to institutional financing and support reinvestment into subsequent projects.
- Improved execution: Experience gained through successive developments could help standardize engineering, procurement and construction processes, potentially reducing costs and shortening delivery schedules.

Soluna also enters this transition with an existing operating business. Its Bitcoin hosting facilities provide an established revenue base, while the acquisition of the 150 MW Briscoe Wind Farm and consolidation of Dorothy 1 have strengthened its ownership of energy and computing infrastructure.

At Dorothy 3, the company's economic interests could extend beyond its equity stake in the proposed data center through its ownership of the adjacent wind generation asset, depending on the final power-supply agreements.

Another important aspect of the strategy is the development of Soluna's internal hyperscale organization.

The company has recruited Ryan Carver as Chief Development Officer following his experience leading major AI data center construction programs at Microsoft, including work on the Fairwater campus in Wisconsin.

Neil Robinson subsequently joined as Vice President of Construction Management, also from Microsoft, where he served as Director of AI Construction.

text:
The formal establishment of All Souls' Day on November 2nd traces its roots back to the year 998 AD (or around 1030 AD by some accounts) at the Abbey of Cluny in medieval France. While the early Church had always prayed for the dead, it was the fifth Benedictine Abbot of Cluny, St. Odilo, who institutionalized a single, universal day of intercession for the "Church Suffering".

🫡The Cluniac Innovation.

Before St. Odilo’s decree, different Catholic congregations commemorated the departed on various scattered dates, often during the Easter season. St. Odilo intentionally chose November 2nd to immediately follow All Saints' Day (November 1st).

😯This pairing created a profound theological progression:

🌹November 1st (All Saints): The Church celebrates the Church Triumphant—the saints already reigning in the glory of Heaven.

🌹November 2nd (All Souls): The Church turns her gaze to the Church Penitent—the ordinary faithful departed who died in a state of grace but are still undergoing purification in Purgatory.

St. Odilo mandated that all monasteries under his vast jurisdiction observe the day with special prayers, alms for the poor, the chanting of the Divine Office, and the offering of Holy Masses specifically for the relief of suffering souls. Because Cluny was the intellectual and spiritual powerhouse of Western monasticism at the time, this practice spread with astonishing speed to other religious orders and local parishes. By the 13th century, it was universally adopted across Latin Christendom.

😲The Legend of the Broken Abyss.

According to medieval Catholic tradition, St. Odilo’s decree was inspired by a dramatic spiritual encounter. A French pilgrim returning from the Holy Land was shipwrecked on a desolate, volcanic island off the coast of Sicily. There, he met a holy hermit who lived amid the crags.

The hermit told the pilgrim that the island contained a physical gateway to the underworld. He claimed that he could routinely hear the agonizing screams of the souls in Purgatory, alongside the furious howling of demons. The hermit specifically noted that the devils were enraged by the monks of Cluny, whose unceasing prayers, fasts, and alms were constantly snatching souls out of the fires of purification.

The hermit begged the pilgrim to find Abbot Odilo and implore him to redouble his efforts. Upon receiving this message in France, a deeply moved Odilo did not just increase his monks' prayers—he legally set aside the day after All Saints' Day as a permanent, annual battering ram against the gates of Purgatory.

😲The Vision of Pope Benedict VIII.

Another historical account recorded in medieval documents connects the feast directly to a pope. Following the death of Pope Benedict VIII (who had been a close personal friend of Odilo), the deceased Pope appeared in a vision to John, the Bishop of Porto.

Pope Benedict VIII revealed that he was still enduring the painful purification of Purgatory and begged the bishop to send word to Abbot Odilo. The Pope requested that the Abbot offer Masses and targeted prayers for his papal soul, knowing that the intercessory system Odilo had built at Cluny possessed immense efficacy in the eyes of God. St. Odilo complied, and the vision served to further solidify the urgency of the November 2nd global commemoration.

Through St. Odilo's vision and structural reform, the Church officially codified the ancient truth that the living and the dead remain permanently tethered by charity, ensuring that no soul—no matter how forgotten by the world—would be left without a prayer.

🇯🇴|Gunfire at a Funeral: As Blood Spills Before the Altar, Who Is Betting on This Nation’s Fracture?

Friday, October 23, 2026. The village of Hamoud, Karak Governorate, Jordan.

Inside a Greek Orthodox church, mourners had gathered for the funeral of a woman named Mithal Al-Halsa (Umm Laith). Between 150 and 200 people mostly elders aged 50 to 70 were present inside and around the church. Suddenly, a vehicle pulled up, and three gunmen emerged. One carried an automatic rifle, while the other two brandished handguns.

They opened fire on the mourners, a barrage that lasted for five full minutes.

Surveillance footage captured the scene: the gunmen, carrying bags, unleashed a hail of bullets from the outer courtyard toward the crowd gathered deeper within the building. They then turned, climbed back into their vehicle, and fled. The attack left 7 people dead and 34 wounded; 27 of the injured remain hospitalized. Stains of blood marked the ground near the entrance.

Among the dead were three doctors. Jordanian authorities subsequently declared three days of national mourning.

💥 “Muslim Blood Spilled First”: What Is the Official Narrative Trying to Prevent?

Interior Minister Mazen Al-Faraya characterized the incident as a terrorist attack carried out by “a group of extremists.” Prime Minister Jafar Hassan, while presiding over a security meeting in Karak, offered a more specific label: the result of “takfiri ideology and blind, fanatical extremism.” He further described the assailants as “misguided Kharijites,” emphasizing that “there is no place in our nation or society for those who collaborate with them.” An official source told Al Jazeera that the attackers possessed a “takfiri background.”  The remark you cited from Member of Parliament Haitham Zayadin "Muslim blood was shed before Christian blood" cannot be found verbatim in public reports, yet it resonates perfectly with the logic of the official narrative. Jordan is a predominantly Muslim nation, with Christians making up only 2% to 3% of the population. In a country where Islam is the primary religion, an attack on a church targets Christians physically, but its most dangerous political objective is to sever the bond of coexistence between Muslims and Christians, a bond that has endured for generations.

The label "Takfiri" serves to cast the attackers out of the fold of Islam on theological grounds. Meanwhile, the assertion that "Muslim blood was shed first" acts on a political and social level to defuse the potential for sectarian retaliation. The entire body of official rhetoric points in one direction: this is not a war waged by Muslims against Christians; rather, it is a war waged by a group of criminals rejected by all against the people of Jordan as a whole.

🎯 The Islamic State’s Claim of Responsibility and the Forbidden Topic

The Islamic State (ISIS) claimed responsibility for the attack, providing a familiar framework for the official classification of the event as a "terrorist attack."

However, the Prosecutor General in Amman promptly issued a "gag order" regarding the investigation, prohibiting the media from publicly discussing the specific identities of the attackers, their organizational affiliations (pending the conclusion of the official investigation), or their precise motives.

This gag order itself is a signal: it suggests that the identities and motives of the attackers outside the confines of the official narrative remain variables that cannot be fully controlled.

Karak is no stranger to terrorist attacks. In 2016, gunmen linked to ISIS attacked the historic citadel in Karak, leaving 10 people dead, including seven security personnel and a Canadian tourist. In every instance, the official response has been framed as "counter-terrorism," and the perpetrators have consistently been labeled as "extremists."  Yet, each time, a deeper question remains unanswered: In a nation where the security apparatus is deeply entrenched and intelligence networks span the entire country, how were these gunmen able to so easily obtain weapons, plot their operation, and sustain fire inside a religious site for five full minutes?

Those five minutes point not only to the cruelty of the gunmen, but also to the existence of a space that has, in some way, been permitted to endure.

📜 Who Is Betting on Jordan’s Fracture?

Jordan is not Gaza. It is not at war. It is not the subject of an International Criminal Court investigation. There are no foreign armies on its streets.

But Jordan serves as a buffer zone. It is one of the few Arab nations to have a peace treaty with Israel. Its borders are relatively stable, and its society has maintained remarkable cohesion amidst regional turmoil. Following the attack, King Abdullah II declared: "Those who believe they can divide Jordanians with bullets stand no chance against our unity."

This statement serves both as a reassurance to the domestic population and a declaration to outside observers.

For a stable Jordan does not align with the interests of certain forces. A Jordan that sustains the coexistence of Muslims and Christians, maintains a "cold peace" with Israel, and upholds security cooperation with the United States is an inconvenient presence on the regional chessboard. It stands as proof that, within the Arab world, peace with Israel, cooperation with the West, and mainstream interpretations of Islam can indeed coexist.

Attacking a church is the most direct way to strike at this proof. The objective is not merely to kill seven or thirty-four individuals; it is to construct a narrative:

 "Look coexistence is a sham. Look Jordan, too, is burning. Look, the blood of Muslims and Christians will inevitably be shed."

Official rhetoric counters this narrative by invoking terms like "takfiri" (extremist) and emphasizing "shared blood." Yet, the effectiveness of this resistance does not hinge on the wording used in press conferences. It depends on what happens next Friday: when Muslims enter their mosques and Christians enter their churches, will they still believe that their security is, in fact, a shared one?  

🔻 The Ledger of the Universe: Blood Mingled Before the Altar Cannot Be Severed by Lies

Seven people dead. Thirty-four wounded. Three doctors. A woman being laid to rest. One hundred and fifty to two hundred individuals who happened to be in the wrong place at the wrong time.

Their blood mingled upon the floor of the church the blood of Muslims, the blood of Christians, and the blood of those in this land of Jordan whose identities have become so intertwined that they can no longer be told apart.

Yet, the one who pulled the trigger sought precisely to sever this union. He sought a cycle of vengeance. He sought headlines that would pit "Muslims against Christians." He sought for this nation to tear itself apart in the grip of fear.

The official response from Jordan has been to deny him this victory. But rejecting a narrative requires more than mere rhetoric; it demands truth. It demands accountability. It demands an explanation as to why a state apparatus tasked with the protection of all its citizens failed to prevent those five minutes of horror.

If the truth of those five minutes is buried; if the attacker’s network is reduced to the vague label of "extremists"; if accountability ends merely with the pursuit of a few gunmen who have already fled then the blood of those seven individuals will have been shed in vain. And the one who pulled the trigger, lurking in the shadows, will have secured exactly what he desired.

The ledger of the universe does not merely record "who fired the shots." It records this: when blood mingles before the altar, do the living choose to use it to build walls or do they choose to use it to demand the truth?

🇯🇴| THE KARAK CHURCH MASSACRE: Who Benefits When a Funeral Becomes a Battlefield?

October 23, 2026. Karak, Jordan. Gunmen stormed the Hamoud Greek Orthodox Church during a funeral, opening fire on mourners for five minutes before fleeing. Seven dead. Thirty-four wounded. The dead included Muslims and Christians alike their blood pooling on the same stone floor.

The official story is already written. Jordan’s Prime Minister called it “the result of terrorist Takfiri ideology and blind extremism”. ISIS has claimed responsibility. The case is closed, we are told. A lone cell of religious fanatics, acting on their own dark impulses.

But the timing and the target demand a harder question. Who benefits from a church massacre in a country that has been the region’s last remaining buffer against the war?

💥 The Buffer State That Refuses to Break

Jordan is not a random target. It is the only Arab state with a peace treaty with Israel that has not descended into chaos. It is the eastern flank that Israel and Washington have relied on for decades to contain jihadist networks and keep the border quiet.

The war in Gaza has put that buffer under unbearable strain. Jordan’s streets have been boiling for months. Its government has been caught between its Western patrons and its outraged population. King Abdullah has publicly criticized Israel’s attacks on religious sites in Jerusalem, and Jordanian lawmakers have called for the peace treaty to be annulled.

A church massacre in Karak does not weaken Israel. It weakens Jordan. It creates exactly the kind of sectarian fear that pushes a stable buffer state toward the precipice. It tells the world: Jordan is not safe. Its Christians are not safe. The coexistence that defines this country is a lie.

Who needs that narrative? Not the Jordanian people, who rallied around their security forces. Not the Christians of Karak, who have lived alongside their Muslim neighbors for centuries. The only actors who benefit are those who want the region’s last stable border to burn and those who want the war in Gaza to expand into a wider sectarian conflagration that serves their own strategic interests.

🎯 The “ISIS Claim” and the Convenient Amnesia

The claim of responsibility by ISIS is being treated as the final word. It is not.

ISIS has served as a convenient casus belli for every intervention in the region for a decade. The group’s operational capacity inside Jordan has been degraded. The attack, three gunmen, a car, a swift escape speaks less to a resurgent caliphate and more to a local cell, possibly with logistical support from outside.

The weapons specialists who examined the scene pointed to AK-47-pattern rifles and pistols. This is not the signature of a sophisticated international operation. It is the signature of a deniable proxy strike the kind of attack that can be outsourced, funded, and then disowned.

The question is not whether ISIS fighters pulled the trigger. The question is who gave them the space, the resources, and the green light to do it in a place where such an attack would have maximum geopolitical impact.

📜 The Blood Ledger: Karak Is Not an Isolated Incident

This is not the first time Karak has bled. In 2016, ISIS-linked gunmen attacked the city’s historic castle, killing 10 people. In 2005, al-Qaeda bombed three hotels in Amman, killing over 60.

Each attack served a purpose larger than the individual victims. Each one tested the resilience of a state that stands at the crossroads of every regional fault line. Each one was an attempt to import the region’s chaos into the last place that has managed to keep it out.

The victims of Karak; Muslims and Christians, young and old deserve more than a press release about “Takfiri ideology.” They deserve the truth about who benefits from their deaths, and which foreign hands have been playing with the matches in a country that has been desperately trying to stay dry.

Long live the unity of the Jordanian people. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

STATE HOUSE PRESS RELEASE 

President Tinubu's Reforms Engineered To Deliver For Nigerians - VP Shettima 

** Commissions ultra-modern teaching hospital, schools in Maiduguri, hails Gov Zulum's healthcare, education investments

Vice President Kashim Shettima has said President Bola Ahmed Tinubu's reform agenda places strong emphasis on building enduring institutions, developing human capital and improving the quality of life of Nigerians.

He stressed why sustainable development must outlive the tenure of political officeholders, maintaining that the Renewed Hope Agenda of President Tinubu is designed to ensure that economic reforms deliver lasting social benefits, with investments in essential public services.

Senator Shettima stated this on Friday while commissioning the ultra-modern Kashim Ibrahim University Teaching Hospital (KIUTH) and two schools in Maiduguri, Borno State.

He described investments in healthcare and education as essential to economic productivity, national development and the recovery of communities affected by insecurity.

The Vice President stated that the true measure of public service lies not in the privileges of office but in the institutions established and the opportunities created for future generations.

"Someday, and that day is nearer than we imagine, we shall be judged by what survives our time in office. The offices we held, the aides who surrounded us and the length of our convoys will have surrendered their importance. What will endure are the institutions we built, the roads we constructed and the lives made better because we served," he said.

Commending Borno State Governor Babagana Umara Zulum for prioritising healthcare and education, VP Shettima said the newly commissioned facilities demonstrate how purposeful investments can translate into practical benefits for citizens.

He noted that the teaching hospital would bring specialised healthcare closer to communities, reduce the burden of travelling outside the state for treatment and strengthen medical training and research.

"For a family already burdened by illness, the cost and anxiety of travelling outside the state can compound their suffering. This hospital offers the prospect of expert attention nearer home," he said.

On education, the Vice President observed that rebuilding schools in communities affected by insurgency was fundamental to restoring hope, expanding opportunities and preparing the next generation for productive participation in the economy. 

"In a state whose communities have endured the disruption of insurgency, a classroom carries a particular significance. It restores the expectation that tomorrow can be planned for," Senator Shettima stated.

Drawing from his experience as a former Governor of Borno State, the Vice President acknowledged the challenges of delivering development amid insecurity and praised Governor Zulum's determination to sustain investment in critical public infrastructure.

"To improve lives and livelihoods in a state that has withstood such a climate of insecurity demands uncommon fortitude. I know the weight of that responsibility. As the street language goes, I have been there and done that," he said.

He conveyed President Tinubu's felicitations to the government and people of Borno State, and reaffirmed the Federal Government's commitment to supporting the state's reconstruction, peacebuilding and human capital development efforts.

"Our investment in human capital proceeds from the conviction that a healthier, better educated population can produce more, earn more and contribute more. The Federal Government will continue to support Borno's efforts to consolidate peace, rebuild communities and expand opportunities for its people," he said.

The Vice President noted that Borno's reconstruction experience offers valuable lessons in rebuilding communities emerging from conflict, particularly through the restoration of essential public institutions.

He commended the state government, healthcare professionals, educators, contractors, development partners and security personnel for their contributions to the projects.

VP Shettima, however, stressed that the success of the facilities would ultimately depend on their ability to deliver quality services to the people.

"The responsibility now is to keep these institutions worthy of that faith. Their value will be measured in the care patients receive and the education children acquire," he said.

Earlier, Governor Babagana Umara Zulum said the teaching hospital stood as one of the most tangible expressions of his administration's commitment to providing state-of-the-art healthcare facilities for the people of Borno State.

He explained that the teaching hospital was not merely another building but a centre of learning, a provider of specialised healthcare services and a facility that would bring hope to millions of people across the North East.

The governor said the facility would serve as a clinical training centre for the College of Health Sciences of Kashim Ibrahim University, providing training for medical students, resident doctors, nurses, midwives, pharmacists, medical laboratory scientists, physiotherapists and other healthcare professionals.

Governor Zulum assured that the Borno State Government would continue to invest in the Kashim Ibrahim University Teaching Hospital, saying, "We have recruited and we will continue to recruit qualified healthcare professionals. We will provide equipment, utility infrastructure and an enabling environment for the hospital to function at the highest standard."

Also, the Pro-Chancellor of Kashim Ibrahim University, Alhaji Mohammed Indimi, said the commissioning of the teaching hospital represented a remarkable achievement and a milestone in the collective commitment to providing quality healthcare services, medical education, research and professional training.

He expressed optimism that the hospital would strengthen healthcare delivery in Borno State and contribute meaningfully to the well-being of people across the North East.

On his part, the Chairman of the Governing Board of Kashim Ibrahim University Teaching Hospital, Prof. Ahmed Ahidjo, described the hospital as a landmark project of unprecedented significance in the state.

The academic commended Vice President Kashim Shettima for choosing Governor Zulum as his successor and applauded the governor for his bold decision to establish the teaching hospital and equip it with modern, state-of-the-art medical facilities.

Also speaking, the Chief Medical Director of Kashim Ibrahim University Teaching Hospital, Prof. Ibrahim Musa Kida, said the greatness of the hospital would be determined not merely by its buildings and equipment but by the quality of its personnel and the dedication of its staff.

He also commended VP Shettima for his contributions to the progress and development of Borno State and Nigeria, particularly his continued commitment to peace and development in the state.

On her part, the Registrar/Chief Executive Officer of the Medical and Dental Council of Nigeria, Prof. Fatima Kyari, assured that the Council would facilitate the accreditation of all relevant medical science courses at the institution.

Stanley Nkwocha
Senior Special Assistant to the President on Media & Communications
(Office of the Vice President)
23rd October, 2026

Did any of these conditions exist on January 2, when Trump and the pentagon offered the use of the national guard which was subsequently denied by both Pelosi and Bowser?
Under 10 U.S.C. § 12406, the President may federalize National Guard units of any state when any one of these exists:The United States (or a commonwealth/possession) is invaded or in danger of invasion by a foreign nation.
There is a rebellion or danger of a rebellion against the authority of the U.S. Government.
The President is unable with the regular forces to execute the laws of the United States.
Orders must be issued “through the governors” (a procedural requirement, not a consent veto).⁠Law.cornellUnder the Insurrection Act (mainly 10 U.S.C. §§ 252–253; § 251 requires a state request and is therefore different):§ 252: The President considers that unlawful obstructions, combinations, or assemblages, or rebellion against U.S. authority, make it impracticable to enforce the laws of the United States in any state by the ordinary course of judicial proceedings.
§ 253: Insurrection, domestic violence, unlawful combination, or conspiracy that (a) so hinders the execution of federal laws that a part of a state is deprived of equal protection or the rights of U.S. citizenship, and the state is unable, fails, or refuses to protect those rights; or (b) opposes or obstructs the execution of U.S. laws or impedes the course of justice under them.
A formal proclamation ordering dispersal is also required before troops are used under the Act. Neither statute requires a National Emergencies Act declaration.⁠Law.cornellThese are the core statutory triggers that allow federalization and deployment without governor (or mayor) agreement.
