The tragic irony of the Vojna Krajina (Croatia's Military Frontier) is that its population was born as an imperial instrument—and twice in history, events in neighboring Bosnia turned them from indispensable shields into disposable pawns.

1. The Creation (1500s) Relentless Ottoman raids turned medieval Croatia's heartland into a scorched, depopulated wasteland (Reliquiae reliquiarum) as native Catholic Croats fled north and west, and the surviving Croatian nobility desperately needed manpower to hold the line. But instead of giving Zagreb serfs, the Habsburg Emperor bypassed the Croatian nobility entirely—seizing the land under direct Vienna rule and importing Orthodox Serb and Vlach refugees straight from Ottoman territory in exchange for perpetual war. Therefore, from day one, the Frontier wasn't just a shield against the Ottomans; it was a privileged, armed Orthodox enclave carved right out of Croatia's historical core.

2. The Bosnian Trap (1878–1881) After Russia crushed the Ottomans in 1878, Vienna cashed in at the Congress of Berlin, winning the right to occupy Bosnia-Herzegovina. Because the broken Ottoman Sultan signed the handover and ordered his regular army not to resist, Vienna’s Foreign Minister boasted that Austrian troops could stroll into Sarajevo "with a brass band." But the locals refused to accept the backroom deal: Bosnian Muslims and Serbs seized the abandoned Ottoman arsenals and launched a fierce 3-month guerrilla war—forcing Vienna to mobilize 268,000 troops, with the Krajišnici regiments doing the heavy bleeding. Therefore, by conquering Bosnia for the Emperor, the Krajišnici pushed the imperial border hundreds of kilometers east and literally conquered themselves out of a job. No longer needing an internal buffer zone, Vienna abolished the Frontier in 1881 and handed them over to civilian Zagreb.

3. The 84-Hour Liquidation (1991–1995) When Yugoslavia fractured in 1991, that dormant 16th-century Habsburg map re-ignited almost to the kilometer as the Republic of Serbian Krajina, and early victories convinced Knin’s leaders they were untouchable—so much so that in early 1995 they refused to even touch the Z-4 peace plan (which offered them a "state within a state" that Zagreb dreaded). But while Knin stayed mentally frozen in 1991, great-power math in Bosnia flipped:• Milošević quietly traded them away for Western sanctions relief ahead of Dayton.• Washington needed a strong Croatia to break the siege of Bihać and prevent a second Srebrenica.• Retrained by US generals (MPRI), guided by CIA drones from Zadar, and backed by US Navy strikes on Serb radar, the Croatian Army became a NATO-style maneuver force.
Therefore, when Operation Storm hit across a 630 km front on August 4, 1995, the frontier collapsed in 84 hours. Roughly 200,000 Serbs fled east on tractors—erasing in a single August weekend the demographic fault line Vienna had engineered four centuries earlier.

text:
The Art of the Deal: Jared Kushner’s Hacked Phone Revealed His Secret Negotiations—Including More Than $700 Million in Transfers
An exclusive excerpt from Princes and Thieves: Jared Kushner and Mohamed bin Zayed’s Secret Plot to Remake the Middle East examines how bank accounts linked the president’s son-in-law—and former senior adviser—to Israel, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia.

October 22, 2026
By Matthew Cole

In late spring 2020, a source I knew to be reliable called me with a story. The Dutch government had hacked into Jared Kushner’s phone and monitored him as he accessed a Dubai-based bank account. What was odd, the source said, was that the money in the account—hundreds of millions of dollars—had come from a bank in Azerbaijan. Most importantly, Kushner appeared to have transferred significant amounts of money from the Dubai account to other individuals, including a warlord, a mercenary and a one-time hit man. The story sounded preposterous, I told my source. And yet.
Six months later, I found myself speaking with someone else about the UAE government and their use of mercenaries in conflicts around the Middle East and Africa when I asked, on a whim, whether they knew anything about Kushner and bank transfers from a UAE account. My acquaintance grew quiet. Then they replied, “Yes.”
Over the next four years, I came to learn that, sometime in late 2017, the Netherlands Defense Intelligence and Security Service (MIVD) made a startling discovery. A General Staff of the Armed Forces of the Russian Federation (GRU) operative, a dark web hacker specializing in stolen bank data, was traveling to the UK for an espionage mission. They reached out to the British government for permission to apprehend him when he arrived. The British agreed.

When the Russian national arrived in England, the Dutch informed him that he had two options: he could work for them against the GRU, or the British would arrest him. Once in UK government custody, the operative would be charged with espionage. If convicted, he would spend years in a British prison. The Russian chose to change his employer.

Later that year, the Russian operative gave the Dutch spies access to one of the GRU’s most sensitive assets. Located in Rostov, Russia, the GRU’s hacking and cyber team operated a remote server on which they stored some of their bounty. During their search through these secret files, the Dutch found something astonishing: screenshots of Jared Kushner’s iPhone.

In The Hague, the MIVD hacking team tried to reverse engineer the Russian penetration of Kushner’s iPhone. Kushner owned what was then the latest model, the iPhone X. Released in November 2017, it featured Face ID, a state-of-the-art security feature that Apple had promoted at its launch. The Dutch team had been trying to pick the phone’s door lock, so to speak, when it occurred to them that the Russians may have found an unlocked window to gain entry instead. Their hypothesis was correct. By early 2018, the MIVD had found a vulnerability in the iPhone that gave them access. The security exploit wasn’t perfect, however. Some malware allows a hacker to turn a victim’s phone into a microphone and video camera, turn the phone on or off, and pull and add files. The Dutch solution did not provide that level of access. Instead, when Kushner used the phone, they could see his screen. Almost as soon as they got inside, the intelligence service began capturing every image of Kushner’s screen as he used it, filing their own cache of surveillance on their internal computer servers.

As they monitored Kushner’s phone, they discovered he used it to log in to a UAE bank account. By the time the Dutch spies had visibility into the phone, the account had received hundreds of millions of dollars from a bank in Azerbaijan. 
Their initial assessment was that the bank account was affiliated with the government there.

“Jared was looking for shortcuts in his diplomacy,” a source who knew of the UAE’s deal with Kushner said.

For the MIVD hackers, the bank account became an intelligence mystery to unravel.
 Nearly everything they worked on had a tinge of Russian conspiracy. A little over a year into Trump’s first presidency, the MIVD, like FBI agents and federal prosecutors in Washington working on the Robert Mueller investigation, had only part of the story.
Kushner, UAE ruler Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ) and Mohammed bin Salman (MBS) of Saudi Arabia, converged at an auspicious moment. MBS wanted to be crown prince. MBZ wanted to blow up Obama’s Iran nuclear deal, and Kushner wanted both to help him force the Palestinians into a deal that Israel would accept. Despite the perception of his wealth, Kushner was not entirely financially independent of his parents, and the family business, Kushner Companies, faced a billion-dollar loan coming due on their trophy property, the Manhattan office building at 666 Fifth Avenue.

Early in the first Trump administration, MBZ and MBS offered to pay for a slush fund dedicated to helping the new administration with foreign policy goals. The idea was to help pay for Trump’s promised wall between Mexico and the US, for example, in an effort to secure a second term in the White House. The two Arab royals initially discussed with Kushner putting more than $10 billion into the effort. Within months, though, as MBZ pushed the Trump administration to help back MBS’s effort to become his country’s crown prince—and future king—the broader foreign policy slush fund idea fizzled. Instead, MBZ and MBS initially, and then MBZ alone, put at least $2 billion into at least two bank accounts for Kushner. It is unclear how the royals organized their $2 billion in combined payments, but they effectively split the cost. For the purposes of explanation, it is best to understand where and how each bank account was controlled.

“The Emiratis and the Saudis do this once a year. A billion or two is nothing for them, and if it gets them what they want, it’s money well spent.”

Bank account Alpha was held at First Abu Dhabi Bank, the largest in the UAE, and was overseen by MBZ’s brother, Tahnoon bin Zayed, who served as the bank’s chairman. Beginning in 2017, the Saudis and Emiratis transferred roughly $750 million into the Alpha account. Alpha would be used as a foreign policy fund. This money would be overseen and partially managed by Kushner and MBZ, who, in their effort to strike a grand bargain to end the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, believed the region’s map needed to be redrawn.

“Jared was looking for shortcuts in his diplomacy,” a source who knew of the UAE’s deal with Kushner said. This person held discussions with both senior UAE and Israeli officials about the secret financial arrangement between Kushner, the UAE, and, at least initially, Saudi Arabia. “Jared promised MBZ that he’d push their agenda with Trump if they participated in a fund. He wanted normalization with Israel so that business could take off.” A slush fund—a shared pool of money for off-the-books diplomatic objectives—was a common form of Gulf Arab government corruption, this person explained. “The Emiratis and the Saudis do this once a year. A billion or two is nothing for them, and if it gets them what they want, it’s money well spent.”

The Alpha account looked like the funding source of a UAE government program, by which MBZ paid his bureaucrats their salaries or funded government-run schools. But how and through whom the money flowed into the Alpha account revealed that it was intended to remain secret, more akin to a covert and illicit scheme, given that it was managed in part by a senior advisor to the president of the United States.

The Dutch spies who monitored the Alpha account noted that all of it was sent by a bank in Azerbaijan in American dollars. Azerbaijan plays a unique role in money laundering. Its central bank maintains high levels of US dollars in its reserves but does not adhere to the highest standards of bank transparency. As a result, Azerbaijani banks have well-established but unadvertised practices of serving as way stations for large transfers, in which a foreign currency is exchanged for an equal amount in dollars. For a roughly 6 to 7 percent fee on the transaction, some Azerbaijani banks will accept a transfer from a client who wishes to move Saudi riyals or Emirati dirhams totaling hundreds of millions of dollars. The Saudi or Emirati client sends the money to the Azerbaijani bank, which then uses a different internal bank account to transfer the equivalent US dollars to the client’s requested destination. For auditors, this shadow trade can’t be discerned.

A shallow audit, as the Dutch tried while monitoring Kushner’s iPhone, revealed nothing more than what appeared to be an Azerbaijani government–linked bank account that sent hundreds of millions of dollars to an account in Dubai. But there was another aspect of the Alpha account that the Dutch couldn’t see or understand, one that helped reveal the secret purpose of the money. Kushner did not own the bank account at First Abu Dhabi Bank. He was a signatory for an account managed and owned by an Emirati charity.

When MBZ and MBS first began contributing to the Alpha account in 2017, the Watani Al Emarat Foundation, a UAE government-funded charity, was run by Dherar Belhoul Al Falasi. Al Falasi was a technocrat and a member of the Federal National Council, and friends with one of MBZ’s closest friends and advisors. As a result, Al Falasi and the Watani Foundation had a second mission. The charity was used as a cover to move money in support of the country’s secret military and intelligence operations overseas. Under the Watani cover, Al Falasi helped facilitate the UAE’s secret weapons-purchasing programs, one confidential source who had direct knowledge of the charity’s proliferation program revealed. This source said that the Emiratis believed that the program’s status as a charity made its international transactions less likely to be scrutinized and therefore served as a useful cover for funding MBZ and his brother’s secret wars.

MBZ and Tahnoon made Kushner a signatory on the Alpha account with Watani. As a signatory, Jared had access to it and could, in theory, make transactions, but it technically wasn’t his account. One way to view what Kushner did with the Alpha account is to imagine him as the director of the CIA. Had he been running the government entity that managed and ran secret foreign programs, maintaining the account, again, with presidential approval and congressional disclosure, Kushner’s conduct would have been within his job’s responsibilities. But he was not the director of the CIA, whose position is approved by the Senate and whose operations are overseen and accountable to Congress. Instead, Kushner was overseen only by his father-in-law, who, according to four senior Trump administration officials—two national security advisors, a White House chief of staff, and a former CIA director—were unaware of any presidential authorization for Kushner to access a foreign government bank account. (Kushner’s counsel, however, said Kushner did not make any agreements or arrangements with leaders or officials in foreign countries that were not agreed to by the President of the United States and in the best interests of the United States.) 

Regardless of whether he was a signatory or the owner, Jared was required by federal government regulations and the Internal Revenue Service to disclose his access to the account. Unless disclosed to and approved by the US government and reported on his tax returns, Kushner’s access to the Alpha account may have violated US law. (A lawyer for Mr. Kushner denied that his client had any knowledge of or connection to Al Falasi, the Watani charity, or a UAE bank account and stated that he had complied with all legal requirements when dealing with foreign governments.)

In addition to the Alpha bank account, MBZ put money into at least one other account intended for Kushner. By the spring of 2018, the crown prince had moved roughly $1 billion to Israel via Azerbaijan for Kushner. We will refer to this account as the Beta bank account. It is unclear how Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu first learned of MBZ’s money for Kushner, but a person briefed on the Beta account told me that the prime minister encouraged Kushner to have the money deposited in the Israeli Central Bank, in what would appear to be a government account. It is also unclear how Kushner used the money the UAE deposited into the Beta account for him, but according to the person with knowledge of the money, its allocation was for Kushner’s personal benefit. But as with the Alpha account, there were clues in the way the Beta account was managed.

Israel’s Central Bank does not operate personal accounts. The bank holds and transfers only government funds. The government accounts use a dual-key system, which requires two authorized individuals to make any transfers from the account as an oversight mechanism. Netanyahu required Kushner to inform him before making any transactions from the Beta account.

To do so, Kushner passed his messages through Ambassador David M. Friedman, who frequently met with Netanyahu. With the money in the Central Bank, it would be difficult, if not impossible, to connect MBZ’s payment to Jared. It is unclear if spies in the Netherlands had any indication of the Beta account. (Ambassador Friedman denied that he had any knowledge of, or involvement with, any UAE money made available to Kushner, or that he passed messages on Kushner’s behalf. “I know absolutely nothing about any of these allegations,” Friedman said, “and the specific allegations about me or my alleged involvement in this alleged scheme are 100% false.” Kushner’s counsel also said Kushner “has no idea” about any such account, and insisted that “there are no accounts and never were.”)

Apparently, Kushner faced the challenge of moving money from the Beta account in Israel to other accounts where he could have untraceable access to the funds. One person who worked with Kushner to move the money out of Israel said that much of it went to bank accounts in Cyprus before being moved elsewhere.

During Kushner’s secret financial arrangement with MBZ, he helped negotiate a third, altogether distinct account. As part of what was, at the time, a secret warming of diplomatic relations between Israel and the UAE, Kushner helped negotiate an agreement by Israel to help defend the UAE from a major Iranian military attack. The UAE needed to cover the cost of the emergency defense, however, and the government secretly made another transfer to Israel’s Central Bank. This was something like a rainy-day defense fund. Combined, the three accounts represented a secret foreign policy negotiated by Kushner with the leaders of Israel, the UAE and Saudi Arabia.

Although Kushner’s position as senior advisor to the president was unpaid, he was an official government employee. Not only did his position require financial disclosures for ethics regulations, but each year he worked in the White House, he had to file both a public and confidential financial form, known as the Executive Branch Personnel Public Financial Disclosure Report, also known as a 278e disclosure. Because he had access to classified government secrets, Kushner was required to disclose any bank account to which he had signatory—or beneficiary—access.

Kushner’s apparent betrayal of the public trust, however, went further than his failure to disclose the secret Alpha account in the UAE or the Beta account in Israel. By giving him access to roughly $2 billion, regardless of how the money was used, MBZ and MBS were paying for his influence within the US government. Any efforts he made to shape US policy that came from a foreign government that had provided him with money would make him an agent of a foreign power. US law requires citizens who lobby on behalf of a foreign power to declare themselves and the country they are working on behalf of to the Justice Department.

One former prosecutor who worked on the Mueller investigation said that if Kushner promised anything to MBZ and MBS in return for the money they offered him—even if it was just speaking to his father-in-law—he may have violated federal bribery laws, as well as the foreign agent statute. (Mr. Kushner’s lawyer denied that Kushner violated any laws while serving in the White House.)

Captagon, War and the Global Narcotics Economy: Military Drug Use, Terrorist Financing and the Struggle for Strategic Control - Captagon and other amphetamine-type stimulants have a documented history of use in armed-conflict environments, including reports concerning Islamic State fighters and other participants in Syria’s civil war. Their association with warfare is not merely a journalistic invention, although the prevalence, organisation and effects of consumption differ between cases.

The decisive geopolitical development was the transformation of Captagon into an industrial criminal economy associated with the former Syrian regime, military-linked structures and transnational trafficking organisations. US Treasury sanctions in 2023 and 2024 explicitly connected production and trafficking to Maher al-Assad’s Fourth Division and networks linked to Hezbollah.

Following the collapse of Bashar al-Assad’s government in December 2024, the international security problem shifted from identifying a dominant political-production structure to tracing surviving inventories, relocating manufacturing capabilities and increasingly dispersed trafficking networks.

The 2026 European Union-supported assessment identifies Iraq and Türkiye as jurisdictions reporting medium-scale domestic Captagon production, alongside indications of manufacturing in several additional countries. This makes Iraq more than a transit concern and gives the UAE an increasingly important role in detecting cross-border commercial and criminal connections.

On 23 October 2026, Iraqi–Emirati cooperation resulted in the seizure of 200,000 Captagon tablets. The Iraqi account further described more than a year of monitoring a network previously associated with movements of narcotic tablets from Dubai into Iraq.

The international market is now exposed to a possible convergence between Captagon, methamphetamine, organised criminal finance and conflict economies. Governments must assess drug consumption by fighters, criminal revenues benefiting armed organisations and the deliberate institutional distribution of stimulants as related but distinct intelligence questions.

The strategic conclusion is that psychoactive drugs are simultaneously a commodity, a possible instrument of operational endurance, a source of criminal finance and a means through which armed and politically connected networks can accumulate economic influence.

Captagon, War and the Economics of Criminal Power: The Global Drug Trade Is Becoming a Test of State Sovereignty
The seizure of 200,000 Captagon tablets in a joint Iraqi–Emirati operation on 23 October 2026 exposes a problem considerably larger than the shipment intercepted: governments are confronting narcotics networks whose industrial capabilities, financial relationships and connections to armed power can survive the collapse of the political systems that once protected them. Syria’s former Captagon economy demonstrated how illicit manufacturing could become a source of revenue for military-linked structures. Its disruption has not eliminated regional demand or the organisations serving it. From the Gulf to Europe’s ports, the decisive vulnerability is the growing separation between the territory where drugs are manufactured, the jurisdictions through which they move and the financial centres where criminal profits can be concealed. The security question is no longer how many tablets a government can confiscate, but whether it can dismantle the economic organisation responsible for producing the next shipment.

The fall of Assad disrupted production, not the economics of trafficking
The collapse of Bashar al-Assad’s government in December 2024 dismantled the political environment in which Syria had become the principal manufacturing centre for illicit Captagon. The extent of that dependence was extraordinary: in March 2023, the British government estimated that Syria accounted for approximately 80% of global Captagon production. The figure described the historical market, not the situation after Assad’s removal, but it exposed the degree to which industrial-scale criminal activity had become concentrated within a state devastated by civil war.

The relationship was political as well as commercial. On 28 March 2023, the US Department of the Treasury identified networks connected to Maher al-Assad, commander of Syria’s Fourth Division, and Khalid Qaddour, a businessman associated with the management of the division’s illicit revenues. Treasury connected the military formation to Captagon production and trafficking, demonstrating how coercive state institutions and privately organised criminal finance could reinforce one another. In October 2024, further American designations targeted trafficking and commercial networks associated with the Syrian regime and Hezbollah. These findings established specific financial and organisational connections, rather than merely suggesting that narcotics happened to circulate through wartime Syria.

The distinction matters after December 2024. Removing the political protection surrounding an illicit industry does not automatically destroy its inventories, technical expertise, customers or financial intermediaries. The 2026 EU-supported assessment of Captagon and methamphetamine trafficking identified medium-scale Captagon production reported in Iraq and Türkiye, alongside indications of manufacturing elsewhere. Production may therefore become less geographically concentrated even as the former Syrian system loses its institutional foundation.

That possibility changes the economics of interdiction. A criminal organisation operating through smaller production networks in several jurisdictions may possess less industrial capacity than the former Syrian system while becoming more difficult to disrupt through pressure on any single government. The decisive indicator is not the number of tablets seized after Assad’s fall, but the proportion demonstrably manufactured after December 2024 and the identity of those financing replacement production.

The numbers expose a market that enforcement cannot measure through seizures alone
The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime’s World Drug Report 2026 estimated that 331 million people used illicit drugs in 2024, equivalent to approximately 6.2% of the global population aged 15–64. The number of users had increased by 34% since 2014. Cannabis accounted for an estimated 256 million users, while 63 million reported non-medical opioid use and approximately 25 million used cocaine. These markets cannot be treated as interchangeable, but their combined scale explains why disrupting individual suppliers rarely extinguishes the economic incentives supporting international distribution.

Europe provides an unusually revealing example. EU Member States seized 330 tonnes of cocaine in 2024, compared with 419 tonnes in 2023, while the number of reported seizures increased from approximately 95,000 to 97,000. The apparent contradiction is significant: fewer tonnes intercepted do not necessarily indicate reduced availability when trafficking organisations are fragmenting consignments and diversifying distribution. During 2024, six Member States also reported dismantling at least 42 cocaine production or processing sites, compared with 34 in 2023. Europe is therefore exposed not simply to imported finished drugs but increasingly to industrial activities undertaken within its own market.

The geographical distribution of interceptions illustrates the difficulty of assigning national responsibility from enforcement figures. Spain reported 124 tonnes of cocaine seized in 2024, France 53.5 tonnes, Belgium 44.6 tonnes, the Netherlands 37.6 tonnes, Germany 23.8 tonnes and Italy 11 tonnes. These quantities reflect differing exposure to international commerce and enforcement operations; they do not establish corresponding shares of European consumption or criminal profit.

The financial distinction is equally important for Captagon. Multiplying seized tablets by an assumed retail price may generate an impressive headline value, but it does not establish the income received by manufacturers, financiers or armed organisations. A shipment’s retail value, wholesale transaction price and net criminal profit are different economic measures. Without verified ownership and transaction records, attributing the entire estimated market value to a government, militia or terrorist organisation creates the appearance of financial precision where none exists.

Dubai and Baghdad reveal the limits of territorial policing
The 23 October 2026 operation between Iraq and the United Arab Emirates illustrates how international trafficking exposes the limits of nationally organised law enforcement. According to the Iraqi Ministry of Interior, Iraqi counter-narcotics authorities supplied intelligence that enabled Emirati agencies to seize 200,000 Captagon tablets and arrest suspects inside the UAE. The investigation reportedly involved more than one year of monitoring, while the suspected organisation had previously moved thousands of narcotic tablets from Dubai into Iraq.

The direction of those alleged earlier movements is consequential. Dubai was not presented exclusively as a destination for an incoming shipment: the reported investigation also concerned drugs moving out of the Emirates toward Iraq. That does not establish Emirati manufacture or institutional complicity. It does demonstrate why a commercial hub must be examined as a possible point of distribution, financial intermediation or onward movement, rather than classified automatically as either a source or consumer market.

Iraq’s exposure is also changing. The 2026 EU-supported assessment identified the country as both an origin and transit jurisdiction and recorded its report of medium-scale domestic Captagon production. Iraqi authorities consequently face responsibilities that extend from border interdiction to manufacturing investigations, domestic consumption and financial tracing. The October operation demonstrated an ability to convert intelligence collected in one jurisdiction into enforcement action in another. Its longer-term significance will depend on whether the investigation establishes manufacturing provenance, criminal ownership and the ultimate beneficiaries of the trade.

The UAE’s position creates a different institutional tension. Its international logistics, re-export activities and financial services depend on commercial openness, while counter-narcotics enforcement requires identifying criminal transactions within extensive legitimate flows. Indiscriminate restrictions would impose costs on lawful business without necessarily reaching network organisers. Weak supervision, however, would leave criminal intermediaries able to exploit the very infrastructure that supports the Emirates’ commercial influence.

Drugs have entered warfare as both substances and sources of revenue
Captagon’s association with armed conflict is supported by documented reporting, not merely by its reputation. UNODC discussed consumption among Islamic State fighters and other participants in Syria’s civil war, while the April 2026 EU-supported assessment identified perceived battlefield performance, productivity, hunger suppression and coping with trauma among reported reasons for use. These findings place stimulant consumption within genuine operational environments where fatigue, fear and endurance influence individual behaviour.

The historical precedent extends beyond irregular forces. German military use of methamphetamine under the Pervitin name and British and American use of amphetamines during the Second World War established that conventional armed forces also sought pharmacological means of sustaining personnel. The military calculation, however, contains an internal contradiction: increased wakefulness does not necessarily produce improved judgement, target discrimination or command discipline. The US Government Accountability Office reported in March 2024 that Department of Defense surveys had repeatedly found a majority of American service members sleeping six hours or less per night, illustrating why fatigue remains a readiness problem even in technologically advanced forces.

The relationship between drugs and violence nevertheless requires precision. Allegations concerning stimulant consumption in the Russia–Ukraine war cannot establish an organised military distribution programme without authenticated procurement, command or toxicological evidence. Similarly, allegations that perpetrators of the Hamas-led attacks against Israel on 7 October 2023 consumed Captagon do not, in themselves, establish systematic administration by Hamas. United Nations investigations documented serious violations committed during the attacks, including killings and hostage-taking; those findings do not depend on a pharmacological explanation.

The more demonstrable geopolitical danger often concerns financing rather than consumption. The US Treasury’s March 2023 and October 2024 sanctions actions linked Captagon trafficking to networks associated with Syria’s former Fourth Division and Hezbollah. Such financial relationships can support organisations exercising armed or political power regardless of whether their personnel consume the substances being sold. Confusing the drug’s possible effects on a combatant with its function as a revenue-generating commodity obscures both military responsibility and criminal ownership.

Europe’s industrial strengths also create criminal-financial exposure
The European Union’s response must account for the fact that its lawful industrial infrastructure and its exposure to illicit markets are connected. Germany’s chemical-manufacturing capacity, Belgium’s and the Netherlands’ international ports, Italy’s Mediterranean commercial connections and France’s extensive distribution economy all create different investigative requirements. Criminal diversion of chemical inputs is not evidence against legitimate manufacturers; illicit use of a port does not establish complicity by its operator. But each case requires institutions capable of identifying criminal relationships within lawful commercial systems.

Italy’s comparative institutional challenge concerns criminal ownership and the reinvestment of illicit proceeds. Its specialised anti-narcotics and anti-mafia investigative structures offer mechanisms for connecting shipments to wider organisations, but the effectiveness of those instruments depends on prosecutions and financial outcomes. France confronts a different balance between international cocaine supply, violent domestic distribution and the burden on health services. Germany must protect chemical commerce while investigating diversion and synthetic-drug manufacturing. The United Kingdom, outside the EU’s institutional framework but closely connected to European markets, faces rising cocaine exposure and the medical consequences of highly potent synthetic opioids.

British data demonstrate why public health cannot be separated from the security calculation. The National Crime Agency reported cocaine seizures rising from 3.4 tonnes in 2015 to 18.5 tonnes in 2025. The Office for National Statistics recorded 5,565 drug-poisoning deaths in England and Wales during 2024 registrations, including 1,279 deaths involving cocaine and 195 involving nitazenes. The figures measure different aspects of the market, but together they reveal a system in which increased interdiction does not automatically translate into reduced mortality.

The Council of the European Union’s decision of 4 June 2026 to advance implementation of its drugs strategy and action plan against trafficking recognises this institutional problem. The challenge is converting coordination among police, customs, financial supervisors, prosecutors and health authorities into demonstrable reductions in criminal capacity. Europol, Eurojust and the European Union Drugs Agency contribute different capabilities, but none can substitute for national investigations and judicial decisions within its respective legal mandate.

International law can reach the money, but only if governments establish ownership
The 1988 United Nations Convention against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances provides the legal foundation for cooperation against trafficking, including confiscation, extradition, mutual legal assistance and precursor controls. Its Article 2 preserves national sovereignty, while Article 5 establishes measures concerning criminal proceeds and property. The combination exposes the central jurisdictional difficulty: an investigation may begin in Iraq, lead to arrests in the UAE and require financial evidence from additional countries before the actual organisers can be prosecuted.

The Financial Action Task Force Recommendations, amended through June 2026, provide standards concerning money laundering, beneficial ownership, suspicious transactions and international cooperation. These instruments matter because sophisticated drug networks can separate physical custody from financial control. The individual arrested while transporting a consignment may be economically replaceable; the financier controlling repeated shipments may be considerably more difficult to identify.

Financial sanctions add another instrument but do not resolve the evidentiary problem. The US Treasury’s October 2024 designations targeted named individuals and commercial networks associated with Captagon trafficking and Hezbollah-related finance. Such measures can restrict access to regulated financial systems, but they are not equivalent to criminal convictions and do not automatically confiscate all proceeds or eliminate replacement intermediaries.

The implication is that a government claiming success through seizure quantities must also demonstrate whether it has identified beneficial ownership, secured admissible evidence, recovered criminal assets and prevented a network from restoring operations. Without those outcomes, enforcement may interrupt transactions while leaving the underlying enterprise financially intact.

The next 24 months will determine whether disruption becomes displacement
Between October 2026 and October 2028, the most consequential test will concern the future organisation of Captagon manufacturing after Syria’s political transition. If forensic evidence increasingly identifies recently manufactured tablets originating outside the former Syrian production system, governments will face a geographically dispersed industrial problem rather than a declining historical stockpile. Iraq and the UAE will require deeper intelligence and judicial cooperation; Gulf consumer markets will remain exposed to replacement suppliers; and authorities will need to distinguish Captagon trafficking from the parallel expansion of methamphetamine and other stimulants.

For the European Union, the 4 June 2026 policy framework creates an implementation test over the same period. A reduction in intercepted tonnage will not establish progress unless accompanied by stronger evidence of disrupted manufacturing, criminal-financial confiscation and declining harm. Italy will bear the institutional costs of investigating transnational ownership; France will continue confronting the security consequences of cocaine distribution; Germany will face the burden of supervising industrial chemical flows; and the United Kingdom will confront the medical and enforcement costs associated with changing synthetic-drug markets.

The financial cost of inaction will fall on legitimate businesses exposed to criminal infiltration, public institutions required to investigate increasingly dispersed networks, and health systems treating the consequences of dangerous and adulterated substances. The security cost will fall on states unable to prevent illicit revenues from strengthening criminal or armed organisations. The political cost will fall on governments whose enforcement statistics improve while the organisations supplying their markets remain solvent.

The decisive measure of policy over the next 12–24 months will therefore not be the value assigned to confiscated drugs, but whether governments can establish who controls production, who owns the proceeds and whether the organisations connecting those functions have lost the capacity to operate.- https://t.co/Ba44zecJmD via @https://debuglies.com

📜 “There Has Never Been a Better or Easier Opportunity Than Now”: The Göcsej Association’s Scheme to Acquire Confiscated Jewish Property in 1944

Zalaegerszeg, Hungary, 1944. As Hungarian Jews were being dispossessed, confined and deported, a regional cultural association presented their persecution as an opportunity to establish a public museum, picture gallery and library.

The Göcseji Egyesület—the Göcsej Association—asked for Jewish-owned paintings, sculptures, tapestries, porcelain, books and cabinets. It also requested ownership of a Jewish house to accommodate its collection. The objects and the property were to be obtained without payment.

The file survives in Reel 144, slides 212–220. Read alongside correspondence preserved in the Zala county archives, it reveals how this local initiative reached the officials responsible for Jewish property and confiscated artworks—and how discussion of museum expansion intersected with demands to seize a named Jewish collector’s pictures.

The surviving evidence establishes the requests, official support and pressure for confiscation. Establishing which objects actually reached which institution remains the essential unfinished work.

📜 What the association actually requested

The original petition is dated 31 May 1944. It describes approximately 3,000 objects occupying three rooms in Zalaegerszeg’s former police headquarters, and ambitions for a museum and public library.

Its justification explicitly excludes Jews from the national community while claiming their possessions for that community. The petition portrays state appropriation of Jewish property as an exceptional opportunity for Hungarian cultural development.

One sentence states, in English translation:

“There has never been a better or easier opportunity than now to establish a public library and a public picture gallery.”

The request extends across the Göcsej region, seeking Jewish-owned paintings, pictures, sculptures, art objects, tapestries, porcelain, books and cabinets for the collection in Zalaegerszeg.

Its operative phrase is “ellenszolgáltatás nélkül”—“without payment or consideration.”

The following paragraph requests a Jewish house for the collection, including transfer of the property’s ownership on the same terms. Cultural purpose was offered as the justification for acquiring both the contents of Jewish homes and a building in which to display them.

The document’s significance lies partly in that breadth. The anticipated benefit encompassed the infrastructure of a cultural institution: collection, library, furnishings and premises. [1]

🏛️ Who promoted the proposal?

Dr. Károly Nagy was a district judge, the association’s managing president and the head of its collection. The museum’s own early history identifies him as a principal organizer. The May petition bears his signature. His judicial profession gives particular weight to a request that treated the dispossession of Jewish owners as an opportunity for public enrichment. [1, 7]

The proposal also received support through Zalaegerszeg’s municipal and county administration. Dr. István Tamásy, the city’s wartime mayor, headed the municipal administration whose submission appears in the file. The city’s official biography records that he was subsequently sentenced to five years’ imprisonment for his role in establishing the Zalaegerszeg ghetto. [1, 5]

Count Béla Teleki, Zala county’s főispán—the government-appointed head of the county—advanced the museum proposal directly. In a letter of 12 June 1944, he asked that Jewish-owned objects from Göcsej support the collection in Zalaegerszeg, while objects from other parts of the county could enrich museums in Keszthely and Nagykanizsa.

Teleki acknowledged the priority of Budapest museums for objects they wanted. For the regional institutions, he offered to meet any required transfer price. He then reported that Dr. Albert Turvölgyi had already indicated his agreement under those conditions.

That is a specific, documented connection between the local museum campaign and the national administration of Jewish property. It is Teleki’s report of conditional agreement; the letter does not establish that a transfer followed. [2]

💼 Dr. Albert Turvölgyi: The official responsible for Jewish property

Dr. Albert Turvölgyi was a senior Finance Ministry official who became the government commissioner responsible for Jewish financial and property affairs. His remit concerned the administration of dispossession on a national scale.

According to the Budapest Holocaust Memorial Center, he studied law and entered the Finance Ministry’s spirits department in 1928. In 1932, he developed the concept of a state spirits monopoly, implemented later in the decade. The Memorial Center describes its implementation as an “Aryanization” of the industry—the displacement of Jewish economic interests. [3]

By early June 1944, Turvölgyi headed the government office dealing with Jewish property. Dénes Csánky, director-general of the Museum of Fine Arts in Budapest, headed the separate commission charged with inventorying and safeguarding sequestrated Jewish artworks. The Göcsej correspondence brings these two areas of authority together: control of Jewish assets and the selection of art for museums. [2–4]

Turvölgyi’s career continued under the Arrow Cross regime: he became a Finance Ministry state secretary on 29 November 1944. His role in this case therefore belongs within a longer career in economic exclusion and state appropriation, rather than being treated as an incidental appearance in museum correspondence. [3]

⚖️ Csánky’s reply: Museum expansion and compulsory seizure

On 16 June 1944, Csánky replied to Teleki that he fully supported the proposed Göcsej Museum. He favored allocating provincial material to local museums where possible and considered it likely that payment would not be required. In that context, he wrote that the Göcsej Museum would receive its designated objects “free of charge”—“ingyen.”

He asked that Dr. Béla Darnay, better known as Béla Darnay-Dornyay, consider the new museum’s interests in his collecting work. Darnay was director of the Balatoni Museum in Keszthely and also Csánky’s local commissioner’s delegate.

The same letter invoked the decree requiring the financial authorities, when requested by the commissioner, to order sequestrated movable property transported to a designated location. For Zala county, Csánky identified Zalaegerszeg.

He then turned to a particular collection. Citing a report from Darnay, Csánky complained that Dr. István Oroszlán, a Keszthely tax official, had repeatedly delayed sequestration of the Zádor collection. He characterized the delay as apparent or actual sabotage and demanded action so that Darnay could begin inventorying immediately.

Csánky also requested an urgent inspection and report on the art collection at the Elek family’s castle in Palin, near Nagykanizsa.

These instructions connect the proposed distribution of cultural property to identifiable collections and demands for compulsory intervention. [2]

🕯️ The owner behind the inventory: Lajos Zádor

Lajos Zádor was a Jewish hardware merchant and art collector in Keszthely. A surviving gendarmerie report identifies him as a married man with one child, a former soldier, and a resident of 13 Kossuth Lajos Street.

His testimony records that he had collected and purchased pictures for decades. He reported them to the financial authorities on 30 April 1944, as the anti-Jewish regulations required. By the time of the investigation, the pictures remained in a room in his home that the local authorities had ordered sealed.

The investigation arose from an antisemitic press allegation that he had attempted to protect his pictures through placement in the Balatoni Museum. Zádor denied commissioning such an arrangement. Other witnesses also denied that he had asked them to act for him.

On 18 May 1944, the gendarmerie reported that the pictures remained at his residence, that the alleged transfer had not occurred and that no criminal offense had been established. It discontinued further investigation.

Less than a month later, Csánky was pressing for sequestration and inventorying of the same collection. The closure of a criminal investigation offered no protection against the separate machinery directed at Jewish-owned art. [2, 6]

A surviving inventory, dated 12 May 1944, contains 32 numbered entries. Among its recorded attributions and titles are:

• Mihály Munkácsy: a portrait and Őszi bánat—Autumn Sorrow.
• László Mednyánszky: Téli tájkép—Winter Landscape—and Az Alpok—The Alps.
• László Paál: two large pictures and one smaller picture.
• István Csók: Bűnbánó Magdolna—Penitent Magdalene.
• József Koszta: Tehénőrző—Cowherd.

These are historical inventory descriptions and attributions. They provide starting points for searches through confiscation records, museum inventories, restitution files and the art market. They do not, by themselves, identify a surviving painting. [6]

🚂 The petition continued as Jews were deported

The occupants of the Zalaegerszeg collection camp were deported on 5 July 1944 and reached Auschwitz on 8 July. The ministry’s forwarding letter in the Göcsej file is dated 7 July. The administrative processing of the museum request therefore continued during the deportation itself. [1, 9]

A further response from Csánky dated 17 August 1944 continued to support the project and contemplated the selection and eventual allocation of objects. It still does not supply the missing evidence of delivery: an itemized handover, a receipt or an accession record connecting particular Jewish owners to the Göcsej Collection. [1]

🏺 Does the collection still exist?

The original association was dissolved in 1946. Much of its collection was lost or dispersed during the war. A surviving remnant became the starting collection of the Göcseji Museum, which began operating on 1 July 1950 and remains active today.

The museum’s own account states that approximately 400 mostly undocumented objects survived and were nationalized. [7–8]

Its first director, Imre Szentmihályi, supplied a more precise breakdown in 1960: 313 ethnographic objects, 81 archaeological objects and six objects in other categories. His breakdown records no fine-art objects in that inherited group. [7]

That distinction matters. The records establish a connection between the prewar collection and the later museum. They do not establish that the museum inherited paintings obtained through the 1944 petition. Nor can the 400 surviving objects simply be labeled Jewish property without evidence of their earlier ownership.

The investigation must reconstruct what entered the collection before the war, what entered during persecution, what disappeared and what was subsequently transferred elsewhere.

🗂️ The wartime losses do not close the investigation

Research by historian Valentin Cseh documents that the material evacuated from Keszthely in January 1945 included artworks taken from Jews alongside museum collections. The railway wagons reached Zalaegerszeg, where bombing on 28–29 March 1945 caused catastrophic losses.

But objects also survived and were recovered. Cseh identifies returns and handovers in 1946 and 1947, supported by municipal records.

Those recoveries are not proof that Zádor’s pictures survived, or that the Göcsej Association received them. They establish why a general statement about wartime destruction cannot substitute for checking the transport lists, surviving inventories and postwar recovery files. [10]

🔎 What should now be made public?

The Göcseji Museum, the Balatoni Museum and the relevant archives can help resolve this history by bringing the surviving records together:

• The association’s acquisition registers and correspondence for 1944–1946, including any response concerning the requested Jewish house.
• Darnay’s seizure inventories, reports and allocation correspondence, particularly for the Zádor collection and Elek’s Palin castle.
• Transfer and receipt records connecting the commissioner’s office, financial authorities and regional museums.
• The earliest museum inventories identifying the 400 inherited objects, including any surviving information about their original owners.
• Wartime packing lists and the 1946–1947 recovery and return records.

Two archival references already provide concrete starting points: Zala county főispán records, 813/1944, containing the Teleki–Csánky correspondence; and Keszthely district chief administrative officer’s records, 3690/1944, containing the Zádor investigation and inventory.

The historical significance is already clear. A regional cultural association openly proposed using the dispossession of Jews to establish institutions serving the wider public, and senior officials supported that aim. The unresolved question is how far the proposal was implemented—and where any objects transferred under it went.

A full account of the region’s cultural heritage must include the Jewish owners whose possessions officials sought to turn into public collections.

text:
If you want to understand what it means to be an American citizen, look at what happened in the Indian Ocean on Easter Sunday, April 12, 2009.

One merchant captain from Vermont named Richard Phillips was being held hostage inside a covered orange lifeboat by Somali pirates armed with AK-47s.

He was not a general. He was not a politician. He was one cargo ship captain who had offered himself as a hostage to save his crew.

To bring that one man home, the United States sent the guided-missile destroyer USS Bainbridge, the frigate USS Halyburton, the amphibious assault ship USS Boxer, and a team of U.S. Navy SEALs who parachuted straight into the black ocean at night.

For four days, the lifeboat pitched violently in rough seas twenty-five yards behind the destroyer.

Then at dusk on Sunday, a pirate pressed the barrel of his AK-47 directly against Captain Phillips' back and prepared to kill him.

On the fantail of the USS Bainbridge, three Navy SEAL snipers lay braced in the dark. The destroyer was rolling in one direction. The tiny lifeboat was pitching in another. If even one sniper missed by half an inch, or fired a tenth of a second late, the hostage would die.

Through night-vision scopes, all three snipers waited for the exact millisecond when three targets appeared in the tiny windows at once.

One word came over the headset.

Three rifles fired as a single sound.

All three kidnappers dropped instantly. Captain Phillips walked onto the deck of the USS Bainbridge without a scratch.

Do not touch a citizen of a country that will drop Navy SEALs from the sky at midnight for one man.

text:
Netflix offered $500 million to turn Xbox games into shows and movies. Xbox asked for $800 million. Now neither side has a deal.

@MattBelloni reported it in Puck on Thursday, citing three sources. Former Netflix content chief Bela Bajaria offered $500M for a seven-year exclusive license on Xbox titles for film and TV. Xbox's Asha Sharma and her business affairs team countered at $800M. Bajaria has since been replaced by Peter Rice, and the offer left with her.

• Spread over seven years, that's about $71M a year from Netflix against about $114M a year from Xbox's ask.
• Netflix CFO Spence Neumann was among those who thought the deal was too rich, per Puck.
• Xbox told Puck it has seen "record-breaking interest" in its IP, and is said to be pursuing smaller deals with more partners. The Minecraft and Diablo animated series are still coming to Netflix.
• Rice is still expected to go after more IP deals, and Netflix has reason to hurry. Belloni also posted the latest Nielsen Gauge numbers this week, with YouTube at 15.8% of TV viewing and Netflix at 7.7%.

So don't expect one streaming home for Xbox adaptations. The games will likely get split across several buyers instead.

text:
Pop Watson is expected to play tonight for the first time since the 3rd of October. UMass has not won a game since he got hurt.

He is not named Pop because of football.

He got it as a small boy in Springfield, Massachusetts, from his grandfather, who thought the kid had an old soul. His dad says the boy "thought he was the father and we were the kids," bossing the house around, and the family started calling him Pop. It never came off.

His dad is Bill Watson. He came up from Brooklyn, played quarterback at American International College in Springfield, and started a youth football program in that city to give the kids there somewhere to develop. He has coached his son his whole life, including at Springfield Central High School, where he is still on the staff.

Pop has been going to 6am workouts since seventh grade.

Here is what he says about his dad.

"I trust him with everything."

Now the part almost nobody knows.

Before Pop Watson had played one single high school game, UMass offered him a scholarship at a summer camp. They were first. Boston College came three games into his freshman season. Tennessee came. Nebraska came, and he committed there.

Then Virginia Tech came in December of his senior year and he flipped.

He went 33 and 6 at Central, won state titles in 2019 and 2021, and was the Gatorade player of the year for the entire state of Massachusetts.

Then he spent three years in Blacksburg and could not get on the field. In the whole 2025 season, Pop Watson threw four passes. He completed two of them.

He entered the portal on the 26th of December. Sixteen days later he committed to UMass, the school that wanted him before anybody.

Here is what he said about it.

"You go where you feel wanted."

Pete Thamel broke that one. His source was Bill Watson.

His first career start was at Rutgers. UMass was a 29.5 point underdog and he went 19 for 22, 197 yards and three touchdowns in a 37 to 21 win that ended a 16 game losing streak.

They got to 4 and 0. A year earlier they had gone 0 and 12.

Now the part that complicates it. Three of those four wins came against teams a level below them, he has started seven college games in his life, and the three straight losses since the ankle say as much about a thin roster as they do about him.

But here is why tonight matters.

The last time UMass played in a bowl game it was 1972, the game was in Atlantic City, and they beat UC Davis. They have been an FBS program since 2012 and have never been back.

Two more wins and they go. Tonight they are at UConn.

Bill Watson has said the thing he actually wants is for his son to be a good man first. The football was always second.

The boy they called Pop because he acted like the father is half an hour from the field where his father still coaches.

text:
You accuse me of falling for propaganda, then offer a claim that falls apart under the slightest scrutiny.

Firstly, Russia has not taken all the territory it wants. Putin continues to demand the entirety of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson, including areas his forces have failed to capture. Only yesterday he was still asserting Russia's territorial claims. If Moscow achieved everything it wanted over a year ago, why is it still fighting and demanding more territory?

Secondly, you're misunderstanding the corpse exchange figures. The number of bodies returned by each side does not establish how many soldiers each army has lost. Russian forces have generally controlled the ground following battles, allowing their recovery teams to collect Ukrainian dead. Ukraine cannot recover bodies from territory it no longer controls.

Even Meduza, an independent Russian news outlet, has explained this. You cannot calculate a war's casualty ratio by comparing the contents of two repatriation convoys.

The CSIS estimates I quoted cover killed, wounded and missing personnel, using a much broader assessment of battlefield losses. They are estimates, not exact figures, but they provide no support for your claim that Russia has suffered only a tenth of Ukraine's losses.

As for forced conscription, Ukraine has certainly faced serious allegations of abusive recruitment practices. Those deserve scrutiny. But Russia has also mobilised men, recruited prisoners and offered substantial financial incentives to sustain its war effort. Neither country's manpower problems should be ignored.

You say the figures are easily confirmed. Then provide an independent military assessment demonstrating that Russian casualties are only a tenth of Ukraine's. Body exchange statistics do not establish it. And perhaps explain why, after more than four and a half years of fighting, Russia is still trying to capture territory you insist it secured over a year ago.

text:
The Soviet proposal was an absolutely terrible deal for Finland, both economically and militarily.

Economically, Finland was expected to surrender strategically located, developed territory on the Karelian Isthmus in exchange for a much larger area of sparsely populated forests and wilderness in Soviet East Karelia. More square kilometres did not mean more economic value. Finland would lose infrastructure, agricultural land and strategically important territory in exchange for largely undeveloped land.

Militarily, it was even worse. Moving the border back would weaken Finland’s defensive position on the Karelian Isthmus, while allowing the Soviet Union to establish a naval base at Hanko, deep inside Finnish territory. This would give Moscow a military foothold from which it could threaten Finland’s southern coast and maritime communications.

And Finland had every reason to distrust Stalin. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania had already been forced to accept Soviet military bases in 1939. All three were occupied and annexed the following year.

So Finland was effectively being asked to weaken its own defences, surrender valuable territory and allow a hostile dictatorship to station troops on its soil, in exchange for some remote forests.

Calling that a generous territorial offer because Finland would receive twice as many square kilometres is like offering someone 200 acres of worthless wilderness in exchange for 100 acres of prime real estate, while also demanding the right to station an army in their backyard.

Finland wasn’t rejecting generosity. It was refusing to compromise its national security and sovereignty. And subsequent Soviet actions demonstrated just how justified those concerns were.

Improving outcomes for mothers and babies starts with addressing the gaps in maternity care.

Assistant Professor of Biochemistry & Molecular Biology Scott Barnett, Ph.D., is leading research on a potential drug that could prevent and stop preterm labor. The research could offer new hope for families, particularly those in maternity care deserts where access to specialized care may be limited.

In Nevada, about one in nine births are preterm. In 2024, approximately 3,500 babies were born preterm or very preterm in the state. Scott and his team are exploring whether existing FDA-approved drugs could be repurposed to address this critical gap.

Listen to Scott discuss the research and the challenges facing Nevada families on KNPR: https://t.co/OSRDoUX9th

text:
Message to the NMMI Community from BG Voris W. McBurnette President / Superintendent:

It is with profound sadness that I share with the New Mexico Military Institute family the passing of one of our cadets. The loss of one of our own touches every part of this Institute, and our hearts are especially with the cadet’s family, friends, fellow cadets, faculty, and staff during this extraordinarily difficult time. As a community built upon fellowship, service, and shared purpose, we will stand together and support one another in the days ahead. Out of respect for the family, additional information will be shared when appropriate. Details regarding funeral and burial arrangements will be communicated through NMMI’s official media and communication channels as they become available.

At moments such as this, we are reminded that membership in the Corps does not end when a cadet leaves our formation. Nearly a century ago, after Cadet George O. Speer ’33 JC lost his life in a polo game, the 1933 Bronco offered words that remain part of the Institute’s tradition of remembrance: “But if they are gone from our ranks, we keep them on our roster, as values once intimately known and available in our recollections and in our hearts. They will remain forever young.” Today, those words carry renewed meaning. We mourn the loss of our cadet, extend our deepest condolences to the family, and will ensure that his life and his place within the NMMI family are remembered with dignity, honor, and love.

Counseling and support services are available to cadets, faculty, staff, and other members of the NMMI community. Cadets have access to support through our CCC and TimelyCare. The Commandant and Chaplain have developed a thoughtful plan to provide cadets with opportunities to express their thoughts and feelings and to seek additional support as needed. Details of that plan will be provided to the Corps in a separate communication. Faculty and staff may also contact the TimelyCare Faculty & Staff Guidance Line at 833-4-TIMELY, at any time, day or night, for guidance when supporting a cadet in distress.

Employees also have access to our Employee Assistance Program, which provides confidential support 24 hours a day, seven days a week, at 833-515-0771. Please use these resources as needed, and please look out for one another. At a time such as this, supporting those around us also requires that we take care of ourselves.

Let us continue to support one another and move through the remainder of this semester together, drawing strength from one another and from the bonds that unite us as one NMMI family.

text:
by Nina David/Farmington New Mexico. For those who think that universal healthcare or Medicare for all is the way to go, please read the following. Canada has what you're asking for, and it isn't a good thing. Most of you know I spent 4 days in the hospital in Nova Scotia Canada, and I wanted to share my experience with Universal Healthcare.  
An ambulance with two very nice paramedics met me on my cruise ship and escorted me to the hospital.  We entered into a very long hallway where there were approximately 25 other patients in gurneys waiting to be seen by an emergency room doctor. I thanked the paramedics for getting me to the ER as I assumed they would be dropping me off and be on to their next call! That’s how we do it in the USA anyway.  They politely explained to me that they would not be leaving my side until I was actually seen by a doctor, which could take several hours as they might be needed to administer any life saving measures in the meantime.  They explained that healthcare is “free” in Canada to Canadian Citizens and that they can’t recruit doctors to work for them due to the high taxes and the low pay.  They told me to prepare for a long night.  Okay…… I started to realize I wasn’t in Kansas anymore. 
It was a cold and rainy night, and it was absolutely freezing in that hallway. I’m so sick and miserable being strapped in that gurney.  The hallways were crowded with us 25 + patients and at least 50 paramedics all staying with their patients.  To pass the time, the paramedics spent most of their time laughing and visiting with the other paramedics.  The lead paramedic was looking over my medical chart from the ship doctor and saw that he suggested I needed a CT scan.  He looked at me and said, “I just want to prepare you that you may not get a CT scan for 2 or 3 days!”  2 or 3 days? WTH! At that point I pulled out my phone to see how far away I was from the nearest U.S. hospital…. 8 hours by car! I didn’t think I could do it and I felt stuck. At 3 a.m. I am finally seen by a doctor and was told they would be admitting me.  They take me to my room and I’m so thankful to be off that gurney!  I look around the small room, and I don’t see a bathroom.  I know the nearest bathroom is a long way down the hallway, and I don’t think I can make it by walking.  I call the nurse for a wheelchair when she tells me if it’s an emergency, I can use the one in the room.  She opens up a cabinet and pulls out a toilet.  Are you kidding me? Well, when you gotta go…. Sitting there with absolutely no privacy some random guy walks in my room!  Ugh! Poor guy! 
The next morning the doctor told me I needed to see a Urologist, and he was at another hospital so I would need to be transferred there.  Thank you, God! I’m getting out of this 3rd world excuse for a hospital. The outside of the building looks decent, maybe things are looking up!  As I’m being taken to the 7th floor I’m paying close attention.  The hallways are filled with cardboard boxes, random equipment and supplies and appears to be mostly used as storage.  I pass several patient rooms, and I can see that each small room has 4 patients in each one, divided by 4 curtains.  My heart sinks. As they take me to my room my attendant told me I was in luck and I would have a private room since I had insurance and was a “paying customer” Whew!  I look around the small room and see a bathroom!  Oh yay! They also inform me “DO NOT” drink the water, don’t brush your teeth with it and don’t shower in it.  I look in my bathroom and sure enough the shower parts were pulled out of the wall.  
The sheet I’m sitting on falls partially on the floor and when I get there, I look down and see the white sheet is absolutely filthy dirty.  I don’t know how often they mop those floors, but it’s obviously not often.  Do I really want them doing anything to me?  Doesn’t seem very sterile. 
The interior of the hospital is in disrepair.  Drywall falling off the walls, broken tiles, and filthy dirty! Get back to my room and it’s pleasant enough, at least I have a window!  There is not a T.V. and no internet, so the days were very long. Luckily a nice nurse brought in a recliner, so Ed was able to stay with me in my room.  Good thing as there were very few hotel rooms available and they were in the $700 a night range! The food was fair, and you were able to order from a menu.  The breakfast menu didn’t offer any eggs or meat.  French toast it is, served cold of course! The next morning, I ordered a “high protein” banana smoothie, should be safe.  Wrong!  I don’t know what was in that 4-ounce smoothie, but I wasn’t trying it! 
The nurses were nice enough; they didn’t bother you very much.  I usually saw them twice per day, during shift changes.  On day 3, I really need a bath and my linens changed.  I asked a nurse for help.  Lucky me, since I didn’t have an open wound, I could have a shower!  Yay me!  She led me down the hallway and opened what looked like a closet door.  She handed me a small plastic container that contained a couple of dingy, tattered wash cloths and a towel the size of a standard kitchen towel.  All well, I’ll take it. My last day a cleaning lady came to “clean” my room.  I don’t know why she even bothered.  She didn’t empty the trash, which was a large container that was more than halfway full.  Had to be there long before I came in.  What really shocked me was the Haz Mat container.  The container was not enclosed and was full of used syringes, bloody equipment, etc.  I just about barfed every time I walked by it. I am thankful for the care I received. 
The doctors seemed knowledgeable and I did get better.  They did not seem in a hurry to discharge me and I’m assuming that was partly due to my ability to pay.  I feel really sorry for the Canadian’s that have to deal with this.  We were told that a lot of them travel to the U.S. for their healthcare.  I can see why. I also realize that we need some reform with our American healthcare, but trust me, Universal Healthcare run by red taped government bureaucrats is not the way to go!  I’m amazed by the number of Americans who want this!  Sounds good until you actually have to live it!  I’m so thankful that I’m not a Canadian, because I would probably still be there! The next time I visit our Montrose Regional Hospital I’m going to kiss the walls!

text: Today is October 23rd. This marks the birthday of great American Alfred Matthew “Weird Al” Yankovic, the accordion player and songwriter who has spent nearly fifty years making parody records, original style pastiches and polka medleys now known all around the world. He was born in Downey, California, in 1959, the only child of Nick Yankovic, a World War II medic of Slovene and Croatian descent who earned two Purple Hearts, and Mary Elizabeth Vivalda, a stenographer from Kentucky. He was raised in Lynwood, CA. The day before his seventh birthday a door-to-door salesman offered accordion or guitar lessons. His parents chose the accordion because, he has said, they figured there should be at least one more accordion-playing Yankovic in the world, and because they were convinced it would revolutionize rock. His mother did not let him outside much, so he practiced inside instead.

text:
The Olympic Games are among the world's largest and most complex sporting events, planned years in advance and attracting millions of spectators. Here's a comprehensive overview.

When Are the Next Summer and Winter Olympics?

Summer Olympics

Los Angeles, California, USA

July 14-30, 2028

Winter Olympics

French Alps, France

February 1-17, 2030

When Did the Modern Olympics Begin?

The modern Olympic Games were revived by French educator Baron Pierre de Coubertin and organized through the newly formed International Olympic Committee (IOC).

First modern Olympic Games: Athens, Greece

Dates: April 6-15, 1896

Participants: 241 athletes from 14 nations

Events: 43 events across 9 sports

While the ancient Olympic Games date back to 776 BC, the modern organized Olympic movement began in 1896.

How Many Sports Are in the Olympics and Paralympics?

Summer Olympics (Los Angeles 2028)

The LA28 program includes 36 sports, including new additions such as cricket, flag football, lacrosse, squash, and baseball/softball.

Winter Olympics

The Winter Olympics traditionally feature 7 major sport categories:

Skiing

Skating

Ice Hockey

Curling

Luge

Bobsleigh

Biathlon

These categories encompass roughly 15 disciplines and well over 100 medal events.

Summer Paralympics (Los Angeles 2028)

23 sports

Record 560 medal events planned.

Winter Paralympics

6 sports

Para Alpine Skiing

Para Biathlon

Para Cross-Country Skiing

Para Ice Hockey

Wheelchair Curling

Para Snowboard

Five of the Most Exciting and Dramatic Olympic Years

This is necessarily subjective, but these Games are often regarded among the most significant for athletic achievement and international drama.

1. Berlin 1936

2. Mexico City 1968

3. Munich 1972

4. Moscow 1980 and Los Angeles 1984

5. Barcelona 1992

How Far in Advance Should You Book Olympic Travel?

Ticket Packages

12-24 months before the Games

Hospitality and premium packages often sell first.

Hotels

12-18 months in advance

Hotels nearest venues can sell out almost immediately after ticket lotteries.

Airfare

6-12 months ahead

Earlier is better for opening ceremonies, finals, and medal events.

Fun Fact

The Olympic Games now involve roughly:

10,000+ Olympic athletes

4,000+ Paralympic athletes

More than 200 nations and territories

Billions of television and streaming viewers worldwide

The Olympics remain the largest recurring sporting event on Earth, surpassed only by events such as the FIFA World Cup in certain global viewership metrics.

f*cking insane. here's the brief I gave my AI chief of staff: "find 20 companies that could each pay us $2,500 a month. put the evidence on my desk before I wake up."

imagine running a small web studio. your best developer is also your researcher, salesperson and the person who keeps forgetting to follow up

before budgeting $200,000 a year for a human chief of staff, I tested the bot with a $20 overnight usage cap

I pick the offer and approve the outreach. the bots get the overnight research shift

the rule:
"find independent manufacturers with websites we could improve. public data only. no made-up traffic, revenue or lost sales. contact nobody without my yes. leave pricing to me."

the night I set up:
→ 9pm split the work into company research, website checks, qualification and draft outreach
→ 11pm collect 180 manufacturers in Ohio. remove directories, duplicates and companies that don't fit
→ 1am shortlist 20 with a specific issue: a broken quote form, unreadable mobile navigation or a product catalog nobody can search
→ 2am draft an opener for each company with a screenshot and the exact page. send zero
→ 3am prepare one offer covering the fixes and ongoing maintenance. leave the price blank
→ 8am I enter $5,000 for the initial fixes, then $2,500 a month for maintenance

20 clients means $100,000 in setup fees and $50,000 a month recurring. target contract values, not money collected

I pay attention to the ones it rejects. "old website" isn't enough reason to email a factory owner

run it again next Monday. exclude every company already reviewed. bring back fresh evidence

180 companies → 20 to review → $5,000 setup + $2,500/month → $50,000/month target → 0 emails sent without approval

open the first screenshot before you write another cold email

text:
WRF 12z update on #StormBoelo. #Hebrides

The situation is largely confirmed, barring unexpected, last-minute changes in the cyclone's path or intensification.

The system is currently over the central North Atlantic, with a central pressure of around 989 hPa. By this time tomorrow, its centre is forecast to be northwest of the Outer Hebrides, after losing around 30 to 40 hPa, associated with explosive cyclogenesis.

The first impacts will be felt tomorrow morning, as the leading frontal system crosses over the islands, bringing gusts of 60 mph or more in exposed locations.

Stronger winds will follow through the afternoon and evening, initially affecting the Inner Hebrides. With the cyclone's centre expected to pass closer to the Outer Hebrides, its position may offer some temporary shelter from the strongest winds during the first phase of the event.

However, as the system continues eastwards overnight and into Sunday morning, the wind field is forecast to shift, bringing the potential for gusts exceeding 80 mph across exposed parts of the Hebrides, particularly along northwestern coasts and over higher ground.

Northeast mainland Scotland and Orkney will also experience the effects of this powerful system, particularly on Sunday as the cyclone moves eastwards.

Winds should gradually ease from late Sunday into Monday as Storm Boelo begins to weaken, although conditions may remain unsettled for a time.

Stay safe, everyone.

text:
22 years here. At 51, sitting in downtown Oklahoma City HR.

HR slides a severance agreement across the table.

HR: "The offer expires at 5 PM today."
Me: "I have five hours?"
HR: "Most people sign in the room."
Me: "Does this agreement release age discrimination claims?"
HR: "Yes."
Me: "Then I am taking my 21 days."

If you are 40 or older, the Older Workers Benefit Protection Act, 29 U.S.C. 626(f), sets the mandatory terms for giving up an age discrimination claim.
The rules:
At least 21 days to consider the agreement.
At least 45 days if it is part of a group layoff or exit program.
7 days after signing to revoke.
The agreement must advise you in writing to consult an attorney.
You can sign sooner if that is your own choice.
The 7 days cannot be waived by either side.

EEOC advice: "If you are being rushed, ask for more time. Put your request in writing."
P.S. Look up the EEOC's Q&A on waivers in severance agreements.
P.P.S. This scene is an illustration, not something that happened to me. It's edutainment to show how the law works, not formal legal advice.
